en: The *Hetubinduṭīkā* composed by the venerable Arcata.
Homage to the Omniscient One.
[The auspiciousness through mental attention to the Victor:
He who, having conceived great compassion to protect all people from misfortune,
has accumulated a vast cause consisting of merit and wisdom, and has shaken off all weariness;

I bow my head to that Sun of the Jina, who, having ascended the mountain of the arising of exceedingly pure wisdom that spreads over all objects of knowledge, dispels the darkness within the hearts of the world. // 1 //

[An Exposition of the Supreme Delight of Dharmakīrti’s Words: Indeed, it is better to chew upon the words of Dharmakīrti even after they have already been chewed; for does not the grape, even when squeezed dry, ever lose its sweetness? // 2 //
[Proclaiming one's own modesty and the promise to explain the treatise:

Where could my words, though profound, prevail over the intellect of one whose mind has conquered the world as a whole when weighed on the scales of the path of logic; and where am I, of dull wit? // 3 //
Nevertheless, there are some of dull intellect even compared to me;
for their sake, this *Hetubindu* is also being analyzed by me. (4)
[The revelation of the purpose of the opening statement: By the words beginning with “parokṣe,” he states the purpose for commencing the treatise.
Some maintain that this is for the sake of inducing the audience to engage with it.
As it has been said:
"For of any treatise whatsoever, or even of any action,
as long as the purpose is not stated, by whom could it be grasped?"

Thus it is said. That is incorrect, because the purpose of stating "this is the purpose of this treatise" is described as follows: since a discerning person, having ascertained that the treatise is a means toward a specific goal, cannot engage with what is not a means, they will engage in listening to and so forth regarding the treatise out of a desire for that goal; therefore, the meaningfulness of stating that purpose is explained.
And this is not tenable;
for the activity of discerning persons who seek a purpose occurs toward the means for that purpose because of their certainty regarding its existence.
This is just as, for example, farmers and others act toward seeds and the like—the means for crops—once they have ascertained the status of those seeds by distinguishing them from what is not seed.
Otherwise, for those seeking a goal who act without having ascertained the means, their very status as discerning persons (*prekṣāvattā*) would be lost.

However, regarding the goal (*upeya*), even if it remains unascertained because the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is impossible there, those who have distinguished the means will think: "This intended effect is incapable of being produced, provided that there is no absence of causal conditions (*pratibandha*) or deficiency (*vaikalya*)."
Thus, by engaging [in the treatise] through such a conviction, they would not lose their status as discerning persons (*prekṣāvattva*);
moreover, certainty arises only from a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*),
and the statement of the purpose (*prayojanavākya*) does not possess the status of a valid means of cognition.
Because there is no necessary connection between words and external objects,

and because— even if they possess validity with respect to the speaker’s intention— there is no rule governing their engagement with actual reality, there can be no certainty that a treatise serves as a means toward a specific purpose.

If it is argued: "Indeed, those who intend to express a certain meaning do not necessarily act in accordance with it, because we observe in the world that those with the intent to deceive speak one way and act another; thus, there is universal lack of confidence.

However, since a specific purpose is presented at the outset of a treatise, a doubt arises regarding its being the means to that [purpose]. Therefore, it is reasonable to engage in the activity for the sake of determining whether that [purpose] exists—just as a farmer engages in the determination of seeds and so forth.
This is not so.
Because doubt regarding whether [the treatise] is a means to a specific purpose exists even prior to its exposition;
because, in the absence of any valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes or refutes it, such doubt is logically established;
and because we observe other treatises intended for the sake of training in inference and so forth—[one must ask: "Is the purpose of this [treatise] the instruction in inference, or something else?"
Furthermore, by what could such a doubt as "is it not even anything at all," which arises beforehand, be prevented?
Moreover, is this [inquiry] purposeless, or does it possess a purpose?
Alternatively, if activity were possible for one who desires to know [the truth] because of a purpose already accepted by us, then the presentation of a statement of purpose would indeed be useless.
Therefore, [it follows that] "that sentence which is devoid of a purpose,
or its meaning..."
That which is neither useful for practice nor conducive to liberation is not undertaken by wise persons to perform or to teach;
such, for example,
are sentences like "ten pomegranates" and the like, as well as the examination of a crow's teeth.
This treatise, or its subject matter, is purposeless;

thus, for one who objects by means of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), the statement of the purpose is presented at the outset in order to demonstrate that such an objection is unestablished (*asiddha*). [This is the consideration of the purpose of the treatise and its subject matter.]
In this context, by the phrase "for the sake of producing that," he states the purpose of this very treatise himself.
For the purpose of a sentence is indeed the comprehension of its respective subject matter,
and that exists here because the meaning of the whole is comprehended through the mutual connection of the words and the intermediate sentences.
For instance: inference (*anumāna*) is the subject matter (*abhidheya*) in this treatise, because it is that which is to be explained;
for it is that very thing which is connected with the word "that" (*tat*).

Although inference is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) in the cognition of an imperceptible object, nevertheless, because the function of words follows the intention of the speaker, it is referred to by the word "that."
Otherwise, how could there even be contact with the primary object?
For it is impossible for words to be inherently connected [to their referents].
Since the very nature of inference is being elucidated by means of the passage beginning with "the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*),
the purpose of this treatise is the correct understanding— that is, the realization of its true nature— of that [inference], because that is what is to be established by it.
For this very reason, he indicates by means of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) that the function of the treatise has as its object the mastery of inference, stating: "for the purpose of explaining that.
Consequently, the relationship between the treatise and its purpose, characterized as that of the means and the end (*sādhyasādhanalakṣaṇa*), is also stated.

Although, according to the literal sense of the words, the function of the treatise—whose object is the mastery of inference—is primary, nevertheless, according to the actual state of things, mastery itself is primary, because it is that which is to be accomplished by the treatise.
And because the other [the treatise] is subordinate as a means to that [inference],
therefore it is understood that the purpose is precisely the mastery of inference (*anumāna*), and not the operation of the treatise itself.

However, by the statement, "Because the comprehension of an object beyond the senses is based on inference," he states the purpose of the subject matter of the treatise, which is the definition of inference.

For a person of discernment does not engage [with a statement] merely because the sentence possesses a result characterized by the cognition of its own meaning; rather, they do so when that expressed meaning is conducive to human goals (*puruṣārtha*).

And such [utility] exists here, since the apprehension—that is, the ascertainment—of an imperceptible object has inference (*anumāna*, i.e., the three-featured logical mark) as its cause, by way of metaphorically applying the name of the effect to the cause.
This is stated in order to demonstrate that it cannot be accomplished by any other means, and for the purpose of refuting the views of others. (Hbṭ 4)
"Āśraya" means the cause;
having analyzed it generally as "that of which inference is the basis," and then,

when there is a requirement for a specific [explanation] as to "of what is it the basis of inference?"— even though [it concerns] the connection between the word and the cognition of an imperceptible object—
Even though femininity is understood, because it is not present in the intellect at the time of the formation of the word-base (*pada-saṃskāra*), it is considered "external" (*bahiraṅga*); thus,

it does not serve as the cause for feminine suffixes, as in the examples *bhūtamiyam brāhmaṇī* ("this Brahmin woman is [as] real as the earth") and *āvapanamiyam uṣṭrikā* ("this little leather bag is [as] a vessel").
[The indication that all cognition of what is beyond the senses is inferential is due precisely to its being born from a logical mark (liṅga).
And by this it is shown that every valid cognition of an object beyond the senses is a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is impossible to cognize such an object through anything else.
It is stated that [valid cognition] is based solely on the mark possessing the three characteristics (trirūpaliṅga), because of the restriction "precisely because it is based on inference.
Consequently, if verbal testimony (*śabda*) and the like possess validity, they must be a form of inference;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that they too must be explained [as such], since the underlying cause is the same.
For instance: every cognition of an imperceptible object that constitutes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not independent;
because it lacks an essential connection with its own object, it cannot necessarily correspond to that object.
Furthermore, because the defining characteristic of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*),

if [cognition] were to arise from something else, it would follow that everything could be cognized by everyone; for even when there is no connection with the subject (*dharmin*), it would produce cognition regarding everything,
since there would be no distinction between proximity and distance.

And since an object that has come to be thus exists as nothing other than the three-fold mark (*trirūpaliṅga*), every cognition of an imperceptible object does not differ from inference, because it is produced by a three-fold mark.

Furthermore, this point—that "the reason (*hetu*) is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) pervaded by its part"—is shown through its connection with the context [of the question], namely, "of what? [The answer is: "of the cognition of an imperceptible object."

Because of the restriction that "only that which is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) and only that which is pervaded by a part of it (tadaṃśena vyāpta) is the cause for the cognition of an imperceptible object," it is established that only the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is a real entity (vastu), and not the universal (sāmānya).

Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "object" (artha) in the phrase "cognition of an imperceptible object" is intended to demonstrate that even inference possesses validity regarding the particular characteristic as its object.
For an object is that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*), and it is precisely the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that possesses this nature.
For this very reason, he will state: "Because the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has as its basis a real entity (*vastu*)."
Otherwise, there would be no engagement with that [object] by one seeking purposeful action based on inference.

Even though the universal is not a real entity, its purposeful action consists merely in being cognition; and since that [cognition] is established as being produced by that [universal], [there is no fault].
For a universal (jāti) is not employed in such functions as burning or cooking,
because it is the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) alone that is effective therein.
If it is argued that activity toward it [the object] occurs due to its connection with that [universal], we say no.
Because that which is eternal cannot be assisted by anything, it lacks any connection [with it];
and even if a connection were to exist, how could there be activity toward one thing upon the cognition of another?
For that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it is argued that activity toward inherence occurs through error because its distinction from other things has not been ascertained due to its subtlety,
then let there be mere error alone;
what is the use of this internal tumor of a "universal" (sāmānya)?
If it is argued that this is because an error without a seed (cause) is impossible;
[we reply that] those very individuals, which produce that single effect, are the seed of the error.
For the cognition of a universal has a form identical to the phoneme and the configuration.
Nor is the universal (sāmānya) of that nature;
how then could it be the seed of error?
For others maintain that error is based on similarity (sādṛśya).

Furthermore, it is precisely the individual instances themselves—distinguished from those of a different class and possessing the nature of a cognition in the form of a universal—that constitute the seed of error;
for there exists within them the exclusion of what is not of that nature.
Moreover, since a real entity as a universal cannot exist in relation to them due to the impossibility of a connection, its presence in them is untenable.

However, by those who conceive of the universal as being essentially identical with the individual, it follows that they have already accepted that the validity of inference has as its object the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
But it must be considered how a universal, which is of the nature of a particular characteristic, can appear in inference;
for no form of the universal other than the form of the individual is admitted.
Because it would entail the consequence of adopting the Vaiśeṣika system...
(Hbṭ 6) [1. General Definition of the Reason (*hetu*)]

[1. Discussion on how pervasion is established by means of the threefold nature of the reason: ... for it has been stated that, since the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*) are proofs by way of affirmation (*vidhi*), they have no operation when a negation (*pratiṣedha*) is to be proven.

Even from non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), there is no certainty regarding the absence of other causes, because that [non-apprehension] is established in four ways: non-apprehension of the essential nature (*svabhāva*), the cause (*kāraṇa*), and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), as well as the affirmation of the contradictory (*viruddha-vidhi*).

Non-apprehension of the essential nature—which consists in the apprehension of another [object]—is accepted as the cause for the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) when it pertains to something possessing a similar capacity for cognition and is associated with the same act of knowledge.
However, another cause (*hetvantara*) is not admitted as being of the nature of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), nor does it possess the aforementioned characteristics.
For if it were [merely non-existent], there would be only a negation of its presence in a particular place and so forth, not an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
However, the two types of non-perception—of the cause and of the pervader—occur only when the relationship of effect-to-cause and pervaded-to-pervader has been established.
And this method is not possible if another cause is admitted to be absolutely non-existent.
How then could those two lead to the cognition of its absence?

Furthermore, since contradiction (*virodha*) is understood through the non-existence of one thing when another exists—provided that the cause of the former is unimpaired—the perception of a contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) is also impossible.
Or, if it were possible, how could there be an absolute negation [of objects] by means of the non-perception of causes (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) and so forth?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "The fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) are other than those. "Other than those" means other than the three kinds of reasons; they are "fallacious reasons" because they are distinct from them, and therefore that [reason] is indeed of three kinds only.
He thinks as follows: in this context, when something is restricted to a certain locus, that restriction is established through the pervasion of its opposite by the negation of that [restriction].

Just as the rule that whatever exists is necessarily momentary— when the necessity of existence for momentary things is stated— is established by the pervasion of non-momentariness (the opposite of momentariness) through non-existence (the opposite of existence),

so too here, when the reason is restricted to being threefold, it becomes necessarily limited to the number three by the pervasion of objects outside the number three through the status of fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa), which is the opposite of a valid reason. Thus, it demonstrates that objects distinct from the three types of reasons possess the nature of fallacious reasons.

Thus, by means of the perception of what is incompatible with its own nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), there is the ascertainment of the absence of causal status for those things other than the non-perception of an effect or a nature;

and the contradiction between the true cause and its semblance is understood precisely at the time of cognizing the definition of the cause, because their definitions consist in mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthitalakṣaṇatā*).
Because it is precisely from a cognition whose appearance is restricted to that [specific] nature that there arises the perception of its opposite as being "other" due to its appearing as such;
for they are mutually determined to lack each other's form.

In this regard, the character of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsatva*), when perceived in objects excluded from the three types of valid reasons, negates the presence of a valid reason (*hetutva*), which is its own contradiction.
Furthermore, those objects that fall outside the three types of causes are neither characterized by absolute non-existence, nor is their status as causes being denied;
rather, it is simply that their causality—well-established elsewhere—is projected or suspected there due to delusion, and is then removed through the perception of something incompatible with it.
Therefore, why is it asked: “How can there be a contradiction regarding that which is absolutely impossible?”

Nor is contradiction characterized solely by non-coexistence, such that this principle would have to be applied in every case; nor is it to be understood that there is a contradiction between a thing and the very locus in which it is negated, such that one might object: "How can there be a cognition of contradiction with something non-existent?"

For it is not the case that the contradiction between cold touch and fire exists only within the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) itself— as in the statement "there is no cold touch here because of fire"— but rather, just as there is a negation of cold touch in the subject of the thesis for that which has been perceived elsewhere as being contradictory to fire, so too is there a negation of the status of being a valid reason (*hetutva*) regarding those objects excluded from the three types of reasons, due to their being observed as fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). Furthermore, a conventional contradiction is perceived even in the case of what is absolutely non-existent, such as the contradiction between momentariness and non-momentariness, because the latter is impossible in any real entity whatsoever.
Or rather, it is like the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), which is characterized by the absence of all causal capacity; enough with such excessive concern for the ramblings of the dull-witted.

This being established, the following was stated—by one intending to demonstrate the negative pervasion (*viparyaya-vyāpti*) with the thought that "causality, when restricted to the triad, becomes necessarily determined therein provided that there is a pervasion of its opposite": "The fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*)..."
"Others have said...
[2. Discussion on the pervasion of the three kinds of external objects by fallacious reasons:

In this regard, it might be argued that the pervasion of the opposite of momentariness by the negation of existence is established by the force of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
But here, by which means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) established that objects outside the three types of reasons are pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)?
To this he says: “Because of the restriction of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).

The meaning is: because even if the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) exists, there is an absence of inseparable connection in any object that is suspected or accepted as a mark (*liṅga*) apart from the threefold reason.
And so he will state: “Since that [reason] does not exist elsewhere than in the three types of reasons, it is said to be restricted to these alone.

Furthermore, the deficiency of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is ascertained to be pervaded by the general property of being a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), such as the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), or the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as seen in the case of [the property of] being knowable (*prameyatva*). Thus, when the state of being a fallacious reason is to be proven, the deficiency of inseparable connection is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

And the deficiency of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is established for those other than the three types of reasons simply by virtue of their being excluded from them, due to the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
For instance, invariable concomitance is pervaded by identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*),
because these two necessarily exist therein.
And because that [probans], not having those two as its nature and not being produced from them, is independent of them, there is no rule of non-deviation from them. As it has been said:

“From the relation of cause and effect, or from an essential nature (svabhāva) that acts as a regulator, the rule of inseparable connection (avinābhāva) is established; it is not based on non-perception, nor on perception.”
“What necessary rule of concomitance could there be for one thing with others otherwise than through a cause that is not a distinct entity, as in the case of color in a cloth?

For even the inseparable connection of taste and so forth with visible form and so forth is not intrinsic, but rather mediated by the non-deviation of their own causes; thus, the very production from those causes is the basis for their inseparable connection.

Otherwise, if one were to postulate an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with something that is not dependent on it, or not dependent on its causes, then everything would be invariably concomitant with all things, as there would be no distinction.

If it is argued that the invariable concomitance between color, taste, and so forth is caused by their inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*), [we reply: surely inherence is also described as belonging only to those things that stand in the relation of the supported and the support (*ādhāryādhārabhūta*).

Furthermore, that relationship of substrate and superstrate (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) is not established because it would lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of [the absurdity that] there is no assistance to its own nature; therefore, "inherence in a single object" (*ekārthasamavāya*) must be understood as simply being dependent upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*).

Alternatively, any other real relationship (*vastubhūta-sambandha*) is impossible, as this has already been demonstrated at length by the author of the treatise in the *Sambandhaparīkṣā*; thus it should be determined from that very source. Or rather—[not so]... even if [it were non-existent]... [ja]na[nvasatyapi ja]...
Whether it be in the relation of producer and produced or in identity,

the fact that the inseparable connection (avinābhāva) exists with that alone and not with anything else must be answered by the very nature of things themselves— those things which exist in such a way, and not by us.
If you say, "We are merely the perceivers," then the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things would be accidental; consequently, it would not belong to anything in particular.
For a restriction of place, time, and substance is not logical for that which is causeless.
For that [thing] might or might not be brought about in some place by something else, depending on whether it is dependent or independent upon that thing in that place.

Otherwise, since there would be no distinction, who could prevent its existence in another place and so forth—just as it exists in a desired place, time, and substance—given the absence of any distinction?
Therefore, when one thing is seen to be invariably concomitant with another, the cause of that non-deviation must be stated by those who contemplate reality.
But one must not rely on a mere "stretching out of the feet" (i.e., a superficial or accidental connection).

Furthermore, since no cause other than that which has been described can be established as an invariable concomitant (*avyabhicārakāraṇa*), those [reasons] lacking it do not possess the characteristics of a valid logical reason (*hetu*). Thus it is said:
"In cases such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like, there exists no such necessary connection."
“Those are not valid reasons,” it is said, “because of the possibility of deviation.

Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): that which lacks both identity (*tādātmya*) and origination therefrom (*tadutpatti*) with respect to another thing is not invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvī*) with it, just as, for example, the state of being knowable (*prameyatva*) and so forth are not invariably concomitant with impermanence (*anityatva*) and so forth.

And since non-existent things cannot possess identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from that (*tadutpatti*) with anything else—because they lack the nature of being an essential property (*svabhāva*), an effect (*kārya*), or an absence (*vyatirekin*)—this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

However, non-perception of the essential property (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is included within the reason consisting of essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*); thus, its connection (*pratibandha*) is characterized solely by identity.

Furthermore, the non-perception of the pervader and the cause establish the exclusion of the pervaded and the effect precisely through the force of the connections characterized by identity and origination from that.
As it has been said:
"Therefore, a nature that is connected with that alone would exclude either the entity itself or its cause, because of the non-deviation of the effect from the cause."

Thus, in this verse, (1) the definition of the reason (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*), (2) the restriction of its number (*saṃkhyā-niyama*), and (3) the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that demonstrates it have been indicated. [3. An alternative explanation of the phrase "due to the restriction of inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva-niyamāt*):
Alternatively, "it is indeed threefold."

Thus, that property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is of exactly three kinds—namely, those called essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalambha*)—and is pervaded by a portion of that [reason]; no other [kind exists].
The connection is that these three kinds are indeed pervaded by a portion of that [reason].
What is the reason?
"Because of the necessity of inseparable connection," that is,
because of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Because the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is necessarily of only three kinds, and because the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is restricted to those three kinds of properties of the subject; therefore, there is nothing other than these three kinds of properties of the subject— consisting of essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalambha*)— that is pervaded by that part [of the reason].

It has thus been stated that the threefold property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), consisting of the effect, the essential nature, and non-perception, is indeed pervaded by its own part [the probandum], and therefore it is not a fallacious reason (*ahetu*). Consequently, those who apply the conventional designation of "reason" to things outside the threefold reason because they lack inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*),
and those who declare the threefold reason to be a non-reason because inseparable connection is necessarily absent [in them], are refuted.
[4. The indication of the fallacious reasons even without stating their definitions:

In this regard, one might argue that the definition of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) should also be stated there, so that students may desist from treating them as valid reasons. To this, he says: "The fallacious reasons are other than those. "Other than those" (*apare*) means other than the definition of a valid reason—namely, "that which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and is pervaded by its part" (*tadaṃśena vyāpta*). Since fallacious reasons are understood precisely as those lacking that definition, their definition is not explicitly stated.
For instance: when it is stated that "it is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*), that which lacks the status of being a property of the subject is not a valid reason (*hetu*).

When it is stated that "it is pervaded by a portion of that" (*tadaṃśena vyāptaḥ*), wherever there is an absence of pervasion by that portion—due to the necessary absence of either the counter-pervasion (*viparyaya-vyāpti*) or the pervader (*vyāpaka*)—those are understood as "pseudo-reasons" (*hetvābhāsa*) because they are deficient in the characteristics of a valid reason; namely, the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

For instance, when an object of a certain characteristic has been taught to a student, he will himself engage in the linguistic convention regarding that object even when it is devoid of that characteristic, because the cognition of its true nature occurs precisely through the exclusion of what is not of that nature; thus, effort in that regard would not be fruitful.
As for the exposition of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) found elsewhere, that is intended for those of dull intellect;
however, this treatise was composed for those of vast intelligence, as indicated by the statement "in brief.
For only they are capable of correctly understanding what is stated in brief, not those of dull minds.

Because there would be no correct comprehension of their meaning without a detailed exposition of them, for this very reason, the definition of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) was described therein preceded by an introduction that implies those meanings.
Thus, in this commentary, [the following are presented]: 1. the definition of the reason (*hetu*), and 2. the restriction regarding the number of reasons (*hetusaṃkhyāniyama*). (Hbṭ 11)

Furthermore, six points are indicated here in this verse: (1) the determination that this [reason] is of three kinds; (2) the cause for both [the definition and the example]; (3) the explanation of the connected presentation; (4) the reason for not stating the definition of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*);

and so forth. Moreover, this also appears sound: "In only three ways" is that reason, distinguished by the divisions of effect (*kārya*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).

Likewise, because it is divided precisely into three types according to the distinctions of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), it is "of exactly three kinds," that is, it possesses exactly three forms.
Since positive and negative concomitance are expressed by the statement regarding the pervasion of that part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*),
the reason is not something that can also possess other forms such as having an uncontradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*).

Why? Because [it is said]: "The fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are other than those"; "than those" means other than the three types, such as essential nature (*svabhāva*), or other than the three forms consisting of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth; "others" refers to the related (*saṃyogin*) and so on, or those possessing characteristics distinct from the "uncontradicted object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) and the rest.
Why?

The meaning is this: because the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is restricted solely to the threefold and three-featured reason (*hetu*), it does not exist elsewhere—neither in that which is distinct from the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, nor in that which possesses another feature.

For an invariable concomitance based on a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is impossible in anything distinct from the essential nature and so forth, nor is another feature possible in that which possesses such [a connection].

And just as the occurrence of another form is impossible when there is no inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), so he will explain with the words "possessing six characteristics" (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*) and so forth.

Even when the definition of the reason (*hetu*) is formulated as "the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmaḥ*), if the "subject" (*pakṣa*) were intended to refer to the entire aggregate (*samudāya*):

If that which is the object of inference were grasped [as the subject], then every reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished (*asiddha*); or, if it were established, inference would be redundant. Thus he says, "The subject (*pakṣa*) is the property-possessor (*dharmin*). But if it is asked: how can the word *pakṣa*, which denotes a composite whole, refer to the property-possessor alone?
“Because of the metaphorical application of the whole to its part.
For the whole known as the *pakṣa* (the thesis) has two parts: the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*).
Therefore, in this context, the word *pakṣa* is applied to the mere property-bearer through the metaphorical application of the whole to the part.

And since being a part of that [whole] is the basis for the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of the whole, there is no possibility of that [designation] occurring elsewhere than in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*). As it has been said:

“Because the whole is what is to be proven (*sādhya*), and because it is a part even though the property alone is not the primary subject, ‘being the thing to be proven’ is metaphorically attributed [to the subject].”
Īśvarasena’s objection to the explanation of Dignāga and its refutation:

This very explanation of the Master (Dignāga) was challenged by Īśvarasena; in order to refute that challenge, [the author] states the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) beginning with the words "In the case of the purpose" (*prayojane*), and so forth.
“For there is no dancing [of words] without a purpose; the primary meaning of a word must not be transgressed.
Thus, in the absence of a purpose, figurative usage is not appropriate.
To this, the opponent says: "Let there simply be the subject (dharmin) and the property (dharma).
[The author replies: "No," because there is no purpose.
Why? Because the purpose or objective is the negation of that subject—whether it be the locus of dispute or any other subject.

Since that metaphorical designation (upacāra) exists because of its nature as such, the reason [stated by the opponent]— “because the purpose of the metaphorical designation is the negation of all properties of the subject”— is unestablished, as there is no such purpose.
What benefit is there in this being the case?

If this is argued, he says: "For in this way," when there is such a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), "the state of being visible" (*cākṣuṣatva*) and so forth— whereby the phrase "because of the crow's blackness" and the like are included under the term "and so forth"— is "avoided," meaning it is rejected as a reason (*hetu*) because it is unestablished due to a difference in locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*).

"But since the term *dharmin-dharma* is used in a general sense, those [other properties] would also have the status of being reasons. [To this, the author replies: "Even without resorting to metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), this is established by the mention of the *dharmin* itself; therefore, metaphorical usage is indeed purposeless. Thus says the opponent: "By the word *dharma* as well"—not only by the word *dharmin*.

"In the establishment of the substratum of the property" (*dharmyāśrayasiddhau*): the "substratum" (*āśraya*) is the resorting to or the grasping of the property-possessor (*dharmin*); it means when that [establishment] exists.
If one asks, "What, then, is the cause for the property's implication of the property-possessor?
[the answer is]: "Because of its dependence on another"—that is, because the "property" is dependent upon the property-possessor—it necessarily implies that property-possessor.

Therefore, the mention of the subject (*dharmin*), being superfluous [if it were merely for identification], indicates the subject as qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*) itself, and not the subject in its mere form.
It might be thought: "From the inclusion of the word *dharmin*, it should be understood that some particular qualified subject is intended here."

But why is that [subject] the property-bearer (*sādhyadharmin*)? To this he says: "By virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). And it is understood that "proximity" here is intended by the force of the word "property-bearer."

In the context of pervasion (*vyāpti*), however, since even the mention of the property (*dharma*) implies the locus (*dharmin*) alone according to logical principle, the explicit mention of the locus would be redundant. Furthermore, proximity belongs to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) itself; therefore, it [the locus] must be mentioned first. (Hbṭ 13)
Because of the demonstration of the reason (*hetu*),
the inclusion of the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) does not result from proximity.
Why?
“Of the example-locus (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) as well,” meaning not only of the subject-locus (*sādhyadharmin*),
because in some cases, when the application is preceded by the observation of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the presence of the reason (*hetu*) is first demonstrated even in the example-locus.
If the establishment of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) does not occur through proximity (*pratyāsatti*), then it will occur by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*).
Because, through the pervasion by that part [of the reason] acting as the cause, the existence of the property is established in the "subject of the example" (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*).

For it is held that without an example, the pervasion of the reason by the probandum cannot be demonstrated. Therefore, since the term "subject" (*dharmī*) is not intended to be distinct [from the subject of the thesis], it is the "subject of the probandum" (*sādhyadharmī*) itself that is understood.

Furthermore, one should not suspect that the mention of the *dharmin* (the subject) is intended for the purpose of connecting it with the word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "by a part of that" (*tadaṃśena*), whereby the *dharmin*—implied by the word expressing the *dharma* (the property)—would be linked [to the probandum].
For that which has no other possible purpose falls under the category of *pāriśeṣya* (exclusion by elimination); however, another purpose for the mention of the *dharmin* is indeed conceivable.

Thinking, "Why then, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), does the mention of the subject (*dharmin*) result in the inclusion of the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*)?", the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) says: "Since its existence in the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) has already been established through pervasion by that part [of the reason],
the further mention of the subject might be suspected of having the restrictive purpose [of implying] that only that which is a property of the example-subject is the reason."

"Furthermore, in that case, only properties such as visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) would be the logical reasons (*hetu*), and not properties such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*); this would be an undesirable consequence. Therefore, a figurative usage (*upacāra*) must be employed. To the question, "But where in the treatises on logic (*tarkaśāstra*) is there seen a statement made for the sake of restriction? he says: "It is seen [only] in those of the same class," and so forth.

"In that regard, although the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason is established by the restrictive particle ‘only’ (*eva*) in the Teacher’s definition of the reason— namely, ‘that which exists in the similar class (*sajātīya*)’ [Nyāyamukha 7]— "
Where?
In the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāve*). This which is stated as "that which is non-existent when that [probandum] is absent" [Nyāyamukha 7] refers to non-existence (*asattva*).
That statement was explained by the Teacher for the purpose of restriction, so that non-existence might apply only where it truly does not exist, and not elsewhere, nor in contradiction;
likewise here too, the mention of the subject (*dharmin*) might be suspected to be for the purpose of restricting existence to that very [subject].
When? Even when the existence of the subject in the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) is already established.
Why? Because of the statement regarding its pervasion by a part [of the subject].
For what purpose is there a restriction of existence?
"In that very [place]," namely, in the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*).
And when a doubt is possible,
from what [source is the certainty]?
From the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), there is the apprehension of the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*).

Now, since that which is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) cannot be a valid reason (*ahetutvāt*), there is no possibility of suspecting that it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārthatā*).

For instance, even if a property were pervaded by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), if it were perceived only in a certain subject (*dharmī*), it would produce the cognition of its own pervader only in that very place and not elsewhere— due respectively to proximity (*pratyāsatti*) and remoteness (*viprakarṣa*).
But how can that which has not been perceived in any locus (*dharmin*) be indicative [of the probandum]?

Or, if it were so, why would it not indicate its own pervader everywhere, since there is no distinction between proximity and remoteness? To this he says: "Therefore, by implication" (*tasmāt sāmarthyāt*), and so forth.
From this aforementioned implication, there arises for listeners of sharp intellect the comprehension of the object characterized by the inclusion of the subject (*sādhyadharmin*).
However, for those who pursue an object that is not explicitly expressed by words, there would be a burden of comprehension.

By this [term], through a mere metaphorical designation— being devoid of the independent inference of an unexpressed object— and by the uniform application of the term "property of the subject" (*dharmidharma*) rather than "property of the thesis" (*pakṣadharma*), the burden of comprehension is avoided.

And by the word "ca" (and) in the phrase "and respect for practice," this is what is meant: those who require instruction from another must understand this matter from the statement of its definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
Why [is it that] a reason (*hetu*) which is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) is not a valid reason, given that understanding occurs according to the definition?
This is the apprehension.
Therefore, for the sake of removing the apprehension regarding the restriction of those who follow the definition, the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is employed.
[7. The establishment of the restriction in the phrase "the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*).]
In this context, because the employment of words necessarily results in exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), one must certainly determine the intended meaning.
Furthermore, regarding the term *pakṣadharma*, no other compound is possible than a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).

Thus, by the restriction that it is "the property of the subject alone" (*pakṣasyaiva dharmaḥ*), the pervasion by its own part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*) is contradicted; pointing out this contradiction in the definition, he says: "But if it is the property of the subject... (*pakṣasya dharmatve tu...*)

"A qualifier requires exclusion from others. Thus, for a property that depends on such a qualifier, there is "non-occurrence elsewhere," meaning it does not occur in the *sapakṣa* (similar instances) other than the subject (*pakṣa*) under consideration.
To explain: that which is qualified by the subject belongs to the subject alone and not to anything else.
For example, he who is Devadatta’s son is his son alone, and not Yajñadatta’s as well.
Because it does not follow through to anything other than that, there is "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇatā*); that is, there would be no commonality (*sādhāraṇatā*).
This means, in short, that it contradicts the pervasion of that which is to be proven (*tadaṃśavyāpti*).
And as for commonality...
Because it is established through pervasion by that part [of the subject].

Therefore, if the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) does not involve pervasion by that part, or if there is pervasion by that part but not the property of the subject, then the definition is contradictory.

Now, it may be objected that what is called "pervasion by a part" (*tadaṃśavyāpti*) is defined as the presence of the pervading property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in the locus (*dharmin*) where the reason (*hetu*) exists, or alternatively, the presence of the pervaded reason only where that very pervading property to be proven exists; thus, it will be stated that its characteristic is inseparability from its own probandum.
And by this [definition], the occurrence [of the reason] elsewhere than in the subject (*pakṣa*) is not necessarily implied.
For otherwise, a contradiction of the definition would be suspected.
To explain: when the reason exists in that very subject which has been made the locus of the thesis (pakṣa), it indeed attains pervasion by its own part;
and that very inseparability from its own probandum within the subject of the thesis is the basis for its capacity to prove, not [its presence] in another subject.
And that inseparable connection with its own probandum is based on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the necessary relation (*pratibandha*);
it is not based merely on observing coexistence frequently or even once in some instance of the similar class (*sapakṣa*).

For instance, [the inference] "diamond is scratchable by iron because it is earthy, like wood and so forth"—even though earthiness is here inseparably connected with scratchability by iron elsewhere, such a connection does not hold true in this case.
And if there were a rule that pervasion must be demonstrated only elsewhere than in the subject (*pakṣa*), then how could existence (*sattva*) establish momentariness in entities?
For [existence] which pervades all things— whether they be...
He desires non-existence because there is no one who would be on his side;

and as for the momentariness of flames and the like that is asserted by some, even that is not established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since the distinction between moments is so subtle that it cannot be perceived.
Furthermore, what is this logic that pervasion (vyāpti) should be demonstrated only elsewhere and not even in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin)?
For if this were so, the definition of the reason (hetu) would be understood as being merely conceptual,
rather than functioning through the power of real entities.

Therefore, because of the necessary connection with its own probandum (*svasādhyapratibandhāt*), the reason is established as being pervaded by it; and since that [pervasion] is established even in the subject of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*) through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the opposite case, there is no need whatsoever for dependence on its recurrence elsewhere.

For this very reason, it has been stated elsewhere: "When something is observed somewhere, for one who knows the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of that [thing] with another, that [observed thing] is the indicator of that [connected thing] in that [latter locus]; such is the nature of reality."

Even regarding the definition beginning with "presence in the inferable subject and in that which is similar to it," therein too, only that which possesses the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*) is called the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).
Therefore, this [definition] has the intended meaning that [the reason] exists only when the property to be proven is present.
Consequently, the actual status of being a similar instance for the subject possessing that property—the subject of the thesis—is not excluded.

Since it cannot be rejected by virtue of its being a "subject" (pakṣatva)—a definition established by the desire [of the proponent] to have it as something to be proven (sādhyatveneṣṭatayā)—it follows that by stating the pervasion (vyāpti) with respect to that part [the subject], one expresses the fact of being invariably concomitant (avinābhāvitva) with one's own probandum, which is based on a necessary connection (pratibandha), for otherwise such [pervasion] would be impossible. Therefore, existence elsewhere is not necessarily implied;
so how was this [existence elsewhere] even suspected?

True; this suspicion should not be raised at all, provided that for every reason, the necessary connection with its own probandum can be ascertained through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within the very subject (*dharmin*) that has been made the locus of the thesis (*pakṣīkṛta*).

This is as in the case of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) characterized by existence when proving momentariness as the probandum, where identity (*tādātmya*) is established through the operation of a subverting cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the opposite.

But regarding the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), how could the necessary connection (*pratibandha*)—which is established through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*)—be grasped with respect to some essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*) when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is beyond the senses?

Therefore, since its establishment occurs only elsewhere, and because that which depends on such a qualification requires that [connection] there, it does not follow elsewhere; thus, its "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇatā*) is suspected by the mere possibility [of its occurrence].

For at that time, since it does not occur elsewhere, and because it is impossible for it to exist outside of both [the similar and dissimilar instances], it becomes a cause of doubt regarding the subject (*dharmin*)—since all possibilities are subsumed by the presence of the probandum (*sādhya*) or its exclusion therefrom.

It might be argued: "In some cases, in order to recall the proof-establishing cognition (*pramāṇa*) of the previously grasped and now forgotten connection (*pratibandha*) of existence (*sattā*) upon a certain locus, the occurrence [of the reason] elsewhere must be required."
He refutes this with the words beginning with "no," [stating]:
"It is not that there is no experience elsewhere."
Why? (Hbṭ 17) Because "non-connection" (*ayoga*) means a lack of relation; for the subject (*pakṣa*) is qualified by the exclusion of that [non-connection].
For qualification does not occur solely through the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), but also through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).
Where the existence of a property in a given subject is doubted, there the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) is logically established.
Here, the example is: “Caitra is an archer. For in the case of Caitra, it is doubted whether archery exists or does not exist.

And thus, the scriptural statement "Caitra is an archer," which establishes his possession of that quality, excludes the possibility of his not being an archer—a doubt raised by the listener regarding an alternative state; therefore, the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) is here logically established.
Desiring to refute the exclusion intended by others, he says: "No,..."
The connection is that "because it is qualified by the exclusion of connection with anything else" (anyayogavyavaccheda), there is "uniqueness" (asādhāraṇatā) due to its non-occurrence elsewhere.
Here too, the example is "Pārtha is the archer.
Although this word "archer" is a general term, through the force of the context and other factors, it functions to denote one who possesses preeminent excellence.

In this case, since Pārtha’s status as an archer is already established, there is no suspicion of non-connection (*ayoga*). However, when there is a suspicion of connection with another (*anyayoga-śaṅkā*)—namely, whether such an excellence exists elsewhere or not—the statement "Pārtha is the archer" logically entails the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*).

This is because the two alternatives presented by the listener's doubt are mutually contradictory; thus, by the force of logic, the exclusion of connection with another follows from the mention of one of them.

Thus, in this context, regarding the doubt as to whether "this property exists in the subject or not," when it is stated that "it is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*), it means it is indeed a property of the subject and not a non-property.

Furthermore, because a property is a qualifier by virtue of being dependent [upon the subject], non-connection (*ayoga*) is excluded; however, connection with something else (*anyayoga*) is not [excluded]. This is because, through the pervasion by that part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*), [the presence of the reason in the similar instance] is established, and thus there is no doubt regarding the example.
"That part" (*tadaṃśa*) refers to its property (*taddharma*).
By that word "that" (tat), the subject (pakṣa) is referred to, not the property (dharma),
because a property cannot possess another property;
furthermore, a "part" (aṃśa) is a property, not a spatial portion.

Because the word "pakṣa" denotes the locus (*dharmī*) alone, it is not a "part of that" (*tadaṃśa*), since it lacks a single part (*ekadeśa*). [8. Pervasion (*vyāpti*) possesses the property of being both the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*).]

The pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that which exists as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) consists in both that which pervades and that which is pervaded, because it is cognized as having the nature of both.

When it is intended to be expressed as the property of the pervader (*vyāpakadharma*), then it belongs to the pervader, which is the object to be known (*gamyam*). In this context, the locative case ending (*saptamī*) primarily signifies "existence" (*sat*), not the locus (*ādhāra*).
Because there is no separate entity among phenomena (*dharma*),
the meaning is this:
wherever the pervaded exists within a subject (*dharmin*), the pervasion is the very presence of the pervader’s own inherent property (*svagata-dharma*) in all such cases.
Therefore, in relation to the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), there is the cognition of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) itself as being pervaded; however,
it is not determined in this way that "only the pervader exists there."
Otherwise, it would follow that there is an absence of a logical reason (*hetvabhāva*), because even non-pervasive properties such as corporeality (*mūrtatva*) exist therein;
nor can it be said "only in that [locus]," for that would result in the fallacy of making properties such as "being immediately subsequent to an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) non-reasons,
and the reason would become "over-common" (*sādhāraṇa*).
Because eternity exists only among those things that are objects of knowledge (*prameya*).

However, when there is the intention to express [the relationship] as a pervaded property (*vyāpyadharma*), then, by virtue of the pervasion (*vyāpti*), it is only when the pervaded— the indicator— is present in that very place where the pervader— the object to be known— is located.
In that case, pervasion means that the pervader exists only where the subject exists, and not even in its absence;
here too, the restriction that "the pervaded exists only there" is not based on the fear of the consequence of the reason's absence.
Because even that which is non-pervasive exists there;

nor is it the case that only that which is pervasive exists there, for this would result in the fallacy that a reason existing in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) is not a valid reason.
Furthermore, it would follow that even a common (*sādhāraṇa*) reason could be a valid reason.
Because knowability (*prameyatva*) necessarily exists in eternal things.

However, the description of the property of the pervaded and the pervader is for the purpose of demonstrating that the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) should not be of a single form due to the property being identical in both cases, as it is in the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

For instance, in the former case there is a restriction by the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), while in the latter there is a restriction by the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*); how then could there be a single form of pervasion in both cases? As it has been said:
“The indicator (liṅga) exists only in the indicated (liṅgin), and conversely, the indicated exists only in the indicator;
if this restriction is reversed, there is no relationship between the indicator and the indicated.
By this, the fault that was stated by the Teacher regarding the capacity to indicate [the probandum] through the force of conjunction (saṃyoga) is addressed.
"And fire is not non-conjoined with it in any respect, nor is smoke [non-conjoined] with it in every way; therefore, the manifestation [of fire] from smoke is established.
It is explained that this [argument] does not apply here.
For instance, this undesirable consequence applies to conjunction because it is indistinguishable in both cases, but not to pervasion.
This is because pervasion as a property of the pervader is not exactly the same as [pervasion] as a property of the pervaded. And so it has been said:
“Although the relation resides in both the coexistent probans and the probandum,
its occurrence is like that of the container and the contained, but not like that of two conjoined things.
Therefore, the pervader is not the pervaded, and the pervaded is not the pervader.
Because of the statement, "The reason is pervaded by a portion of that [subject]," the fault mentioned regarding the position of conjunction does not apply;
nor does it follow that both are simultaneously the cognizer and the cognized,
since from the definition of the reason as stated, it is understood that only the pervader is the object of cognition.
Because it is only the pervaded (*vyāpya*) that is understood as the means of cognition (*gamaka*).
[9. Indication of the nature of pervasion as positive and negative concomitance:

If, then, the definition of the reason (*hetu*) is "the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) which is pervaded by a part of that [subject]," then the reason would have two forms: the state of being a property of the subject and pervasion by a part of that [subject].
And since the three-fold [reason] has been stated elsewhere, how is there no contradiction?

To this he says: "By this"—namely, by the statement of the pervasion by that part—it should be understood that "either the positive concomitance (anvaya) or the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is stated. The underlying sense is that pervasion consists in the nature of both positive and negative concomitance.

For it is thus: that very thing which is concomitant with another, and which ceases when the latter ceases, is said to be pervaded by it. Since pervasion consists in this very nature, the statement of pervasion expresses both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*);
therefore, because two aspects are expressed by the statement of pervasion, there is no contradiction. [10. The ascertainment of pervasion is by means of perception or inference.]
And these two are ascertained by virtue of being the reasons for making known;
furthermore, their ascertainment is not by means of a single pramāṇa alone, but rather by each according to its own respective pramāṇa—
that is, by whichever pramāṇa is its own determinative means.

And that valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) which determines each [of these] will be explained later: "Either positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to indicate their equal status.

Therefore, since one of the two types of formal arguments—those based on similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—implies the other through the nature of affirmation and negation, there is no need to present both, even though there is a difference in their exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), because they are in reality identical (*tādātmya*).
This is indicated:

for the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), which is the property of the logical mark (*liṅga*) to cease when the probandum ceases, is an inherent property; thus, its positive form (*anvaya-rūpatā*) is not in fact contradicted. And [it is said]: "It is also a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)."
What [is it]?
The connection is that it has been stated: "ascertained by its respective means of valid cognition" (Hbṭ 20).
In this context, that [inference] is also set forth by way of an incidental discussion (prasaṅga), in order to explain that what is ascertained (niścita) is the means of cognition (gamaka).
The word "also" (api) is used for the purpose of demonstration.

“Even though [the object] itself has the form of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), its establishment [as such] occurs because it generates an immediately subsequent conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a universal (*sāmānya*).

This is called ‘ascertainment’ (*niścaya*) in a figurative sense (*upacāra*), in order to show that the conceptual construction following upon direct perception lacks the capacity to apprehend an object not already apprehended.

Therefore, although the mark (*liṅga*) is established in the form of a universal, nevertheless, the very cognition of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the basis for that establishment; thus, [it is established] through direct perception that the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) resides in the locus of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*).”
Establishment (*prasiddhi*) is being stated;
this will be clarified immediately hereafter.
Alternatively, establishment is the ascertainment (*niścaya*) of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in the locus of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*) by means of inference.

And because there is a distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*), he says that "by inference" (*anumānataḥ*) means "ascertainment by means of inference. Regarding this example, it is stated in due order: "as, for instance, in the case of smoke in a location," which refers to the ascertainment of the generality of smoke (*dhūmasāmānya*) through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). [11. Having refuted the view of Uddyotakara, the statement is made that the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) is a means of cognition when it depends on place and other such factors.]
But as for one who thinks:

"That portion of space which is in contact with fire is imperceptible; whereas that which is perceptible—consisting of the form of a portion of the sky, light, and so forth—is seen to possess smoke, yet it does not possess fire. Therefore, how can there be a cognition of smoke in that location through perception?"

Therefore, it is logical that smoke alone is the subject (*dharmin*); the relationship between the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) is thus: "This smoke possesses fire because it is smoke.
However, even for that [proposition], the smoke-part that possesses fire is not perceptible.

Furthermore, since that which is currently perceived exists in the upper portion and is not co-located with fire, how can the universal "smoke" be established through perception in the subject (*dharmin*) where the probandum resides?
If it is argued that the composite whole (*avayavin*) consisting of smoke is perceived, we say no.
Because it does not exist apart from its constituent parts,
or— if its unity is established through worldly convention— then the imagined unity of even such a spatial extent is not precluded.
Furthermore, people perceive fire only in its specific location, not in the smoke itself;
and it is only by depending on factors such as place and time that the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) functions as a means of cognition. As it has been said:
"Even in the case of a contradictory effect, dependence on place, time, and so forth is accepted."
Otherwise, it would be inconclusive, like ashes used as a means to prove that fire is not cold.
Thus:

"Therefore, when fire is being established in dependence upon a location and so forth, it is not contradictory for the location being apprehended as possessing smoke to function as the locus (dharmin)."
Just as a tree or other object possessing cranes establishes the presence of water with respect to a particular location and so forth;

or as the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) in the case of sound [establishes its impermanence] through inference such as "being differentiated by a difference in cognition" (*pratyayabhedabheditva*).
[This is the response to Kumārila’s objection: "How can non-conceptual [perception] grasp a universal?"]

In this regard, Kumārila— failing to understand the intended meaning of the well-described establishment of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in the locus of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*) through perception—
asks: "How is it even possible for perception, being non-conceptual, to grasp the essential nature of a mark (*liṅga*) such as smoke, which is by nature a universal?"
"Or rather, how could there even be the apprehension of its connection with the subject (*dharmin*)?"—thus he objected.
For by that [objection], the following *bhāṣya*—"And because inference and the rest are preceded by perception, they are not means of knowledge regarding *dharma*"—is addressed:
"How can inference and the rest be preceded by perception?"
When, due to the incapacity for recollection, the cognition of the non-conceptualizing sense faculty [arises].
"And there can be no apprehension of a mark that is not conceptually constructed, nor likewise of its connection with the subject"— having raised this objection:
As for the claim that there is no apprehension by perception because the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth are free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
that is not accepted, since even conceptual construction is helpful in the form of the object itself.
There exists a first cognition of perception which is non-conceptual,
resembling the cognition of infants, the mute, and others, and arising from the pure object itself.
Furthermore, that cognition by which the object is subsequently determined through properties such as genus and so forth is also accepted as being of the nature of direct perception.
(Hbṭ 22)

By saying this, [the author] means: "This defect—characterized by the non-apprehension of the mark (liṅga), the subject (dharmin), and their relationship—belongs only to the Buddhists for whom perception is exclusively non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka); it does not belong to us, who maintain that perception is also conceptual (savikalpaka)."
This is what has been stated.
Then, in order to counteract the faults described therein, he says: "For [the fire] with smoke," and so forth.
The collective meaning here is as follows: for perception indeed apprehends that which stands before one, such as the region of smoke and so on, in their spatial sequence of above and below.

By way of affirmation, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of smoke and so forth— which is excluded from all homogeneous and heterogeneous things— because all causal capacities (*sāmarthya*) are established in their own intrinsic natures and are mutually non-confused, produces two subsequent conceptual constructions of affirmation and negation that imitate its location as it arises through that capacity; by means of these, there arise the property-bearer (*dharmin*) known as "smoke" and the location, as well as their spatial relationship of "above" and "below."

One conceptualizes that "this is so, and not otherwise," because conceptualizations arise through the cooperation of other conditions such as the proficiency of practice, based upon experience. Consequently,
the determination of the essential nature of both the property and the substratum, as well as the determination of their relationship, is established as being grounded in perception.
For instance, this very determination that "this [fire] is here [in this place]" is the ascertainment of the relationship between smoke and location.
And that [relationship] is indeed established by non-conceptual perception in the manner already described.

Furthermore, there is no relationship characterized as the state of container and contained that is anything other than the two entities situated in a vertical relation; for if such a thing existed, it would have to be conceptualized later on because it was not experienced by perception.

Because that which has become a real entity is negated elsewhere, this [conceptual construct] is merely superimposed by imagination based upon those two objects as they actually exist. Therefore, the worldly convention of "relation" and "related," as property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*), occurs through the exclusion or non-exclusion of other distinctions; it is not, however, ultimate (*pāramārthika*).
Even common linguistic usage is extended only by relying upon entities that are excluded from those of a different class, and is thus merely superimposed by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

This is because those very distinct entities, through the medium of experience, are by their very nature the causes of a single-form reflective cognition (*parāmarśa-pratyaya*) precisely as they are excluded from what is of a different class. And so it has been said:

“Even though they are distinct, certain things are restricted by their own nature to the accomplishment of a single purpose, such as a single reflective judgment, a cognition of an object, and so forth, just like the sense organs and other [causes]. (Hbṭ 23)

Therefore, because the form of smoke appearing therein—which possesses a nature excluded from dissimilar classes—is grasped by perception itself as a universal through the mediation of the generation of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), [it follows that it is not a memory].
For the exclusion from dissimilar classes (*vijātīyavyāvṛtti*) is not something other than the excluded object itself such that its non-grasping by perception would occur.

Consequently, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of smoke and so forth, exactly as it was perceived, is conceptualized as having a nature excluded from others; thus, by virtue of the determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) of the cognizer, this is nothing but a memory.
Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is of two kinds: that which follows upon perception and that which is entirely without an object in reality.
Therefore, as it has been said regarding the non-experience of a universal: "He who would say that this cognition is a memory [of something] through non-differentiation..."
"Even for the son of a barren woman, there must surely exist the capacity for memory"—
this [objection] is also refuted.
[13. Response to Kumārila’s objection that inference would lead to an infinite regress if it were to have the universal as its object:

Alternatively, another point stated by Kumārila is as follows: "Perception has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, while inference has the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object. According to this statement, the universal such as smoke is indeed apprehended solely by inference. In that case, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because the inference that apprehends the logical mark (*liṅga*) itself arises through the power of another logical mark distinct from it.

And since that [universal] is a general form, it is the object of inference based on what is other than itself; likewise, the same applies to anything else. Thus, the cognition of even a single probandum (*liṅgin*) is not possible even in a thousand aeons, let alone within the span of a single human life. And so it has been said: "That for which the universal is not cognized without inference..."
Furthermore, inference does not function when it is devoid of a logical mark (liṅga).
Furthermore, no one accepts that what is unique [to the subject] can serve as a logical mark (liṅga);
nor is there any unperceived mark that can act as a revealer.
Furthermore, the cognition of that [object] would have to occur through another inference;
and its arising would result from a logical mark (liṅga) associated with the knowledge of a universal.

Moreover, its status as inference arises from a logical mark (liṅga), and that [mark] is known through yet another inference; such being the case, this would lead to an infinite regress in the conceptualization.

Anticipating the objection that "because signs (liṅga), the signified (liṅgin), and inferences (anumāna) are infinite, a comprehension of even a single signified object does not occur even in many thousands of yugas," he says: "For [the fire] with smoke," and so forth.
He thinks as follows:
"Let this fault apply to one for whom the universal (*sāmānya*) is not cognized without inference;
however, for us, the universal is cognized even by a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurring subsequent to perception (*pratyakṣa*), due to a natural delusion."

Furthermore, because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding a logical mark (*liṅga*) is based on the perception of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it possesses non-deceptiveness through an indirect connection with the real entity (*vastu*), just as the error of perceiving a jewel in the luster of a jewel [is non-deceptive regarding the jewel itself].

Likewise, even the status of being an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) belongs to the universal smoke (*dhūmasāmānya*) appearing in conceptual construction; for that universal is established as a logical mark by being based on the perception of the effect and by the determination (*adhyavasāya*) thereof.
For it is not logical to establish the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of smoke as a logical mark (liṅga),
because that which is unique lacks occurrence in the similar class (sapakṣa) and thus cannot be pervaded by a portion of that [subject].
And because it is impossible to perceive a real entity when there is a conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*) of the probandum and the probans.

As for what was stated— that "inference has the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object"— it is not determined therein that inference has *only* the general characteristic as its object.

Since even the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises subsequent to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) has that [particular] as its object, and since other conceptual constructions do not, it is determined that inference has only the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object; this is for the purpose of negating its having the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object. In that context, "accompanied by smoke" (*sadhūma*) means that which exists together with smoke.
This was stated for the purpose of establishing the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
And this alone is the seed of the conceptual construction of affirmation (*vidhivikalpa*).
The connection is with the words "for one who has seen that place as possessing smoke" by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣeṇa*).

What is meant by "having a form distinguished from other things"? The analysis of the compound is as follows: its form (*rūpa*) is distinguished (*vivikta*), that is, unmixed (*asaṅkīrṇa*), from other things, namely from those of the same class and those of different classes. This is because all entities are established in their own respective natures (*svabhāva*), and thus there is no confusion of natures.
Otherwise, if everything were applicable everywhere, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
By this, the cause for the conceptualization of negation has been explained, as well as the seed for the imaginative construction of universals (*sāmānyotprekṣā*). As it has been said:
"The mutual exclusion [of particulars] is the [cause] of the ultimate..."
"The seed is the conceptualization (saṃjñā) for which it has purpose.

For instance, when one perceives the exclusion of other objects among things that are mutually distinct yet similar, a conceptual construction arises that conceals their differentiated form and superimposes a non-differentiated nature—
namely, "by way of its own uncommon essence," meaning by way of a nature excluded from other objects.
But it is not as Kumārila thinks—
that "the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntaraviveka*) is grasped by the means of non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*) and is not determinable by perception (*pratyakṣa*).
