For it is impossible for perception, which arises through the power of real entities (*vastubalabhāvin*), to perceive otherwise, as that would entail the consequence of its being erroneous (*bhrāntatā*).
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: for a person who has perceived by means of that very self, immediately thereafter "the cognition of the mark based on memory arises.
"Smārta" means nothing other than memory (*smṛti*).

"Cognition appearing as a mark" (*liṅgajñāna*) refers to the conceptual cognition that arises subsequent to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). By this, [the author] states the formal establishment of the "mark" (*liṅga*) regarding that universal (*sāmānya*) which appears in such a conceptualization.
What, then, is its object in the ultimate sense?

[The determination of validity and invalidity regarding conceptualizations of the affirmation and negation of perception: “Having as its object the ultimate reality of the distinctions as they have been perceived... [14. The determination of validity and invalidity regarding conceptualizations of the affirmation and negation of perception: He undertakes an investigation into the validity and invalidity of conceptualizations that affirm or negate perception.
“In that regard,” among those alternatives concerning the injunctions and prohibitions regarding perception;
“the first of them” is this: “For there is indeed an initial cognition of bare observation.”

That which is called "the first" (*ādyam*) is the vision (*darśana*) whose object is the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), having an uncommon object, occurring at the beginning of the activity of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); that alone is the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not even the conceptual constructions of affirmation and negation, because it alone possesses the definition of valid cognition while those two lack it.
For instance, the definition of valid cognition consists in having as its object that which has not been previously apprehended and that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
That [capacity] belongs to perception alone.

In this context, "the first" refers to its nature as a cognition of an object not previously known; "having an uncommon object" refers to its having as its object that which accomplishes purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), because only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the accomplisher of purposeful action.
[15. Establishing the Invalidity of the Conceptualization of Negation:
Regarding that, first demonstrating that the conceptualization of negation is a form of memory because its object is an entity already grasped by perception, he says:
"In that"—namely, in the unique—"such" entity, whose nature is unmixed with other things, "by means of seeing"—which arises through the power of that unmixed nature—...
"When [the object] is seen," that is, when it has been apprehended.

For instance, even by one who maintains that the aspect of non-existence (abhāvāṃśa) is distinct from the aspect of existence (bhāvāṃśa), the aspect of existence must be conceived as having a nature that is unmixed [with others];
otherwise, that very aspect of non-existence could not be established.
Furthermore, if there is no state of being unmixed by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
then even if a distinct portion of non-existence were present, that [state of being unmixed] would not be logical;
for it is impossible to abandon an entity whose mixed nature has been brought about by the power of its own causes, even if an ineffective portion of non-existence were to occur.
Nor can that very same [cause] bring about its own destruction, because it will be demonstrated that a cause for destruction is logically untenable.

Furthermore, if destruction were to consist in a confusion of forms, it would be better for things to arise by their very nature as distinct forms from their own causes; what is the point of resorting to the "logician's sweetmeat" (parivrāḍmodaka) analogy?
Therefore, the non-existence aspect of entities consists precisely in their being devoid of the nature of others by virtue of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and not anything else.
And that which is of such a nature is indeed apprehended by perception.
When that which is of such a nature is seen, that object is "common" (*asādhāraṇa*)—that is, it possesses a similar intrinsic nature—with "that" [other] thing.

It does not exist [in others] because its nature is deficient in that form; it expresses this very point by stating its "unshared nature" (*tadasādhāraṇatām*), which is its lack of identity with those various things that do not possess that form.

Thus, through the power of perception, a memory arises—directing itself toward and manifesting the "distinction" (*bheda*) or difference from other objects, namely, the fact that "this is not of another form"—by way of operating upon the perceived dissimilarity.
The point is that if, however, it were produced by the power of the inferential mark (*liṅga*), then even memory would not have exclusion as its object.
What is its object?
It has "the exclusion of what is not that" (*atadvyāvṛtti*) as its object.
By the word "that" (tat), there is a reference to the object that is the domain of perception.
"Not that" (na tat) means not of a different class (vijātīya). Exclusion from what is not that is "exclusion from the non-that" (atadvyāvṛtti).
That which has that as its object is "tathā" (so). Alternatively, this was stated because even I postulate a difference from other objects, based on the determination of the cognizer.

Because it is ultimately devoid of an object, that [cognition] is "not a means of valid cognition" (na pramāṇa); the meaning is that it is not the result of the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (abhāvapramāṇa).
For it is not logical that validity should be established merely by its capacity to produce recollection.
Why is it not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
Because it apprehends a particularity—the form of that which was perceived—which depends upon other conditions such as proficiency in practice;
for an object is not apprehended by conceptualization merely as "that which was seen."
Because there would be no distinction in perception, it would follow that conceptual constructions would arise with respect to all aspects;
rather, only a certain [aspect] arises depending on conditions such as repeated practice. Thus, he explains it by means of the apprehension of an aspect.
Let it be the apprehension of the aspect exactly as it is perceived.

Showing that the opponent’s definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is lacking, he asks why it does not qualify as such: "Previously" (*prāk*), at the time when the initial sensory awareness (*ālocanājñāna*) arises, one perceives the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*), that is, the unmixed form; yet, for one who "expresses" (*abhilapataḥ*), that is, conceptualizes, [the thought] "this is not the uncommon form of another object," there is no "attainment of a previously unknown object" (*apūrvārthādhigama*) by means of that conceptual exclusion (*pratiṣedhavikalpa*). Thus, it is not a means of valid cognition.
This is because it lacks the cognition of a previously unknown object (*apūrvārthavijñāna*).

The point is that you state that valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is precisely the cognition of a previously unknown object. [16. Establishing the lack of validity for this conceptual construction of an injunction.]
If conceptualization through negation is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the manner described, then conceptualization through affirmation will be a valid means of cognition;
for it is impossible that it lacks the quality of being a cognition of an object not previously known.

Since the universal form (*sāmānyākāra*) appearing therein—which persists [through various instances]—is not apprehended by a perception that relies upon a unique particular (*asādhāraṇarūpa*), how can there be invalidity for this [cognition]? Regarding this, it was said: "Thereafter, however, the object...
and so forth. Having raised this objection concerning the statement of Kumārila, [the author] establishes the validity even of affirmative conceptual cognition (*vidhivikalpa*).

He says, refuting [the opponent]: "Because the particular (svalakṣaṇa), which is the means for accomplishing purposeful action (arthakriyā), has already been seen by the sensory perception (ālocanājñāna), and because its nature as the means for accomplishing purposeful action—which was previously unseen—is not apprehended by conceptualization (vikalpa), conceptualization that functions as a positive affirmation (vidhivikalpa) is not a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa).

Even if it is described that it apprehends a universal (sāmānya) not yet apprehended by that [sensory perception], nevertheless, that [universal] is not the means for accomplishing purposeful action; therefore, one who apprehends it is like a cognition belonging to those with ophthalmia or similar defects.

Conceptual construction regarding the procedure is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). "Thereafter, however, the object is determined by the intellect through its properties such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth."
And thus it is said.

Furthermore, by the mention of "the thing" (*vastu*) therein, it is stated that there is a conceptual determination (*avasāya*) by means of a conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) of that very thing which is the object of non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpapratyakṣa*), as qualified by genus (*jāti*) and so forth.
Furthermore, since that [universal] is apprehended solely through non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpajñāna*), it lacks validity (*prāmāṇya*) therein;

and because a universal lacks causal efficacy (*arthakriyāsādhanatva*), even when it is apprehended as something not previously known, it lacks validity—just like the cognition of [illusory] hair and the like.
For this very reason, direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*) is also impossible, because there is no sensory contact (*samprayoga*) with a universal that is devoid of the capacity for causal efficacy.
By the word "and" (*ca*), there is a conjunction of the previously stated reasons, namely "because it is a memory" (*smṛtitvāt*).
That this is indeed a memory will be demonstrated later:
"like inference" (*anumānavat*). (Hbṭ 28)

This is the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Just as when a locus (*dharmin*) called a "place" is apprehended through perception as the means for accomplishing a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), there is no such apprehension of fire— which is not yet apprehended, which is the means for accomplishing a purposeful action, and which is imperceptible (*parokṣa*)— by means of a conceptual construction (*vidhi-vikalpa*), because it is impossible to cognize it in its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) rather than in a generic form.
An object that accomplishes purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is apprehended in its general form,
because it is apprehended by that very same sensory perception (*ālocanājñāna*).
In that [perception]...
"That this is merely memory, and not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
[17. Justification of the validity of cognition whose object is the accomplishment of purposeful action.
Why is it that "only that which has as its object the accomplishment of purposeful action is a valid means of knowledge, and nothing else"?

If this is argued: "For a person who seeks purposeful action (arthakriyā)—that is, one who seeks to attain the beneficial and avoid the harmful—is 'everyone,' not just some rare individual by way of the 'crow-and-palmyra-fruit' maxim; such a 'discerning' person (prekṣāvān), acting with prior reflection, would always engage based on a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) alone, and never [engage] based on what is not a valid means of cognition (apramāṇa)."
Because deception is possible,
one "seeks both" not out of mere curiosity;
therefore, he declares that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has as its object only that which accomplishes purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Because that [cognition] serves as a factor for activity in the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*),
whereas the other does not, being the opposite of that;
for even in common worldly usage, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is said to be non-discrepant and non-deceptive.

Furthermore, if one does not apprehend that which accomplishes a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) and thus does not engage with it, how could one possibly attain it? How then could a person acting with circumspection declare such a thing to be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) on the grounds of its non-contradiction?
[18. Detailed Proof of the Non-Reality of the Universal (*sāmānya*):]

If it is argued that since the universal (*sāmānya*) is likewise a means for accomplishing purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), then the affirmative conceptual cognition (*vidhivikalpa*) directed toward it will be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he replies: "And not" (*na ca*)— indeed, the universal "does not bring about" (*upakalpayati*) any "purposeful action," whether it be the one characterized by non-distinct cognition and designation which is accepted as being accomplished by it, or another [action] such as that accomplished by the individual (*vyakti*).

Of what kind [is it]? It is "grasped by a conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*) produced through the power of that" "after" (*urdhvam*), i.e., at a later time, "the apprehension of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇapratipatti*)," which is the apprehension of the individual (*vyakti*) known as sensory perception (*ālocanājñāna*).
Here, the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to the apprehension of the particular characteristic.
"Furthermore, after that, the object (*vastu*)."

By stating "thus, etc.," [the author] speaks in this way precisely because others have asserted it, in order to refute the status of perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises subsequent to a sensory perception.
However, every universal (*sāmānya*) whatsoever does not contribute to any purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
As for that universal which is grasped by inferential conceptualization, it arrives by way of the ascertainment of a logical mark (*liṅga*) that is connected to a cause or a pervader (*vyāpaka*).

Because it brings about a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) concerning an object that is a means to an unattained purposeful action— by way of a connection to what is already connected— the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) having that as its object is a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This [sensory perception], however, is not like that,
because the means to the purposeful action has already been apprehended by the initial observational cognition (*ālocanājñāna*).

An illustration for this is: "Just as, upon seeing blue, in the cognition 'it is blue'... the word "appearing" (*pratibhāsamāna*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. The connection with the context is that "the universal does not accomplish any causal efficiency. Now, one might object: "The universal appearing in the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the subject under discussion; why then is something else cited as an example?"

This is in order to refute, by means of an equal logic, the status of perception as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—as accepted by others—for every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises subsequent to a sensory perception. Furthermore, what kind of universal (*sāmānya*), appearing in the conceptual cognition "What is blue? which follows upon a sensory perception, does not provide for causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*)?
If [it is argued] that it is the efficacy to be accomplished by the particular (*vyakti*);...

In that case, another entity would also not provide the causal efficiency belonging to something else; thus, because it would not accomplish its own causal efficiency, the consequence would follow that it is a non-entity.
If, on the other hand, you mean its own specific causal efficiency, that remains unproven.

Anticipating the objection that [the means of cognition] produces its own effect characterized by non-differentiated cognition and designation, he says: "For that very same" blue particular (*nīlasvalakṣaṇa*), i.e., the individual instance of blue, which was not apprehended in the perceptual awareness (*ālocanājñāna*) at that time, "is the performer of such a purposeful action" (*tathāvidhasādhyārthakriyākāri*). By the word "such" (*tathāvidha*), it is the universal (*sāmānya*) that is intended here.
Because this [particular] is a synonym for that [universal],
and because its common form is of that same nature;

therefore, it is so called because it is the habit of this particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) to perform such an effectual action (*arthakriyā*) characterized by non-differentiated cognition and designation, which has as its object to be proven (*sādhya*) the generality of blue (*nīlasāmānya*).

He thinks as follows: just as distinct individuals, despite being separate, assist that single, undivided universal by means of a certain proximity characterized by their restriction to that single effect—
even without connection to another universal—
otherwise there would be the consequence of an infinite regress.
In this way, they will accomplish purposeful action (arthakriyā) even through that which consists of non-differentiated cognition and designation.
What is the use of accepting a universal (sāmānya) that lacks any means of valid cognition (apramāṇaka) and is contradicted by valid cognition (pramāṇabādhitena)?
For instance, in cognitions such as inference, we do not perceive in individual particulars the kind of indistinct form that appears [in that cognition].
For at the time of perceiving a particular individual, we clearly discern only a single form, such as blue.
How then could we deceive ourselves by postulating something unseen?
If it is argued that [the universal] is not discerned because of its association with the form of the individual, like fire in an iron ball—that is not so.

Because it would follow that the distinction between difference and non-difference would be non-existent everywhere; for this same rebuttal is easily applicable elsewhere as well. Furthermore, a universal does not possess two forms—a distinct one and an indistinct one.

For [an object] would appear through one [cognition] in perception and through another in inferential and other types of knowledge; this would entail the consequence of admitting two distinct entities,
since it is precisely the difference in appearance that serves as the basis for establishing a difference in reality in all cases.
Because it would follow that a universal must itself possess another universal, and because this [universal] is admitted to be devoid of further universals;
by this, the following is also refuted, which he [Kumārila] said:
“And the cognition regarding all things arises as having the nature of both exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and inclusion (*anugama*);
and that [cognition] is not tenable without a dual nature.
Nor is either one of these two here considered to be an error through metaphorical designation.”
"Because cognition is always stable, the error belongs to those who claim that it is erroneous.
This is because, if this is said with reference to sensory cognition (*indriyabuddhi*),
then it is unproven (*asiddha*).

Because an indistinct form such as blue is not perceived there when there is a distinct appearance of blue and so forth; and because even if there were a second distinct [form], it would be a recurring one.
Furthermore, if that were the case, how could there be a persistence of that [form] for something that reaches even the interval between two individuals?
And when that which exists is perceptible, how could there be a non-perception of it therein?
For it is impossible for it to possess both a manifest and a non-manifest form simultaneously.
Because it is one. Thus it has been said:

"If that universal were omnipresent because it is manifested in a single individual due to its non-difference from that individual, then it would be perceived everywhere; nor does it depend upon individuals."
Thus, when even a single individual instance is perceived, would its form—which pervades the entire triple world or pervades all its own substrata—not be seen [in its entirety]?
For there can be nothing of a single thing that is either seen or unseen, as is the case with momentariness and so forth.
If it is argued that even when one is seen, the determination of seeing occurs only in relation to that specific substratum and not everywhere, we say: no.
Because it is accepted that [the object] is seen by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
For it is not logical that something which has been made the object of a certainty should also be uncertain.
Consequently, if the form of everything-pervading were seen, it would follow as a logical consequence that all objects would be seen.
For when that [object] is perceived, it is not logical that its concomitant— which is perceivable and possesses an identical nature— should not be perceived.
Therefore, how can sensory cognition possess a dual nature?
Now, as for cognition through inference and so forth:
since even in that [cognition] the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear, how could it possess a dual nature?
For in those cognitions which grasp universals (*sāmānya*), there is no appearance of the particular characteristic perceived as indistinct, as is the case with the form of an individual (*vyakti*).
Because those [cognitions] would still arise even in the absence of that [object],
and because it does not appear in its own cognition under any other form; for it is impossible for a single [entity] to possess multiple forms,
and because it would lead to an over-extension (apratiprasaṅga).

Therefore, this non-distinct conceptual cognition (*sāmānyabuddhi*) which grasps distinct objects does not appear as something arising from particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Rather, being produced by the latencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless habituation to false conceptualization, it appears in that manner. Furthermore, the "firmness" of a cognition does not consist in its indestructibility.
Because of the acceptance of momentariness, [the definition of valid cognition] is simply "that which is not sublated"; however,
this is not possible for this [cognition], since it has been stated that there is even a slight sublation.

In detail, however, the refutation should be understood from the *Syādvādabhaṅga*, which will be presented here and there as the occasion arises. Therefore, just as individuals function toward that single [cognition] without another universal, so too will they operate toward a single cognition and designation; thus, that very blue particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) performs the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) accepted as being accomplished by a universal. [20. Demonstration that Kumārila’s objection does not invalidate the Buddhist position.]
But as for the one who says: "If a universal is not admitted as something distinct, then what restricts its occurrence? Why is the cognition of 'cow' not restricted even in the absence of cowness?"

"Just as, despite an equal degree of difference, there is occurrence [of a term] in some instances and non-occurrence in others— such as the case of *gotva* (cowness) and so forth, which occurs even without a specific cause— so too will cognition be.
Having thus raised the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the author proceeds:]
"For it is not accepted that cognitions arise without an object;
therefore, they certainly accept a universal as something distinct from the particular."
"For those [particulars] would be false if they were produced without that [universal], even in the absence of an object;
however, the existence of the universal here is not impaired by being without another [particular].
(Hbṭ 32)

Thus, the fault of the consequence of falsity has been stated; however, it does not invalidate those whose intellects are purified by the system of the Tathāgata’s doctrine, because they accept that falsity is based on subverting cognitions for those with ordinary intellects. For instance: "Why is 'cowness' restricted only to those things possessing a dewlap and so forth?"
Because it is of that nature;
if one asks why its identity with that [nature] exists, let it be understood that it is due to its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because of this statement:
"The universal has the individual as its nature;
nor is it uncommon [to the individuals], even during the arising and destruction of those individuals."

It has been stated that [the self] "is not subject to arising and passing away," because otherwise there would be the consequence of difference due to the imposition of contradictory properties. And he said:
“If it is held that the universal is identical [to the individual], then why is it not accepted that when the individual is born, the universal is unborn,
and when it perishes, the universal does not perish? And likewise, why is there no lack of concomitance?”

If it has not been produced at the birth of the manifest individual, nor has it come from another substratum, and if it did not previously exist in that location, how could it have become conjoined with it?

If it is argued that [the universal] is not destroyed when the individual is destroyed, yet it has not gone to another individual, nor does it abide in a place devoid of those individuals— then tell me, where is that universal?

"Even though the individual instance (vyakti) is subject to birth and so forth, if it is not admitted that the universal (jāti) possesses these, how could identity (tādātmya) be accepted by those whose minds are unclouded?
[21. Establishment of the invalidity of the conceptualization of blue.]

If the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) of blue itself performs the causal function (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by the universal, then the conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) apprehending that very [particular] would become a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). To this, he says:

"And that" unique particular of blue "is indeed seen" by the sensory perception (*ālocanā-pratyaya*) "in its own nature," that is, as possessing the intrinsic character of performing the causal function to be accomplished by blue.
Therefore, how could a conceptual cognition—which produces no further distinction in an object for which the function has already been accomplished—be a valid means of knowledge?
Now, it might be thought: "In that case, let the conceptual cognition of blue, which apprehends the universal itself, be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);

and that universal is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), because, acting together with the blue [particular], it will perform the very same causal function that is to be accomplished by the blue."

For universals are indeed of the very same nature as individuals; thus he says: "And not"—meaning certainly not—"that [universal] which exists at a time subsequent to the apprehension of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)," i.e., that which has the habit of occurring after the perception of a blue individual.

The sense is that it is possible to establish a universal—whether imagined or real—as having the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) accomplished by the individual, in the manner previously described, only for that [universal] which exists at a time subsequent to the apprehension of the inferential mark (*liṅga*).
“By the object of the conceptualization of blue,” that is, by the universal of blue (*nīlasāmānya*), “the causal efficiency to be accomplished by blue,” such as dyeing and so forth, “is performed.
This is because, given the impossibility of [that universal] possessing the nature of a particular (*vyakti*), it is impossible for a conceptually constructed form (*kalpitarūpa*) to possess it.
Furthermore, no other causal efficiency to be accomplished by blue is performed by the object of the conceptualization of blue, which bears an eternal nature.
He considers that this is because of the contradiction between succession and simultaneity.
Thus, having seen blue, [one perceives] "blue."

Having thus established that the universal appearing in cognition does not accomplish any purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), [the author] shows that the definition of valid cognition provided by the Mīmāṃsakas—“valid cognition is the cognition of an object not previously known”—must include a qualification, because otherwise there would be the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) following upon perception, even though their objects do not perform purposeful action. Thus he says: “Therefore,” since [conceptual cognition] has as its object that which does not accomplish purposeful action...

It is illogical for the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises subsequent to perception (*darśana*) to possess validity. Therefore, having rejected our own accepted definition of valid cognition as "valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge," [others] propose other definitions out of mere self-aggrandizement, such as "valid cognition has as its object an unapprehended thing," or "in that regard, valid cognition is the cognition of a previously unknown object. Even in this case...

When formulating the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a qualification must be employed to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*). How should it be qualified? It should be qualified as "with respect to a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) not yet cognized. For by this qualification, the validity of inferential conceptualization is established.

And since the validity of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises subsequent to the knowledge of direct observation (*ālocana-jñāna*) is excluded, everything is well-established. Thus, having refuted the validity of the affirmative conceptual construction (*vidhi-vikalpa*)— on the grounds that its object is not the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), even though it apprehends a universal (*sāmānya*) not previously apprehended—

the author now addresses, by means of the word "and" (*ca*), the fact of being a memory (*smṛtitva*), which is a common cause of invalidity shared with the negative conceptual construction (*pratiṣedha-vikalpa*).

Demonstrating this, he says: "But when the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has been apprehended by the sensory cognition (*ālocanājñāna*), the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)— which arises through its power, exists by the force of that apprehension of the particular characteristic,

and imitates it— is said to be such because it does not arise directly [from the object], but rather imitates the clear form of the particular characteristic of blue due to the influence of the impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the perception, and because of the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized."
In reality, however,
this [cognition] does not imitate anything at all;
it is simply memory.
Why? Because its objectivity is due to its functional effect (*kārya*), not in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).
Here, the "functional effect" consists in the person's engagement with the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) thereof.

And because it has that [particular] as its object only by way of its effect, memory—and thus the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) produced by the force of perception—is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For even in the case of memory, which has as its object a portion of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) previously experienced, there is no objective reality (*paramārtha*) to that object;
for the particular does not appear in memory with a clear form, as it does in sensory cognition.
However, it arises precisely from the object as previously described;
and since that is the same even in the case of a conceptual construction of affirmation (*vidhivikalpa*), how could this not be a recollection (*smṛti*)?
[23. Establishing the validity of inference by distinguishing it from the conceptual construction of affirmation.]
In this regard, it might be argued: "But surely even an inferential conceptualization (*anumāna-vikalpa*), though of the nature of memory, is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For instance, that very thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*) which was previously experienced in the kitchen as excluded from non-fire is remembered upon seeing smoke in a particular location. In the same way, an affirmative conceptualization (*vidhi-vikalpa*) will also be a valid means of knowledge. To this, he says: "Because there is no apprehension of the form of an object not [already] apprehended."

He thinks as follows: that which was previously experienced in the kitchen and elsewhere as a mere entity excluded from non-fire is not remembered by the inferential conceptualization solely in its relation to that specific place and so forth;
rather, it is remembered in its relation to the particular location where it was not previously experienced.

Therefore, because there is the apprehension—by means of the exclusion of non-connection (ayogavyavaccheda)—of the nature of an entity excluded from non-fire, which was not apprehended by the two perceptions grasping the property-bearer of the probandum and the property-bearer of the example, its status as a valid means of cognition is justified.
But it does not apply to the conceptual construction that follows upon perception,
because that is the opposite of it; thus,
the establishment of the means of valid cognition has reality as its basis.
And the nature of a real entity (*vastu*) belongs exclusively to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

If it is argued, "Even if it does not apprehend the form of an entity that has not yet been apprehended, why would it not still be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?", he replies: "Because it has a real entity as its basis," and so forth.

Furthermore, the statement that the "establishment of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇavyavasthā*) has reality as its basis (*vastvadhiṣṭhānatva*) is said with reference to the object of the operation of the means of valid cognition, not in the sense of having it as its objective support (*ālambana*).

Otherwise, since inference would have a mentally constructed universal as its objective support, it would lack a basis in reality, and thus the establishment of the means of valid cognition would be non-pervasive (*avyāpin*).
If the establishment of the means of valid cognition is based on reality, how [can it apply] to an object that is remote? (Hbṭ 35)
If it is argued that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), [we reply:

even in that case, since the very conceptualization of the *pradhāna* and so forth is what is to be proven by virtue of not being the material cause of existing things, that [non-apprehension] likewise certainly has a real entity as its substratum; thus there is no fault.
Now, why is it that the establishment of a means of knowledge must necessarily have a real entity as its substratum?

Thus he says: "Because those who seek that [object]—that is, those seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) characterized by pleasure and pain—engage in activity characterized by acquisition and avoidance toward that which is 'suitable' or capable for such purposeful action, [the object] is its domain.

If it is asked: "Even if there is activity on the part of those seeking purposeful action toward what is not suitable for purposeful action, how can the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have a real entity as its basis?
For in that case, it would have something other than what is suitable for purposeful action as its basis."

He says: "That which is 'capable' (yogya) regarding 'purposeful action' (arthakriyā) is indeed the 'definition' (lakṣaṇa) of a 'real entity' (vastu). Therefore, the meaning is: since it is the locus of what is capable of purposeful action, why should it not be the locus of a real entity? And this demonstration of the establishment of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) based upon the real entity is stated [in the phrase] "when the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) has not been apprehended," lest the opponent might say: "The establishment of the means of valid cognition is indeed dependent solely upon the real entity."

It is not based solely on the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, even if it does not apprehend a particular characteristic that has not been previously apprehended, conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) will nonetheless possess validity (*prāmāṇya*) because it apprehends the nature of an object (*vasturūpa*) that has not been previously apprehended. To point out that this [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), it was stated: "Regarding the nature of an object not previously apprehended," and so forth.

And when the charge of its being unestablished is raised, as to why validity belongs only to that which apprehends the nature of an object not yet apprehended and not to any other, the reply is given: "because it is capable of purposeful action" (*arthakriyā-yogya*), and so forth.
Thus, even for one who asserts that validity has a real entity (*vastu*) as its object, it is effectively stated that its object is exclusively the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
He considers that this is because the definition of [validity] consists in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), whereas the universal (*sāmānya*) is the opposite of that.
Furthermore, he states an additional reason to refute the validity of the conceptual construction of "blue" (*nīlavikalpa*) which arises at a time subsequent to the direct experience:

“From that too”—that is, not only from the experience of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of blue as previously described, but rather “in the object itself,” namely in the particular characteristic alone, “by the determination of that” (i.e., by the determination of the particular characteristic), because otherwise activity toward it would be impossible; thus, when a person has acted—that is, when the particular characteristic has been apprehended—the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from its capacity is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is the connection [of the words].

Previously, it was stated that [perception] lacks validity because it does not apprehend the nature of an object not previously apprehended; now, however, it is stated that it lacks validity because it apprehends only what has already been apprehended. Thus, there is a difference between the two arguments in terms of their positive and negative formulations.
Alternatively, this [present argument] clarifies by way of an additional supporting reason that which was previously stated: "because its object is [the effect] through its causal efficiency."
[25. The absence of separate validity for conceptual construction due to its being seen as distinct from perception:

If it is argued that even though a person’s activity toward an object occurs through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that [conceptual construction], why is its validity not accepted as separate from perception—which grasps the previously unapprehended universal (*sāmānya*)? To this, he says: because in "activity"—which occurs only with respect to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—it shares the same "acquisition and preservation" (*abhinnayogakṣema*) as "perception," which is called the cognition of mere observation (*ālocanājñāna*).
Yoga is the attainment, characterized by the discernment of an object not yet attained;
kṣema is its preservation, characterized by the performance of its purposeful activity. That which possesses both yoga and kṣema as non-different is described as such.

In this regard, the non-differentiated application (*abhinno yogaḥ*) of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) with non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpapratyakṣa*) occurs through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

It is "non-differentiated" (*abhinna*) because it is secure (*kṣema*), since, like the sensory cognition of observation (*ālocanāvijñāna*), activity proceeds toward the particular characteristic itself even from conceptualization.

This is his intended meaning: if conceptualization were to have as its object a differentiable objective (*prameyāntara*) distinct from the non-conceptual mind, then it should direct the person toward that very [different object] in order to attain the causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by it.
Or rather, one should not engage [with it] at all;

for the universal, which is intended to be its object, is admitted to have only a single causal efficiency characterized by non-differentiated cognition, and that [universal] is established precisely through the arising of conceptual construction.
Indeed, cognitions of yellow and so forth, which have other objects of cognition as their domain, do not cause a person to engage with a blue object simply because of the experience of blue.
Or, [if it were so], the fulfillment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) would never occur anywhere.
Therefore, this [subsequent cognition] does not have a different object of cognition (*prameya*) than the initial awareness (*ālocanājñāna*).
This is especially so for those who explain it as follows:
"By means of non-conceptual cognition, there is the apprehension of an object even though it consists of two aspects.
Therefore, it is logical that only non-conceptual perception of blue possesses validity (*prāmāṇya*).
For conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*), like memory, is indeed perceived as distinct from that [perception] whose utility is non-different from it;

otherwise, for one who postulates another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that would be fruitless, it would follow that memory, desire, aversion, effort, and so forth are also means of valid cognition, and thus the fixed number of means of valid cognition would collapse.
(Hbṭ 37)
[26. Validity and invalidity of successive cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*) with respect to the yogi and others:

When a series of sensory cognitions arises regarding one and the same object, such as blue, then—because the subsequent sensory cognitions share the same *yogakṣema* (identity of acquisition and preservation) as the preceding one—it would follow that those subsequent sensory cognitions are not valid.

But this is not the case; therefore, [the opponent] shows that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and the proponent of the convergence of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-saṃplava-vādin*) says: "By the preceding moment of perception," and so forth.
He refutes this: "No," for it would follow that the subsequent [cognitions] are also valid.
Why?
“Because their acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) are distinct.
For instance, at every moment, the acquisition (*yoga*), characterized by the discernment of objects,
and the preservation (*kṣema*), characterized by the performance of purposeful action and consisting of protection, are different.

Therefore, because it does not occur in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), the reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). When is there a lack of commonality in acquisition and preservation (*ayogakṣema*)?
It is "when there is a desire for an object to be accomplished through a specific moment."

When yogis, aiming for the benefit of others, have a desire— namely, the wish to attain or avoid— for an object characterized as beneficial or harmful that is to be accomplished through a specific moment, because it is useful to someone in some way or another at some time;

then, just as on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) suppresses the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) of those underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Because it generates an intention contrary to that [affliction].
The dharma-knowledge regarding suffering produces the attainment of nirvana, characterized by separation from the afflictions,
because it generates a firm intention contrary to the latent tendencies (anuśaya).
Therefore, the cognitions of others' minds that apprehend these [objects] are indeed distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And for the Blessed Ones— who have undertaken the vow to establish the welfare of others, whose inner selves are illuminated by the light of knowledge pervading the full extent of all things— only a certain momentary object is conducive to some particular benefit for another, or conversely, it is an obstacle.

For those whose perceptual consciousness observes all entities at every moment, the moments that constitute those objects possess distinct causal efficiencies (*arthakriyā*) and thus have different fates (*yogakṣema*).

Therefore, if this is stated with reference to those who perceive the distinction between moments at every instant, then because they have distinct utilities and are individually valid cognitions, there is no inconclusiveness (*anekānta*).
However, if it is stated with reference to conventional persons who determine oneness across all things, then [the objection applies to] the whole [of their cognition]. (Hbṭ 38)

Since [cognitions] determine a single object as a blue continuum, possessing a stable nature, and its corresponding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) as being of a single essence, the validity of subsequent [cognitions] is also certainly undesired [by the opponent]. How, then, can there be any inconclusiveness (*anekānta*)?
Showing this, he says: "For that which is common...
This refers to that which is common to all the moments occurring within that continuum, which are determined as one by those engaged in worldly transaction (*vyavahartṛ*).

Although the objects such as blue and so forth— which consist of coloring and the like— are distinct in every moment due to having different causes, they are nonetheless clung to as a unity through cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*) from the perspective of ultimate reality; in that regard, there is "no difference" in the "capacity"— that is, the power to reach the object— of those aforementioned moments of cognition.
Since activity proceeds from those [subsequent cognitions] toward the very same object as the initial moment of direct perception, validity belongs to that first one alone in that regard.

For instance, for those seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) who employ the conventional term "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) for a cognition capable of bringing about its means, it is logical that the distinction in the conventional usage of validity regarding cognitions arises solely from the distinction between the means of achieving purposeful action—provided they possess unimpaired intellects. Otherwise, how could one ward off the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even memory and the like would be valid?
Or would a discerning person regard the establishment of the means of valid cognition as fruitless?

To the question, "In what way is there no difference in capacity regarding a common effect? he says: "Just as in the case of those 'successive' 'smokes' which have been 'cognized' by them [the senses] when they are 'near the fire'."

Just as in the case of inferential cognitions regarding objects such as fire— when one desires an action like kindling that is achievable by mere fire— the distinction in validity is not tenable for the wise because there is no difference in the individual instances that bring about the attainment of that purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), so it is here as well. However, when one wishes to perform the "five-fire" penance (*pañcatapa*), then even for those inferences whose objects are proximate fires cognized through various instances of smoke, validity is certainly not precluded, owing to the difference in their respective capacities.
[27. The resultant meaning of the refutation of the validity of conceptual construction:

Thus, having refuted the validity of the conceptual construction of "blue" in the example, "Just as, having seen blue, there is the cognition 'it is blue'," he applies this to the subject at hand, saying: "By this"—that is, by the refutation of the validity of the conceptual construction of blue that arises subsequent to the perception of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of blue.

By Kumārila stating, “Therefore, because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which assists in the form of the object, is desired [as a means of cognition],” he refers to the conceptual construction of the substratum (*dharmin*) that arises subsequent to the perception of the location and so forth.

Therefore, at the time of apprehending the relationship, there is the conceptualization of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), which has the universal fire as its object and arises through the power of perceiving the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire;
and there is the conceptualization of the mark (*liṅga*), which manifests the universal smoke and arises subsequent to the cognition that perceives smoke;
and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [other such cognitions are implied].

Furthermore, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the relationship between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), which arises subsequent to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is preceded by the perception termed "mere observation" (*ālocana*) whose object is solely the essential nature of the substratum and so forth, [is required];
for "without conceptualization, there is no such apprehension of the mark (*liṅga*) and its relationship with the substratum."
Thus, because of the fear of such an objection, that which was accepted as "validity" has been "answered," i.e., rejected.

It is established by the aforementioned reasoning that only the prior perception whose object is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—which is designated by others as "indeterminate cognition" (*ālocanājñāna*)—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from its power; for [the latter] lacks the property of the subject in the locus of the probandum (*pakṣadharmasya sādhyadharmiṇi*).
"Establishment" means certainty, whether through perception or inference.

Thus, by stating that the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is ascertained through perception, and by incidentally refuting the validity of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises subsequent to sensory observation,
[Dignāga] established that "perception is free from conceptual construction" (*pratyakṣaṃ kalpanāpoḍham*).
Thus it has been established. [28. Demonstrating the Primacy of Inference:
If this is so, why was it said that "this [treatise] is commenced for the purpose of explaining inference," rather than [simply] in general terms?
Is it for the purpose of elucidating right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)?
In this regard, misconceptions concerning number and so forth, which have that [right knowledge] as their object, are also already refuted.
For the comprehension of objects beyond the senses, inference alone is the basis.

Why? Because it has been stated that only that which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and is pervaded by a part of that [subject] (*tadaṃśena vyāpta*) is the cause (*hetu*) of that [inference], and nothing else; thus, all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose objects are imperceptible things are included within inference. In this way, the disagreement regarding the number [of means of valid cognition] concerning the object of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) has been briefly refuted. Furthermore, since the part that is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is understood as the object of comprehension, it is declared—by the statement "pervasion by a part of that"—that inference has the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object and not the specific individual characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because the latter is unique (*asādhāraṇa*).
Furthermore, because that which is unique cannot be a pervader,
and because it is not an object of conceptual construction,
one who asserts that "among those, the first has the unique as its object" has thereby stated that perception has only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.

(Hbṭ 40) By the statement "perception alone is the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), it is indicated that the means of valid cognition itself is the result (*phala*), because that [perception] has the nature of the cognition of the object.
Likewise, since it will be stated that "its application is twofold," inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) will be explained.
Since that [treatise] consists in the exposition of the three-fold logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*), the systematic elucidation of inference (*anumāna*) is also intended in brief.
And since that [exposition] exists everywhere [in this work], why was it stated: "for the purpose of elucidating inference"?
True; however, that [term] is mentioned because of its predominance.
For it is thus: since the reality characterized by the Four Noble Truths—which is conducive to the primary goal of the person—is ascertained through inference alone, it possesses predominance.
Likewise, even regarding an object of direct perception, when the possibility of dispute arises, [inference is required].
Furthermore, its preeminence follows from the fact that there is no basis for definitive certainty other than inference.
Its preeminence also derives from its being the motivator;
for instance, when one has experienced a result that is a means to pleasure or pain, [one acts accordingly].
Alternatively, that which is currently being experienced or perceived is the object of engagement because the fruit has already been produced.
Therefore, even in the case of a future fruit—a means to pleasure or pain that is directly perceived—inference alone is what prompts engagement.
For perception does not determine its capacity for future pleasure or pain.
Because the fruit is imperceptible, as it has been said: "For when the effect is not perceived, there is no cognition of the causal relation.

Therefore, even regarding an object that is currently perceptible, the determination of its suitability for a future result occurs through its similarity to the means of previously experienced pleasure and pain, and not through direct perception itself.
And so it has been said: "That which is established in such a way through similarity with what has been perceived does not transcend the status of being an object of inference.
How, then, is there the capacity to motivate action for both [perception and inference]?
It has been stated: "For one who acts after having determined an object by means of these two is not deceived regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)."

Since the nature of water, fire, and so forth—which are the means for achieving pleasure and pain—is established through direct perception, and their capacity regarding future results is established through inference, both serve as motivators.

Furthermore, it has been stated that the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful are preceded by correct knowledge; however, this does not apply to the capacity regarding future results, because that is not determined through direct perception.
For those of limited vision cannot ascertain the suitability for a future result from that [present state];
therefore, because it is primary, the mention of inference is made—enough of this excessive detail.
(Hbṭ 41)
[29. The determination of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the case of the essential nature as a reason (*svabhāvahetu*) depends upon its own means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):

In this regard, the determination of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) for the essential nature, the effect, and non-perception has been stated without distinction because it is to be accomplished by the same means;
however, since the determination of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) is to be accomplished by different means, it must be explained with distinction.

First, demonstrating that the ascertainment of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is based upon its own means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: “The ascertainment of the positive concomitance (*anvayaniścaya*) also. The word “also” implies that not only has the ascertainment of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) been stated, but the ascertainment of the positive concomitance is also stated “in the case of an essential reason. “The mere existence (*bhāvamātra*)” of the probans-property—that is, its mere presence—without depending on other causes such as a hammer and so forth; “the connection (*anubandha*)” with that, which is its following or pervasion (*vyāpti*); the “establishment (*siddhi*)” of that is what [is meant].
Of what is there the establishment of the necessary concomitance with the mere existence of the probans-property (*sādhanadharma*)?

[It is] "of the property to be proven" (*sādhyadharma*). It is called a "property" because it is that which is to be proven—since it is unestablished—and because it is a constituent part of the aggregate of the property and the locus (*dharmin*). The establishment of this meaning—that wherever there is the existence of the probans-property, there also exists the property to be proven, independent of any other cause—is the determination of the positive concomitance (*anvaya-niścaya*) in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
But how, then, does the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) follow upon the mere existence of the property that proves it (sādhanadharmabhāvamātra)?
[It follows] "by being its very nature" (tadbhāvatayā): that is, by being the state of having as its nature (bhāva) or intrinsic being (svabhāva) that proving property.
For how could a proving property that is the very intrinsic being of the property to be proven not follow it?
Because it would follow that [the reason] lacks a nature (*nīrūpatva*).
[30. On the establishment of the relationship between the probandum and the probans even when there is identity in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*):
But surely, if [the reason] has that very nature, how can there be a relationship of probandum and probans given the absence of difference?
Thus he says: "In reality" means from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*).

However, at the time of conceptualizing the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), because they appear as distinct within a conceptual cognition—which is based on various excluded objects (*vyāvṛtta-padārtha*) through a conventional succession—the relationship of probandum and probans is not undermined. For this [conceptual distinction] does not depend upon an ultimate difference between the properties of the probandum and probans and their locus (*dharmin*), such as in the case of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth.
Because, in the absence of a relationship, the state of being the probandum and the probans is untenable.

If it is argued that the relationship between "being produced" (kṛtakatva) and "impermanence" (anityatva), etc., is inherence in a single substratum (ekārthasamavāya); [we reply: no, for even that [inherence] would be a different entity from those [properties].
"This is the inherence of these two in this object"—
since the absence of a relation remains in that state,
and because the postulation of another relation would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress.

Furthermore, if one assumes that [a property] exists through inherence (*samavāya*), then properties such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) would also exist in things like the self (*ātman*), which are considered eternal.

For the very same inherence by virtue of which "being produced" exists in sound—and because of which it exists only there—is the very same [inherence] in those things considered eternal, since it is accepted as being unitary (*ekatva*). Thus, who could prevent "being produced" and other such properties from existing in the self and so forth?

Now, if it is established that "those properties such as being produced (kṛtakatva) reside in that very entity which has the nature of coming into being after not having existed, and which, having come into being, has the nature of ceasing to exist—that is, an unstable form," then what is it that serves as the basis for the conceptualizing intellect (*kalpanābuddhi*) whose object is the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of the superimposition (*samāropa*) of a nature contrary to that [unstable form]? It is precisely that very state of having the nature of coming into being after not having existed, and the state of having an unstable nature once it has come into being. What else could it be?

Since the two properties, which are non-different in the ultimate sense, reside in the subject (*sādhyadharmin*) by that very fact, what is the use of accepting an intervening "lump" (*gaḍu*) such as "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, which possesses exclusion (*vyatireka*)?

For instance, properties such as "producedness" do not serve as the basis for the comprehension of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) merely by their existence; because they would be constantly present, it would follow that the cognition of that property would occur incessantly.
However, [these properties] appear only within conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

And that conceptual construction, following after the very form appearing within itself— which has been determined (*adhyavasita*) as an external entity— realizes the object's nature of being produced, impermanent, and so forth,
even though in ultimate reality it does not actually contact that form.
Because it is their material cause through a continuous succession;
whereas other dharmas are merely postulated as the efficient causes for their arising,
it would be better if that very basis for such postulation were itself the cause for the production of such conceptual constructions.

Since that [non-existence] must necessarily be accepted, and since once it is accepted the properties possessing negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) have already fulfilled their purpose, enough with the postulation of that [separate non-existence].
Furthermore, even by way of a separate impermanence, one necessarily understands the very entity itself to have a non-abiding nature.
Because one engages [in an inquiry] out of a desire for an object that performs a function corresponding to it;

otherwise, since [the object] would be eternal due to its distinct impermanence, this person— desiring a function to be accomplished through impermanence and suspecting that sound and so forth are eternal— why would he engage in an investigation into impermanence?
Have you grasped the point?

(Hbṭ 43) If impermanence is understood as something distinct [from the object], then let the activity [of the means of knowledge] apply to that very thing; why then should it apply to the eternal nature of sound itself?
If it is argued that [the object] is apprehended by means of that [conceptualization],
then what is the use of this mediation?
It would be better for there to be an apprehension of the object itself without any mediation.
"Because of being sought by that very [means]"—if this were to be discussed further, it would become excessively profound; so let it rest for now.
As for those followers of Jaimini who think:
"This fault belongs only to those such as the Naiyāyikas for whom properties possess absolute difference;
however, for us, since properties—which possess both difference and non-difference in some sense—have that [subject] as their very nature, this fault does not apply.
Even for them, if they were to admit in reality that the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) has the form of the probative property (sādhanadharma), [the same fault would follow].
If one were to somehow admit a difference [between the means and the end], we do not perceive any result [in doing so],
since the relationship between the probandum and the probans is established even through an imagined difference.
Furthermore, in the case of absolute identity, a difference of any kind is not logically tenable.
If it is argued that because they are non-different from a single intrinsic nature,
there nonetheless exists some degree of both difference and non-difference between the two, we say no, for that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress.

For instance: since two properties, though distinct even from that single nature, possess that very nature as their basis, another non-distinct nature must be admitted to serve as the cause for their partial non-difference;
and likewise, yet another must be admitted for that one as well. Thus, there would be an infinite series of distinct and non-distinct natures.
Furthermore, an infinite series of such dual-natured natures does not appear in the conceptualizing intellect; so why do you deceive yourselves with such a fabrication?

And since some degree of difference is admitted, how can there be no occasion for the faults that arise from the position of absolute difference? Furthermore, with reference to which self [is it said]:
"These two are dharmas"?

If it is established that "this is the substratum" (dharmī) by means of that [attribute], then if there is difference, there is only difference; so how can there be the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda)?
Or, if there is non-difference;
Then [one identifies]: "This is the property that serves as the means of proof (sādhanadharma); this is the property to be proven (sādhyadharma)."
And since this [subject] is a "possessor of properties" (dharmin),
how could the triad be established as ultimate (pāramārthika)?

Therefore, because properties (*dharma*) and their substrata (*dharmin*) appear as if they were distinct within a conceptual cognition that relies upon the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of various other forms, there exists the relationship of the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*).

However, thinking that "in reality, the necessary concomitance (*tanmātrānubandha*) is logically possible only by virtue of [the property] being that very nature (*tattatsvabhāvatā*)," he stated: "in reality, by being of that nature" (*vastutastadbhāvatayā*).
(Hbṭ 44)
[31. By means of the subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) itself, there is identity between the probandum and the probans in the case of an essential nature as the reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
But what is this "being that very thing" (*tadbhāvatā*) in reality, by virtue of which the concomitance of the property to be proven with the mere existence of the proving property is established?
To this he says: "That" being that very thing in reality is the "opposite" (*viparyaya*), that is, the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), of the "probandum. In that [counter-example],...

“From the reason”: that which is the “subverting proof” (bādhaka-pramāṇa) establishes a property contrary [to the one intended]; by this, the reason being subverted does not function therein, because the coexistence of two contradictory [properties] in a single locus is impossible.

Its "function" (*vṛtti*) is its "operation" (*pravṛtti*), namely the operation of the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa-vṛtti*). Because the state of being that [probandum] in reality is to be established by that [proof], it is called the "operation of the subverting proof. For when that [proof] exists, the reason, having been excluded from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), occurs only in the subject (*dharmin*) possessing the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*); thus, the fact that the property to be proven—which is not a separate entity—is of the same nature as the proving property (*sādhanadharma*) is established. And by means of that—namely, the state of being that [probandum] in reality—the necessary concomitance (*anubandha*) of the property to be proven with the mere presence of the proving property is established; this is "the ascertainment of positive concomitance" (*anvayaniścaya*).

The form [of the statement] arises as: "Wherever there is the property of the means of proof (sādhanadharma), there is the property to be proven (sādhyadharma). An example for this is: "Whatever exists is necessarily momentary."
By means of the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*), he states the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

This form has been declared to be the necessary concomitance (*anubandha*) with the mere existence of the property to be proven (*sādhanadharma*); for it is shown that something is momentary simply by virtue of its being existent, without any other cause.

And since that [existence] is established in reality as having that nature, he demonstrates the means of its establishment— the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*)— as follows: "If there were non-momentariness," that is, in the case of the opposite of momentariness, "because of the contradiction with causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā-virodhāt*), meaning because of the contradiction with the "efficiency of the object"— the accomplishment of an effect— "that which has that as its definition," namely, that whose definition is causal efficiency, i.e., "reality" (*vastutva*), which consists in the capacity for causal efficiency.
That has been stated as such.
For it is by means of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) that the nature of a real entity (*vastutva*), which consists in its capacity for such [efficiency], is characterized.
Thus, this kind of reality "is lost," meaning it ceases to exist.
Because it entails the non-existence of that which is of a nature contrary to it.

Furthermore, this subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), which consists in the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), will be explained by [the author] himself later when its opportunity arises.
Thus, through the operation of this subverting proof, the fact that the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is in reality the very nature of the proving property (*sādhanadharma*) is established.
And because it exists as that very nature in reality, there is an invariable concomitance with the mere presence of the property of the probans.
Determination of the ascertainment of positive concomitance in the case of the effect-reason.]

Having thus established the certainty of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the case of the essential nature as a reason (*svabhāvahetu*) through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary, which establishes identity (*tādātmya*), [the author], now demonstrating it in the case of the effect as a reason (*kāryahetu*), says: "In the case of the effect as a reason, the certainty of positive concomitance" is the subject under discussion.
But what, then, is this existence (*bhāva*) of cause and effect?

“Effect-ness” and “cause-ness”: the “establishment” (*siddhi*) or cognition of these is the ascertainment of the positive concomitance (*anvaya-niścaya*) in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*). Demonstrating how the establishment of the relation between cause and effect occurs, he says: “Just as,” and so forth.
The word "yathā" (as) has the sense of illustration.
The grammatical connection is: "this," such as smoke and so forth, "is perceived" when there is the "perception of 'this'" fire.
By this, he states the operation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in establishing the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
And it is not only perception that establishes the causal relation beyond doubt;
rather, he says—“that which has attained the conditions for perceptibility is unperceived”—in order to show that [perception] is assisted by a prior non-perception.
If that smoke and so forth had attained the conditions for perceptibility while other [conditions] were present...

While existing as something perceptible among the conditions for perception, it is not apprehended prior to the presence of the causal complex such as fire; however, when the causal complex consisting of identity and so forth is present and being apprehended, that effect is established as being apprehended.
It is not, however, [established] while remaining in a state where the capacity for apprehension has not yet arisen due to the deficiency of other conditions for perception.

Even though it is present in that location, it was not perceived prior to the presence of the causal complex of fire and so forth because it had not reached the conditions for perception (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatayā*).

And since there is no non-perception of something that has reached the conditions for perception, there can be no arrival from elsewhere prior to the presence of the causal complex of fire and so forth;
rather, there must be its production from things such as straw mats already present in that place and time.
And by stating "absence from that place," these three [objections] are refuted;
for it is only through these many modes that the state of not being its effect could possibly arise.

Therefore, by means of non-perception (*anupalambha*), the suspicion that [the effect] might not have that as its cause is dispelled; thus, the causal relationship—founded upon the perception that the effect exists when the cause exists—is established beyond doubt.
Nor should it be suspected that smoke might arise from some invisible entity whose presence is restricted to the existence of fire, fuel, and so forth;
for smoke conforms to the specific variations of fire, fuel, and the like.

Since this [fire] is observed to have variations corresponding to the differences in its fuel— such as sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, wool, and so forth— and since fire that produces effects of small or great magnitude from its fuel must be of a corresponding nature;
furthermore, it is not logical for something whose nature is invisible to have a fixed presence whenever fire and fuel are present,
because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
Or, if there were an obstruction, there would have to be either the state of being its effect or the state of being its cause.
If it were its effect,
the production of smoke would not occur immediately after the contact of fire and fuel.
And its status as an effect of that [fire] follows precisely from the fact that it conforms to the presence and absence of that [fire];
and this is the same in the case of smoke as well.
Nor can fuel and so forth be the cause of something whose nature is imperceptible.
Since we observe that fuel and the like arise from their own causes, such as trees and the like,
the same response must be stated even in that case if one imagines their existence in that manner. If the objection is raised again, that very same refutation applies, leading to an infinite regress.
By this, dependence upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*) is also refuted.
Furthermore, fire and the like would be considered the cause of smoke solely because smoke conforms to their presence and absence;
and that [conformity] is equally present in the case of fire and so forth as well.
If it is argued that even that [the presence of the fuel] may be the cause there, we say no;
for when fire and so forth are present, there is no reason to postulate another thing as the cause which is necessarily present,
since the postulation of a causal state is based on the absence of the effect.
Just as fire, fuel, and so forth do not exist in the absence of either one of them,
let there be causality for another factor as well when it is invariably present;
however, that does not entail the loss of the causal status of fire and the other factors.
For if one were to act based on the certainty [of fire] derived from seeing smoke, there would be a discrepancy with reality.

Indeed, even though the diversity of the world is produced by the sovereign power of the karma of all sentient beings, those who act based on the observation of its effects—without abandoning the visible causes—do not fail to obtain what they seek; so enough of this digression.

Furthermore, what is the nature of this causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) which is based upon perception aided by non-perception? He says: "Its presence when that is present, and its absence when that is absent."
For it is precisely when that which is considered the cause exists that that which is considered the effect exists;
and "in its absence," when that which is considered the cause is absent, there is "necessarily an absence" of that which is considered the effect.
That alone is the relation of cause and effect, and nothing else.
For if it were something other than those two, it would either exist as a distinct entity whose nature is not perceived in things that do not possess the form of cause and effect,
or it would exist by its very nature as the essence of cause and effect themselves.

If the first position were true, then it would apply to every object whatsoever, even to those things that stand in neither a causal nor a non-causal relationship, because there would be no cause for such restriction; consequently, everything would be the effect of everything.
(47) Furthermore, that which lacks a certain nature by its own essence does not acquire that nature even through conjunction with another.
For entities do not, upon abandoning their restricted nature, assume a different form even when conjoined with something else;
because this conjunction with another does not destroy their prior nature, as there is no cause for destruction, which will be explained later.
Nor does it produce something previously non-existent, for that would entail the consequence of its being a different entity from them.
Indeed, when those [entities] have been produced, it is not logical for there to be an unproduced nature or one with a different cause;

for this distinction or the cause of distinction consists in the superimposition of contradictory properties and a difference in causes. Therefore, if there were no such distinction, there would be no difference at all.
Because there would be no other cause, it would follow that the universe would be a single substance, and so forth.
For even a difference in appearance does not transcend the superimposition of contradictory properties by way of being mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*).
Consequently, the two preceding entities remain in that very same state; thus, even if they were joined with something else, they could not attain the status of cause and effect.
Now, if it is the second position,
then since those two possess the nature of cause and effect by their very essence, how could another such state not experience futility?
Furthermore, the cognitions of "cause" and "effect" are based solely on the fact that they arise when that [other] exists, and do not have a separate entity as their cause.
Because that [cause], which has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), does not appear as a distinct form differentiated from its effect;
