and if one were to conceive of the apprehension of such a thing, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it has not reached the conditions for perception, how could there be cognitions of cause and effect based upon it?
For that [object] does not, by its mere existence as a distinct entity, cause those two cognitions to arise;
otherwise, because it would be constantly present, there would be the undesirable consequence of those two arising at all times.

Furthermore, since an unperceived qualifier cannot be the basis for a cognition of its own qualified object, it is incorrect to claim that it has reached the state of being characterized by non-perception (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
Nor is it logical that something which is actually perceived should remain unobserved, because the cognitions of cause and effect are admitted to be based upon it;

for it is not reasonable that a determination of something as being "that" should occur elsewhere with respect to an object that does not possess the cognition of "that," while the cause of that determination remains unobserved.
Just as there is no determination of a staff in Devadatta when the staff is not perceived,
a relationship between a distinct entity (arthāntara) and its effect or cause is not tenable; for if one were to postulate another relationship, it would lead to an infinite regress.
If one accepts the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), then existence (*sadbhāva*) cannot coexist with either the effect or the cause.

Consequently, since it is absent at the time of the cause and the effect, how could it be the cause of the cognition of cause and effect? Furthermore, if one constructs the notion of that [existence] by mentally supplying two things that have already ceased, then the determination of causality would have only a conceptual object as its domain, not a real entity as its object.
And since that [cognition] is already accepted as being based on the presence or absence of a specific entity, what is the point of postulating a different object?
For if the determination has a conceptualized object as its domain, that [conceptualization] would be useless; moreover, cause and effect cannot exist simultaneously.
If it is produced by those two,
how can there be a causal relationship when each one produces it individually?
And when it is produced by the cause, is it produced together with its own effect?
Now, what of the isolated [cause]? Is the isolated [cause] prior to its own effect,
or is it posterior?

If it exists together with its own effect, then because both [the cause and the effect] would exist from some other source, there would be no mutual relationship between them, and thus its connection to the effect would be lost.
Alternatively, if it exists alone prior to its own effect,
then since the cause perishes immediately after producing that very [effect] due to its momentariness, how could it perform the activity of its own effect?
And if that [cause] does not exist, how can its status as a cause be dependent upon it?
And if that [cause] does not exist, how can a causal relationship be produced by something that is not a cause?

Furthermore, if it were produced after having first performed its own effect, even then, since it has already perished at the very time of its own effect, how could that which is non-existent produce the causal state of the effect occurring at a subsequent time?
And that state of being [the cause] is called the relation.

Alternatively, if the complete causes produce the effect by their very nature (*svarūpataḥ*) in its capacity as something produced (*janyatā*), what obstruction to their power (*śakti-vyāghāta*) is there in the effect that would necessitate postulating [an auxiliary cause] elsewhere?

In that case as well, if there were a requirement for the conjunction with another causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, the complete collection [of causes] alone is the producer. And their status as causes is inferred from the absence of the effect when each one is missing; thus he says: "even though other causes" included within that complex "are present," [the effect does not arise]. (Hbṭ 49)

Because each of these is a producer [of cognition], the phrase "in its absence" refers to the object of non-perception (*anupalambha*) by specifying that which is intended as the producer; thus, through the statement "it does not occur," the scope of non-perception is stated.
However, the operation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as previously described, is devoid of non-perception and is connected with the apprehension of existence when that [cause] exists.
And so, what is the means of establishing this causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), namely, that "when this exists, that exists" and "when this is absent, that is absent"?

Thus he says: "Established by perception and non-perception" (*pratyakṣānupalambhasādhana*). Non-perception preceded by perception—consisting of a perception that grasps an object other than those two [the cause and effect]—is the means of establishment (*sādhana*) for this; thus, "the causal relation is established by perception and non-perception. However, that which was previously stated as being established by a perception dependent upon non-perception is called "established by non-perception and perception," because its means of establishment is a perception preceded by non-perception.
It must be said:

the "establishment" (*siddhi*), that is, the ascertainment, of that "causal relation" (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) which consists of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), occurs "by means of the aforementioned" perception and non-perception; thus it is connected [to the statement] that there is an ascertainment of positive concomitance in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).

Now, one might object: surely the so-called "ascertainment of positive concomitance" is the determination that the effect, as it arises everywhere, follows upon the existence of its own cause; so how can this be called simply the establishment of the causal relation?

Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "For it is only the causal relation... [and so forth]. This is stated in order to show that the certainty of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is based on the establishment of the causal relation; thus, by metaphorically applying the term "effect" to the cause, he demonstrates that [the goal] cannot be accomplished by any other means.

Furthermore, showing that this was said for the purpose of refuting the view of those who maintain that [concomitance] is based merely on observation, he says: "For it is only when the causal relation exists..."—that is, "only when the causal relation exists, indeed."

Because it was previously stated that the certainty of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) arises precisely from the certainty of identity (*tādātmya*), which occurs through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary of that which is not distinct—that is, the "other object" (*arthāntara*) distinct from the probandum (*sādhya*); thus, the term "other object" is employed.
Of that other object, "it would be thus."
How so?
By the rule: "Wherever there is smoke, there must necessarily be fire."
The certainty of positive concomitance (*anvayaniścaya*) takes the form: "the existence of fire is there.

However, as for the certainty of positive concomitance of taste with another object through its color—even though there is no relationship of cause and effect—that is due to their dependence on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatayā*); thus, it occurs precisely by way of the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) from its own cause, and so there is no fault.

(Hbṭ 50) Now, even if smoke is indeed the effect of fire, why is it that wherever that [smoke] is, fire must necessarily be there, such that the determination of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is said to be based on the establishment of the relation of cause and effect? To this he says: "Only when fire exists"—that is, only when it has being (*sattā*).
For this reason: since "existence" (bhāvaḥ), that is, the being (sattā) of smoke, is its "being an effect" (kāryatvam);
therefore, it is only when the relation of cause and effect exists that there is the aforementioned certainty of positive concomitance (anvaya).

For if smoke were not necessarily accompanied by fire wherever it occurs, then, because it could exist even in the absence of fire, its very nature as an effect—defined by its existence only when fire exists—would be lost. [33. Explanation of the means for determining positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the case of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*): Now he states the determination of positive concomitance regarding non-perception: "Even in the case of non-perception," meaning not only in the cases of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the effect (*kārya*) reasons.
The certainty of positive concomitance (*anvaya-niścaya*) has been stated; however, the certainty of positive concomitance is also asserted in the case of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).

What is its nature? To this he says: since the object of proof is both the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—namely, the conventional usage of "non-existent"—and its fitness (*yogyatā*), what is intended here is the conventional usage of "non-existent" together with that fitness.

The "non-apprehension" of that [object], which has reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), consists in the apprehension of something other than it; this, being restricted to that alone (*tanmātre*) and independent of any other cause, is the "functioning"—that is, the activity—of the linguistic convention of non-existence.
The "establishment" (*sādhana*) of that, its proof, is the ascertainment of the positive concomitance (*anvayaniścaya*) of non-apprehension.
But why does this conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) occur solely on the basis of that [non-perception]?
To this he says: "Because of the demonstration of the absence of any other cause.

For when it is established that there is no cause for this conventional usage—such as the absence of cognition, designation, or causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—other than the aforementioned non-perception, then [the usage occurs] solely on the basis of that aforementioned non-perception.
Thus, its function is established;
and by that means, there is certainty regarding positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the case of non-apprehension.

For otherwise, if there were a suspicion that it depends on some other cause, then even when the aforementioned non-apprehension is present, the absence of the conventional usage of "non-existence" would not be certain; how, then, could there be certainty regarding positive concomitance?
The absence of other causes, however, has been explained in detail in the *Vādanyāya*, and thus should be understood from that very source.

Alternatively, that which is the cause for the conventional usage of "existence"—namely, the existence of an object that meets the conditions for perceptibility—is a "different cause" because it is distinct from the cause for the conventional usage of "non-existence. It is stated in this way by means of whatever instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) demonstrates the absence [of that object] due to its non-perception therein.
Therefore,
when the object exists, because its impossibility is certain, there is a certainty of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in non-perception;
and we shall demonstrate that in our consideration of its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
(51) Thus, the ascertainment of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) for all three types of reasons has been explained according to their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), it is based on the establishment of identity (*tādātmya*) through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary.
In the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), it is because the causal relationship is established by means of perception and non-perception;
and in the case of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), it is because the means of valid cognition that establishes the absence of other possible causes serves as the ground for establishing that absence.
[34. Explanation of the method for determining the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the effect and the essential nature.]

Now, desiring to demonstrate the ascertainment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-niścaya*)— which is based on its respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— for all three types of reasons, he says: "The ascertainment of negative concomitance also"— not only the ascertainment of positive concomitance (*anvaya-niścaya*), which for those two [the first two reasons] was stated to be based on their respective means of valid cognition— but rather, "the ascertainment of negative concomitance also" for the reasons of effect (*kārya-hetu*) and essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*) is said to have its cause in their respective means of valid cognition.
What, then, is this?
It is "the establishment of the absence [of the reason] when the probandum is absent.

To the extent that those two types of reasons—namely, the essential identity (*tadātman*) and the effect (*kārya*)—are the establishers of the probandum in the form of a cause or a pervader, there is for them the establishment of their own absence when the probandum is absent.
By what means of valid cognition?

"By the non-perception of the cause and the pervader. In the case of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), the certainty of its absence when the probandum is absent is established through the non-perception of the cause.
In the case of the essential nature as a reason (*svabhāvahetu*), [the non-existence of the probandum is established] by the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
But when do these two non-perceptions become the means of proof for that?

When the relationship of cause and effect and the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader have been established—specifically, when the causal relationship has been established through perception and non-perception—the non-perception of the cause serves to prove the absence [of the effect] in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) when the probandum is absent.
And because its existence is not established through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) in the case of the opposite,

once the relationship of pervader and pervaded is established, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) serves to prove the absence [of the probandum] when the probandum is absent in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*).

By stating this, it is effectively said that in both cases, the ascertainment of both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) arises solely from the ascertainment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*).
For this very reason, it is stated elsewhere: "Or because of the relation of cause and effect," and so forth.
Of what kind are they? They are described as "having a perceptible object" (*dṛśyaviṣayābhyām*), meaning those two for which the object is perceptible.

If the cause and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) meet the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), then their non-perception establishes the absence [of the effect and the pervaded] when the probandum is absent; this is the meaning.
But when is the qualification "having a visible object" required for those two?

To this he says: "Of that whose object has been specified. That is to say, when the demonstration is being made of that absence [of the probandum] in the case of the absence [of the reason], wherein the "specified" (*uddiṣṭa*)—meaning stated—object—the substratum characterized as the negative example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*)—is present.
If it is asked why, even in that case, the condition of having a perceptible object (*dṛśyaviṣayatā*) is required, he says: "Non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*), etc.
"Otherwise," if the qualification of having a perceptible object were not required for the two types of non-apprehension;

When one employs an object that has not met the conditions for perception (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) as a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*), then even if a cause or a pervader exists there despite its being unperceivable, since the absence of a cause or a pervader that has not met the conditions for perception cannot be established "in some" remote object such as Mount Sumeru and the like, how could the non-existence [of the probandum] be established by means of these two when the probandum is absent?
The intention is that the non-apprehension of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) and the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) are themselves unestablished.

Now, one might ask: "Even when demonstrating a non-existence whose object has not been specified, why is the qualification 'having a perceptible object' (*dṛśyaviṣayatva*) not required for the two types of non-apprehension?

To this he says: "That which has an unspecified object"—that is, a non-existence in which the object, namely the form of a counter-example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*), has not been specified.

Since that [non-perception] establishes the mere presence of an impediment when the absence of a reason is being made known— even without the qualification of having a perceptible object— it follows that in that case, regarding the establishment of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) for a subject not explicitly mentioned, no requirement for the qualification of "having a perceptible object" is admitted for non-perceptions (*anupalabdhi*).

For instance, even when speaking by way of a general rule that encompasses all categories of things, whatever has a nature that is necessarily bound to something else—by virtue of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*)—will certainly not exist in the absence of that [bound-to] thing; otherwise, it would follow that it lacks an intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) or is causeless (*ahetukatva*). As it has been said:
"Even in the case of an intrinsic nature, there is an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) which follows from the mere existence [of the nature]."
"In the absence of that [cause], there would be the absence of the entity itself, because they are non-different.
Likewise: "Smoke is the effect of fire because it follows the properties of an effect;
if it were to exist even in the absence of that [fire], it would overstep its state of having a cause."
The point is this: since the requirement for the object to be visible (*dṛśyaviṣayatā*) is not auxiliary to the matter at hand, it contributes nothing to the case.

By the phrase "in the establishment of mere invariable concomitance" (*pratibandhamātrasiddhau*), he demonstrates the impossibility of that [negative concomitance] for those who do not describe the invariable concomitance of the reason, but rather assert its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based on mere non-perception; for instance, if there were no invariable concomitance, and all things devoid of the probandum (*sādhya*) were visible, then the absence of the probans (*sādhana*) would be established for those [visible things] in which it is not perceived.
Kumārila also says:
"Even after having gone again and again to those places, if the object is not perceived..."
"Then, due to the absence of any other cause, it is understood to be non-existent.

Even though [the object] is not perceived because it is remote in terms of space and so forth, since mere non-perception is possible even when that [non-existence] is the probandum, this negative concomitance (vyatireka)—characterized by the absence of the probans wherever there is an absence of the probandum—is doubtful; for such [mere non-perception] belongs only to...

Because it is expressed by means of the two distributive terms—"wherever there is an absence of the probandum (sādhya), there is an absence of the probans (sādhana)"—the ascertainment of positive concomitance (anvaya-niścaya) has also been described as being based solely on the previously mentioned necessary connection (pratibandha). Therefore, for those others who desire the establishment of positive concomitance based on observation, its non-existence has also been stated;
for it is impossible for inferents to observe all things that possess a cause as being endowed with the property to be proven (sādhyadharma).

Furthermore, because the concomitance of the probandum with its entirety— including all locations and so forth— is established through the use of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) in the form "wherever there is the reason,

there is the probandum," pervasion is not established merely by observing the coexistence of the property of the means of proof (*sādhana-dharma*) with the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) many times in a few locations and so on;
for in the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), it is possible that even those things observed to be frequently so in some cases may turn out otherwise.
Because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) to the contrary in that case.
[35. The non-statement of the means for ascertaining negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) regarding non-apprehension.

Now, with reference to non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), he says: "The ascertainment of negative concomitance occurs in the case of non-apprehension"—the word "is said" (*ucyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
What is its nature?

To this he says: "From the non-existence of non-apprehension"—which consists in the apprehension of that which is distinct from it—of that which is "existent" (sataḥ), meaning present, in the form of the absence of the probandum, [and] which has reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), meaning from another existing cause of apprehension and from a perceptible nature.

That which is a perceiving direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of an existing thing is its "seeing" (*darśana*); it is shown—that is, it is made known—by this, hence it is called "seeing. It is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that demonstrates [the absence]. In the case of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), the determination of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-niścaya*) consists of that very [means of cognition]. And because it is the cause of that [determination], it is likewise called a "means of valid cognition."
For if an entity that possesses a perceptible nature were not perceived even though it exists and its other conditions for perception are present, how could it be said to have a perceptible nature?
Indeed, only that which, when other conditions for perception are present, becomes directly manifest is designated as having a perceptible nature.
Therefore, when such [an object] is present, it must necessarily function as a perceptible object;
otherwise, it would never possess perceptibility, since there is no difference [in its nature].
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever has a specific cause necessarily occurs when that cause is present.
For example, a sprout has as its cause only the totality of conditions such as the seed.

And since perception has as its cause only the presence of an object that has attained the aforementioned characteristics of perceptibility, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

By this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), in the case of the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)— characterized by the absence [of the probans] where the probandum is absent— is ascertained. Furthermore,
this very means of valid cognition is also the cause for the ascertainment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*),
because by means of it alone, the absence of non-perception is demonstrated in other instances [where the probandum is present].

Regarding the non-apprehension of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) and the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), which will be discussed later, the very means for establishing the two types of necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is the basis for determining positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Since that [means] has already been demonstrated in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*), it is not stated separately here. To explain: the absence of the cause and the pervader is necessarily accompanied by the absence of the effect and the pervaded; and when there is the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of the absence of the effect and the pervaded—characterized by their presence—the [absence of the cause and pervader] is necessarily excluded because of the presence of the cause and the pervader.

Otherwise, it would follow that the effect and the pervaded (vyāpya) would be causeless and devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva); therefore, there is nothing further to be stated separately. [This concludes the designation of the names for the three types of reasons.
By this much of the text, the definition "the reason is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) that is pervaded by its part" has been explained.
Now, in order to explain the statement "it is indeed threefold," he says: "having this characteristic" (*etallakṣaṇaḥ*).
That which has the characteristic defined as "being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) while being pervaded by a part of that [subject]" is "that which has this characteristic."
The word "he" (*saḥ*) is explained as "the cause" (*hetuḥ*); the phrase "in exactly three ways" (*tridhaiva*) is analyzed as "of exactly three kinds" (*triprakāra eva*).
He enumerates those reasons by their respective names: "essential nature (svabhāva), effect (kārya), and non-perception (anupalabdhi).
The word "and" (ca) serves to aggregate them as reasons.
The word "iti" indicates completion and clarifies the sense of restriction.
"For example," when something such as sound is the "probandum" (*sādhya*) as being "impermanent," the presentation of the "essential nature" reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is "existence" (*satva*);
when a location possessing fire is the "probandum," the presentation of the "effect" reason (*kāryahetu*) is "smoke."

"And in the case of non-existence" means that in the conventional usage regarding non-existence, there is the presentation of non-apprehension as "the non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension. [This is the demonstration of the means of valid cognition regarding the fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) that lie outside the three types of valid reasons.
Why, then, is the reason only of three kinds?

Anticipating this objection, [the author] says—demonstrating that the fallaciousness (*hetvābhāsatā*) of those things other than these three is established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇavatī*) because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the nature of a reason is restricted to the three types of reasons alone due to their being distinct from the threefold reasons:

“In this very threefold reason,” namely those called essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), “because of the restriction of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). The meaning is: because there is an absence of inseparable connection in objects other than the threefold reasons.

Therefore, it follows that those things which lack invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)—being distinct from the three types of valid reasons consisting of essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*)—are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), just like "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth.

Furthermore, the absence of invariable concomitance is understood through the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), because it is excluded from the three types of valid reasons; for identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), which pervade invariable concomitance, are absent there.
[38. Determination of Invariable Concomitance]
Now, what is this inseparable relation (avinābhāva)? To what does it belong?
Or how is it said to be restricted to this very [inference] alone?
Therefore, he says: "The pervasion as previously stated belongs to the pervader"—by way of being its cause and by way of being its very nature;
wherever that which is pervaded, whether an effect or an essential nature, is present, there the pervader must necessarily exist.
Or, [the pervasion belongs] "to the pervaded"—whether it be the effect or the essential nature.

Wherever that which is called the nature of its cause—the pervader—is present, there alone [the effect] exists in the subject (dharmin), and not even when that [cause] is absent; this pervasion (vyāpti) described as the state of being a pervaded property of the pervader is what is meant by "the aforementioned pervasion is inseparable connection" (avinābhāva).
Of what [is it said]?
“Of the property of the subject” means of the property belonging to the locus of the probandum.
“That” refers to such an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). “Threefold” [is the nature of the reason].
On account of the aforementioned threefold reason, [the probans] "does not exist" in any other object— that is, in an object distinct from that [subject].
For in these three types [of reasons], there exists the pervasion by way of the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*).

Because there is a relationship of pervaded and pervader between these two—just as between "being produced" and "impermanence"—it is said that [the reason] is "restricted" (niyata) to this very threefold reason by way of its absence elsewhere.

By this, the meaning of the statement "other than that are the fallacious reasons" (*hetvābhāsās tato 'pare*), together with its justification "due to the restriction of inseparable connection" (*avinābhāvaniyamāt*), has been demonstrated.
And how there is no inseparable connection elsewhere than in the threefold reason has already been explained.

Alternatively, if "another object" (*arthāntara*) means an object different from its own nature (*svabhāva*), then that [other object] would be either different from the effect, or the cause, or neither.

There is also something other than the aforementioned non-apprehension, namely mere non-apprehension or apprehension of that which is to be negated, whether it be something else that is contradictory or not contradictory.

In that regard, if "another thing" (arthāntara) refers to an immediate effect, it cannot serve as a logical mark (aliṅgatva), because it is impossible for those with limited vision to discern it through its distinction from others.

Even if one were to determine the distinction by observing the effect, the determination of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) occurring after the establishment of the probandum, as well as the process of positive concomitance (anvaya), would be redundant.

Even a cause that is temporally remote is not an inferential mark (*liṅga*) of its effect, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the potential occurrence of obstacles or deficiencies in the intervening period. As it has been said:
"In regard to the transformation of the potencies of the causal complex and its fruit..."
"There is inconclusiveness regarding the effect, because an obstruction is possible."
Thus, in the case of an inference based on capacity (*yogyatā*), there is no other [separate] logical mark (*liṅga*);
nor is it both [the mark and the probandum],
because it would be impossible for it to be a means of cognition (*gamaka*) without a necessary connection (*apratibandha*).
If it is asked, "How is the determination of the proximity of Rohiṇī [to the moon] based on the cognition of the rising of Kṛttikā?"—

surely that too is not tenable in the absence of a causal connection, because it has already been stated that, due to the lack of any specific distinction, this would lead to the absurd consequence of every cognition occurring from everything.
Therefore, some cause for the transition of the circle of constellations must be postulated, mediated by an interval of time.

Just as the agitation of the elements is to be inferred as the cause of rain occurring at a later time through the inference of a causal property (*hetudharmanumāna*), it must be understood as arising from the mark of an effect (*kāryaliṅga*).
Even mere non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is a cause for doubt,
because the absence of an object is not established even when the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have ceased to function.
How could even a perception establish the non-existence of that which is to be negated,
given that the absence of a non-erroneous perception is impossible?
Rather, it is the perception of a contradictory [object] that establishes the absence of its counter-positive.

However, since that contradiction is established precisely because others are not perceived when it exists, it is non-perception itself that is employed by way of that [contradiction]. Otherwise, the absence [of something] would not be established, as the perception of what is not contradictory would remain unrefuted.
Furthermore, the perception of what is not contradictory is inconclusive regarding negation.
Because coexistence is possible for those things that are not contradictory,
and since no other mode is possible, inseparable connection does not exist elsewhere.
(Hbṭ 57)
[2. Examination of the Essential Nature as a Reason (svabhāvahetu) / 1.

Stating the Definition of the Essential Nature as a Reason] Now, first, he states the definition of the essential nature as a reason: "In that regard"—that is, among the three types of reasons—the definition of the essential nature as a reason is stated first.
That by which something is established is the *sādhana* (the means of proof).
That [means of proof] is also a property (*dharma*), and its state is "the state of being that" (*tadbhāva*).
This very thing is "the mere existence of the property that serves as the means of proof" (*sādhanadharmabhāvamātra*).
Its "concomitance" (anvaya) is that which belongs to it; [this refers] to that [subject], because the term for the whole is metaphorically applied to its part, namely the property to be proven.
In that case, there is the "essential nature as the reason" (svabhāvahetu).
Since the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is what is explicitly stated [in the reason], it is understood that this [reason] is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of that [property].

But how can this be the nature of the property to be proven, given that it is perceived as distinct from it? To this he says: "From each and every other," meaning from that which is non-existent and from that which is non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*). What [is the nature]? It is that which...

"Even though there is a difference between the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and the proving property (*sādhanadharma*)— a difference based on that 'exclusion' (*vyāvṛtti*) which is itself conceptually constructed through a distinction in its limits (*avadhibheda*), and which serves as the cause [of the inference]— nevertheless, in reality, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is nothing other than the very nature of the mark (*liṅgasvabhāva*);
that is, it is the very nature of the property to be proven."
For instance: that very thing which is excluded from what is non-existent is also excluded from what is non-momentary.

Therefore, because there is no difference between them as a single factual entity (*dharmī*), the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*) are also not distinct in the ultimate sense.
[2. To refute the opinion of others, the qualification "merely the existence of the proving property in the property to be proven" and so forth is employed.]

If, in reality, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is indeed identical in nature (*svabhāva*) to the probans (*liṅgin*), then why is it qualified as "that which follows upon the mere presence of the property that serves as the means of proof" (*sādhanadharmabhāvamātrānvayin*)?
For how could that which is the very nature of something not follow upon that [nature] alone?

Because [otherwise] there would follow the consequence of being formless (*nīrūpatva*), or else [the probandum] would lack that nature; therefore, he says: when the probandum-property (*sādhyadharma*) has a cause that is its very nature—that is, when the probandum-property is "of the nature of the cause" (*hetusvabhāva*)—there is "no deviation in the positive concomitance" (*anvayavyabhicārābhāva*), because there is no deviation in the positive concomitance of the mere presence of the proving-property (*sādhanadharma*).
A qualifier is appropriate when there is both possibility [of the property existing in the subject] and deviation [from the reason].

But here, since there is only possibility and no deviation, a qualifier is indeed inappropriate. Nevertheless, when the definition of the essential-reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is being formulated, that which is stated as "by the concomitance with only that" (*tanmātrānvayena*) regarding the "property to be proven" (*sādhyadharma*)—

The qualification "that [non-apprehension] is in relation to the opponent's view" is made by following the mere presence of the property to be proven; it is in relation to the divergent views of the Naiyāyikas and others, and not in relation to one's own view.
(Hbṭ 58)

Showing that very same misconception of others, he says: "For others," namely the Naiyāyikas and so forth, [hold that action is] "caused by a different entity. That is to say, it is caused by an entity other than the productive object, such as the conjunction with a substance possessing velocity (*vega*). For they say this: from the conjunction with a substance possessing velocity, motions arise in the parts; from those, the disjunction of the parts [occurs].
Consequently, upon the destruction of that conjunction, the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) initiated by it is also destroyed.
Thus, there is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) as the cause.

For this very reason, because [the property] is absent even when the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth exists, it is said to "depend on a distinct entity as its cause" and to "not follow merely from the presence of that [state]."

The "existence" (*bhāva*) of that [property] such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is its "being" (*sattā*); that alone is the "mere-ness" (*tanmātra*). The "concomitance" (*anvaya*) is that which belongs to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), characterized by impermanence. That which is the opposite of this—namely, the "nature" (*svabhāva*) of being produced and so forth—is what they intend by the word "also" (*api*). Since [the opponent] accepts this, the qualification was made. By means of that qualification, the author of the definition states that destruction caused by an external factor is not of the same nature (*atatsvabhāvatā*) as that [impermanence].

Because it is indicated by the qualification that "the nature of being exists only in that which arises from its own existence alone, and not elsewhere," [it follows that] when destruction is to be proven as having a cause, the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is fallacious. Likewise, he states that when that [destruction] is to be proven as being caused by something else (*arthāntara*), there is a "fallacy of the reason" (*hetu*), namely, its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*).

An example of this is as follows: when "destruction being caused by a cause" is the probandum (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*) "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) possesses "the state of not having that as its nature" (*atatsvabhāvatā*) and "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*). Now, one might object: since impermanence is admitted by others to be distinct from the nature of being produced, it is certainly not accepted [by them] that it is the very nature of being produced; so why is it said that "they also accept a nature that is concomitant with the mere absence of that"? The intention is this: even by those who admit that the two properties called "being produced" and "impermanence" are distinct, [it must necessarily be accepted that...]
One must accept that "coming into being after not having been" and "ceasing to be after having been" constitute the nature of non-abiding;
otherwise, since there would be no distinction [between these and other things], even the self (*ātman*) and so forth would possess the qualities of being produced and impermanence.

Therefore, let the relationship of probandum and probans (sādhyasādhanabhāva) exist between those very two— the coming-into-being after not having existed and the ceasing-to-be after having existed— which constitute the non-abiding nature of an entity, by means of the conceptualization that manifests the distinctions of "producedness" and "impermanence" arising through the power of perceiving them.
What is the use of postulating a distinct property (*dharma*)?

For even after such a postulation, it is the entity itself (*vastu*), by virtue of being the basis for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), that must be considered by those who seek that [result]. As it has been said:
(Hbṭ 59)

“By means of the distinction between the positions of existence and non-existence, those who do not deny the referents of words investigate the real entity itself; for the arising of the fruit is dependent upon that very entity.”
"What is the use of investigating the variations of that which is capable of purposeful action for those who seek it?
What is the point of a lustful woman examining whether a eunuch is handsome or ugly?"

Thus, even though entities have been perceived and determined in some respect through their exclusion from others, they may not be determined in another respect—namely, through an aspect excluded from what is not that [entity]—because of the presence of causes for error. Therefore, when there is a determination of the connection between the determined and undetermined aspects by means of another instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is established by inference regarding the object standing before one. Consequently, it is logical that "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), which is the very nature of impermanence, serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*) with respect to destruction.

And thus, the very nature of destruction is intended by them as the reason called "being produced" (kṛtakatva) according to the aforementioned logic. If that [destruction] does not follow from that alone [i.e., being produced], its lack of that nature is stated by means of a qualification, because it would have another cause.

It might be thought: "By means of being produced, destruction itself is directly inferred as possessing the reason; thereafter, impermanence is established as existence qualified by prior non-existence and destruction, or as inherence in that [existence]."

For this very reason, there is no consequence of impermanence regarding the self (*ātman*) and so forth. Furthermore, we do not consider "destruction" to be the non-existence of an entity characterized by annihilation (*pradhvaṃsa*);
rather, being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is its inherence in the existence of its own cause.
It is argued that by qualifying it [as "destruction"], there is nothing undesirable in making known its lack of inherent existence (*asvabhāvatā*).
This is incorrect.
Because such a destruction would contradict its having a cause,
as the Teacher himself will state later;
and nothing is established by that which is merely inferred.
Because that [entity] lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-sāmarthya*).
For those who, having understood the means for achieving pleasure and pain, desire to act accordingly, investigate something out of a practical intent and not out of mere addiction.
Therefore, by this very fact, the instability of the nature of the entity must be inferred.
And that [non-existence] itself must be conceived as having a cause;

otherwise, since the non-existence of destruction—which is not distinct from the entity itself—would remain unchanged even when a hammer or other instrument arises, that entity would persist in its very same state. In that case, how could existence characterized by it, or the inherence of it, constitute impermanence?

Furthermore, if the existence and inherence [of a thing]— which are qualified by the non-existence resulting from destruction caused by a hammer or similar instruments— are impermanence for an entity whose nature is unchanging,
then why would this not also apply to the self (ātman) and so forth?
Thus, the logical consequence (prasaṅga) remains exactly as it was.
Furthermore, even the inherence in its own causes cannot be established for one who does not accept that something comes into being after having not existed.
Indeed, it is precisely the existence of that which comes into being after having not existed that is described as "being produced.

Moreover, since both existence (*sattā*) and inherence (*samavāya*) are accepted as eternal and thus devoid of any qualitative distinction, it is not logical to qualify them with prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and subsequent destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).
And if it comes into being after not having existed, let that very state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and the lack of a stable nature (*asthirasvabhāvatā*) be what constitutes destruction.
What is the use of postulating a separate entity that is fruitless, lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇika*), and is contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇabādhitā*)?
Thus, even for our opponents, the identity (*tādātmya*) of being produced and destruction is necessarily established.

Therefore, if destruction—characterized by non-duration—is admitted to have a cause distinct from the object itself, then the fact that "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) does not possess that as its intrinsic nature (*atatsvabhāvatā*) is made known by the qualification [of the reason].
This is because it is impossible for that which is unproduced when the former is produced, or which has a different cause, to have that as its intrinsic nature.
Likewise, in that case, the reason "being produced" would be inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the probandum.
For instance: those things which depend upon other causes in a given case do not necessarily occur there, just as dyeing occurs in cloth.
And since the absence of destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva) in produced entities depends upon other causes, this is an "observation of the pervasion of the contradictory" (viruddhavyāptopalabdhi).

But surely, since the dyeing of a cloth has a limited cause, and since the presence of that cause depends upon its own specific conditions, and since its substrate is unstable due to the occurrence of contrary factors, it is logical that its occurrence is not necessary;
however, this is not the case for destruction.
Because its causes are infinite, there must necessarily be the presence of at least one among them in jars and other such things.
Furthermore, no one destroys the substratum of destruction prior to the presence of those causes,
such that destruction would fail to begin due to their absence.
That is incorrect;
for although causes of destruction are generally abundant, nevertheless, because their presence depends upon their own causes,
and because even when those causes are present, there may be an absence of opposing factors due to the obstruction of their power, it does not necessarily follow [that destruction occurs].
If it were the case that "causes possess their effects," then nothing would ever perish; thus, the deviation [of the reason] is not removed.
Now, one might object: even if this dyeing of cloth were dependent on other factors, if it were observed everywhere, why would it not be necessarily present?
It would be so, if it were perceived in that way;
however, it is apprehended otherwise.
If this is the case, then one should not allow the mind to be distressed by the suspicion that what is perceived everywhere might undergo a change of state through destruction.

How much more so, then, for you, whose light of knowledge pervades the entire expanse of all things, that you should speak thus? Or, if such were the case, how could the operation of inference not become fruitless when applied to what is already perceived?

However, even when someone observes destruction produced by a cause, they may still observe that things whose birth depends on causes can exist otherwise; thus, having developed doubt, how could such a person determine the state of things remote in space, time, or nature? Furthermore, this person regards destruction—which is characterized as the cessation of an entity—as eternal, because if that destruction were to perish, it would follow that the entity would re-emerge.
Furthermore, no cause for its destruction is perceived, as is the case with things such as a jar. As it has been said:

"Just as causes for bringing about destruction are observed in the case of jars and the like, [but] there is no such [cause] for destruction; since it is without a cause, how could it come into being?"
Thus [it is argued]. Then, why is it not accepted that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) by that very same [reason] when "being produced" (kṛtakatva) is the probandum for destruction?
If it is argued that this property of entities is indeed absolute (aikāntika), from what is this further determined?
If it is argued that this is because no change in their nature is perceived, [we reply]:
surely this non-perception, even if it exists, does not exclude the existence of the self and so forth; how then can it exclude change in other things?

If it should be argued that [the object] is apprehended through inference, then one must ask: how does non-apprehension itself exclude the presence of the reason in the counter-example (vipakṣa) within that very inference?
Thus, this is trivial.
Therefore, it was rightly said: "..."

He states that if destruction were caused by a cause, then the property of being produced would lack its own essential nature (asvabhāvatā) and would be subject to deviation (vyabhicāra); thus, enough with this excessive chatter. [4. Examples of the application of similarity and dissimilarity in inference for others.]

Now, although inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) is the subject at hand, nevertheless, because some people understand [the logic] solely through the practice of observing formal syllogisms (*prayoga*), and since that possibility exists even within inference for oneself, he speaks in order to explain inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) by way of a digression: "The *prayoga* of that"—that is, of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*)—"is twofold," meaning the verbal formulation that demonstrates its three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*).
He shows that very [formulation]: "That which has a common property" (*samānadharma*), the state of being such, by that... [the probandum]. (*Sādhya*)... [is established]."
One [type of] application is by way of similarity (*sādharmyeṇa*);
the other is by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*), which is the state of that which has a dissimilar property.
He states the examples for these two respectively: "For example, whatever exists... and so forth.
The word *yat* in the phrase *yad yat sat* is primarily distributive (*vīpsā-pradhāna*). Likewise, the word *tat* in *tat sarvam* is also primarily distributive.
Here, by the inclusion of the term "all" (*sarva*), everything without exception is encompassed, thereby excluding the fallacy of external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*).
Regarding the phrase "just as jars and so forth":

for one who possesses the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between existence and momentariness as it applies to jars and the like, the statement of the example is intended to provide a reminder of that [connection] in that context, not for the sake of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*),
because the probandum is not established by the mere presence of an example.
For it is not the case that because one thing exists in such a manner, everything exists in that same manner, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
"Sound is existent" is the application of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma-upasaṃhāra*).

An example of the formulation by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-prayoga*) is as follows, beginning with the word "tathā. The word "tathā" signifies conjunction; thus, the formulation by way of dissimilarity is being illustrated.
Here too, the term "all" (*sarva*) should be connected by changing its case-ending: "in the absence of momentariness," there is an "absence of existence" in "everything.

Demonstrating the purpose of the inclusion of "all" in both formulations, he says: "In every subject (*dharmin*) possessing the property of proof (*sādhanadharma*), and not merely in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*)," the "application" (*upasaṃhāra*)—that is, the bringing forward (*ḍhaukana*)—of the "property to be proven" (*sādhyadharma*).

Therefore, "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) is of the nature of "the necessary presence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) wherever [the pervaded] is," and so forth; the demonstration or establishment of that very [pervasion] is the "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) for those two, and thus they are described as such.

Consequently, those who exclude the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) and demonstrate external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*)— arguing that even if the probans (*sādhanadharma*) is pervaded by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), the establishment of the thesis is nonetheless untenable because this [pervasion] does not exist as such everywhere— are thereby refuted;
for the pervasion of the probans by the property to be proven exists everywhere when that [property to be proven] is present.
Why is such a case not demonstrated, by which external pervasion (bahirvyāpti) would be declared ineffective? For it is not as if [one were to say]: "He is dark-complexioned, because he is his son."

In the case of "like a son who is currently being seen," even though the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that sonhood with darkness is demonstrated outside the probandum (*sādhya*)— namely, in a son who is currently being seen— the establishment of the probandum nevertheless occurs.

Therefore, that very pervasion (*vyāpti*)—which is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), based on an invariable connection (*pratibandha*), and is capable of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*) through a universal synthesis (*sarvopasaṃhāra*)—is the one that must be demonstrated for the sake of its recollection.
Furthermore, even when pervasion is demonstrated through universal synthesis, the locus (*dharmin*) qualified by the property (*dharma*) is not perceived at that very moment;
for if it were, the inference occurring at a time subsequent to the presentation of the property as residing in the subject (*pakṣadharma*) would become a mere recollection (*smṛti*).

Because that [recollection] is impossible prior to the demonstration of the reason—which is inseparable from the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—as the basis for the cognition of that very reason within the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*);

and since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is preceded by that [demonstration], how could the subsequent inference, which has a particular object as its domain, be a recollection? [5. Even in the formulation of dissimilar instances (*vaidharmya*), the demonstration of pervasion is appropriate.]

But surely, it is logical that the formulation by way of similarity has the characteristic of demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*), because it demonstrates the necessary presence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) when the property that serves as the proof (*sādhanadharma*) is present; however, how is this the case for the formulation by way of dissimilarity?
For in that case, only the absence of the reason when the probandum is absent is stated, but not that the probandum must necessarily exist when the reason is present.
This is not a fault.

For in this context, the absence of the reason in the absence of the probandum is not shown as being of the nature of a mere non-entity (*tuccharūpa*), because that would contradict its status as a reason;
for a reason, such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth, is indeed a property of a real entity (*vastudharma*).
Since that very self does not exist, how could it possess the nature of a reason (*hetu*), such that the reason might have its three characteristics? Rather,
by means of an application based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-prayoga*), the property of having the nature of ceasing upon cessation— which is an internal property of the subject— is demonstrated.
And when the property serving as the means of proof (sādhana-dharma) is of such a kind, the existence of the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma) is necessarily understood;

otherwise, it would be impossible for it to possess the character of being absent when that [probandum] is absent. Therefore, it is not unreasonable for the application of the dissimilar instance (vaidharmya-prayoga) to have the characteristic of demonstrating pervasion (vyāpti).
[6. The Uselessness of Stating the Proposition (pratijñā):]

[Objection: "But in both types of formal argument, the employment of the thesis (*pratijñā*) has not been shown; how then can its meaning be understood? Moreover, the employment of the means of proof (*sādhana*) is intended for the purpose of communicating that meaning. To this, he says: "In these two arguments, because the meaning of the thesis—which consists of the aggregate of the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) and is the probandum (*sādhya*)—is understood solely by the power of stating the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and its connection [with the example] (as will be explained later), the employment of the thesis is not shown."

An opponent, failing to understand the underlying capacity [of the statement], says: "If you think that when the object of cognition (*prameya*)— the probandum (*sādhya*)— is not indicated by the words, there can be 'no' understanding whatsoever of it— that is, no understanding of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*)— then who would be the one to 'indicate' the object of cognition during the time of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), when one is practicing comprehension 'by oneself' without another person acting as an instructor?"
No one at all [is required].

Rather, one understands the object of cognition (*prameya*) by oneself through the perception of the probans (*sādhana-dharma*) which is invariably concomitant with the probandum (*sādhya*). Likewise, in inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), let the understanding of that [object] arise from that very same [probans]; what is the use of stating the proposition (*pratijñā*)?
If, at the time of one's own comprehension, there is no one to point out the object of cognition, how then does its comprehension occur?

To this he says: for one who has "perceived"—that is, seen by direct perception—the "smoke," which is the probans (*sādhana-dharma*), as being "located in a particular place" (*pradeśastha*) within the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*); when there occurs the "recollection of the pervasion" (*vyāpti*), i.e., the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) previously established through the force of the ascertainment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of that smoke with "fire," the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*), on the basis of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

“Precisely by the force of that”—namely, by the very force of grasping the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—the understanding of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) arises in the form “there is fire here,” even without the employment of a formal proposition.

One might think: “Even in that case, something such as a ‘ear-demon’ (*karṇapiśācikā*) tells him the object of cognition (*prameya*). To this he says: “And not”—indeed, not at all—is there “anyone,” such as a ‘ear-demon,’ who is invisible, “there” at the time of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
With the words "Agni is here," he thus "announces" or declares the object of knowledge to this respondent;
if you were a speaker of truth, you ought not to speak in such a manner.
For instance, we too, upon seeing smoke in a particular location, cognize fire by depending on the recollection of its pervasion (*vyāpti*) with fire;
yet no one informs us, "Fire is here."
And since there is the apprehension of that [object], it is equally appropriate for the apprehension of anything else as well.
If it is argued: "Even if no one points it out, one will nevertheless establish the object of cognition for oneself and then follow the logical mark (*liṅga*) to apprehend it," [we reply:]

He says: "Nor indeed"—meaning not only does no one inform [him], but even "prior to" the operation of the inferential mark (*liṅga*), he himself does not "cognize" anything such as fire and so forth. Why? If this is asked, it is because "[he would do so] without a means of valid cognition," that is, without a reason (*hetu*).
Because there is no basis for the cognition "fire is here," as [the opponent] understands it;
for the three-featured reason (*trirūpa-hetu*) is indeed the basis for the cognition of an imperceptible object (*parokṣārtha*), so in its absence, how could that cognition arise?
Now, if one were to say that such a cognition occurs even without a logical mark (liṅga), then, since that cognition is being asserted, the logical mark would be useless;
for its purpose is the comprehension of the object to be inferred (anumeya).
If that comprehension occurs without it, how could it not be devoid of purpose?
Demonstrating the extreme delusion of the opponent, he says: "Having himself," that is, independently, established [the premise] that "there is fire here.
How does he establish it independently?

"Without cause" (*akasmāt*) means by way of establishing [an object] without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). "For the sake of its comprehension" (*tatpratipattaye*) means for the purpose of comprehending the object of cognition (*prameya*) established without a basis.
"Subsequently," one "follows the mark" (*liṅga*), which is the basis for that [comprehension]. What kind of sequence or order is this regarding comprehension?
For instance: first there is the following of the mark; [then the comprehension of the object].
"Therefore, the understanding of the probandum [arises] from that"—this is the sequence for the wise.
But this [proponent] is a unique inferer who relies on the opposite of that;
thus [the author] mocks him, for this sequence is equivalent to what is said in the world: "Having shaved one's head, one asks about the lunar mansion."

Therefore, one realizes [the conclusion] for oneself solely through the power of grasping the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and recollecting the pervasion (*vyāpti*); and since that which establishes [the conclusion] has already been stated, there is no purpose whatsoever in mentioning the object of cognition (*prameya*).
Even if it is granted that one realizes the probandum (*sādhya*) for oneself at the time of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), that is indeed appropriate.

Since the logical mark (*liṅga*) is also apprehended there by oneself alone, whereas in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), one must apprehend the object of knowledge (*prameya*) from another just as one apprehends the logical mark from another, the employment of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is indeed appropriate; therefore, he says: "Even by another"—meaning not only by oneself when establishing [the matter] beforehand.

Even when stated by another proponent, that object of cognition (*prameya*) "floats away," because such a statement— by virtue of expressing a doubtful meaning— is not a factor for the ascertainment of the probandum (*sādhya*); for it does not fathom the depth of the object of cognition, and being neither directly nor indirectly connected to it,
it remains suspended above, being based merely on the speaker’s intention.

If it is asked, "Why does it float? [the answer is]: "Because of the absence of utility. That is to say, it has no utility whatsoever toward the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*), because that which is capable of communicating it has not been stated.

(Hbṭ 66) Anticipating the objection that an opponent might perhaps say this is merely an application [of the reason], he says: "The indication of the object" means that the object of the reason—the probandum—is indicated; this is the utility of the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*). If it is thought [that this is sufficient], he replies: "by that very object."
The word "first" (*tāvat*) indicates sequence.
If the subject matter being presented were meaningful, then the presentation of that subject matter would constitute the purpose of the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*).
However, since the subject matter itself is what is being shown, what is the point? What is the purpose? What is the meaning?

Now, it might be argued that the purpose of indicating the object [of inference] is both the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the cognition of the application based on similarity with the probandum (*sādhyadharman*); therefore, such an indication is the function of the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*). For instance, if the presentation of the probandum were absent—
When it is stated, "Whatever is produced is impermanent," one asks: "Is this an argument based on similarity (sādharmya-vat)?"
Or is it one possessing dissimilarity (*vaidharmyavān*)?
This would not be known.
For both are suspected here: that which possesses similarity (*sādharmyavān*) when proving impermanence by means of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), and [that which possesses dissimilarity].
"By being eternal, it possesses a dissimilarity [to sound] in its uncreatedness";
for when the thesis statement "sound is impermanent" or "it is uncreated" is uttered, both meanings are understood without doubt.
Furthermore, there would be no cognition of reasons that are contradictory or inconclusive;
however, in a formal argument preceded by a proposition (pratijñā),
such as "Sound is impermanent," [the logical structure is maintained].
From the statement "because it is produced," the status of being a reason (hetu) is understood,
[and] "it is eternal,"...
In the case of "because it is produced," there is contradiction;
likewise in "it is non-eternal because it is produced after effort."
Thus, there is inconclusiveness; furthermore, the three-fold nature of the logical reason would not be understood,
because its establishment depends upon the probandum.

When the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is present as a member [of the syllogism], by means of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of the whole for its part, the subject of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*) is called the "thesis" (*pakṣa*); thus, the state of being a property of the thesis (*pakṣadharmatva*) belongs to "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) as it exists therein.

Furthermore, the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) is an object similar to the thesis by virtue of the commonality of the property to be proven; thus, the existence [of the reason] in the similar instance (*sapakṣe sattvam*) belongs to that which exists therein.

And since the "non-similar instance" (*asapakṣa*) is that which is not a similar instance, the non-existence [of the reason] even in the non-similar instance (*asapakṣe 'pyasattvam*) would be understood as its not existing in that which is devoid of the property to be proven.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "If [the] cognition"—meaning the determination characterized by certainty regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), and the ascertainment of the essential nature [of the reason] from the application of similarity (*sādharmyavat-prayoga*) and so forth—"would not exist 'otherwise,' that is, without the statement of the proposition (*pratijñāvacana'), then" what was stated—that the presentation of the object is for the sake of establishing the probandum and for the sake of knowing the application of similarity and so forth—"all of that would be appropriate. However, since even at the time of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), [these functions occur] without the statement of the proposition.

It has already been explained that cognition characterized by the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) indeed occurs through the apprehension of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and the recollection of the [logical] connection (*sambandha*).
This will be the same for inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) as well.
Therefore, when this proponent of the formal employment of the thesis (*pratijñāprayoga*) himself realizes the probandum in such a manner, [he employs the thesis].

At that time, when the person himself has already "cognized" the object to be proven (*sādhya*), the subject is presented by means of the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*); yet, even "without" that [statement], one who "understands"—that is, one who ascertains the *sādhya* solely through the power of the logical mark (*liṅga*)—[does not require it]. When we are acting as those who provide instruction, then, seeing us as the "clients," he clearly "seeks the price" characterized by the employment of the proposition.
Like what? "Like the Parvan Brāhmaṇa.

Just as a Brāhmaṇa who lives by the *aurdhvarathika* profession eats at other times even without a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), yet on occasions such as a *śrāddha* festival, he says to a faithful supplicant: "If you give me one coin for each *ghṛtapūra*, then I shall eat; not otherwise."

"You are also equal to him. Furthermore, as for what you say— that at the time of inference for the sake of others, just as the probans (*liṅga*) is not understood by the person to be convinced when it is not stated by the opponent, so too is the probandum (*sādhya*)— this would be appropriate only if that person, having ascertained even the probans merely from the words of the proponent, were to understand the probandum in accordance with it.
And since we too at that time seek to convince others, why do we not likewise employ a thesis-statement devoid of the statement of the logical mark (*liṅga*)?
For our own words alone serve as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that person, and from those very words, the realization of the object to be inferred arises.
Because that statement would then have fulfilled its purpose.
But this is not the case;

for [the word] "even from our words" (*asmadvacanād api*) implies that it is not only at the time of one's own inference (*svārthānumāna*)—that is, even without our words—the particle *api* (also/even) being used.

But even when our statement is presented, he does not "even understand the logical mark (*liṅga*) from our statement"; how much less will he rely upon it for the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*)?
Rather, if that logical mark is established for him by himself through some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then our statement merely serves to provide a "restoration of memory" regarding it.
At that time, relying on the logical mark as established by himself, he understands the probandum.
"He does not drink even water because of our word.
Therefore, what is the difference between these two states—one consisting of the statement of the proposition and the other consisting of its non-statement?
There is none at all, since in both cases the understanding of the probandum arises solely from the power of the reason (*liṅga*) established by itself.

Therefore, since there is no difference regarding the pursuit of a mark (*liṅga*) already established for oneself, or regarding the resulting cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*), the presentation of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is likewise useless even in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*).
For if that [mark] were not stated here, [the inference would still function].
One should remember for oneself what is already well-known from before; why, then, is the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) employed, which expresses a meaning that is already established?
It might be argued: "Even if the statement of the proposition is of no use for the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*), let there be no employment of it for that purpose;
nevertheless, its employment remains necessary for the sake of understanding the application of similarity (*sādharmya*) and so forth."

Because its comprehension would otherwise be impossible, he says: "And it is observed that from an application [of a syllogism] possessing similarity (*sādharmya*) and so forth, comprehension occurs even without the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*).
Therefore, the introduction of the proposition for that purpose also does not appear appropriate.
But how can there be comprehension from an application possessing similarity and so forth when there is no indication of the probandum (*sādhya*)?
Thus he says: "From the mere statement of the property of the subject and its connection.
He thinks as follows: for no one would ever state merely this much, namely, "whatever is produced is impermanent."
Because he is defeated precisely due to the deficiency of his proof (*sādhana*), he must necessarily apply the reason (*hetu*) to the subject (*dharmin*).
In that case, if [he says], "And sound is produced" (*kṛtakaś ca śabdaḥ*);
If he should say this,
then there is the cognition of an application possessing similarity;
or [if he says], "and it is impermanent."

If one were to say this, then from the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) preceded by the statement of the relation [of the reason] as possessing the property of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the two types of formal argument (*prayoga*) are understood.
Furthermore, the fallacies of the reason—namely the contradictory (*viruddha*) and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)—are not recognized merely by the statement of the property of the subject;
but when the statement of the relation is also made, how could they not be recognized?

For instance, when the statement of the property of the subject— “whatever is produced is impermanent”— is uttered, the reason is understood, because there is a pervasion (vyāpti) of the thing being restated by that which is being enjoined.
In stating "whatever is produced is eternal," there is a contradiction,
because of the pervasion by the opposite.
In the demonstration that "whatever is produced is immediately preceded by an effort," there is the determination of inconclusiveness due to deviation;
yet, the three-fold character of the reason is indeed understood.

Since, at the time of demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*), the pervading property (*vyāpaka-dharma*) is understood as that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), and since the pervaded property (*vyāpya-dharma*) is subsumed under a subject (*dharmin*), that [subject]—being understood as qualified by the pervading property—is recognized as the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*) because it is a portion of the whole complex of the probandum (*sādhya*). Thus, when that pervasion is demonstrated in a subject where the subsumed pervaded property resides, that object is perceived as being similar to the subject by virtue of the generality of the property to be proven; this is what is meant by "in the similar instance" (*sapakṣe*).

Existence [in the subject] is understood; and by implication, that wherein the absence of the pervader is determined to entail the absence of the pervaded is the "non-similar instance" (asapakṣa); thus, non-existence in the non-similar instance is also ascertained.

If there were some purpose served by the subject (*pakṣa*) and other members being known [by name], then those engaged in practical discourse would not need to rely on conventions regarding the subject and so forth for the comprehension of an imperceptible object.
For such is the way things stand in the world: when something is observed in a certain place, that which is connected to it serves as its indicator for one who knows that connection.
There is no dependence on the apprehension of conventions such as "the subject" (pakṣa) and so forth.
In that regard, for the sake of understanding the form of the argument, the authors of treatises may formulate definitions according to their own conventions or otherwise, as they please;
however, at the time of actual usage, following those [conventions] is of no utility whatsoever.
However, it is precisely that form of the indicator as described—which is established through convention—that is useful for those engaged in linguistic practice.

If that [form] is understood, the establishment of the probandum is accomplished by that alone; thus, even if one is unaware of the conventions regarding the subject (*pakṣa*), the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and so forth, nothing is lost.
For this very reason, the venerable Teacher [Dignāga] stated:
"Perception of an object necessarily connected [with another] is inference for one who knows that [connection]"—
thus it has been established that the mere form of the means of cognition is independent of conventions such as the "subject" (pakṣa) and so forth.
As for the fact that some people, due to their own intellectual failings, proclaim even there defects that do not exist, what can we say to that?

"Therefore," even for the sake of knowing the formulation based on similarity (*sādharmyavat-prayoga*) and so forth, the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā-vacana*) is improper, because—as explained by the aforementioned method—cognition occurs through the mere statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and its connection [to the probandum]. "What is the utility" (*upayoga*) "of that" statement of the proposition? None at all. Furthermore, this proponent, having bypassed the very sequence by which he himself understood the object of inference (*anumeya*), and resorting to a different sequence for the sake of convincing another, is perceived as nothing but a rogue due to his deceitfulness.
Demonstrating that he is not merely well-behaved, he says: “Just like one’s own certainty,” and so forth.

Just as the production of certainty has been accomplished for oneself, so too is the "proof" (sādhana) stated by those devoted to the welfare of others for the sake of producing certainty in others as well.

“In this regard,” given this principle, this proponent himself, at the time of his own inference (*svārthānumāna*), even “without” a statement that serves as a “demonstrator” by means of “pointing out the object of cognition” (*prameya*), “having understood” the object of cognition, “instructs” another person— such as one who is doubtful— and communicates what he himself has understood.
