While making the object of knowledge known, what is the reason for resorting to a "different sequence" (*kramāntara*)— that is, something other than the "sequence" or means previously experienced at the time of one's own comprehension when the object was first understood?
There is no reason at all, except for the purpose of deluding others.

For instance: if the sequence of one's own realization is the basis for understanding, why abandon that and resort to another sequence? How could one have realized it by means of that [other sequence]?
Since this is so, "therefore there is no purpose whatsoever" for the "statement" called the thesis (*pratijñā*) regarding the "object of cognition," which is the probandum (*sādhya*).
Why?
Because, as the conclusion states, "even otherwise"—that is, even without it—"comprehension" occurs, meaning the realization of the probandum arises.

[7. The non-membership of the application, conclusion, and so forth, in the syllogism: Having thus removed the thesis from the syllogistic statement, he says—extending the same reasoning already stated—in order to remove other elements such as the application and conclusion imagined by others: "By this" reasoning, "the application, conclusion, and so forth"—by the inclusion of "and so forth," doubt, desire to know, and so on—"are refuted," that is, rejected.
In that context, "the application [is] 'thus,' depending on the example" means:
The application (*upanaya*) is the statement that "it is not so," or it is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*); this refers to the proposition itself.

By the word "by this" (*etenā*), he demonstrates exactly this: "because the cognition of the probandum (*sādhyapratīti*) occurs—meaning it arises—by this much alone, namely by the mere statement of the connection between the property and the subject (*pakṣadharma-sambandha-vacana*), even without the application and the other members."
Regarding this, the author [Uddyotakara] says: First of all, the thesis (pratijñā) must necessarily be stated for the purpose of specifying the object [of the inference],
since people first determine the object to be cut and so forth before acting.
Consequently, one employs the means of action, such as an axe and so forth.

Furthermore, as long as the reason (hetu), whose efficacy has been observed in the example, is not applied to the subject (dharmin) by means of the application (upanaya), how can there be a cognition of the probandum (sādhya)?
Moreover, it is shown by this [application] that the purpose of the reflective cognition (pratyavamarśapratyaya) is what is observed in inference for oneself (svārthānumāna).
For instance: in inference for oneself, one first perceives smoke in a particular location;
then one recalls the pervasion (*vyāpti*) thus: "In every place where I have seen smoke, there I have also seen fire."
Then, one reflects again by saying, "And here there is no smoke"; that purpose of reflection is expressed by the application (upanaya) in an inference for the sake of others.
The conclusion (nigamana) must also necessarily be stated;
for although it was previously asserted that "sound is impermanent," certainty regarding this has not yet been established by that alone.
But now, the object established by the force of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is concluded by this [verse] for the sake of its clear comprehension;
furthermore, the operation of all means of valid cognition is subsumed by this.
For instance: scripture is the thesis (pratijñā).
The reason (*hetu*) is inference (*anumāna*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is perception (*pratyakṣa*), the application (*upanaya*) is comparison (*upamāna*);
thus, the operation of this entire fourfold set of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is concluded by the conclusion (*nigamana*). How, then, could this [conclusion] not be purposeful?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Having abandoned the passion of the Ḍiṇḍikas"—the Ḍiṇḍikas are naked teachers who are addicted to fruitlessly writing names one after another; therefore, like them, one must abandon the misplaced obsession that thinks, "When another has spoken, I must certainly state something over it, even if it is useless because it is inappropriate.
Having done so, "closing your eyes"—that is, withdrawing external distractions—"consider for a moment":
“Will there be a cognition of the probandum by means of this much—a mere statement of the property of the subject and its connection—or not? To this we reply:

Since we have already granted that only as much as is to be expressed in an inference for others is required, and since exactly that same amount—neither less nor more—is observed to be the cause of cognition even in an inference for oneself, what contradiction of its power is there here?

By which [means] would he not achieve comprehension even in the case of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*)? Since comprehension occurs when the existence [of the probandum] is understood, what is the use of the "proliferation" (*prapañca*) characterized by the proposition, application, and conclusion, or characterized by the description of its utility for deceiving the foolish?

For instance: even when employing the formal members of a syllogism—the proposition (*pratijñā*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*)—if the probans (*sādhanadharma*) were not ascertained by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being pervaded by its own probandum (*svasādhya*), or if it did not exist in the subject (*sādhyadharmin*), then it would have no capacity whatsoever to cause comprehension.

However, when that [ascertainment] is present, even in the absence of the proposition and the other members, it cannot be prevented from functioning because the form of the indicator (*gamaka*) is complete, just as in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*). Therefore, why this misplaced insistence?

For it is not logical that the ascertainment of the probandum (sādhya) should result from the mere statement of the proponent regarding the property of the means of proof (sādhana-dharma), if that property lacks the capacity to imply the probandum;
otherwise, there would be the consequence of the futility of adducing the reason (hetu). Or, if that capacity does exist, then the same applies to the statement of the proposition (pratijñā).

As for what was stated— that "the thesis (pratijñā) is for the purpose of indicating the object"— the author of the treatise himself has already provided the answer to this. Furthermore, by one who employs a proof (*sādhana*), [it must be accepted that...]

Having determined the object by thinking, "I shall establish cognition regarding this particular goal by means of this particular instrument," that [inference] is employed; thus, there is no transgression of worldly convention.

Otherwise, if the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) arises for someone from a means of proof (*sādhana*), then that very person must determine the object of action (*karman*); how else could there be the establishment of the probandum in an inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), which is based upon a means of proof, in the absence of such determination?
Furthermore, one who has established the relationship between fire and smoke in the mind...

"Where is the fire? Where is the fire?"—thus he searches for the fire; yet, in that location, he perceives the fire from the mere sight of smoke. How, then, could there be a reflective cognition (*pratyavamarśapratyaya*) in the case of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*)? If, on the other hand, it is argued that because he has seen it there at some time, its mention is included even in the inference for others (*parārtha*), then why not also [mention] the eating of curd and so forth, since he might have perceived the fire from smoke after having eaten curd and such at some point?
What is the basis for that which is occasional?
Furthermore, as for what was stated,
"the scripture is the proposition," [that too is explained].

In this regard, if the mere statement of the proponent were the *āgama*, then since the probandum would be established from that alone, the introduction of the reason (*hetu*) and other members would be useless.
Alternatively, if the proposition (*pratijñā*) is considered *āgama* because the meaning of the proposition is recited in the *āgama*,
then since it is not recited anywhere in an *āgama* that "there is fire in this place," how could the proposition have the status of *āgama*?
The claim that "the reason (hetu) is inference" is also incorrect,
for the mere property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) is not the reason.
Because that [inference] possesses three forms,
and because not every example is perceptible, how could it be said that "the example is perception"?
But analogy (*upamāna*) is not even a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
how then could its function be subsumed by the conclusion (*nigamana*)?

Moreover, if the reason (*hetu*), whose capacity has been observed in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), must necessarily be applied to the subject (*dharmin*), then let that application simply be the application (*upanaya*); what need is there for [the conclusion]?

By the statement "because of being produced," which indicates the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), he will himself subsequently present the reason whose efficacy has been observed and demonstrate its presence in the subject; therefore, there is nothing [further] required by that [statement].
Therefore, since the initial employment of the proposition (*pratijñā*) itself is not accepted, how could there be a conclusion (*nigamana*) consisting of its restatement?

Thus he says: "Therefore, for this reason, in a statement of proof (*sādhanavākya*), only this much—the mere statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and its connection—is the superior employment; it is established that it does not consist of five members.
[8. There is no fixed order for the statements of the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) within a formal argument.]

In this syllogism of proof, not only is the employment of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth inappropriate, but there is also no fixed rule regarding the sequence, such as "the reason (*hetu*) must be stated first and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) afterwards," even if it were accepted by the opponent.

Why? Because in every case, whether the reason (*hetu*) is stated first and the pervasion (*vyāpti*) afterwards, or the pervasion is stated first and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) afterwards, it remains a means of cognition (*gamaka*).
(Hbṭ 73)
[9. Refutation of the threefold application of the reason:
But is it not the case that your statement—that its application is twofold—is incorrect?
For the Naiyāyikas maintain that the reason (*hetu*) is of three kinds: positive (*anvayin*), negative (*vyatirekin*), and both positive and negative (*anvayavyatirekin*).
Therefore, it must be stated that its formulation is threefold: by way of similarity (*sādharmya*), by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), and by way of both similarity and dissimilarity.

To this he says: "Even when stating the [logical] connection (*sambandha*)," not only is a fixed order of sequence not appropriate, but "there is also no difference in meaning," because the presence of the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) exists in both cases alike.
Therefore, every reason is indeed both positive (anvayin) and negative (vyatirekin); the point is that there is no such thing as a reason that is exclusively positive or exclusively negative.
How, then, could there be a threefold classification of formal arguments (prayoga)?
Thus he thinks.
But why is there no difference in meaning?

To this, he says: "In both ways"—that is, whether in application by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), even though [the statements] take the form of affirmation and negation—

Although a difference between the properties (*dharma*) is perceived, nevertheless, it is precisely the state of being that very [nature]—namely, the fact that the probans-property (*sādhana-dharma*) has the same essential nature as the probandum (*sādhya*)—that is "manifested" through the applications of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
Now, in the application of similarity, the existence of the probandum follows from the existence of the reason; [is this not so?]
And in the case of dissimilarity (vaidharmya), the absence of the reason in the absence of the probandum is understood from the word [of the statement],
not identity (tādātmya). Why, then, is it said...?
Because that very state [of being of the same nature] is what is being made known, he says:
"For not," and so forth.

If, in the formulation based on similarity (*sādharmya-prayoga*), that state were not implied, then why would there be the existence of the probandum (*sādhya*) "exclusively" (*ekāntena*)—that is, necessarily—in the presence of the probans (*sādhana*) which does not have that as its intrinsic nature (*atatsvabhāva*)?
Let it be granted that [the reason] is occasional; however,

when the reason exists, the absolute concomitance of the probandum with it— expressed as "whatever is produced is impermanent"— is stated through pervasion in the application of similarity (*sādharmya-prayoga*).
And since that [invariable concomitance] is not possible for a non-distinct entity without identity (*tādātmya*), it implies that [identity] by the force of the context.

How is it that the existence of something whose nature is not that [of another] does not entail the existence of the other exclusively? To this he says: "In the case of being produced," and so forth. If being produced exists even without being immediately preceded by effort, then it lacks that nature; and this same situation applies to impermanence as well.

Furthermore, because of the absence of identity (*tādātmya*), there would be no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between "being produced immediately after an effort" and "impermanence," nor would there be a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) such that the latter ceases upon the cessation of the former; how then could the latter be understood from the former?
This is not a fault.

Because it is precisely the nature of a thing that follows immediately upon effort which is proven by that [reason] as being impermanent, and because identity (*tādātmya*) exists there, positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are unimpeded. However, with respect to the relationship between impermanence and being produced (*kṛtakatva*), its lack of identity has been stated here. [Objection: But surely, even when fire ceases, the cessation of smoke—which does not have that [fire] as its nature—is observed, and thus there is positive concomitance. To this he says: "of the effect" (*kāryasya*).
For the basis of positive and negative concomitance is the necessary connection (pratibandha),
because by that [connection] they are pervaded; in its absence, those two [concomitances] would also be absent.

In that case, since smoke is a distinct entity from fire, there exists a "connection characterized by origination from that" (*tadutpatti-lakṣaṇa-pratibandha*) which is the cause of positive and negative concomitance; thus, those two [concomitances] may exist. However, where those two are said to belong to what is not a distinct entity, the intention is that there must necessarily be identity (*tādātmya*). An example here is: "Just as in the case of these very two—being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and being immediately following effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*)—there is no cessation of one upon the cessation of the other when they are reversed."
"That which is not invariably concomitant with effort is also not produced";
since this is so, therefore, when the presence and absence [of the reason] correspond to their definitions, the probandum necessarily exists whenever the reason exists.

And since the absence of the reason is necessarily concomitant with the absence of the probandum, even a single [reason]— whether employed by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)— implies the second,
because it implies its own pervader (the probandum) through a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), and that [pervader] is likewise pervaded by the other.

Therefore, since the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) are understood in both cases—one through the word and the other through the meaning—it is established that even when the relationship [between the reason and the probandum] is stated, it is only the formal application (*prayoga*) that differs, whether by way of affirmation or negation, but not the meaning. Consequently, its application is twofold: by similarity (*sādharmya*) and by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
But it is not by both similarity and dissimilarity,
because its meaning is revealed by either one alone.
Concluding that every reason is in fact only positive-negative (anvaya-vyatirekin), and that in reality there is no such thing as a purely positive or purely negative reason, he says:

"Thus, in a single [locus], in a statement of proof (*sādhanavākya*), the 'employment'— that is, the direct verbal presentation— of both the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not desired,
because it would be 'useless,' as there is no purpose in making known what has already been understood."
(Hbṭ 75) Clarifying that very same understanding of the other in terms of its actual meaning, he says: “By virtue of having that as its nature,” and so forth.

If the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the reason with the probandum is established by virtue of having that as its nature, then for that very reason, “the absence [of the reason] in the absence [of the probandum] is also established.”

Because that which has such an intrinsic nature cannot exist by itself as a selfless entity in the absence of that [nature]. Likewise, when the non-existence of the probandum is established through its being of that intrinsic nature, and the non-existence of the probans is established, it is precisely from that [establishment] that the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the reason with the probandum is also established.

As for those who explain: "In an application based on similarity (*sādharmyavat*), the manifestation of the non-existence of the reason in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) occurs only in the absence of that [probandum]."

"It may be that [the reason] exists neither elsewhere than in the counter-example (vipakṣa) nor in the contradictory [example], because it would follow that the reason is non-existent [therein], and because it would follow that exclusion occurs only through contradiction; thus, the formulation of the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is for the purpose of demonstrating this restriction.
This too is incorrect for that purpose.

Why? Because [the term] "also" implies that it is not only the absence of that [property] which constitutes the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), but also that which is other than it or that which is contradictory to it. For that which has something else as its counter-example, or which possesses another property, is not necessarily the non-substratum of the intended property;
or it may be contradictory by way of the specific contradiction characterized by non-coexistence.

Nor is it a counter-position by virtue of being defined by mutual exclusion; for if [the reason] were to reside in an object that possesses properties other than impermanence, such as non-selfhood and so forth,
it would follow that the reason is absent [from the locus of the probandum], which is an absurdity.

Furthermore, when heat is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), if one were to argue that fire is not definitively established as hot because there is the possibility of its exclusion from other things—such as that which is neither hot nor cold—due to the presence of a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*) like coldness, then this would be a flaw in his position. Regarding this, the Master has stated: "If the status of being a counter-example (*vipakṣatva*) is desired for a single thing, then let it be desired for the absence of that very thing."

It does not [exclude] that which is contradictory or anything else, because even in other cases where there is no substratum for the intended property, both [the contradictory and the other] exist; for it is impossible for those two to be "other" or "contradictory" without the absence of that [intended property].
However, for us who accept all three types of counter-examples (vipakṣa), including one that does not serve as a locus for the property intended to be proven—this is the sense.
[10. Proof that existence has momentariness as its intrinsic nature.]

If, in the case of a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*), the fact that the property of the probans has the nature of the probandum is the basis for both positive and negative concomitance—and if, by means of expressing either a similar or a dissimilar formal argument (*prayoga*) through positive or negative concomitance, the implication of the other is stated by way of implying their identity (*tādātmya*), then the fact that one has the nature of the other must be established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as their basis, and not merely perceived through words alone. With this intention, he says: "How is this? and so forth.
"By 'existent' (yena)" means by way of having the nature of perishing;
that is to say, by way of the nature of momentariness of the reason characterized as existence (*satva*).
And the intention of the questioner is this: here, existents are of two kinds—those that are produced, such as jars and the like, and those that are unproduced, such as space and the like.

In that regard, as for those things which are unproduced, they do not even possess impermanence— let alone momentariness— because they lack the characteristic of impermanence, namely, "being existent and causeless is permanent. Thus, existence does not have momentariness as its intrinsic nature.

Even for those things that are produced (*kṛtaka*), since their destruction follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of hammers and other such causes, destruction possesses a cause; therefore, in the absence of those causes, there is no destruction. Consequently, even for that which is of a produced nature (*satva*/*tattva*), the essential nature of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva-svabhāvatā*) does not exist at all, and thus the possibility of positive and negative concomitance [proving it] is not present. Furthermore, destruction must necessarily follow the positive and negative concomitance of the staff and so forth.

Because it is observed as such; for it is said: "Without the presence of causes such as a blow, contact with fire, or destruction, destruction does not occur through association with jars and the like."
Furthermore, even elsewhere, the Buddhists themselves accept that conformity with presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) alone is the basis for the conventional usage of "having a cause.

Since this [conformity] exists here as well, why is that conventional usage not applied? Now, by one who establishes the certainty of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the fact that [the effect] has that [cause] as its nature was already established previously through the operation of subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).

Since there is the statement, "The ascertainment of positive concomitance [occurs] also in the case of the essential reason (svabhāvahetu)," how could there be any occasion for this prima facie objection?

True; however, since the former teachers, when proving momentariness from the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), have stated that because opponents necessarily admit that for produced things there must be destruction at the end caused by a specific cause, they have presented the proof of the impossibility of such a cause as a subverting argument (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary [position] regarding destruction— thereby establishing identity (*tādātmya*)— and this was done by way of a reductio (*prasaṅga*) specifically concerning the characteristic of being produced.
This is presented as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to demonstrate that [existence] leads to the identity of that very entity and not of anything else;

and furthermore, although it was previously stated that the definition of the contradiction of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāvirodha*) applies to all existence, it is now set forth in detail by means of the mere thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*).
However, an existence characterized by being uncreated is simply impossible,
because without a determining cause, a restriction regarding place, time, and intrinsic nature would be untenable. Therefore,

the former teachers did not attempt to establish its identity with that [uncreated state], on the grounds that its permanence— defined as "being existent and without a cause" (*sadakāraṇavat*)— is impossible due to the deficiency of even one of its necessary conditions.
The author of the treatise, however, [establishes] in a general sense that existence has a momentary nature,
and that even that which possesses the characteristic of being produced—
and even that which is remote in terms of space, time, and intrinsic nature— has that very nature by the very state of things, through the contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Since destruction is necessarily inherent and lacks a cause—there being no distinction [between things] due to this lack of causality—it will be demonstrated that it would follow that a thing perishes as soon as it has arisen.
[This is a critical examination of the nature of existence (*bhāvasvabhāvatā*) in order to refute the view that destruction has a cause.
In this regard, it was stated by the former masters: [The text continues with the citation: "Therein..."
"Since for every existent thing that is produced, destruction caused by a cause is necessarily present at the end"—
in order to demonstrate the independence [of destruction] with respect to that which is thus maintained, he begins by stating, "Because a cause of destruction is impossible.
If, then, there is no cause for destruction, [how can it occur?]

Why is the destruction of those things that have been produced necessarily certain? For no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) whatsoever can be logically established as being accidental; thus he says: "by its very intrinsic nature" (svabhāvata eva).
The word *bhāva* signifies a cause, in the sense that "from this, the effect comes into being."

Therefore, from their own causes alone, entities arise within themselves as "perishable"— that is, having the nature of perishing— and as non-abiding, like mustard seeds on the point of a needle. For these existing entities, which possess the characteristic of being produced and have been brought forth by their own causes, there is no "arising of destruction" from "anything else," such as an external blow.
Why? Because that [cause], such as the impact or contact with fire which is accepted as its cause, lacks the capacity [to produce destruction].
For instance, at the time of contact with fire and so forth, we perceive a triad: that very wood and so forth which is to be destroyed; [the cause]; and [the destruction itself].
The various states such as charcoal and so forth,

as well as non-existence characterized by the cessation of wood and so forth— which is of a void nature— are not anything else in which the operation of the contact with fire and other factors could be conceived.
And given this state of affairs, it is not logical for a cause of destruction to possess any efficacy whatsoever in this context.
For a cause of destruction does not produce a nature characterized by instability in an entity—such as fuel—which has already arisen from its own causes with a stable form.
Why? Because that fuel and so forth have already been brought about solely by their own causes.
For it is not possible to effect a change in nature in that which has arisen from a stable self;
for if that [change] were to occur later due to another cause, it would follow that it is a different entity altogether.
Because it is impossible for that very thing to undergo alteration, and because it is impossible to conceive of the operation of a cause upon it.

Alternatively, when the triad is examined: first, as for that which is to be destroyed, such as wood and the like, the cause of destruction—such as contact with fire—does not produce its own nature, since that [nature] has already been established by its own causes.
[12. Examination of Kumārila’s position regarding the nature of a different entity (bhāvāntarasvabhāva):

Kumārila, however, maintains that it is not the very nature of the entity itself that is produced by contact with fire and so forth, but rather the non-existence through destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva) of the fuel and the like.
And this [non-existence] is simply a subsequent different entity (bhāvāntara), such as the embers, which is devoid of the form of the fuel and so forth. As it has been said:
“The non-existence of milk in curd is characterized as non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*);
and the acceptance of such a form of non-existence as having a cause is not at all contradictory.
Thus, someone has said:
“An entity devoid of any other entity is here considered a non-entity, like [the absence of] perception; why then does that [non-entity] not arise from a cause?
Refuting this view of the followers of Kumārila, he says: “Nor indeed,” and so forth.

If the subsequent effect, being of the nature of an entity, is indeed "another entity" that constitutes non-existence, then we certainly accept that the contact with fire and so forth operate toward the production of charcoal and the like.
However, if it is accepted that "another entity is produced," then because fire and the like would have no operation upon the fuel and so forth, the fuel and such would remain exactly as they were.

Consequently, just as there was the perception of the fuel and so forth prior to contact with fire, and a distinct purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by it, so too would there be the consequence of [continued] perception and so forth even when charcoal and the like are produced.
Now, [one might argue] that of the other entity, namely destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*)—

If [the fire] were of the nature of an existent entity (*bhāvarūpatā*) at the time of its arising, then since fuel and so forth would have been destroyed, how could there be the consequence of perceiving them as such when they are non-existent?

True; this is what is intended: lest everything else, such as fuel or even a cow, likewise become that [nature], one must state the basis for establishing the destruction of the embers and so forth. In that case...

If you say that "when [the cause] exists, there is the cessation [of the effect]," oh, what eloquence in speech! For, since you do not admit that cessation has the nature of a non-entity (*tuccha*), you are simply calling that very other entity—such as the embers—the "cessation.
Thus, the resulting meaning is this: when the state of embers and so forth exists, the destruction of the wood and so forth is the state of the embers and so forth themselves.
Furthermore, its existence [as charcoal] does not occur when it is in the state of [fuel such as] wood, because it is impossible for something to be a cause with respect to itself.
If it is argued that its nature is destruction because it is said to arise from fire and so forth, and because it becomes charcoal through the crushing of the fuel and so on—
then what is this so-called "crushing"?
If cessation were characterized solely by charcoal and the like, it would not differ from the previous state;
therefore, it is better to hold that wood and such things cease by their own inherent nature, whereas the production of charcoal and the like results from fire and other factors.
Otherwise, why would it not follow that wood and other such things are likewise perceived [as non-existent]?

Furthermore, if the non-existence of destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) were a distinct entity, then for those things such as lamps or cognitions— which perish without having undergone any transformation— what distinct entity could be established as their destruction?
If it is argued that they too rely upon non-manifestation (*avyaktatā*), the nature of the self (*ātmabhāva*), modification (*vikāra*), or destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), we say no.
For there is no evidence for the existence of non-manifestation as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) in the case of lamps and the like.

If non-manifestation were the attainment of a state of potentiality (*śakti*), then—since potentiality is a form inferred from the observation of its effects—how could lamps and the like be conceived as existing in the form of potentiality in the absence of those effects?
Now, if non-manifestation is the attainment of a nature devoid of fitness for perception,
there is likewise no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existing in that state;
and the wise do not respect words that lack a basis in valid cognition.

Since the self (*ātman*) does not exist, how could there be its state as a modification or transformation (*vikāra* and *pariṇāma*) of cognition and so forth? Because a refutation has already been established elsewhere, it is not elaborated upon here; enough of this digression. It might be thought: "Because fuel and the like are covered by another entity such as embers, their perception and so forth do not occur in that way. To this, he says: "Nor even... and so forth.

Furthermore, it would not be logical for there to be an "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*) of another thing, such as fuel and so forth, while that fuel remains in its "unchanging state," that is, while it exists in its unaltered form; for even an obscuration would be impossible—not only non-perception and the like—[Hbṭ 80] [13.
An examination of the position that [an entity] both exists and does not exist].

Not only is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity or another distinct entity not produced by a cause of destruction, but even the non-existence (*abhāva*) of an entity is not produced; thus he says, "Nor... and so forth.
If one asks why, [the answer is]:

if the non-existence is accepted as being produced through a positive formulation (*vidhi*), that is, by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) as something "other" than the intended entity, then is this [non-existence] simply of the same form as the fuel and so forth?
Or is it a different object? In that case,
because one cannot avoid the alternatives of being either distinct or non-distinct,
the very same fault already mentioned applies there as well.

Now, it might be argued: "Surely this [non-existence], being of the nature of a non-affirming negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) and consisting of a mere void (*tuccha-rūpa*), is accepted as being produced by fire and other such factors.

And since fuel and the like lack intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) when that [non-existence] exists, how can there be any occasion for the aforementioned fault? Furthermore, because it necessarily conforms to the presence and absence of fire and so forth, it must be their effect; for even in other cases, the conventional usage of the term 'existence' is based upon that. As it has been said:
“Since that which has been projected as the object of awakening is not perceived when it exists, how can its destruction not be a destruction? How could it not undergo the state of being an effect?”

"Just as an entity that did not previously exist comes into being from causes, so too, having come into existence, it does not continue to exist from causes. Therefore, he says: "In the negation of an entity," and so forth.

This is the intended meaning: if destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) were merely a void consisting of simple passing away (*cyuti*), independent of any connection with other entities, then the operation of causal factors (*kāraka-vyāpāra*) would not be possible therein, since such an operation is possible only in that which possesses the nature of coming into being (*bhavana-dharmin*).
If it is argued that its status as an effect (*kāryatā*) is not contradicted because it too undergoes the transition from non-existence to existence, we say: no.

Because that which has the nature of coming into being would attain the state of being an existent entity, its status as a non-existent entity would be lost; for it is called an "existent" (*bhāva*) precisely because it comes into being (*bhavati*),
and there is no other basis for the application of the term "existent" even in the case of a sprout or similar things.
If it is argued that [it exists] because of its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*),
then how can this [entity], which is devoid of all capacity, be an object of cognition? For that which is not a cause cannot be an object of cognition.

Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument]. Or else, how could there be an understanding of its being possessed of a cause, or its being a real entity, if it is not an object [of cognition]?
To this it is replied: "That real entity is indeed of a non-void (atuccha) nature."
Or, if it generates cognition, how is it not connected by way of causal efficiency (*sāmarthya*)?
If you ask, "How can there be existence for that which is not the object of the cognition 'it exists'?", [we reply:
how, then, can it have the status of being an effect?
If it is argued that [an entity exists] because it arises from its own causes,
then how is it that it is not the object of the cognition "existent"?
For if it is understood that it exists when it arises from its own causes, then it would also be understood as "existent."
Because the wise say that what "is" exists;
yet there is no existing, becoming, or being.
If it is argued that there is no ultimate difference in meaning among words such as "existent" (sann),
and that this [word] exists solely by virtue of having non-existence as its nature, we say: no,
because that is contradictory.
Since that which does not exist is called "non-existence," how can it be designated as "coming into being"?

If you argue that it is called "not existing" because it does not manifest within its own cognition in any established form, then it would follow that the eyes and other sense organs—which are entirely beyond perception—would also be non-existent. This is not so.
If it is argued that this is because they appear as the cause of knowledge, we say no;
for even this [cause] appears as something that exists.
Furthermore, how can there be a connection between the absence of all forms and existence?
For emergence in some form is indeed manifestation;

and because this [non-existent thing] is equal to that [existent thing] in its appearing as the cause of that [cognition], since it is impossible for something without a cause to be an object of cognition.
But our cognitions of non-existence, following from the ripening of their own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), are indeed devoid of an object.
Furthermore, if non-existence were itself an existing entity, how would the exclusion-by-implication (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) differ from the exclusion-by-restriction (*paryudāsa*)?
If it is argued that it differs because the former is an affirmation of a negative form while the latter is an exclusion-by-restriction, we say no.
Because the coming into being of that which lacks the nature of existence is a contradiction;

for the expression "it comes into being" (bhavati) is connected with "becoming" (bhūti), that is, with existence (sattā). In that case, how could there be an affirmation of that which possesses the nature of existence?
The meaning of the negative particle would have to be exclusively a paryudāsa (presuppositional negation), because in all cases the affirmative injunction is primary;
or else, that [negation] would not exist at all.
For if something were to be excluded from something else, then that [exclusion] would touch upon what is distinct from it by means of its negation;
but that is not the case,
because when it is said that "there is an exclusion everywhere," this is due to the affirmation of some other entity.
In that case, he would have stated merely another entity,
not the distinction between those two; and if there is no distinction, there can be no exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
Furthermore, there would be the fault of stating something irrelevant;
for while the negation of existence is the subject at hand, what is being established is merely another entity that is non-existent by nature.
Nor is this [entity] non-existent by its own essential nature.
Because it is contradictory for that which is non-existent even in its own nature to be an effect;

and since, in terms of another's nature, every entity is of the nature of non-existence, there would be no distinction between this [non-existence] and things such as a jar. Or, let this be non-existence; why then are firewood and the like not perceived when fire and other [causes] are present?

For instance, since fire and the like have already fulfilled their purpose in performing another action, fuel and the like would still be perceived from them just as before, because they have not ceased [to exist].
If it is argued that this is not so because destruction arises through the annihilation of those [causes], such as fire;
How is that [fuel] destroyed? It cannot be by way of absolute non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*),
because that [non-existence] is absent at the time when the fuel exists.
Not by fire and so forth,
because their function is admitted to consist solely in the manifestation of destruction;
nor does the produced non-existence through destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva) destroy the fuel and other such things.
Because it would entail the consequence of simultaneity; and because, even if destruction were caused by annihilation (*dhvaṃsa*), the threefold dilemma would remain as it was;
and consequently, there would be an infinite regress.
If it is argued that this very destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of fuel and so forth, produced by fire and the like, is the cessation [of those things], and therefore there is no perception of them;
how then can one thing be the cessation of another?
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument].
Furthermore, if this [self] possesses causes, why does it not experience a difference in its own nature according to the difference in those causes?

Even sprouts of rice, barley, and so forth, which experience a difference in their own nature that is utterly distinct due solely to a difference in their causes, are determined by direct perception itself.
Destruction, however, is not like that; it does not involve the association with another entity, but is characterized merely by the passing away [of the thing].

Even though its causes—such as impact or contact with fire—differ, destruction appears within the cognition of itself as having a single form, because its nature is sheer non-existence (*tuccha*). Indeed, apart from the voidness of the entity, we perceive no other form therein.
This has been examined in detail in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi*, so let it suffice for now.
Therefore, at the time of contact with fire and so forth, it is logical to accept that "nothing happens to it; it simply ceases to exist.
For this [entity] is not called "destroyed" by virtue of becoming something else, but rather, because it exists as inherently unstable in nature, it is therefore called "destroyed."
Therefore, for this [entity], there is no other existence or anything else whatsoever.

And thus, since there is no such thing as something possessing the nature of coming into being (*bhavana-dharman*) that could be produced from somewhere, the conjunction with fire and so forth would merely be a negation of action (*kriyā-pratiṣedha*).

Such being the case, since the conjunction with fire and so forth does not become an "agent" (*kartṛ*), it follows that what is not an agent is not a cause; therefore, there is no cause of destruction whatsoever.
[14. The impossibility of a cause for destruction even on account of its futility:

Not only is a cause for destruction impossible due to incapacity, but also "due to its futility. He says this very thing: "If it were perishable by its own nature"—that is, if it were of a nature to perish, unable to remain in itself, like a mustard seed on the point of a needle—"for that [entity], there is no..."
“By some causes of destruction”?
What is the reason?
“Because it perishes by itself.”
“Precisely by virtue of having that as its nature” means precisely by virtue of having an unstable nature.
For indeed, when something is inherently incapable of remaining stable, effort toward its stabilization—such as placing a mustard seed on the point of a needle—would not be fruitful.
(Hbṭ 83)

Right here he demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the words “For whoever,” and so forth. “But when that exists”—that is, when there is that very nature—[the effect] does not depend on another cause from the productive cause.
The explanation of the example is provided by the passage beginning with “For illumination and so forth.”

He demonstrates the pervasion—that being of that nature does not depend on any other cause—by means of the proof establishing identity: "Of that which is of that nature" (tadātmanaḥ), i.e., whatever is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of something; [if there were] "in the absence of identity" (tādātmyābhāve) with that nature, then for that which depends on another cause, even though it has been produced from its own cause, there would follow the consequence of "selflessness" (nairātmyasya), that is, the lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā), because it would lack the state of having that very nature.

"Similarly," like light and so forth, "not again" later, "in its state of being that [nature]"—that is, in its nature as having the property of non-abiding—it "requires another cause"; this is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). "If it has the property of non-abiding," meaning if its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is perishable, then "the entity is produced from its own causes by way of its intrinsic nature"; this is the application of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*).
And this is an observation of the pervasion of the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*),
because there is a contradiction between dependence on another cause and independence [from it], since they are defined by their mutual exclusion,
and because being of that very nature is pervaded by independence from another cause.
[15. Dispelling the fault of inconclusiveness regarding the reason that proves inherent perishability:
And here, anticipating the opportunity for an objection from an opponent, he says: "Like seeds, etc. He analyzes this very point with the words:
"It might be argued... they do not produce [the sprout] alone," and so forth.

If it is asked, "Why?"—it is because water, earth, and so forth are required for seeds and the like, which possess the nature of producing sprouts and so on, even though those seeds are distinct from their own causes;
and therefore, once that [nature] has arisen, they do not require any further cause for its existence. Thus, the reason is inconclusive (*anekānta*).

“In the same way, an entity such as fuel, though produced from its own cause as having a perishable nature, would [require] ‘destruction’ for that state of perishability to occur”—this is the application of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*).
[The opponent replies: “No; it is not inconclusive (*anekānta*), like the case of seeds and so forth.
Why? Because seeds and the like, which possess the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of producing sprouts and so forth, do indeed produce sprouts and the like.

This is because, in the case of being that very nature (*tadātmatā*), there is no dependence on any other cause. Furthermore, regarding that which does not produce [the effect] while depending on soil and so forth—as in the state of being within a granary—it lacks that nature; for "that which is non-productive lacks that intrinsic nature" (*ajanakasya ca atatsvabhāvatvāt*), meaning it lacks the nature of producing sprouts and the like.
Therefore, the reason characterized as being that very nature (*tadātmatā-lakṣaṇa*) simply does not apply to such a case, and thus there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) by means of it.
[16. The establishment of a stable, single entity is not possible through recognition, because it is sublated by direct perception.
Now, one might object: "By the very direct perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the seed and so forth are observed to possess a single nature.
In that case, how can there be this distinction characterized by having the nature of producing or the nature of not producing, from which [distinction]—(Hbṭ 84)"
There would not be uncertainty;
nor is recognition (pratyabhijñā) invalid, because it possesses the defining characteristics of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), such as "the cognition of an object not previously known."
Recognition is indeed perception, since it arises from the contact of the sense organs with existing objects and from their actual presence;

and there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) more authoritative than perception, by virtue of which this [recognition] might be rendered invalid through the experience of sublation (*bādhā*) resulting from the establishment of a difference in its object. Anticipating this objection, he says:
Therefore,
precisely because of being a producer and a non-producer, due to the imposition of contradictory properties upon those two states.

In the states of being a producer (*janaka*) and a non-producer (*ajanaka*), a "difference in reality" (*vastubheda*)—that is, a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*)—must be "ascertained," meaning it must be determined.

For instance, a rice seed possesses the intrinsic nature of producing that [specific] sprout, as this is understood through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because the presence of a rice sprout is observed when the rice seed is present;

whereas a barley seed possesses the intrinsic nature of not producing it, as this is understood through the non-perception of the rice sprout when the barley seed is present, by means of a direct perception that apprehends the barley seed as distinct from it.

In the same way, why is it not determined here as well—in these two states—that the rice seed possesses the nature of being both a producer and a non-producer of its own sprout, by the very force of perception which grasps the states of the seed as being distinct from and non-distinct from that sprout?
If it is argued that "the difference between the two states is indeed accepted, but there is no difference in the possessor of the states," we say: no.
For it would follow that the state (*avasthā*) would appear in perception as a distinct form (*rūpāntara*) differentiated from the possessor of the state (*tadvat*).
Indeed, it is not logical for something to possess perceptibility if it does not appear in its own cognition as differentiated from what is not its own nature.
If it is asked: "Since there is no difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) between the state and its possessor, how can it appear as a distinct form?"

Now, if no distinction of form has been acquired by the self from its states, then just as there is a distinction among the states, the non-distinction of the self does not cohere when such a distinction exists.
Consequently, for this [self] which experiences a distinction of selves just like that of the states, how can it possess the status of being the substratum (*avasthātṛ*)?

If it is argued that there is no fault because, despite the difference in states, the self is established as having an undifferentiated form, since there is also some degree of distinction; [we reply:]...
If one were to place this self (ātman) at the forefront [of thought], thinking,
"This is the abider, and these are the states";
Thus it is said; therefore, the difference between the state and that which possesses the state is indeed a difference.
Consequently, the phrase "in some way" (*kathañcit*) is a mere empty word.
Consequently, the undesirable consequence— that it would appear as a distinct form differentiated from the nature of non-self— does not cease even when it is manifest to perception.
If, on the other hand, there were no difference [between the states] and the self,
then the substrate would necessarily be subject to differentiation just like its states.
Or [if it is argued that] there is non-difference between the states and the possessor of those states;
and if it is further argued that even for those two there is some kind of difference and non-difference—
then one would have to accept a distinct nature for those two, which possess difference (namely, the state and the self of the possessor of the state), that is somehow without a cause.
And thus, that [state] also has some kind of difference from those two;

otherwise, because it would be absolutely non-different from their single nature, there would follow the consequence of absolute difference and non-difference between the state and the possessor of the state.
If there is some kind of difference in another form, then there must be yet another form as its basis.
Likewise, for this [cognition] as well, there would follow an infinite number of forms for each single object, since it would have "that" and "the other" [forms].
And we do not experience a perception that manifests an infinite number of forms.
Not experiencing such a thing, how could we deceive ourselves by imagining it?

Therefore, because that which has attained the conditions for perception is not perceived as distinct from its states, and because it would follow that it possesses infinite forms, the substrate of the states—which possesses both difference and non-difference in some respect—must indeed be non-existent. Furthermore, since those states are directly perceived as possessing a distinction in their intrinsic natures (svabhāva) as being productive or non-productive, how can recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), which determines their identity, be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?

For, while experiencing such sublation, [the argument] would result in the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of the previous reason, since even things like seeds, whose natures consist in producing sprouts and so forth, would depend on other causes despite having that very nature.
Let there be some persisting entity; even for that, this very same [argument] establishes its difference.
For instance: "of those two"—referring to the states of being a producer and not being a producer—this is a locative dual. Thus it occurs.

Thus, the meaning is this: the "distinction"—that is, the diversity of intrinsic natures—of the "entity," characterized as the substratum (dharmin), between its state of being a producer and its state of not being a producer, must be "ascertained" through a conventional usage defined by certainty; this is because it is established by perception precisely on account of the [entity's] having the nature of being both a producer and a non-producer.
This is because one observes that the object possesses the characteristic of being superimposed with contradictory properties.
Nor can it be argued that only the states possess the nature of producing the sprout and so forth, while the substratum does not;
for that would entail the non-existence of the substratum, as it would then be characterized by a total absence of all causal capacity.

Therefore, how could that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of entities as having a single form be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), given that it is sublated by the experience based on perception—which establishes the distinction between the natures of being a producer and a non-producer at earlier and later times?

Furthermore, if the undifferentiated form appearing therein is unreal, then even though this [recognition] possesses an operation arising from the sense organs, it lacks the quality of being born from the contact with an existent object; thus, like the cognitions of those suffering from ophthalmia and other such defects, how could it possess the status of direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*)?
Furthermore, apart from the nature that is based on causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), there exists no other ultimate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in things such as seeds,
through the apprehension of which recognition could become a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Since that which exists in the ultimate sense is characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*),

this determination of reality must be understood as purely erroneous— like [the perception of] hair or a plantain trunk— occurring only because the hearts of those whose minds are captivated by mere similarity of form are bound by the production of subsequent similar moments.
Therefore, although there is a difference at every moment even for what exists, it is not perceived by the foolish.

But when, due to the occurrence of adverse conditions, there arises a production of a dissimilar subsequent state, then the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that determines identity does not rely upon actual existence.
Nor is there any other similarity [than this] apart from its being the cause of a cognition that reflects a single form.

And even though the difference [between entities] is no different, it is by virtue of their own nature, acquired through the power of their respective causes, that only some [entities] produce a cognition characterized by a reflective awareness of a single form, such as the cognition of an object and so forth.
The author of the treatise has already explained in the *Pramāṇavārttika* that [only certain things] perform a causal function and others do not; therefore, it will not be elaborated upon here.
Furthermore, since recognition is sublated even by inference, the existence of a permanent entity cannot be established on its basis.

To demonstrate that a difference between entities must necessarily be understood—as stated—between the states of being a producer and a non-producer in the case of seeds and so forth, [the following] inference regarding non-difference is presented:

He states the refutation: because there is no change in the "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) of "entities" (bhāvān), such as seeds and the like, which is that which produces its own effect while they exist, it is impossible for them ever not to produce it; therefore, since that "intrinsic nature"—the nature of producing sprouts and so forth—would result in the "production of its own effect even before," at the time of remaining in the granary and so on, just as it does "later," when the conditions such as water are present.
For instance, even when water and other conditions are present, a seed and the like produce their effect by means of their own nature alone,
not by means of another nature.
And that intrinsic nature of theirs which produces that specific effect—
If it exists even previously,
then because the recognition "this is that very same thing" involves the determination of the identity between the present producer-nature and its former form,
why does it not produce that effect even previously?
The formal argument is as follows: Whatever has the nature of producing something at a particular time, that necessarily produces it at that time;
for it is contradictory for that which is not a producer to possess the nature of being a producer, or else anything else would also incur the status of having that same nature.

For example: even at times when that very seed and so forth are in proximity to water and other conditions, and even while in states such as being inside a granary, this seed and so forth is established by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) as having precisely the nature of producing its own effect; thus, there is the consequence of a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
And it does not produce [it];
therefore, it does not have that nature of producing it.

The application of the contrapositive is as follows: whatever, at whatever time, does not produce a produced effect that has the nature of being produced by it, does not at that time have the nature of producing it.

For example, just as a kodrava seed does not produce an effect that is brought about by the nature of producing a rice sprout, and likewise, prior to the presence of causes such as water, it does not produce its own effect—a seed and so forth—which is brought about by the nature of producing that specific effect; this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
Therefore, since recognition also experiences sublation by means of inference, how could it be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?

But surely, since the inference being sublated by this [perception] lacks validity, how can it possess the power of sublation? And if its status as a valid means of knowledge is not certain, how can there be sublation? Nor is there the fault of mutual dependence.

This inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is invalid; rather, it is so because of its necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with its own probandum (*sādhya*).
And that connection is ascertained by the force of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) in the case of the contrary.
[18. Refutation of the Superiority of Perception over Inference:
If it is argued that there is no means of valid cognition more authoritative than perception, we say:
no, because recognition is not established as being perceptual in nature.

We do not say that this [perception], being of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), is sublated by inference (*anumāna*). Furthermore, on what basis is the superiority of perception established? It is called a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it does not occur when its object is absent; and since this is equally the case for inference—because it is produced from a mark (*liṅga*) that is necessarily connected to the object—it has no distinction whatsoever from the other.

If recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) were to be considered a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) even while contradicting inference, then why would the cognition of a flower that is not blue—not being blue—be invalid, since it perceives its identity based on the similarity of its form?

For the difference inferred from the observation of effects such as flowers and fruits does not experience such a state through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, the detailed refutation of the validity of recognition has already been established in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi*; let this matter rest for now.

“Since it is so,” that is, because there is a difference in the nature of the seed and other things between their states as producers and non-producers according to the manner described, “therefore, that final particular state” immediately after which the production of the effect, such as a sprout, occurs— “that alone has the nature of producing the sprout,” because its nature as a producer of that [effect] is inferred from the observation of the effect.

If, then, that very [seed] possesses the nature of producing the sprout, how can those preceding distinct states— which, by their nature, do not possess that capacity for production— be designated as its causes?
Or why would those seeking a sprout take them up [as the cause]?
To this he says: "But those preceding states"— namely,

those existing at the time of abiding in the granary and so forth— are the "causes" of the final specific state of the sprout's cause, because "from them that [final state] arises" through a succession of particularities imparted by other conditions.
Therefore, in those cases, there is a figurative designation of them as causes, and they are taken up by those seeking a sprout;

for that which possesses the nature of producing a seedling or the like does not depend on another cause, whereas that which depends on something else for its production does not possess the nature of producing it.
"Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness [of the reason] because of its being of that very nature, like a seed and so forth"— this is the conclusion regarding the logical reason.

Thus, when recognition is asserted by others as a means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) for the sake of establishing stability—intending to demonstrate its inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) through examples such as seeds and the like—it lacks the nature of that [perception] because it is sublated by both direct perception and inference in the manner already described. Since this is so, how could there be oneness of entities from which inconclusiveness might arise? This has been demonstrated.

But when others state as a reason that seeds and so forth possess a single nature across prior and subsequent times because they are recognized [as the same], then this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).

For it does not exist anywhere within the subject (*pakṣa*); thus he says: "because there is an absence of identity (*aikyābhāvāt*) in things (*bhāveṣu*) which we maintain to be momentary (*kṣaṇikeṣu*)"—this is the connection [of the words].

[19. The removal of the fault of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) once again regarding the argument "because of having that as its intrinsic nature" (*tatsvabhāvatvāt*): Now, even for one who holds that entities are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), although there is an absence of identity from moment to moment in the case of seeds and so forth, because no distinction is perceived, all of them—even those whose intrinsic nature is to produce [a sprout]—would depend upon water and other conditions with respect to that production, just like the final moment; thus, the fault of inconclusiveness remains exactly as before.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Because of arising from one after another," there is no inconclusiveness even with respect to momentary things.

Since momentary things arise at every instant from various preceding conditions, they possess distinct capacities; therefore, because they lack the nature of being producers [of an effect] like the final moment, how could there be any inconclusiveness on their account either?

For it is not logical that things whose births are conditioned by a diversity of causes should possess an undifferentiated nature even when their specific distinctions are not perceived; otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence of their being causeless.
And as he will state: "..."

"Although conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*), which possess distinct capacities at every moment due to their connection with various successive conditions, appear to be of an identical form because of some similarity, they are nonetheless distinct; therefore, only a specific [factor] is the cause of a specific [effect].
This is as it was stated: "Because it produces that which has its own nature."

Raising an objection against this [position] by pointing out its lack of exclusivity (anekānta), the opponent says: "Those" seeds, soil, and so forth, being "final" (*antya*)—meaning occurring at the end—are individually incapable of producing the sprout;
since you maintain that an effect does not arise from causes taken in fragments, why do they not each produce [the sprout] individually?
Consequently, among these, only one certain [seed] produces the sprout, while the others, though possessing that same nature, do not; this is because it is their very nature to produce [the effect].
Thus, there is an inconclusiveness (*anekānta*).

Similarly, the opponent thinks that the inconclusiveness remains just as it was, because seeds and so forth—even while in states such as being in a granary—though possessing the nature of producing sprouts and so forth, will not actually produce them.
To this, he replies: "Thus" (*iti*)—meaning, since you think in this way.

Because it was stated by means of a general [principle], he gives the reply by means of a general [principle]: "They certainly produce [their effects]"; "here," in the production of their own effects, "there is no possibility of being otherwise," that is, one should not suspect non-productivity.
Why? "Because their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not subject to alteration. For those things which would not produce [their effects] would not possess the very nature of producing them.
The point is this: since those things are held to have that very nature, they necessarily produce [the effect];

and thus, how could there be any inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*)? [This is the refutation of the objection raised by some, who feared that if each individual [cause] were capable of producing the effect, others would be of no use.]

Considering that if each of the final [causes] were individually productive, then since the effect would be produced by one alone, the utility of the others would be rendered objectless and thus they would simply not produce it, the opponent says: "When those final co-operating causes (*sahakārin*)— those whose nature is to act together simultaneously and which are admitted to possess a capable nature (*samartha-svabhāva*),
i.e., to be fit for the performance of that effect— are present, what is the utility of the other [causes], since the effect has already been produced by one alone?"
"Not at all anyone [produces it]. So why is it said, 'they certainly produce it'?"
He addresses this [objection]: "By no means" (*na vai*);
indeed, "sentient deliberation" (*prekṣāpūrvakāritā*), that is, action preceded by intelligence, does not belong at all to "entities" (*bhāvānām*) such as seeds and the like.
"Because," due to acting with foresight, [they think]: "Even this one among us is individually capable of producing the effect;
what is there for us to do here?"

Having reflected thus, [he considers that] "others might desist" and, adopting indifference (*audāsīnya*), would not exert themselves toward the production of that effect. For those entities, such as seeds and so forth, have "operations devoid of intention," meaning their operations are free from deliberation; yet, when an effect arises from one cause, all of them without exception exert themselves toward it.
And regarding an effect that is subject to coming into being, their operation consists precisely in their prior existence,
because anything other than that is impossible.

For if the operation were indeed distinct from the agent who performs it, then since the production of the effect would arise from that [operation] alone, the status of being an agent belonging to the possessor of the operation would be lost.
If it is argued that this [entity] is an agent because it possesses that activity,
then— since the application of activity is metaphorically attributed to it despite its lack of utility for the effect— the entity's status as a real agent would be lost.
Furthermore, what is the relationship between this [entity] and its activity?
If it is argued that [the cause possesses activity] through inherence (*samavāya*), no;
for that has already been refuted.

Furthermore, if [the cause] possesses activity by virtue of inherence, then it would follow that anything else, even if not contributing to that effect, would possess that same state [of being a cause].

If it is argued that there is no over-extension [of the definition] because inherence (*samavāya*), as the cause of the cognition "it is here," is uniform everywhere due to its oneness, and because the production of that operation occurs only through that which is intended and engaged [in the act],
we reply: surely, the production of that [cognition] by means of that [intended entity] is precisely what is called inherence in that context.
And that [effort] is the same in all cases.
Why does it not produce the very effect by means of that exertion through which it generates an operation? For what reason is an intervention resorted to?
And just as this [cause] produces an activity merely by its own presence and not by means of another activity—
since that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress— in the same way, it follows from that very point that the effect [is likewise produced], as has already been largely explained.
Therefore, regarding an effect that is yet to come into being, the very prior existence of the cause constitutes its causal operation.

Since this [prior existence] belongs to all [causes], it is designated that "all" are operative in the production of the effect. Thus, "that effect arises from all [causes]" because its existence occurs only when all [the causes] exist.
For there is no production of an effect other than the very existence of that which is considered its cause;
for if it were otherwise, since the causal operation would occur within that [cause] itself, the performance of the effect by these [causes] would be impossible.
Consequently, even when the causes are present, how could there be the existence or the perception of this [effect]?
If it is argued that [the universal] exists because it causes the birth of its related [particular], we say no; for there can be no connection with that which is non-existent.
Alternatively, if it were existent by itself, the purpose of "birth" would be untenable.
Furthermore, since the self is perceived at the time of birth, it would follow that it must have been perceived even prior to that;
for if it existed in another form [previously], it could not be said to exist [as the same entity],
because a difference in existence is characterized by a difference in form.
Therefore, because it is not perceived prior to its own birth, it lacks existence;
how then could it have a connection with birth?
Consequently, since the effect itself comes into being from a state of non-existence within the causal state, its birth is indeed its very becoming; thus, it is born from all [causes].

If it is argued that since even a single [cause] possesses the capacity to produce that [effect], the operation of others characterized by their mere presence is indeed useless, and thus the existence of others there is not logically consistent, he says: "From its own cause"— that is, from the causal complex (sāmagrī) characterized by earth, seed, water, and so forth— there is a "transformation" (pariṇāma), which is the production of a subsequent moment endowed with a specific quality conducive to the arising of the effect, wherein an excellence is being superadded at every moment.

Therefore, those for whom "proximity" (*upanidhi*)—that is, presence at the place where the task is to be performed—is their "duty" (*dharma*), being thus situated at the place of action, "do not deserve censure. They do not deserve to be questioned with the reproach: "Since even a single one among you is capable of performing this task, why are you all present here?
Thus, they are not subject to such an objection.
For it is not possible for even a single one of them to exist there without the presence of the others.
Why? Because of its "nature" (*tatprakṛteḥ*); that is, because it has that as its nature (*tatprakṛtitvāt*). This is an expression emphasizing the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*).

Since each individual capable factor has a nature produced by the transformation of the totality of causes such as earth, seed, water, and so forth, how could there be the occurrence of any one of them in isolation when those [others] are absent?
Because distinct causes denoted by the term "sāmagrī" (causal complex) initiate their own respective efficient specific characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*),

and because an excellence (*atiśaya*) is thus produced and accumulated at every moment; and because isolated [causes] lack the nature of producing that [result], since the nature of the cause capable of producing it is generated through its conjunction with other conditions.
And this will be clarified in various places as the occasion arises.

Therefore, whatever entity has a nature produced by a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*), that entity cannot come into being even if one [factor] is absent, due to the deficiency of a cause; thus, the coexistence of those things born from a single causal complex is necessary. Since the effect exists only when all of them exist, it follows that all of them together produce it.
"Therefore, because [the effect] is produced from that which has that very nature,
there is no inconclusiveness" (Hbṭ 92).
Revealing the intention with which he asked, "Why do those final [moments], though capable, not produce [the effect]?", he says: "They are capable," and so forth.
The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) also reveals the intention behind his statement that [the causes] "indeed produce" [the effect], as follows: "No,"...
"In that very [text]," and so forth.
He explains this very point with "of that very [thing]," and so forth.
This is the intended meaning: '...'"
"This is capable here; this is incapable"—
thus it is designated through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), which are established by perception and non-perception.

Because there is an absence of any other cause, and because those two—positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—are observed in relation to one and the same effect, and not in relation to various different ones, they are understood to be capable of producing that single effect alone; thus, there is no production of anything else.
Now, when those [causes] are seen producing [the effect], are they at that very moment of the nature of producing it?
Or rather, [does it exist] even before?
On this point there is a dispute.

In that regard, if it possesses that same intrinsic nature even before, then just as [production occurs] later, production would follow even before; thus, it is said that there is a difference at every moment.
[21. The Jains and the followers of Jaimini, who accept that the diversity of effects arises from the diversity of causes, raise the objection of inconclusiveness (anekānta).

Furthermore, in another way, the Jains and the followers of Jaimini, raising the objection of inconclusiveness, say: "From those [causes] such as the eye, which possess 'distinct'—that is, mutually exclusive—'natures' and act as 'cooperating causes' (sahakārin) simultaneously, there arises 'one'..."

When there is the arising of an effect characterized by consciousness, since there are many causes of distinct natures while the effect is a single entity of non-distinct nature, "there would be no difference in the effect despite the difference in the causes.
Consequently, the eye and other [faculties] should not be accepted as producers of a single effect through their own distinct identities.

However, one must admit that these [factors] possess a common nature (*sāmānyabhūta-rūpa*) which is undifferentiated and productive of a single effect, by virtue of which they produce an undifferentiated result.
And that [nature] produces that effect only when in a complete state, not when in a disordered state.
Nor does its absence follow from the absence of any one individual member.
Because it is impossible for that which possesses a universal nature to ever be non-existent;
nor can it then have a non-productive nature,
