for that would entail a difference between its states of being complete and incomplete, as it would possess both a productive and a non-productive form.

And thus, there is a loss [of its nature] through its universal essence (*sāmānyātman*). Therefore, that form (*rūpa*) which is the producer of this [cognition] when the eye and other factors are complete, does not exist even when any one of them is absent; yet it does not produce [the cognition], because production occurs from that which possesses the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of producing it.
"Thus, it is not non-exclusive (anekānta).
[22. The proponent of the established tenet (siddhāntavādin) offers a rebuttal:
The proponent of the established tenet says: "No."
"According to their respective [natures]," and so forth.
He thinks as follows: "What, then, is this cause intended by you?
If it is each individual [sense organ] such as the eye," (Hbṭ 93)
That is incorrect, because an effect has as its intrinsic nature that which is produced by a causal complex (sāmagrī), and it is that very complex which constitutes the cause.

But surely, in that state, since it is admitted that each individual among those things denoted by the term "causal complex" possesses the nature of producing [the effect], the eye and so forth are causes individually.

If this is so, what is this restriction that when [an effect] arises from many, it must be produced by many? There is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for the opposite case; nor do we perceive any reason for a restriction that such an effect must be performed by one alone.
And how is it determined that it performs only a single effect?
If you say, "Because [the effect] exists when that [cause] exists," this is equally true in the case of multiple [causes] as well.
As it has been said: "Those [causes] which are capable of producing that very single [effect] are not capable of producing another; thus, there is no production of a succession of different things.
Nor does it follow that from multiple [causes] a multiplicity [of effects] arises, because for us, unlike for you, it is not the case that the cause itself assumes the nature of the effect.
Since there is a multiplicity of transformations, the effect would necessarily be manifold because it possesses multiple forms.
However, [the effect] arises as something entirely new (*apūrva*) only when certain [causes] are present.
And since that [new thing] exists only when those multiple entities exist, it is called their "effect"; how, then, could the consequence of its being manifold follow?

As for that undifferentiated form which is said to be the producer, since it exists even when [the other causes] are present in isolation and because its nature is to produce that effect, it would follow that the effect must be produced from it alone; or else, since there is no difference in it when others are present, it would not produce it even then.
Therefore, those factors in whose presence or absence the effect is seen to be present or absent are themselves the producers; so how can there be any inconclusiveness?
Now, if it is argued that "there would be no difference in the effect due to a difference in the cause" by relying on the totality (sāmagrī) as the cause,
that is not so.

"According to their respective [causes]" (*yathāsvam*): by way of the distinction between the specific nature belonging to whichever causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is "the application of those particularities" (*tadviśeṣopayogataḥ*). Regarding that effect characterized as consciousness, its "particularities" (*viśeṣāḥ*) are natures differentiated by the differences in the causal complexes; through the application of these—that is, through the operations of the diverse causal complexes—there arise specific natures of the effects. Because of the non-confusion of these, which consist in their mutually exclusive forms, [the effects remain distinct].

Since effects possess distinct forms precisely due to the difference in their causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), how could it be that there is no difference in the effect resulting from a difference in the cause? To illustrate: one causal complex, characterized by mental attention (*manaskāra*), its excellence (*tatsāguṇya*), and so forth, gives rise solely to conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*).
Another [form] has the characteristic of mere mental attention and the sense faculties;
from that, the arising of deluded sensory consciousness occurs;
yet another consists of the object, the sense faculty, and mental attention.
Furthermore, since non-erroneous cognition arises [from these], there is indeed no confusion among the specific natures of effects produced by distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).
Thus, due to the difference in causes characterized as causal complexes, there is a difference among effects.
[Objection: But when cognition arises from the object, the sense faculty, and mental attention, since the object of their utility is one, how can there be no confusion?
Since such a commingling is accepted, there is no fault.
As it has been said: "In that very same [place], by virtue of its capacity," and so forth.
How, then, do they possess the status of being producers of that [cognition]?
If the effect does not differ because of that difference [in the causes],
then how indeed do the complete [causes] possess the capacity to produce distinct effects, such that in their absence that [distinct effect] would not occur?
For their capacity to produce is established precisely by the fact that something arises only when they are present.
In that case, when one or many [effects] arise, it is said that those [causes] possess the capacity to produce one or many [results].
[23. Explaining the distinction among effects even when they are produced by a single causal complex:
Now, if multiple [effects] arise from a single causal complex, let there be a distinction from those produced by other causal complexes; however—
But how is it so with respect to one another?
For entities are held to possess either that nature or a different nature because they are produced from causes that possess either that nature or a different nature.

In that case, when consciousness arises from the eye, visible form, and mental attention, since the moments of the eye and the visible form also exist at that time, they would have the same nature as consciousness because they are produced from causes non-different from those of the consciousness.
Or else, why would it not follow that consciousness itself possesses that same nature? As it has been said:
"Entities that possess a certain nature are born from causes that possess that same nature;
why then is this [object] of such a nature not considered knowledge, since it is produced from causes non-different from those of consciousness?"
This is not a fault,
because they are utilized as the objective cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*) respectively according to their own distinct natures;
for mental attention (*manaskāra*) is indeed the material cause of consciousness.
For the eye, which is capable of producing its own consciousness, the [simultaneous] cause is the auxiliary cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*) at the moment of its arising;
likewise, this should be stated for the other [faculties] as appropriate.
Therefore, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces a moment of the eye is of a different nature [than that which produces consciousness].
And since consciousness and the other [factors] are of a different nature, the difference among effects arises precisely from that difference [in their causes].

This might be argued: if all [effects] conform to the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of the moments of the eye and so forth, then from what does this distinction arise—that in one case it is employed through its status as a material cause (upādāna-bhāva), while in another it is not?
But in other cases, it is by way of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāribhāva*),
because there is deviation or non-deviation regarding its existence depending on whether it imitates or does not imitate the nature of consciousness and so forth.
For instance, consciousness imitates the cognitive nature of mental attention (*manaskāra*),
but not the state of insentience (*jarāḍatva*) and so forth belonging to the eye and other [sense organs].
Other cases should be understood in the same way.

Furthermore, if there is necessarily only the existence of consciousness alone, then the operation belongs to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and not to the eye and so forth.

And when a subsequent moment of the eye arises, it is not from the previously existing eye that the immediately preceding condition derives its status as the cause for the suitability of its own consciousness.
The same should be said for visible form (*rūpa*) as well.

Therefore, even though there is a difference in states, that which serves as the basis for a cognition that apprehends a single form, and which is the cause for the production of effects falling within its own continuum, is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). That which serves as the basis for the arising of a particularity in another continuum, depending on its prior state, is the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*).
And this is the nature (*prakṛti*) of entities, arrived at through a succession of their own causes, by which some effect becomes the basis for the establishment of its own continuum.

And since they produce another [moment] which serves as the basis for the designation of a different continuum, there is no contradiction in the mutual distinctness of the moments of visual consciousness from the eye and visible form, because this is produced by specific internal differences within that very causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
[Thus, even when the causes are multiple, the effect is a single unity; and when there is a difference in the causal complex, there is a difference in the effect.]
Therefore, if "due to a difference in causes"— that is,
due to the multiplicity of causes— there is a "difference" or multiplicity of the effect, then [the reason] is inconclusive because of the absence of an invariable concomitance (pratibandha).
And since that [distinction] is not admitted, there is no harm whatsoever. Now,

if it is argued that the distinction of a cause characterized as a causal complex (sāmagrī) from another complex constitutes the distinction of the effect, and that this is called the effect's having a nature different from those things which are not its causes—
then, since that [distinctive nature] exists here, how could it be that there is no difference in the effect due to the difference in the cause?
With this intention, he says: "No"; [otherwise] there would be no difference in the effect due to the difference in the cause.
Why?
The phrase beginning with “yathāsvam” has been stated.
Demonstrating that both of these [principles] are observed in the case of effects through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says “yathā,” etc.
For, although there is a multiplicity of causes in the case of a jar produced from a lump of clay and so forth, there is no multiplicity of forms [in the effect].
Nor does it have an identical nature with that which is produced by another causal complex; this is the meaning of the example.
In this regard, he first demonstrates its difference from what is produced by another causal complex with the words, "from the lump of clay," and so forth.
Here, [the factors are] the lump of clay, the potter, and the string. (Hbṭ 96)

Causes characterized by distinct natures, when combined with other factors, produce effects—such as bricks and the like—that possess natures different from those produced by other [causes]. When these same causes are complete, they produce an effect consisting of a jar that is indeed distinct from them. For instance, a lump of clay independent of a potter and so forth is observed to produce, by way of being the material cause (*upādāna*), an earthy effect that is distinct from a tree or other things produced by different causes.
Even when accompanied by the potter and others, [the lump of clay] produces a jar that consists of that very nature;

and because it possesses a specific quality imparted by those causes, it has a distinct intrinsic nature from the mere lump of clay and is indeed different from bricks and other such things produced by those same causes.

Likewise, whatever effect the potter and others produce in conjunction with other material causes as cooperative conditions, that is distinct [from other effects]; whereas that which is produced by the lump of clay together with its causes and endowed with the specific qualities imparted by them is of the nature of a jar.
The collective meaning is that it produces an effect.

In this context, the nature of the jar is distinct from the lump of clay; it arises from things such as trees, which do not possess the nature of clay because they do not serve as its material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*). From the potter—acting as a cooperative cause (*sahakāribhāva*) by means of the excellence imparted to the lump of clay as its material cause—it is [produced] "of that very jar."

Because it has clay as its material cause (*upādāna*), that which exists as the essence of clay possesses a "particular configuration" (*saṃsthānaviśeṣa*)—namely, a form such as a broad base and belly. By virtue of having that [configuration] as its nature, its own-being (*svabhāva*) becomes distinct from others; that is, it is different from those things like bricks for which the lump of clay, together with other auxiliary causes, is not the material cause. From the "thread"—that is, from the specific qualities imparted by the causes of the lump of clay, the potter, and so forth—there arises [the cognition] of that very jar, which consists of the particular configuration of clay.

Because the lump of clay and the potter possess the inherent nature of producing it, the jar is endowed with their form; and because those two—the thread and the cause (the potter)—possess specific qualities conferred by the weaver and the potter respectively, they have a distinct nature from their state independent of those [qualities]. Thus, the "nature" of the jar becomes "differentiated" or "separated" from the wheel and other such factors. Therefore, the jar produced by the three aforementioned causes arises with a nature that is indeed distinct from any other single effect or any pair of effects; this is due to the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

Effects are indeed distinct, possessing mutually unmixed natures; thus, the non-confusion of the specific effects resulting from their respective applications is established. Furthermore, because each [effect] follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of its own specific cause existing in that particular state, and because it does not arise piecemeal, even though it is produced by each [cause] individually, in reality, it is not observed when other causes of the same genus as those individual ones are present.
Because that specific quality is observed only in the presence of the other,
those who investigate reality discern: "This [effect] is produced by that."

For this reason (Hbṭ 97), those who seek a specific effect undertake the acquisition of multiple causes through a succession of effects mutually providing assistance, for the sake of bringing about the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) capable of producing the desired effect.

Since it is thus, due to the difference in causal totalities, the effects—characterized as a jar produced from a collection of bricks or a jar produced from a collection of clay—are indeed distinct. Therefore, in the manner described, [the jar] arises from the potter when he is devoid of the lump of clay, being included within another causal totality.
Nothing possesses the nature of clay [as its cause],
because it is only that whose essence is assisted by the cause— the lump of clay— that serves as the specific cause for that [effect].

Nor does the mere clay, existing outside of that causal complex, possess the specific configuration, because it is only the clay assisted by the potter’s material cause that serves as the cause for the effect consisting of that specific configuration.

[25. The unity of the effect despite the multiplicity of auxiliary causes: Having thus demonstrated, by way of example, that the effect is distinct due to the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), he now says—demonstrating that there is an absence of manifoldness even though the auxiliary causes are multiple: "And not of those two," namely the clay and the potter, when they are conjoined and their natures are assisted by one another's material cause (*upādāna*).

That specific capacity which is a distinct fitness resulting from a state associated with other conditions— although there is a difference between its object and the object of any other state, just as it differs from anything else,
so too "there is no difference by way of intrinsic nature" (svabhāva).
“Even in terms of its own nature, there is no plurality,” meaning the effect does not possess a manifold essence.

The specific quality produced by those two—consisting of the particular clay and its particular configuration—is itself distinct from what is produced by other causal complexes; this is its differentiation.
But how is this known?

"Since there is no difference in its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) [between the clay and the jar] other than [the difference from] something else," he says: "Of the clay and the configuration," and so forth.
For if, between the clay and the potter—which exist in those respective states—the object of a specific capacity consists of the specific nature of the clay and the configuration, [then...]
If [the clay] were distinct from that [other thing] by its own nature, as if it were something else, then— due to the lack of mutual identity between the clay and the configuration,
that is, because they would lack the nature of each other— the clay would not appear through the specific configuration,
nor would the specific configuration appear through the nature of the clay.
Just as it does not appear in the form of something else; for that which is not the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of a thing does not manifest in the cognition apprehending itself in that [other] form,
just like color in relation to taste.
Alternatively, it is logical that cognition, arising through the power of an object that lacks such a form, should conform to that form;
for otherwise, the consequence of its being erroneous would follow, and by virtue of that, the non-establishment of the object would result.
Therefore, clay and its configuration possess an identical nature; thus, it is not an absolute rule that because the cause is manifold, the effect must also be manifold in nature.

Since it is contradictory for a single effect to arise from cooperative causes such as the eye and so forth which possess distinct intrinsic natures, one must either accept that they perform a common action toward a single effect by virtue of having a single form, or that they produce a common effect despite having distinct forms.
And this "agency toward a single effect" is stated with reference to a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), however, because that which is included within a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) initiates another moment of its own kind, and because it is also a constituent of another complex, it produces other effects as well; thus, just as there is nothing whatsoever produced by a single condition, so too is there nothing produced by multiple conditions.
Therefore, even if one accepts that the multiplicity of causes results in the multiplicity of effects, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Therefore, if one were to entail multiplicity based on their having a single function, there would be a fallacy of doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekatā*);
furthermore, if the proof is made in a general sense, it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
[This concludes the refutation of the position—accepted by the shameless ones and others—that substance and its modifications are both different and non-different.]

But surely, even if clay and its particular configuration possess a single nature, the shameless ones (ahrīka) and others maintain their distinction based on differences in number and so forth; how then can this serve as an example for the unity of that which is produced by multiple conditions?

For in all cases, the distinction between substance and mode is maintained through differences in number, name, characteristic, and function, while their non-distinction is maintained through the identity of place, time, and intrinsic nature.
As in the case of a jar and its color and other qualities.
For instance: "one jar" versus "many colors and so forth" is a difference in number;
"jar" versus "colors and so forth" is a difference in designation.
Substance, characterized by persistence, is eternal, whereas particularities, characterized by exclusion, are momentary; however,
for the follower of Jaimini, some [particularities] also endure for a period of time— such is the difference in their definitions.
The fetching of water is performed by means of a jar, whereas the coloring of an object is performed by means of its color and other qualities; thus, there is a difference in their effects.

In this way, in all cases, there is a difference between substance and mode (dravya-paryāya) in terms of number and so forth, but non-difference in terms of location and so forth. Therefore, because clay and its shape are in some sense different, the effect produced by both the clay and the potter is indeed manifold.
However, just as there is oneness [of the effect], so too its production from a non-different nature by those two [causes] means that whatever has multiple causes is indeed multiple;
whereas that which is single is a single cause precisely because it is produced from a non-different form of its auxiliaries—thus, there is no deviation [in the rule].
(Hbṭ 99)

That is incorrect; for if a difference [between them] is not admitted by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then difference cannot be established otherwise, since there is no contradiction in a single effect arising from multiple causes.

Or, if a difference by way of intrinsic nature is admitted, then it would be difficult to avoid the consequence that the shape and the clay—being mutually identical with one another—would fail to appear as distinct through their respective specific natures of shape and clay.
For if there were no difference between the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin) by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
then there would be no difference even due to differences in number and so forth;
for numbers and the like, even when they differ, being of a different form, are not capable of subverting the non-difference that constitutes their own essence.
To begin with, a difference in number is incapable [of establishing a distinction],
because we observe the usage of the plural even for a single substance,
as in the case of "the teachers" (*guravaḥ*).
Nor can it be that form and so forth (*rūpa-ādi*) are the cause here simply because the plural number is not invariably observed;
for if form and so forth were the cause, the term "teacher" (*guruḥ*) would never appear in the singular.
If it is argued that only the possible nature of the substratum (*dharmin*) is intended to be expressed, we say no.
If one intends to express that [substance] as a unity, there would follow the undesirable consequence that neither its entirety nor its weight would be apprehended.

Furthermore, since the word "rice grains" (*vrīhayaḥ*) expresses a genus (*jāti*), it does not denote the substratum (*dharmin*) nor its qualities such as color and so forth; thus, no answer is forthcoming.

Moreover, since a real entity (*vastu*) which possesses both forms is what is denoted by the word "heavy," how can there be an intention to express the form of the substratum—which exists therein—as a unity?
Furthermore, because the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) seen in the expression "one teacher" (eko guruḥ) shows that synonyms also fall within the scope of the number one,
and yet those synonyms differ in their specific forms,
how can difference be established on the basis of a difference in number? Thus [the objection].
A name, too, is based on convention,
and since its application depends upon the will [of the speaker], how could it be the cause of a difference in objects?
Furthermore, since we observe different names applied even to a single thing, how can it serve as the cause for differentiation?

If it is argued that, just as in the case of "Indra," "Śakra," and "Purandara," a distinction in powers is understood here from the acts of ruling (*indana*), being able (*śakana*), and shattering (*dāraṇa*), we say no; for the entire [set of names] refers to the performance of a single effect.
For it is not only the power that moves, is capable, and tears asunder;
what then?
The substratum itself also [possesses these qualities].
This is because those two are admitted to have a single intrinsic nature (*ekasvabhāva*),
and because words such as "is able" (*śaknoti*) are observed to be used in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with terms expressing that [nature].
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to assume a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) on the grounds that they are the objects of a cognition whose occurrence is unerring (*askhalad-vṛtti*).
And regarding those synonyms for which there is not even a slight correspondence in meaning, what more need be said?
Furthermore, a difference in defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*) is not a valid reason [for proving difference], because it is unestablished (*asiddhatvāt*).
For no single entity is established anywhere as being a persisting concomitant (*anvayin*).

For instance, substance is not accepted by the shameless as eternal by way of unchanging permanence (*kūṭasthanityatā*), because they admit a permanence consisting in transformation (*pariṇāmanityatā*);
and that [transformation] occurs through the continuous succession of preceding and succeeding moments.
For its destruction does not occur in the same manner as that of the modes;
rather, it is accepted that the substance is eternal because it is held that only the modes cease in their mode-form, while the substance does not.
Furthermore, this kind of immutable eternity is not possible in the case of a substance.
Since a substance distinct from its modes is not established— because such a substance, even if it met the conditions for perception, is not perceived apart from those modes—
the notion of a "substance" among the modes themselves, which perform similar forms of functions, belongs only to those of dull intellect;
it is not perceived as something distinct from them.

However, the distinction of effects is indeed unestablished for us, because certain [qualities] such as color-form (rūpa) and so forth themselves perform those functions. Nevertheless, even while granting this, it is said: "For an effect is of two kinds."
[The relation] is both of different times and of non-different times.
In that regard, that which exists previously would be the basis for differentiation if it were possible here;
however, that is not possible because the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin) are simultaneous.
However, [the reason] "having the same time" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) regarding a difference in effects,
because it is possible in the case of cloth and other things that possess distinct transformations;
for cloth and the like, though possessing distinct transformations, are observed to produce multiple effects.
Nor do they differ in their nature as substrata (*dharmin*),
because there is no contradiction in a single entity performing multiple actions;
for in this case, it is not the cause itself that assumes the nature of the effect.

Since, if a single causal entity were to assume the nature of a single effect, it would lack any other form and thus could not assume the nature of any other effect; rather, an effect is something entirely new that comes into being where it previously did not exist upon the presence of something else. In that regard, when the object, the sense faculty, and mental attention—each possessing distinct forms acquired through mutual contribution—are present, and a specific moment arises as distinct from others, there is the admission of multiple functions because each conforms to the presence and absence of those [causes].
It is not contradictory;
for even in the case of a single action, the fact that it is permeated by the existence of that [nature] is the very basis,
and that [basis] remains the same even in the case of multiple actions.
But surely, since the effect characterized as consciousness occurs in their proximity, their very nature of producing that [consciousness] is established,
because a cause exists in a generative form in dependence upon the nature of its effect.
Therefore, how could another effect possibly arise from those [atoms], each of which has the nature of producing consciousness?
Or, if that [consciousness] were present, they would have the nature of producing something other than that;
consequently, they would not produce consciousness at all,
because their nature would be to produce something else.
This is not a fault,
because they possess a nature capable of performing multiple functions.
For instance, in that state, each of them consists in the production of a specific moment of its own kind as well as other moments.

Because their very existence is observed to be immediately followed by that [cognition], it is precisely the nature of producing consciousness that is established; thus, its nature of not producing [consciousness] is excluded, since that alone is the counter-correlative (pratiyogin), and not the nature of producing anything else.
Nor does this imply that they possess a manifold nature.
Because a single unique essence (ātma-atiśaya) is the cause of multiple effects;
for an entity, when expressed by multiple words based on its exclusion from others, does not thereby acquire a multiplicity of forms,
since it is that very same distinct singular essence which is thus designated.
For example, [the statements] "form is visible" and "form is resistant.
In these cases, the words are not based on a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
because that would entail the impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
If it is argued that there is no fault because those causes exist together in one place, we say no; for it is impossible for them to be so unless they depend on that single [effect],
and if they do depend [on it], how could a single [cause] not produce multiple effects?
If it is argued that this is because [the cognition] functions through multiple selves, we say no;
for the fault of the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) would remain as it was.
Furthermore, we do not perceive any difference in the nature of blue and other such objects through direct perception.
Nor can the difference in the self be inferred solely from the difference in effects,
because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) and because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend such a connection.
This is because, through direct perception, even entities that have multiple effects— such as lamps and the like— are observed to possess a single nature;
nor can it be established through inference,
because even in that case there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary.

Furthermore, if one does not admit that a single entity performs multiple functions, then this observed regularity of the coexistence of specific forms, tastes, smells, and tangibles in certain instances would not exist;
for it is impossible for things with distinct causes to be subject to a rule of coexistence.
Moreover, even for those causes themselves, whose arising depends on that same single cause, a fixed concomitance is impossible.
If it is argued that there is a rule of coexistence in one place because they possess the nature of a single substratum (*dharmin*), we say no;
for the very fact that a single thing possesses multiple natures is what must be examined.

Furthermore, since [the cognition] experiences a single nature through many [aspects], multiplicity would be difficult to avoid in that case as well; otherwise, how could there be a distinction between properties (*dharma*) and the property-possessor (*dharmin*)? (Hbṭ 102)
Is the difference not absolute? For instance, when this substratum (dharmin) and these modalities (paryāyas) are established by taking a certain self (ātman) as the basis,
if there were a difference [between them], then there would indeed be only difference.
Even for multiple [causes], there would be no single effect;

for it is not logical that the object, the sense faculty, and mental attention—being independent of the mutual assistance provided by their respective material causes (*upādāna*)—should simultaneously initiate a single effect.
Nor does any single thing ever produce anything anywhere.

Consequently, the very relationship of cause and effect would collapse everywhere, because a plurality cannot produce a unity and a unity cannot produce a plurality, and because there is no other possible mode [of causation].
Nor is the universe without a cause.
Because of the necessity of place, time, and nature,
there is therefore a restriction on the coexistence or the restriction on the performance of a single effect only for those things whose arising depends upon the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Consequently, how could a single entity— which simultaneously assists its own moment in the continuum and another material cause— not have multiple effects?
Then, how could a distinction [between substance and modes] be postulated on the basis of a difference in their effects?
And how can one who proclaims that substances and modes possess a single nature not be considered insane for rejecting the fact that a single entity has multiple effects?
For it is the very nature [of the entity] that constitutes its reality.

Otherwise, it would follow that it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). Furthermore, if substance and its modes (*dravyaparyāya*) were of a single intrinsic nature, then the difference in their effects would be based solely on a single entity; thus, one who asserts a distinction based on the difference in effects is clearly shameless and deserves to be ignored. [27. The objection raised by the Vaiśeṣika—that a single thing cannot produce multiple effects—is also not tenable.]

Even the Vaiśeṣika, by asserting that a single substance is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of substances, qualities, and actions, and by rejecting the notion that a single action can be the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of conjunction, disjunction, and impression— thereby performing multiple effects from a single [cause]— is struck down by the very wrath of his own established doctrine (*svakṛtānta*).
Nor is a difference in potency (*śaktibheda*) the basis for this [distinction].
Since these powers are independent of any single auxiliary cause, how is it that they are restricted to specific substrates?
Why, then, do they not pervade all individuals without exception?
Therefore, it must be due to some excellence within its own nature that this [entity] possesses the assistance of multiple powers.
Therefore, even the performance of multiple effects arises from that very same source;
so, enough with this overly prolix discussion.
[28. Refutation of the claim that non-difference in place, time, and intrinsic nature establishes non-difference.]
Furthermore, the non-difference that is asserted on the grounds of the non-difference of place, time, and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is likewise untenable.
To explain: even if place and time are non-different, color, taste, smell, and touch differ in the form of their respective modes (*paryāya*); therefore, how can non-difference be established?
As for intrinsic nature, if it consists of both continuity (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), then it must belong to each of the two—substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*)—individually.
In that case, there would be two distinct entities, like a jar and a cloth, rather than a single entity possessing two forms; how then could non-difference be established from that?
Furthermore, it is not logical for persistence and exclusion to be the very nature [of a single thing].
Because those two depend upon the persisting and the receding [respectively],
one must state that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the persisting and the receding is something other than them;
it is not the case that their very persistence and recession constitute their intrinsic nature.
Because being (*bhāvatva*) is dependent upon that which exists (*bhavitṛ*);
for memory is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the rememberer.

Furthermore, if both persistence (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) were the intrinsic nature, then a distinction between the intrinsic nature and its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) would have to be stated.
If it is argued that the nature [of things] consists in their being clay and so forth,
and if by "non-difference" in this context you mean similarity,
then that is possible only where there is indeed difference.
Because similarity has as its locus that which is similar;
consequently, there would be only two distinct entities, rather than a single entity possessing two forms.
Now, if it is accepted that identity consists in the absence of a second form—that is, non-difference—then how can there be a state of having two forms?
For here, by the word "form" (rūpa), intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is denoted. And if that [nature] is one, how can there be a twofold form?
For it is a contradiction to claim both oneness of intrinsic nature and a twofold form.
Furthermore, if oneness is not accepted by way of intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
how then can that which is manifold be called "one"?
It cannot be so because of being produced from a single cause.
Because a difference in causes is established everywhere through the distinction between the material cause (*upādāna*), the efficient cause (*nimitta*), and the instrumental cause (*kāraṇa*);
nor [is it established] by virtue of producing a single effect,
since even for a single [cause], a distinction between effects is admitted based on whether their transformation is differentiated or undifferentiated.
Nor can there be identity [of all things] on the grounds that they are denotable by a single name, because even a single thing can possess multiple synonyms;

and because of the capacity [of language], since it is impossible for everything—whether produced or unproduced—to be denotable by a single name in every instance. Furthermore, this has been stated in response to one who asserts a difference of objects based on a difference of powers.
Nor is it one because it is the object of a single consciousness, since even in a single instance multiple cognitions may arise.
For example, many people behold the rising of the moon; how then is its oneness admitted?
Furthermore, since it is possible for many things—such as blue, yellow, and so forth—to be the objects of a single cognition, it would follow that they are one and the same.
Thus, the claim that a single entity possesses two forms does not cohere in any way whatsoever.
Rather, a cognition arising as a reflection of blue is designated as distinct by way of its exclusion from the appearance of yellow and other colors.
Furthermore, it does not possess two forms in reality.
Rather, because substance and mode are fused together—like the man-lion (Narasimha)—it is said to have two forms due to its variegated nature.
That is incorrect.
Because it is not established that Narasiṃha has a variegated form;
for he consists of an aggregate of many atoms,
and those atoms individually do not possess the form of Narasiṃha.
Its upper portion is in the form of a lion,
while its lower portion is in the form of a man; and it constitutes a distinct species from both the human and the lion.
It is not of a variegated form;
for a variegated form is called "mixed," and variegation consists in having diverse intrinsic natures.
And how can there be unity when there is a diversity of intrinsic natures?

Thus, this is merely a delusion of the dull-witted, caused by the observation of a single function among many things—such as the conventional usage of "army" and so forth—even though there is multiplicity.
Therefore, in this way, direct perception is first shown to be no proof for establishing the unity of place, time, and intrinsic nature.
Even when combined, they are subject to deviation through their various modes (*paryāya*).

For instance, the modes possess identical location, time, and intrinsic nature, yet they differ in the form of the modes themselves; furthermore, because of the previously stated refutation of both property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*), the doctrine of both [substance and mode] is impossible.
[29. Refutation of the Non-absolutist Doctrine of Substance and Mode (*dravyaparyāyānekāntavāda*)]
And it is said:
"Because it consists of substance and mode, an entity is indeed twofold in form; even though these two are of one essence, they are distinct by virtue of differences in designation and so forth. (1)
For the object of words is not at all the form of a real entity that appears in sensory cognition;
so by what [reasoning] could there be a distinction based on a difference in names? (2)
Likewise, because of such statements as "being solely intent upon the ultimate reality," [the object] does not appear in the cognition of one whose eyes are not engaged with the word. (3)
Regarding the object, just as in the case of perception, those words have a conceptualized domain;
for if the distinction of that [object] were due to a difference in names, it would belong only to the conceptualized.
There might be some distinction in terms of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*),
but in no way could there be one in the thing itself (*vastu*).
Even the distinction in number is not considered anything other than a distinction in verbal expression. (5)
Even from that, the distinction could somehow belong only to the imagined [nature],
according to such statements as "words are dependent on things," but not to the real thing itself.
Non-destruction is persistence, while destruction is said to be cessation. If modes are perishable while the substance is indestructible, how can they be of the same nature as it? // 7 //
If they have perished in the form of their successive states while remaining in their substantial nature, what other form do they possess? If not, how can there be such a thing as destruction?
If the substance persists as the self, then those [qualities] that arise later would also have that as their essence;
even if there is the superimposition of contradictory properties, by what [means could they be distinct]?
And what is that which is real, from which [it arises]? // 9 //
In that case, synonyms are postulated if a form of difference is intended;
for a synonymous form would indeed be distinct [from it] only if it were different from the form of the substance. (10)
In that case, this might be so; however, if there were non-difference, this statement would not be applicable:
"One thing would result in being both born and unborn, and both destroyed and undestroyed. (11)
When it is accepted that substance and mode possess a single nature, there can be no distinction between the two on account of a difference in their characteristics. (12)

If there were a difference between those two [cause and effect] due to a difference in their effects, then because of the non-difference of their intrinsic nature (svabhāva), there would be no difference [between them]; such being the case, there would be no distinction.
Why is difference not proclaimed as being due to the very difference in intrinsic nature? For a difference that arises later cannot be the differentiator of those effects. (14)

Since intrinsic nature is also an effect, it cannot be subject to a cause of destruction; furthermore, if these two were absolutely distinct, they would be two separate entities, and that [intrinsic nature] as well. (15)

By which of the two [is it established]? Since that which is non-different from two distinct things cannot itself be divided, if it is argued that the non-difference of those [two] is established by means of this non-different [entity], then: (16)

If another intrinsic nature were to be postulated for that [first nature] as well, in order to establish its non-difference from it, yet another intrinsic nature would have to be postulated; thus there would be an infinite regress. (17)
Furthermore, the infinite nature [of the object] does not appear in a cognition that arises through the power of the object, such that one could accept it as being so. (18)
If there were absolute non-difference between two things that are distinct from one another, then difference itself would dissolve, because of their non-distinction from that [single] unity. (19)
If non-difference is not relinquished, then difference must be a product of conceptual construction;
or, if that [difference] were not false, then there would be falsity even in the absence of difference. (20)
Since the existence of one thing among those whose nature consists of mutual exclusion is caused by the non-existence of the others, therefore a single entity cannot possess a dual nature. // 21 //
Furthermore, if the modes were of the nature of mutual non-existence, they would not be distinct;
otherwise, how could the substance remain undestroyed when they are destroyed? // 22 //

Why is immutability not accepted as permanent in a substance, while momentary destruction is accepted in its modifications? If you say it is because of contradiction, then the very definition of "modification" is not accepted [by you]. (23)
In that case, why is a single universal, which follows after all individual instances, not accepted?
And why is there no oneness between the mother and the wife? // 24 //

Furthermore, why would the faults already stated regarding difference and non-difference not apply to those two [if they were accepted]? Why would those faults that attach to each individually not also apply when both are present? // 25 //
If jaggery were the cause of phlegm and ginger the cause of bile, then this preparation known as *guḍanāgara* would be something entirely different, arising from those two roots combined. (26)
For not everything that is sweet is a cause of phlegm, as is the case with honey; nor is everything sharp considered to generate bile, as is the case with *māgadhikā* (long pepper). // 27 //
Why is it not observed that whatever is the cause of each [humor] individually is of a mixed nature by its own essence?
For example, a bean (*māṣa*) is both unctuous and hot, yet it produces phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*). (28)
And the effect would depend upon capacity, being bound solely to the qualities;
for since those [capacities] are absent everywhere, only a specific thing [would produce] a specific [effect]. (29)
How could the faults that are possible in the case of mere difference or mere non-difference apply here?
A wise person would say that even if those [faults] were present, they would not occur in this case. (30)
Even if a fault were not produced due to the presence of its opposite, it would not cease; for as long as that [fault] exists, its very nature does not depart, even if it is undesirable. (31)
Only parts appear as they are situated in such-and-such a way; however, no possessor of those parts ever appears as something partless. (32)
Mutually dependent upon one another, they remain fixed in their respective forms;
yet, by the power of karma, they exist inseparably.
Those entities which, by their configuration, bestow pleasure or pain upon living beings are indeed produced by [past] actions; for they are inseparable from those very actions.
And these [particulars] might somehow be denoted by a single word, but they are not non-distinct;
furthermore, the referent of a word does not appear in the cognition of a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). (35)
For those very [entities] are understood from words even when their forms are indistinct;
therefore, with what could there be a conceptualization of them as being either different or non-different? (36)
And how can it be accepted that that which is indivisible possesses parts occupying multiple distinct locations?
If you say it is because of perception, [we reply] that perception experiences the destruction of things in every moment. (37)
If those successions which are perceived as possessing stability and joy are thought to arise from another means of valid cognition, then any sublation [of that claim] here would be equal to it.
Because they are not distinct from one another, difference and non-difference between those two are necessarily absolute;
or else, the difference between the property and the substratum is fixed as being mutually exclusive.
There would also be a difference between those two [modes] if there were a distinction between them by way of their own nature;
that is, if the distinction between "mode" and "substance" existed by way of that very nature.
In that case, there would be only difference; for a single entity cannot possess two natures.
Nor is there anything else here [in this world] besides the forms of substance and mode. (41)
If an intrinsic nature were to arise from a cause, there would be a conceptualization of identity between the two;
for if they were non-different, it would follow that the [nature] loses its own self-nature. // 42 //

If its difference from those two [the property and the substratum] is also [due to them], and if that substratum and that property are such that their difference consists in the very nature of the one being other than the nature of the other; (43)
If, on the other hand, even in that case, a difference distinct from them is postulated for the sake of establishing their non-difference, then the same reductio ad absurdum as before would apply.
"In that case, its status as a subject (dharmin) would likewise depend upon those two [the property and the locus], because it is dependent on them.
But this is not understood; therefore, this argument is devised by a fool.
Enough with such extensive talk.

Thus, since clay and its configuration possess a single nature, no difference between them is possible in any way; therefore, even though the auxiliary causes are manifold, the effect is not manifold—this is the illustration for this point. [30. This is an allusion to the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) formulated by the Vaiśeṣikas regarding the non-difference of substance and quality.
Here, having raised the Vaiśeṣika position as an objection, he says: "It is indeed something else," and so forth.
“Configuration” (*saṃsthāna*) is said to be the arrangement of parts; and since that is characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), it is of the nature of a quality (*guṇa*).
Therefore, it is distinct from the substance of clay, because substance and quality possess unmixed natures.

Therefore, if it is said that the potter’s activity pertains to the clay-piṇḍa’s nature as clay, while [the activity of the lump] pertains to its specific configuration, then because of the absolute difference between these two, there would follow a multiplicity of effects due to the multiplicity of causes.
To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) replies: “It has been stated in this regard.”

The refutation of the difference in intrinsic nature between clay and its configuration has already been stated in such passages as, “Because clay and configuration are not of the same nature” (Hbṭ 108); therefore, the configuration is not something other than the substance of clay.

Consequently, by means of the potter—who possesses an excellence imparted by the material cause of the lump of clay and acts as a cooperative condition for that causal moment—his own nature being assisted by that material cause, [the jar is produced].

Since the lump of clay, acting as a cooperative cause for that moment of the effect, produces the entire effect consisting of the clay's form in its entirety by itself, there is no multiplicity in this [effect] despite the multiplicity of causes.
To provide further supporting reasons for this very point, he says: "Moreover," and so forth.
If that configuration residing in the jar were different from the clay, then why does the potter not produce it separately?
For there is no necessity for things that are distinct to be inseparable;

moreover, since the potter is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to be the cause of that configuration which is of the nature of a quality, he would therefore produce it even as something separate.
The opponent says: "Regarding the phrase 'of a quality,' etc.:

because of the definition of a quality—'that which resides in a substance, is devoid of qualities, and is not a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions, being independent [of other causes]'—a quality is always dependent upon a substance; how then could it ever be separated from it?"
The Vaiśeṣika himself, anticipating the Buddhist objection, says: “That configuration,” and so forth.

If, by its very nature, that configuration—which consists of qualities—possesses the nature of a substratum because of such statements as “that which has action, that which has qualities,” etc., and if that clay substance, or such a configuration, is essentially contained within the potsherds, then why does it depend upon the activity of the potter?
"Why does it not arise from itself?"—this is the intention of the objector.
Anticipating this objection, the Vaiśeṣika offers the following rebuttal: "No."
Regarding the passage beginning with "tataḥ":

that which is the clay substance and that which is the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) consisting of the broad base, belly, and so forth—the relationship between these two, characterized as that of substratum and superstratum—insofar as there is a "capacity" (*yogyatā*) therein, both of these are obtained from the potter; therefore, it "depends upon the potter."

He states the fault in the absence of dependence on a potter: "Otherwise"—if there were no dependence on a potter regarding the mutual suitability for connection between those two [the lump of clay and the specific shape]—then the lump of clay would, by its very nature, possess the suitability for connection with such a configuration.

And since that [suitability] exists, because the entity itself possesses the essential property (*dharmatā*) characterized by suitability for connection with that configuration, it would follow that even prior to the presence of the potter, there would be a connection with a particular configuration; this is the Vaiśeṣika’s response to the objection.
(Hbṭ 109) [31. Establishing the non-difference between substance and quality.
The proponent of the established doctrine says: "In this way," and so forth.
If [the clay] depends upon the potter for its fitness to enter into mutual relation, then it follows that "this fitness of the clay-substance arises from the potter.
Yet there is no "difference"—that is, no distinctness—in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these two: the clay-substance and its fitness.
For if such a difference were to exist, then the separation of the fitness from the substance would entail the same consequence as before.

Now, if one were to argue that even capacity (yogyatā) is inseparably established from the substance because it is dependent upon what is capable, then— lest its inclusion [in the substance] prior [to its production] be denied on the grounds that it is a property of the thing— one must accept that a further capacity, distinct from the capacity for relation with the substance, arises from the potter. Yet, since that too would entail the consequence of being separable, it cannot be admitted to have a nature different from the substance.
Alternatively, if one were to insist on their distinction, the same objection would apply to that position, and the same response would have to be given again;
thus, due to the consequence of infinite regress, one must necessarily admit that the potsherd and the clay substance, as well as their respective capacities, possess an identical nature.
What is established when this is the case?
To this he says: "There is, first of all," and so forth.

Since the substance of the potsherd, which is capable of being related through a specific conjunction, is produced from the lump of clay and the potter, then it is established that even though a single thing possesses a unitary nature, it may yet possess specific qualities imparted by multiple conditions.
This is our position.
Therefore, why this excessive persistence of ours in proving that clay and its configuration possess a single nature?

If, by relying on functional capacity (*yogyatā*), it is established that there is no consequence of multiplicity for the effect—because it is a unity despite being produced by multiple conditions—then our purpose is achieved.
The intention is that there is no purpose here in refuting the doctrine of substance and quality, since that has already been refuted elsewhere.

Furthermore, by the insistence on [the identity of] clay and shape, their oneness is indeed established through this reasoning: because clay and shape do not possess a mutual nature, it would follow that they would not appear as distinct from the specific natures of shape and clay respectively.

He explains that even though other arguments (*yukti*) are possible, no insistence characterized by their explicit statement is made, because the point at hand (*prakṛta*) is established even otherwise:
[32. Summary of the difference in effects due to a difference in causal complexes, and the unity of the effect despite a difference in causes.]

Having thus demonstrated that, due to the difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), there is a distinction from those things produced by other complexes, and that the unity of the effect is not contradictory even when the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are manifold, he concludes by saying: "Therefore, by the auxiliaries," and so forth.
This means that when there is an accumulation of other conditions, a different causal complex is formed from that which was deficient in them.

And that [effect] produces a distinct effect altogether, different from what was produced by the preceding causal complex; for although the auxiliary factors (sahakārin)— which are the objects designated by the term "single causal complex"— are manifold, there is no contradiction in multiple factors performing a single action,
since we observe a single effect that conforms to their positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), and thus its unity is established by its very nature.

For that reason, conditions that possess the nature of acting together and are included within a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*) do not have "the same object of application" (*naikopayogaviṣaya*) when considered alongside other causal complexes; that is, they do not become those for whom there is a single object of application.
This is because, by the force of logic, it is understood that they have distinct objects of application precisely when considered alongside other causal complexes.
By this, that which was previously conceptualized—

"If by the word 'cause' the causal complex (sāmagrī) is meant, then because of its differentiation, there is indeed a differentiation of the effect from those produced by non-complexes; so why is it said that 'there would be no differentiation due to the differentiation of causes'?"— is concluded as demonstrated by this example.

Now, if by the term "cause" (kāraṇa) one refers to the auxiliary factors (sahakārin) that constitute the scope of the designation "assemblage" (sāmagrī), then it is certainly not denied that a distinction characterized by multiplicity in the effect arises from the distinction—characterized by multiplicity—of those [causes], because there is no contradiction in multiple things performing a single action, and because we observe the production of a single thing from multiple causes. Thus, he concludes the demonstration that clay and its shape are of one essence: [The text continues: "...[therefore]..."
Even though the nature of the effect,
which consists of the form of the clay,
is one;
"Even though there is no diversity in reality"—
that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth— even though they appear as if distinct, like clay and its shape, within the conceptualizing mind.

Having thus established in the example that the difference among effects arises from a difference in their causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), and not a multiplicity of the effect due to a difference in the cognitions directed toward a single complex, [the author] applies this to the case at hand— the eye and so forth— and says: "Just as in this example there is a 'difference of causes,' namely a difference in the causal complexes characterized by a triad consisting of the potter, the deficient lump of clay, and the additional factors such as the string."
In the case of distinct particulars,
which possess diverse intrinsic natures;

Just as the [causal] complexes characterized by bricks and so forth that constitute an undivided jar and those that constitute a divided jar have different functions—and thus do not share a single effect—but rather possess distinct effects;

"in the same way," by that very principle, when consciousness arises from the eye and other [senses], one should infer that the difference in causes characterized by their respective causal complexes results in multiple distinct effects.
Explaining this very point, he says: "For instance," and so forth.

That collection [of conditions] which is devoid of the eye and visible form—consisting of the consciousness characterized as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and depending on other conditions—from that [collection], the nature of awareness (*bodharūpatā*) is perceived as being the material cause (*upādāna*) of consciousness, whether it be conceptual or otherwise; that same [nature of awareness] belongs to visual consciousness as well.
“Of that very same” visual consciousness;
of what kind?

“Of it existing as having the nature of apprehension,” that is, while it is arising, at that very same time, [it arises] together with the visual faculty which is restricted to that same single effect.

Due to the presence of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) which provides its material cause (*upādāna*), there arises from that [condition] "the specific determination of the apprehension of form," meaning the specific determination of the aspect of form;
for it is precisely such an effect— possessing a distinction from the aspects of sound and so forth—
that is produced by the causal complex consisting of the eye together with the immediately preceding condition.

“From the object,” that is, from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) which exceeds the mere object, and from the sense faculty—by means of that object, there is “similarity of form.

This indicates that it is not merely the appearance of a form, as in the case of a deluded cognition; rather, it is the effect of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) characterized by the object, the sense faculty, and mental attention (*manaskāra*).
Any other effect produced by one or two [of these causes] must be understood by oneself.

In this case, although there is in reality no difference [in the effect], the nature of the "effect"— characterized as visual consciousness— is indeed distinct from the individual natures of the "causes"— namely the object, the sense faculty, and attention— even when these causes are taken individually; it is likewise distinct from other things that do not produce it.
These [cognitions], characterized by the nature of awareness and so forth, "come to be.
And because they are considered in relation to what is not produced from them, although they possess a single nature, they are indicated as being many.
Since this is so, therefore, even when there is a difference in causes...

Just as there is no non-difference [of the effect] despite the difference in the conditions included within a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it is not the case that there is non-difference despite the difference in the causes characterized by their respective complexes; for [the effect] is distinct from those produced by other complexes—namely, the "specific effect," that is, the particular effect. "If the effect remains undifferentiated even when there is a difference among the auxiliary causes (sahakārin), then let it remain undifferentiated even when there is a difference in the causal complexes (sāmagrī). Alternatively, if it becomes differentiated due to a difference in the causal complexes, why does it not also become differentiated due to a difference among the auxiliary causes? For there is no distinction [between the two cases].
Thus, that [objection] is refuted.

For instance: due to the mutual approach [of causes], based on specific conditions (*pratyaya-viśeṣa*), and through the mutual assistance of their respective continua directed toward a single effect, there arises from the emergence of cooperating factors (*sahakārin*) with restricted capacities a single effect;
this is distinct from other causal complexes (*sāmagryantara*).

But since distinct effects arise from other causes that are bound by the capacities for producing different effects, and because these possess distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), how can there be an absence of distinction?
[33. Being a producer (*janakatva*) alone constitutes being a substratum (*ādhāratva*), not being a stabilizer.
Now, is it not the case that every effect is common [to many causes], just as derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is?
For it is accepted by you that when [consciousness] arises from the elements, it depends upon those very elements;
likewise, other effects such as consciousness and so forth must also depend on some cause.
Therefore, even this [consciousness] must rely upon some cause.
Furthermore, regarding that cause, its status as a producer occurs first, whereas its status as a substratum for the effect occurs later; it is not a simultaneous act of generation.

Therefore, because [the opponent claims] that [the substratum] generates that very nature [of the effect], the inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) remains exactly as it was. To this, he says: "These very ones" refers to those "distinctions of causal power" (kāraṇaśaktibheda)—that is, the specific powers of causes—just mentioned immediately prior.

Of what kind are they? "According to their own [nature]" means that those auxiliary factors, which are characterized as distinct causal powers, possess an unimpeded power—that is, a power that cannot be obstructed or hindered—in the production of their respective effects, which are distinguished from those produced by other causal complexes; by virtue of this state of having "unimpeded power," they are "present" with a power that necessarily brings about the effect.
Being thus engaged, because there is no such thing as the "effect of a totality" produced by a single condition alone, they maintain that every effect belongs to the totality itself;
therefore, they say that the nature of the effect of a totality depends upon its persistence.
But why is its power said to be unimpeded?
“Because of momentariness.

For the power of that which is momentary cannot be obstructed; for by the time an obstructor exerts itself to produce another intrinsic nature, the momentary entity has already ceased after having performed its own effect.
But how, then, is it logical for a cause that is not simultaneous [with its effect] to be a support?
To this he says: "For thus," and so forth.
Because that effect characterized as consciousness arises from those [causes], such as the eye and so on, collectively, in the form of awareness—
Because it possesses a "distinct nature" from other things that do not produce it— since the effect is not produced in fragments and the whole arises from each individual [cause]— it is born as one;
therefore, those [causes] are called its supports (ādhāra).
For there is no benefactor other than the producer;
nor can that which does not provide benefit be a substratum, as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Therefore, the status of being a substratum for that which exists at a different time is not contradictory.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the primary elements (bhūtas) serve as the support for derived matter (upādāyarūpa), that too is simply their being the producer of it in its own location; nothing becomes a producer first and subsequently attains the state of a sustainer, such that there would be an inconclusive [reason].
[34. The production of an excellence is not "auxiliary causality" (sahakāritva), but rather the performance of a single purpose.

Furthermore, anticipating the opponent’s objection that this is an inconclusive argument because it produces a nature different from itself, he says: “In those whose powers are unobstructed”—that is, those whose power is such that no obstruction or impediment exists.
And the state of having unobstructed power [belongs to those dharmas] because their effect follows immediately;
for while those that, having arisen, produce their effect after a lapse of time might have their power obstructed, this is not the case for those that produce their effect immediately upon arising.

By this, he states the absence of any harm toward things that perish moment by moment. He also states the lack of any benefit: "in those wherein no excellence can be produced. And that state of having no excellence produced is expressed by the term "in momentary things."

For it is not possible to deposit a distinction in things that are momentary, because that which deposits the distinction, being co-existent with them, produces [the distinction] immediately after [the moment],
and at that time, the [momentary thing] has already ceased.

In such conditions as these, what is the meaning of "cooperation" (*sahakārārtha*) among them, by virtue of which they are called "cooperators"? But has it not already been established that there can be no cooperation precisely because no excellence (*viśeṣa*) can be imparted [to the cause]? Why then is it said, "in those whose power is unobstructed"? For one who obstructs the power [of another] is certainly not called a "cooperator."
True;
however, this was stated in order to make it known that [the auxiliary causes] are in every way incapable [of producing the effect].
Furthermore, by removing the obstruction to its power, he refutes the notion that auxiliary causes provide assistance.

Therefore, since auxiliary causes that could impart an excellence [to the entity] are impossible, the capacity to produce for momentary things is strictly dependent upon their own causes alone. And such a capacity exists at all times;
yet, they do not produce [the effect] when alone. Thus, because this nature produces [the effect], it is considered that there is indeed no inconclusiveness [in the reason].

He refutes this: "By no means" (*na vai*) is it the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*) that constitutes joint action (*sahakriyā*), such that in its absence there would be no auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
Where, then, is it not the case that the production of an excellence constitutes the joint action of conditions?
"Everywhere" (*sarvatra*).
Indeed, in no case is a cooperative action characterized by the production of an excellence possible among co-existent things.
What, then, is cooperative action? He says: "The performance of a single purpose," that is, the accomplishment of one effect by "many."
The particle "api" is used in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*).
By the force of logic alone, we conceive of such a cooperative action (*sahakriyā*) in all cases, and not any other.

An illustration of this is: "as in the case of the final [moment] of the causal complex (*kāraṇakalāpa*), that is, the totality of conditions (*pratyayasāmagrī*), for the effect which is the immediately following sprout and so forth."
[35. Performing a single effect is indeed the primary form of cooperation; the other, however, is secondary. It might be argued:

"This cooperation is merely figurative (aupacārika), whereas the production of an excellence (atiśaya) is the primary [form]. To this he says: "That very" [cooperation], characterized by the performance of a single effect, is the "primary cooperation," not that characterized by the production of an excellence.
Because that [final cause] alone is primary;
this will be explained later. Why is this so? He says: "Because that very last one" is the "cause" with respect to the intended effect.
Furthermore, the designation "cooperative cause" (sahakārī) applies to that which is a cause, not to that which is not a cause;
for those things are called "cooperative causes" because they act together simultaneously,
and it is precisely the final collection of causal factors that is of such a nature.

Just as the final [moment] possesses the state of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) by performing a single function, so too should it be understood that the preceding collection of causes—which initiates each subsequent, distinct, and superior moment—possesses this same nature; for the final one is cited merely as an illustration.
Therefore, every effect, such as a sprout and the like, or whatever is characterized by specific qualities, is produced by multiple conditions.

In all cases, the state of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) for a collection of causes that produces effects which increase or decrease consists precisely in performing a single purposeful action, not in the production of a specific excellence (*atiśaya*). It might be argued: "Let there be both the performance of a single purpose and the characteristic of producing an excellence therein as the state of being a cooperative cause. To this he says: "And in that final moment, because it is impossible to produce a specific excellence."
Nor is "cooperation" the production of an excellence [in the cause].
Why is it impossible to produce a distinction? To this he says: "Because the nature of the one, which is partless, is indivisible."

For in that case, there is no distinction such as: "this part has arisen from its own causes without having any excellence produced [in it], whereas this one has had excellence produced by its auxiliary causes."
If indeed there is no distinction [between the two states], why then is a specific difference not produced?
To this he says: "Because the production of a specific quality is characterized by the arising of a different intrinsic nature."
And since there is no division [in the ultimate], how could there be the establishment of another intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
It might be thought: "Let the particularity (*viśeṣa*) of the ultimate be precisely of a different intrinsic nature. To this he says: "Another entity" (*bhāvāntara*), etc.
If the particularity were characterized as another entity...
In that case, its very status as the last would be lost.
If it is asked, "Let it be lost; what is the harm?"—

"And therefore," because of its infinity, "it would not be a direct cause. Since this is so, "therefore there is no production of a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) from the auxiliary causes (*sahakāribhyaḥ*) of the primary cause"; thus, being an auxiliary consists precisely in performing a single purposeful action. Now, one might object: "If no specific quality arises from the auxiliaries, then their capacity to produce an effect is not logical. To this he says: "They are capable," and so forth.

For if they were to arise as inherently incapable, then one would have to admit that their capacity arises from auxiliary conditions. However, those final conditions, being inherently capable, arise together, delayed by only a single moment. Because they are restricted to a single moment, there is no state of existence prior to, after, or separately from them.

And since the effect arises immediately after them, and not after an interval of time, "cooperation" (*sahakāritva*) in such cases consists precisely in the performance of a single purposeful action, and is not characterized by the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*). Thinking that the birth of what is already capable is illogical—because the existence of capacity by its very nature is contradictory [to its being produced] and because mutual dependence is not admitted—the opponent says: "From where does the capable [cause] arise? and so forth.
The proponent of the established doctrine says: "From their own causes. However, this is stated as "by way of intrinsic nature" from the perspective of the opponent's view;
for the opponent [regards] that which has already arisen as being [produced] by another.
The statement "by its own nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*) is intended to negate the claim that a cause possesses efficacy [only] through auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*);
however, nothing whatsoever is produced by its own nature, because that would entail the consequence of it being causeless (*ahetukatva*).
[36. The establishment of the restriction of performing a single purposeful action among momentary entities:
The restriction of performing a single purposeful action is itself untenable for momentary entities, because we observe even isolated [moments] that are similar to the final moment.
For instance, it is distinguished by perception and non-perception as follows: "This is of such a form, and not otherwise.
In that regard, earth and the other elements are perceived exactly as they are when alone, just as they are when in proximity to other causal conditions.
Then [the opponent], thinking that even when they are alone— as if accompanied by others— they would each initiate their own subsequent moment capable of producing a sprout; and therefore,
because even a single [cause] possesses the nature of producing a sprout and so forth, yet does not produce it,
the reason "because that which has such a nature produces [it]" is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), says the opponent (Hbṭ 116).
He says: Why do those [factors], their own causes such as earth and seed, produce this [seed] when it is capable only upon the "presence" (*sannidhāna*) of another condition?
Why not alone?
If it is argued that they always exist only in combination, he replies: "Sometimes," at a certain time, they "might also be otherwise," meaning they could even exist alone.

For instance, it is observed that internal and external factors, when combined with certain others for a particular effect, are seen to produce exactly that same effect even when devoid of those others.
If it is argued, "Let them alone, being capable, produce [the effect]; what is the fault?
