he says: "And therefore," because even single factors are possible as producers of the capable [effect], "even one"—not merely many—[is sufficient].

“If [a cause], being capable and having arisen in a certain place and time, such as soil and seed, were to ‘produce’ an effect, such as a sprout, then that nature must necessarily possess the power of production.

The opponent objects: “But it does not produce [the effect] when alone, even though its nature remains present; therefore, there is an inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) regarding that nature. Anticipating this, the author says: “aparāpara-” and so forth.

Furthermore, through various conditions—such as the rice granary, the effort of the person removing it, the basket, the act of throwing [the grain] into it, carrying it to the field, and scattering it—the "conjunction" (*yoga*) occurs; by that cause, [seeds] possess "distinct powers at every moment. They never possess a single power existing across preceding and succeeding times.
For if they were to have non-distinct powers despite the difference in causes characterized by the conjunction with successive conditions, it would follow that they are causeless.

Furthermore, since even in the case of rice, barley, seeds, and so forth, the difference in capacity is based on a difference in causes; "formations" (*saṃskāra*), being produced by conditions through their meeting and combining, "continuing" (*santanvantaḥ*)— that is, existing as a continuum—
even though they possess a certain uniformity characterized by the production of a conceptual cognition of a single form due to similarity in color, shape, or some other manner.

"Those which have a common form" (*sarūpāḥ*) means they are "similar. They are "perceived," that is, they are recognized. "Nevertheless," just as with artificial and natural gems, pearls, and so forth, due to the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) characterized by distinct conditions for each, their "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is indeed "distinct," meaning dissimilar; it is not non-distinct or of a uniform form merely by virtue of recognition. Since this is so, "therefore" [the following applies].

Because moments are established as having distinct intrinsic natures or distinct potencies, and because they are produced by various successive causal complexes, only a specific thing such as earth or a seed is the cause of only a specific effect such as a sprout, or of that which is capable of producing it;
not everything is the cause of everything.

And thus, for disjoined factors such as soil, seeds, and so forth, there is no inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of producing a sprout, nor is there an inherent nature of producing a capable moment; for that which produces possesses such a nature, whereas that which does not produce lacks that nature. Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) in this argument.
This is because whatever possesses a certain nature arises from its own causes as being precisely of that kind, and it does not depend on another cause for the existence of that nature.
Thus, there would be an inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) here.

Furthermore, since recognition—which has similarity as its object—is sublated by the fact that its nature possesses distinct potencies inferred from the difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), it lacks validity; therefore, similarity is not established on its basis.
And previously [it was stated]: "For this very reason... [the rest of the citation follows].
By the passage beginning with "the difference between the two states must be determined as a difference in the entity," recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) whose object is identity has been refuted;
however, the distinction here is that its object is similarity of nature (*tulyasvabhāvatā*).
This too [is stated] therein:
This has already been stated by the phrase "because of the arising of one after another";
however, it is presented here again for the sake of further elaboration.
[37. Explanation of the determination of the relationship between cause and effect among momentary things:

It has been stated that "only a certain thing is the cause of a certain other thing. Regarding this, in order to demonstrate what is the cause of what—even though such a determination is possible—one says "In that regard," and so forth.
"In that regard" means: among those momentary entities which, at every instant, possess a nature of causal capacity.

"Absence of obstruction" (*avyavadhāna*) refers to that by which something is obstructed; those things beginning with it—such as being too distant or too near—which are absent in a certain location, that is the "location characterized by the absence of obstruction and so forth.

That which has form (*rūpa*) and the sense faculty (*indriya*) as its beginning—namely, attention (*manaskāra*) and the rest—is "form-faculty-and-the-rest. This, together with the collection of causal factors (*karaṇakalāpa*) characterized as a totality (*sāmagrī*), is what is thus described.
This collection of causes— consisting of form, the sense faculty, and so forth, located in a place that is unobstructed and so on— is the cause capable of producing consciousness, and nothing else;
for it exists only when that [consciousness] exists,
and it does not exist even when other things are present.
And because the distinction between the capable and the incapable is based solely on this [proximity],
[the phrase] "of those," namely the sense faculties and so forth, refers to their "mutual approach," that is, their coming toward one another.
By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the removal of obstructions [is also implied].
"Because it depends on a causal complex, there is no contradiction.

Having thus demonstrated this faultless determination of the relationship between cause and effect regarding internal phenomena, he extends it to other cases as well, saying: "By this same principle," and so forth.

This principle of the specific determination of the relationship between cause and effect, which has just been stated, is to be seen as applying "everywhere" (*sarvatra*). By using the word "everywhere," he intends to prevent the notion that this applies only to non-momentary things; thus he says, "at every moment" (*pratikṣaṇam*), and so forth.

One should understand that this specific determination regarding the performance of a single purpose by auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) pertains to those capacities (*śakti*) which, occurring at each and every moment, follow upon various distinct intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-bheda*).
However, this [term "one"] is included so that stability might not be attributed even to those entities imagined by others as having a stable,
unitary nature, since such stability could be designated even in relation to a continuum (*santāna*). The term "stable" (*sthira*) is included because unity also exists in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
[38. The absence of the performance of a single purposeful action in that which is non-momentary:
Why, then, is this not accepted in the case of things that possess a stable, unitary nature?
To this he says: "By its own nature," and so forth.
Granted that an entity might not exist by itself;
however, it is not possible for an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to undergo alteration through its own essence.
Consequently, if a stable object possesses an intrinsic nature capable of producing an effect, then its non-action is untenable, and thus it would necessarily act at all times.
If, on the other hand, its nature is incapable, then too action is untenable;
the implication is that it would never act at all.
As for the claim that [a thing] sometimes acts and sometimes does not, this is untenable.

Consequently, if non-momentary things possess a nature capable of performing that action, then because they would have the same form in both their associated and unassociated states, it would follow that even those things existing alone would perform that action.
Thus, how could there be "cooperation," characterized by the restriction to the performance of a single effect?
On this point, the opponent says: "Accompanied by another," and so forth.
Even though the nature of a non-momentary entity is capable even when alone, nevertheless, it produces [the effect] only when accompanied by another, not when alone.
For this too is its very nature: that—
"One must perform its own function in conjunction with another, even though it possesses a capable nature when alone.
To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) replies: "What [is the point] of the 'alone'? and so forth.

This question is posed by one who considers that the claim "one must perform its own function only in conjunction with another, not alone" is only logical if the thing alone possesses an incapable nature, and not otherwise.
But another, whose intention is not understood, says: "It is capable.
For even a non-momentary entity possesses a nature that is indeed capable; otherwise, its very non-momentariness would be lost.
The proponent of the established tenet (siddhāntavādin) says: "Why does it not act?
For there is no non-action on the part of that which is capable;
as it is logical [only] in the state when it is accompanied [by other causes], one who desires action only for the accompanied must admit that the solitary [cause] possesses an incapable nature.
Now, if it is thought that even if the head of the isolated [entity] were cut off, it still would not act, to this he says "not acting," and so forth.
For capacity is to be inferred from its effect; and since there is never any production of an effect by the isolated [entity], how can its capacity be postulated?
There is no such rule that one whose nature is capable must necessarily produce an effect.
Thinking that [the effect] is seen even otherwise, the opponent says, "The weavers and so forth," and so on.
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin), mocking him, says, "One whose nature is play," and so on. [He means:
"Devānāmpriya" is one who is upright yet foolish, because of being raised in comfort, and thus having a playful disposition.
Playing is the characteristic of a child; by analogy with that, he demonstrates a deficiency in wisdom,
specifically a lack of application toward the treatises due to being raised in comfort.
For one who is unpracticed and of poor intellect, even though a task has been performed, he causes it to be done again and again—meaning he has it re-established—because of his forgetful nature.
Where, then, has this been refuted?
To this he says: "For instance," and so forth.
This has already been thoroughly examined under the introduction: "There is no inconclusiveness [of the reason], as in the case of seeds and so forth.
Thus, if that which is non-momentary possesses a capable nature, there is a contradiction in its possessing a nature that performs an action only when conjoined [with other factors].

Concluding the demonstration that it is untenable for the isolated [cause] to lack activity, he says: "Therefore, because a change in nature is impossible for that which possesses that nature— namely, that which is capable of performing an action— and because there is never an absence of capability, the occurrence of its property— that is, the performance of the action by that which has the property of performing an action— is unavoidable, just as in the final state, as if in the state of conjunction."
[39. Refutation of the Mīmāṃsaka-accepted capacity consisting of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities:
It might be thought: "This non-momentary entity is indeed incapable when alone;
therefore, it does not act when alone."
However, its capacity in the state of association arises from auxiliary factors;
therefore, it is only when associated that it acts. To this he says: "When capacity arises in the final state," of what kind [of entity]? Of one that was "previously incapable.
Regarding "that capacity" which arises for it, if its "having that as its nature" (tatsvabhāvatva) is maintained by the Mīmāṃsakas and others: [the argument follows].
(Hbṭ 120) For they do not maintain that there is a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) between those [entities] and their capacity (*sāmarthya*).
They believe that even if there is some kind of difference between them, it is perceived precisely as having that [entity's] own intrinsic nature.
"That is simply the arising of the unprecedented" means that the arising of the capacity, which has that [entity] as its intrinsic nature, is indeed the arising of a previously non-existent thing.

For it is not tenable that, while possessing a single nature, one [moment] possesses efficacy while the other has newly arisen as inefficient; for this would entail a difference in their intrinsic natures,
since the superimposition of contradictory properties is the defining characteristic of difference.

If it is asked: "But how can the arising and non-arising of the capacity and its possessor, as well as their identity of nature, be denied when they are indeed perceived? We say: No, because that perception is not by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); otherwise, you, who follow what is perceived, would not be able to deny even things such as a double moon.

If it is argued that those [alternatives] are rejected because of the existence of subverting evidence (*bādhakapramāṇa*), then why is subverting evidence not accepted here as well—namely, the mutual contradiction between the arising and non-arising of an entity that possesses a single intrinsic nature (*ekasvabhāva*)? Furthermore, how could one perceive a distinction between earlier and later times for a subject (*dharmin*) such as a diamond or a stone, which remains fixed, if its capacity for that intrinsic nature has arisen? For there would be no appearance of any differentiation between the two times.

If it is argued that because the non-arising or simultaneous arising of effects such as consciousness would otherwise follow, one must conclude that this capacity—which was previously non-existent—arises when the eye and other factors are present, and thus occurs sequentially; then, if this were so, the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) concerning an object under discussion which arises with a single form across earlier and later times would not be accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is because such recognition would experience sublation (*bādhā*) through inference or presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), since it would be grasping stones and the like whose appearance of a newly arisen capacity has been excluded.

Likewise, since there is a contradiction in the identity of nature between arising and non-arising, why is it not accepted that only a previously non-existent entity arises, while the delusion of oneness among those with limited vision is produced by the perception of a subsequent similar occurrence—just as in the case of hair, nails, and the like that have been cut and grown back again?
[40. Refutation of the Naiyāyika-accepted capacity consisting of the intrinsic nature of entities.]

Now, if the Naiyāyikas and others should think that efficacy (sāmarthya) is merely characterized by the proximity of auxiliary conditions (sahakāri-pratyaya) and thus does not constitute the thing's own nature (atatsvabhāva), so that there is no consequence of the production of something new (apūrva-utpatti), [the author] says here: "If efficacy is held to be non-natural (atatsvabhāvatve), then that entity, such as a seed, would remain non-productive even afterwards, just as it was before, because it has not abandoned its previous form."
Why?

Because the Naiyāyikas accept that what is called "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*) characterized by the proximity of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*), and that this very thing is what is denoted by the term "excellence" (*atiśaya*).

Furthermore, it is precisely from that [capacity] that the production of the effect occurs through the principle of "the existence of the effect following the existence of the cause" (*tadbhāvabhāvitva*).

If those auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) were also non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*), then this same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would remain unavoidable even in their case. Therefore, for one who accepts that "auxiliary causality" (*sahakāritva*) is characterized by the restriction to a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyāpratiniyama*), momentariness itself must be accepted.
Furthermore, he states the cumulative reason (*upacayahetu*) to refute the restriction of a single purposeful action among non-momentary things, beginning with the words: "Moreover" (*api ca*).
As for that non-momentary entity which is asserted to produce its own effect when all auxiliary conditions are present, why does it not produce it at that very time?
For by whatever reason it produces it then— namely, by virtue of having the nature of performing that action— it [should produce it] by that same [reason].
Or, because of its stable nature, it would have to act even previously;
therefore, how could there be for it a restriction to performing a single causal function? This is the intended meaning.
Thinking that "what other reasoning is sought? As it is seen, so it is"—that this reasoning is everywhere unimpeded—Kumārila said: "It is seen acting," and so forth.
Since I saw him performing the action at that very moment, we say that "he acts by the power of seeing"; what is the use of stating another justification for this?

Since he was not seen performing that [action] previously, the restriction regarding the performance of a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyā*) is established even for non-momentary things; for an entity produces its effect by virtue of having the nature of producing it, and not by the power of being seen, since it performs its own effect even when unobserved. Therefore, this response is not relevant. Mocking [the opponent], he says: "Oh, what great capacity! and so forth.

Your great power is seen in your great capacity, because of this: even though entities are devoid of the nature of performing an action, if entities were to perform an action simply by virtue of having the nature of performing an action, why was this very answer not stated?

Since the demonstration of the performance of an action has been made the primary point—namely, that [the Lord] "employs" them in various kinds of activities "by mere nature," that is, by the mere existence of their own essence—how is that a great capacity?
Would it not be so?

And I have no intolerance in this matter; however, [the phrase] "if indeed some" reason, by "some means," should "transcend the range of perception" of one who is either disregarded or distracted—[the term] "Your Honor" (*atra bhavataḥ*) being a word of respect (Hbṭ 122)—then "alas" (*hanta*) expresses a manifestation of dejection.

The nature of this [entity] is non-productivity; therefore, this thought of ours—that "this which is of a non-productive nature might [nevertheless] have its continuum departed" (i.e., become active)—afflicts the mind.
The opponent says: "Indeed, we do not," and so forth.
We certainly do not claim that entities devoid of the intrinsic nature of performing an action produce an effect merely by virtue of our perception of them.
However, those entities possess by their very nature the capacity to produce that effect;
therefore, they perform their own function. Observing them, we simply recognize: "These possess the nature of being causal agents."
For the function of perception (darśana) lies in the cognition of an object as it actually exists, not in the activity of a nature that does not exist.
The proponent of the established doctrine says: "True, this too exists.
Do we, out of a fondness for logic, merely observe what is logically consistent?
Furthermore, having become somewhat gratified by the thought that you yourself, though always devoid of reasonable speech, have somehow spoken reasonably, he asks: "What is that?

He says: "The nature (*svabhāva*) of those entities (*bhāva*) is the property of performing an action (*kāryakriyā-dharma*), meaning the property of producing an effect; for that reason, it is not the case that there is a lapse into indifference on the part of those whose auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) are all complete (*samasta*), without their having produced the effect."
It is true that there is no state of indifference; this statement of yours is also logical.

However, you must be asked this: "Does that nature which possesses the property of propelling [the effect] exist for them only at that very final stage—that is, at the complete stage immediately preceding the production of the effect—or did it also exist previously, even during the stage when they were mutually separated?"
In that case, if it has arisen at that very moment with that intrinsic nature (*tatsvabhāvatva*), it is simply a new production;

if it does not have that intrinsic nature, then it is not an agent at all. Fearing the aforementioned faults, the opponent says: "It existed. Why? Because it is both fallen away and arisen; thus, it is "fallen away and arisen" (*pracyutotpanna*).

The refutation of that [position] is as follows: for those entities whose nature is stable, unitary, and neither fallen away nor arisen, it is a contradiction for some previously perceived nature to be absent at any time. For if things were indeed momentary, a nature observed at one time would not exist at another, because in that case, it would be something else.
"Not in the case of stable entities whose prior and posterior forms have neither fallen away nor arisen.
To this, he says: "In that case, what now," and so forth.
It might be thought: "Our statement is not at all similar to this one. To this he says, "Or who [is responsible for this]," and so forth.

If this [statement] were not equal to that, then the meaning of the following assertion must be explained: "Even prior to the state of all the auxiliary causes, this [entity], being by nature non-delaying in its action—that is, having a nature that performs its effect without delay—does not yet produce its effect."
The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that the determination of things as having the nature of being causal or non-causal depends upon the presence or absence of auxiliary causes,

and not upon their intrinsic nature; therefore, even though a thing possesses a single, stable nature that neither perishes nor arises, it does not have the nature of producing its own effect even prior [to the presence of auxiliaries].
But [if it is argued that] it is only when all auxiliary conditions are present; anticipating this view, he says: "Accompanied," and so forth.
He refutes this with: "In that case, another," and so forth.
If it is the case that the combined entity has the nature of producing its own effect, while the isolated entity possesses a contrary nature, why does their difference [of state] occur?
To this he says: "Difference in intrinsic nature," and so forth.

For "difference in intrinsic nature alone is the defining characteristic of difference in entities. If that [nature] differs by way of being of a form that either produces or does not produce its effect, [then there is indeed a difference].
How could there not be a difference in existence, as in the case of rice, barley, seeds, and so forth?

For there is no entity other than its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), such that it would not differ even when that [nature] differs, for that would entail the consequence of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).

Now, it might be argued: "Since it has been stated that there is no lack of both the productive and non-productive natures *per se*, and since the states of being productive or non-productive depend upon the presence of other conditions, how can a difference in the entity (*bhāva*) follow even when those [conditions] differ?
For such a state is characterized by a difference in nature that does not depend on anything else. To this, he says: "For it is not [the case] even in conjunction," and so forth.
This response of yours would be applicable only if the entity—that which is considered another and brought into proximity—were the agent in its own form, and not in its intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).
And this is not the case;
for if that were so, then in ultimate reality he alone would be the supreme agent. In that case, however, the designation of "agency" would be nothing but a construction of conceptual imagination.
Furthermore, causal efficacies do not conform to conceptual construction;
for a young boy is not employed for cooking simply because he is metaphorically designated as "fire.
Consequently, an effect would not depend upon that [cause] which provides no assistance; therefore, it arises from those very things that lack such [conceptual] status.
It would arise from the auxiliary causes;
or else, it would not arise even from them,
because they too would lack agency in their own form, since agency belongs to them only through another form.

Therefore, since all things are thus non-agents by their own nature, they must also be non-agents in the form of others; consequently, there would be a total abolition of agency, and nothing whatsoever would arise from anything.
Thus, the position that "an entity is the agent of its own effect only through its own nature and not through the nature of another" leaves no room for this [opponent's] rebuttal.
Consequently, the distinction that "one is accompanied by others while another is solitary" remains entirely unshakable.

Now, if that very nature by which this [cause] is a producer exists for it at all times, in both its combined and uncombined states, then that nature of this stable entity which produces its own effect must have existed even prior to the combined state— that same nature which possesses the character of non-delayed action during the combined state.
Therefore, there can be no cessation of the production of the effect under any circumstances.

Alternatively, someone might argue: "This [cause], having been produced with its own causes as possessing a nature that generates its own effect while depending on other conditions, does not act when alone;

yet there is no difference in its nature between the states of being accompanied and unaccompanied, because its nature of producing its own effect while depending on other conditions exists at all times. To this, he says: "For even in the state of association... and so forth.

The sense is this: since its agency belongs to its very nature, and since that nature exists even prior [to the causal complex], it is impossible for it to depend on other conditions; for there can be no excellence (*atiśaya*) of the self to be gained from them, as agency is defined by the characteristic of "assistance" (*upakāra*), otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Thus, since the performance of the effect by the solitary [entity] is unavoidable, how could there not be a difference between it when it is acting and its state when it is associated [with others]? This is the intended meaning.

The statement that "its nature is to perform its own function while depending on other conditions" means that for that which is a non-agent by its own form, there is agency at a time characterized by the proximity of other conditions, but not prior to that.
Consequently, by asserting that its nature of performing an action is occasional and not constant, how can you say that its nature of producing an effect is constant?
Surely, in this way, a difference in its very nature between those two times—that [time when it acts] and the other [time when it does not]—would be established.
Therefore, it is established that for non-momentary things, there is no such thing as cooperative action characterized by the restriction to a single purposeful activity.
The opponent, seeking to show that the fault is equal for both sides, says: “For whomsoever also,” and so forth; this is easy to understand.
[The opponent asks: “Even if they are momentary, why does [the same problem] not occur?”
Thus he says: "It has been stated what kind [of entity] performs an action when not separate from its auxiliary causes.
In this context, it is said: "Those final conditions, which are momentary and for which there is no prior, posterior, or separate existence, arise together as being by their very nature capable."

“How can that which exists in a single moment”—that is, whose nature is to exist only in the final moment—"be otherwise"? That is, how could it exist before the final moment, after it, or separately from it? "And that which exists otherwise" does not possess the same nature as that which exists in the final moment—namely, the nature of being assisted by a continuum of auxiliary causes and the property of acting without delay; therefore, this "reductio ad absurdum" (prasaṅga) raised against the non-momentary position does not apply to the position of momentariness.
Why?
[It is said: “Of the agent and the non-agent,” and so forth.
The agent is the last one; the non-agent is other than that. Their “intrinsic nature” (svabhāva), though distinct, is stated as a unity because the distinction is not intended to be expressed.

Likewise, that which is the penultimate cause of an agent and that which is the cause of a non-agent— though distinct from one another— are spoken of as a unity through the intention to express their non-difference.
Consequently, there is a contradiction between the two natures of the agent and the non-agent within a single substratum (*dharmin*).

Likewise, regarding the two causes that produce those two intrinsic natures— one producing the nature of an agent and the other producing the nature of a non-agent— there is a contradiction between them in a single substratum (*dharmin*), provided they are distinct.

Since the non-agent nature produced by the cause that produces the nature of a non-agent is distinct [from the agent], the consequence that "that which exists is itself that which does not exist" does not follow.
[41. Refutation of the view that only the effect depends upon auxiliary causes:

Another, however, has postulated a restriction regarding the performance of a single purpose among things that have different forms; he presents that view with the words, "He who also thinks," and so forth.
For the nature of an entity is always its very essence of non-delayed activity.
But it is not as some assert— that the determination of things as having a productive nature depends upon the presence of auxiliary conditions, and not on their own account.
Since that which is not a causal agent by itself cannot become one through the form of another, it would follow that the established order of causal agents would be destroyed.

Such a nature never requires association for the production of its own effect, because otherwise there would be a distinction between one thing being associated and another being solitary, based on a difference in their natures as causal agents or non-agents.
If it is asked: "If it is always of that nature, why does it not produce the effect at all times?"

Since the effect has a nature that depends on other conditions, even though that [cause] always exists as a producer, the effect does not arise from it alone; therefore, in this case, the fault lies solely with the effect itself.
Since that [entity], although established as the sole producer, still depends upon other conditions,

it follows that because its effect arises only from them acting in combination, the state of being a cooperative cause— defined by the performance of a single purposeful action— is possible even for non-momentary things.

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī), demonstrating that this [opponent] has not escaped the aforementioned fault, says: "For him as well"—that is, for one who speaks thus—"how can that entity, which is intended to be eternal, act alone?
This is because of the statement: "Its very nature is such that it possesses the property of non-delayed action."
And an effect arises from [factors] acting in combination alone,
because of the statement: "Its nature is to be produced by a causal totality (sāmagrī)."
Therefore, [the argument] that "it does not arise from the cause alone" refers to the "contradiction in that state" which was previously mentioned.

To explain: if it possesses the nature of non-delayed action (*akṣepakriyā*), then it must necessarily produce its effect; if it does not necessarily produce it, how can it have the nature of non-delayed action?

Since the nature of non-delayed action is understood from the observation that the effect is produced without delay—and not otherwise—the author says "not alone," etc., anticipating the opponent's objection.
I have not said that [the entity] acts alone; rather, I have said that its nature is to act without delay.
To this, he replies: "How then," and so forth.
If it is not accepted that [it] acts alone, how can it be described as having a nature that acts without delay?
Now, if it is stated in that way, then indeed this very point is illuminated—that is, expressed—by these words: "He certainly acts. What is that? It is: "He acts."
For that alone has the nature of unimpeded activity which necessarily acts; how could that which does not necessarily act possess such a nature?
As for what was also said:
The claim that "this is merely the fault of the effect,
in that it requires other conditions while it remains as the producer [of itself]" is also incorrect.
For this reason: how could this non-momentary entity, which is the effect and is capable even when alone, disregard another condition while it is being depended upon? It could not.
What would it do if it did not disregard it?
He says: disregarding—that is, setting aside—another condition, it would forcibly—that is, by violence—produce this effect.

If it is asked, "What is the merit of truth in this case?", he says: "For in this way," by one who performs his own task through sheer force while utterly disregarding another— even though he is capable as a solitary individual— that "capacity" which belongs to him alone is "demonstrated," that is, made manifest.
Otherwise, because [the cause] operates only when conjoined with another and never operates alone, others might have the thought: "This [cause], even when isolated, is not capable."
In that case, how could this [effect] appear as if its own power were eclipsed?
Therefore, it is incorrect to say that an effect depends upon other conditions.
Demonstrating that the contradiction remains as it was even with respect to the effect, he says: "The effect is dependent on another," and so forth.
By stating that the effect depends on something else, you declare that it does not arise from the cause alone;
[yet you also claim] "that [cause], even when alone, is capable."
By saying this, you are asserting that the effect arises from [the cause] alone.

Yet these two—arising and non-arising—from the very same single cause regarding one and the same effect are mutually contradictory; how could they both exist in a single locus, namely the subject (dharmin) called the "effect"?
Because the superimposition of contradictory properties is the defining characteristic of difference; by asserting both [properties] in a single locus, you would be saying,
"She is both a mother and a barren woman."
By saying, "You speak in a manner similar to this," you do not escape the previously mentioned fault;
for even speaking thus, you state only a contradiction and fail to perceive that "therefore" (*tat*), "this" (*ayam*) proponent of non-momentariness,

in the face of the proponents of the momentary position attaining faultlessness through the irreproachable nature of their thesis, possesses the very sting of envy characterized by indignation (*amarṣa*).
Because it is the cause of internal suffering, his vital organs (*marmāṇi*) are pierced and tormented by it; thus, he whose vital organs are pierced by the thorn of envy is a wretched man.

Due to the instability of his mind, failing to perceive even contradictory statements, he "cries out" or laments "distraughtly"—meaning agitated, incoherent, and lacking logical sequence. Thinking "thus," one should disregard the words of such an unstable mind, for there is no point in exposing his faults.
Because producing suffering excessively is like pouring salt upon a wound, "only equanimity" is "fitting for the wise who possess compassion.

Having thus demonstrated that in non-momentary entities, cooperation—characterized by the restriction to the performance of a single purposeful action—is in no way possible, he concludes by saying: "Therefore, this," and so forth.

For those things which, by virtue of having a stable nature, can exist even separately— that is, for those non-momentary entities— it is impossible to establish a rule of cooperation based on the reason that "they are capable of producing an effect individually" while simultaneously acting together; therefore, this definition of cooperation as the performance of a single purpose belongs only to momentary entities.

Because those phenomena—which possess the nature of being brought about by the transformation of their own causes and depend upon one another—cannot exist separately, since they are produced by a single totality (*sāmagrī*) consisting of mutual substantial and cooperative conditions; [it is only in the case of momentariness that cooperation in the form of performing a single purposeful action is established].
[Objection: But surely, cooperation characterized by the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*) is also observed among entities. How then was it stated previously?
"In all cases, cooperative action (*sahakriyā*) does not consist in the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*); rather, it is simply the performance of a single purpose by many.
To this, he says: "But where [it occurs] through the assistance of the continuum," and so forth.
(Hbṭ 128) In all cases, cooperation is characterized solely by the performance of a single purposeful action; nowhere is the production of a further excellence possible.

However, in cases where entities become causes for a desired effect through the assistance of a continuum—by generating successive moments that are increasingly more distinguished than their predecessors due to prior conditions—as occurs, for example, when fire, water, and so forth act as cooperative factors in the production of cooked rice from rice grains and the like.

Furthermore, when a sprout arises from a seed and so forth, earth and other factors are involved; in this context, what is called the "cooperative activity" (*sahakriyā*) of conditions is their production of a specific quality.

This occurs by relying on a continuum (*santāna*): based on the moments of the continuum—wherein the effect, characterized by the second and subsequent distinguished moments, depends upon the preceding moments—and through the conceptual determination of identity between the preceding and succeeding moments, one thinks, "this is an excellence of that very [same thing]. It does not occur by relying on a substantial entity (*dravya*).
This is merely figurative and not ultimate.

However, when successive distinctions arise from preceding moments whose natures are conditioned by the transformation of their own causes, the collection of prior causes possesses, in the ultimate sense, the status of "cooperation" (sahakāritva) characterized precisely by the performance of a single purposeful action; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Why is it not accepted that an excellence (*atiśaya*) is produced by means of a substantial entity (*dravya*) as its substratum?
Because no distinction (*viśeṣa*) can arise in a momentary substance, since that [distinction] would have to exist as the nature of the immediately subsequent moment.
If, then, no distinction arises in a momentary substance such as rice and so forth, [how can there be transformation?]
Let it be that this [simultaneity] does not exist even immediately after [the cause].
Therefore, just as momentary things, although not attaining any mutual distinction from one another, act only when combined and not individually, so too do non-momentary things.
Therefore, for these [causes], their state of cooperation (*sahakāritva*) will consist precisely in their performing a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyā*).
Nor can it be argued that "whatever is a nature that was previously non-productive of something must remain so even later";

for instance, the sense faculty of one who has entered a dark chamber from a bright space is observed to perform the cognition of an object later, even though it did not do so [before]. As it has been said:

“For it is not the case that because objects do not appear to those who have just entered [a house], they are therefore no longer apprehended by the sense faculties when they are in cool inner chambers and the like.
To this, he says: “For [it is not the case] with rice and so forth,” and so on.
Since proximity, in the absence of a specific transformation, is equivalent to non-proximity, rice and other grains would not produce cooked rice even when fire and other factors are present.

Likewise, for one who has entered a dark chamber from a bright place, if the sense faculty does not gradually acquire an excellence (*atiśaya*) from those factors that assist it, then it would never produce the cognition of an object later on, just as it did before.
Therefore, when an effect that is impossible [in a certain thing] is observed in another, that [other thing] is indeed different from it—

just as the seed of *kodrava* is different from the seed of *śāli*. Thus, because it produces that effect through its excellence (*sātiśayatayā*), it is simply something distinct from that which lacks such excellence (*niratiśaya*).

Thus, it has been demonstrated that where an effect arises from auxiliary causes (sahakārin) sequentially, the status of being an auxiliary cause—characterized by the production of an excellence (atiśaya)—is merely figurative; whereas the primary [status] is indeed characterized by the performance of a single purposeful action (ekārthakriyā). But in cases where auxiliary causes produce an effect without delay, through mere proximity to the object, does there also exist the production of an excellence based on a continuum (santāna)?
To this he says: "In those that act without delay," and so forth.

For, in the case of the sense organs and other factors—which arise from their own causes in locations such as those without obstruction—and which act without delay, no production of a distinction [in their nature] can occur through mutual influence, because they are momentary.
This was stated previously.
If there is no production of specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), then how can things that are devoid of specific qualities become causes for cognition?
To this, he says: "In that regard, according to their respective [conditions]," meaning by those conditions which belong to each [thing] as its own.

“Those [atoms] which have arisen from their being the substrata of mutual approach, separation, and so forth— and which exist in a location that is suitable because it is free from excessive proximity or excessive distance, and which abide in such a state of unobstructed space— attain the status of causes for cognition by virtue of the very fact that their own nature has been produced; in this regard, what need is there for mutual [causality]?”
Is it by means of a produced distinction that is sought after?

For if they were not produced from their own causes— which consist in their mutual proximity and so forth— as possessing a specific state characterized by being situated in a suitable location and so on, capable of generating their own effects, then the production of a distinction among them from one another would have to be sought.

But this is not the case when such things arise from their own causes alone. Therefore, since this is so, "in that regard"— that is, with respect to those sense faculties and so forth which act without delay— "the performance of a single purpose" is the primary "cooperative activity," whereas that which is established by relying on a continuum and characterized by the production of an excellence is secondary.
Now, why is the state of being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) not established as having the characteristic of producing a specific excellence (*viśeṣotpādana*)?

For that too must indeed be established because it is well-known in the world. Therefore, he says: "But in the case of an effect where the cooperative causes do not function as conditions merely by coming together in a location without intervention—as is the case with the sense faculties and so forth—but rather [function] in accordance with the production of the intended effect... (Hbṭ 130).

Producing a distinction that is enhanced at every moment, the "causal continuum"— characterized by the existence of successive moments— requires other auxiliary conditions for the sake of attaining its own specific excellence (*ātmaniśaya*) when a task is to be performed that occurs over a lapse of time; however, it does not require a causal moment that is simultaneous with it.

“From those,” meaning from those other causes, “the acquisition of another nature”—characterized by a succession of specific qualities conducive to the production of an effect—is spoken of in the world with respect to a continuum (*santāna*) that is conceptually apprehended as a unity.

However, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), even there, each preceding complex of conditions (*pratyayakalāpa*) is restricted to a specific subsequent moment that is conducive to the production of a later effect; thus, it experiences cooperation (*sahakāritva*) characterized solely by the performance of a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyā*).
But how do they acquire another intrinsic nature (*svabhāvāntara*), such that they produce their effect sequentially? To this he says: "In that regard, by their own force," and so forth.
"In that regard" means: in that causal continuum, those causes which are termed material causes (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) and those conditions (*pratyaya*) designated as cooperative factors (*sahakārin*).

Those which are the first moments of initial occurrence, since they cease by their own nature without depending on a cause of destruction, from those very first moments as they cease by their own nature, there arises a moment distinguished by a specific quality conducive to the production of an effect; from those [moments], there arise third moments possessing even more conducive specific qualities.
From among those [causes], there arise fourth moments possessing specific qualities that are most conducive [to the effect];

thus, until a final, infinitely superior collection of causes has come into being, the effect is produced. In this way, from the auxiliary causes, there is the acquisition of a different inherent nature (svabhāvāntara), and the production of the effect occurs with a delay.

Here, an opponent objects: "From the 'cooperative causes' (*sahakāriṇaḥ*)—that is, from the causes characterized by acting together (the singular number is used for the genus)—arises that which has produced a specific quality in the manner just described; from that cause, characterized as the final moment of the causal complex (*antyasāmagrīkṣaṇa*), [the effect arises]."

If the production of effects such as sprouts is desired, then the very first particularity— which is conducive to the production of the effect and is held to be its generator through gradual intensification— would not arise; for the moments occurring in the first instant do not acquire particularities from one another, being undifferentiated and [by your own admission] not admitted [to possess such differentiation].

If it is argued that [the causes], though not having acquired any distinction from one another, will initiate a distinction conducive to the production of the effect, he replies: "From the undistinguished"—that is, if the production of a "distinction" conducive to the arising of the effect were desired from those [causes] which are mutually undistinguished, then the "effect," such as a sprout and so forth, would have to arise;
the intention is that this cannot be so because of the absence of any distinction.
Consequently, the auxiliary causes would produce the effect while remaining entirely independent of the production of mutual distinctions among themselves.

If it is asked, "What is established by this being the case? he says: "Therefore," by which [reasoning], even though they are momentary, [the causes] produce their own effect while remaining independent of the production of mutual distinctions.

They perform a single function characterized by a specific restriction and thus attain the status of being cooperative causes. For that reason, the proponent of non-momentariness (akṣaṇikavādī) brings his own position into parity with the momentary position, [arguing]: "Even for non-momentary things, there would be causality, and there would be no arising of a superior nature from those things to be depended upon. As he says:
“Who could speak thus with any sense of propriety, unless they were devoid of shame or ignorant; for in that case, everything would be the same even regarding momentary things.”
“The conditions for those [effects] cannot in any way serve as causes of distinction, because, like eternal things, moments are indistinguishable. To this,
it might be argued that even in the first moment, the earth, seed, and so forth, exist only after having produced distinctions from one another.

"By whatever [means] there is a connection for someone, that [connection] exists even for one situated at a distance"—according to this principle, since the relation of cause and effect exists even for those located in distant places, he says "Now, by means of an auxiliary," etc., raising this doubt. Even though auxiliaries lack mutual contact, they assist one another by the very nature of things; thus, at the time of contact, it is precisely that which has been rendered specific [by the auxiliary] for the sake of producing a particularity conducive to the arising of the effect, [that acts] by means of the auxiliary.
If this were the case, there would be an infinite regress.

For instance, even for the production of that particularity, another particularity produced by a cooperative cause must be admitted; and likewise, for the production of that as well, yet another must be admitted.

Now, if the auxiliary causes do not produce another distinct quality that serves as the cause for the specific excellence conducive to the production of the effect, since they are by their very nature capable in that regard, he says: "And not," etc.
For indeed, the auxiliary causes—earth, seed, and so forth—do not [produce] that specific excellence which is conducive to the production of the effect, nor do they [produce] its generation.

"Always," at all times, the state of being ready; "by which," by that state of readiness, "constantly adhered to" (*nityānuṣakta*), meaning constantly bound to these [factors] such as the earth and the seed, would be a particularity (*viśeṣa*) that produces a specific quality conducive to the arising of the effect, from which [the effect arises].
"The production of a specific quality from that which is non-specific would also apply to the effect"—this objection too is refuted.
Why is this so? He says: "Because of its means," and so forth.

This is because the manifestation of the effect is observed when there is the presence of the means for those things, such as the earth and the seed, in a suitable location; and because the non-production of the effect is observed when there is their absence, that is, when their mutual contact ceases.

For if they were always in a state capable of producing the specific qualities conducive to the arising of the effect, then that specific quality would also exist at all times. Consequently, the effect, which arises from that successive series, would also exist at all times; thus, the production and non-production of the effect would not correspond to the presence and absence of its means.
Therefore, the auxiliary causes do not exist at all times in a state capable of producing the specific qualities conducive to the arising of the effect.

For this reason, a specific quality produced by an auxiliary cause standing apart—due to the fear of infinite regress—is not present; nor is it accepted or even logical that such a quality could arise from mutual interaction among those factors existing at the very first moment of contact.

Consequently, the initial specific quality conducive to the production of the effect does not arise from the auxiliaries for the sake of the earth, seed, and so forth, which, being simultaneous with it, cannot provide any assistance.
And it is accepted that this [effect] arises;

therefore, just like the state of being complete, because there is no distinction among all the moments occurring in the state of being incomplete, even though they possess the nature of producing it, they do not produce it, since production occurs only in the state of completeness.
Just as momentary things have cooperation characterized by the restriction to a single purposeful action, so too do things of stable nature.

Thinking "it will come to pass," the proponent of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikavādin*), having exhausted all other means, like a sick man, highly prizes this very [position] and has placed his full reliance upon it.
The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*), mocking the opponent in a subtle manner, says: "But for us, not again and again," and so forth.
If, even when spoken repeatedly, the world understands the principle, we shall speak even a hundred times.
How much more so, then, when [the meaning] is stated three times?
For us, who are engaged in the welfare of others, there is no weariness in repeating ourselves again and again.

And as for those who strive to avoid the charge of tautology when the author of the treatise, speaking in such a manner, clarifies that very same point through a different formulation elsewhere—it is merely a misplaced effort on their part.
If there is no agitation, then alas, let it be said; to this he replies: "Not merely from the production of a distinction," and so forth.
For, in the ultimate sense, the status of being a cooperative cause for cooperating factors is not possible anywhere solely through the production of a distinction.

For if seeds and the like existed only at the first moment, then—since that [subsequent state] would be absent—at the time when a specific quality conducive to the production of the effect must be produced, there would be a lack of auxiliary cooperation (*sahakāritā*). However, it is through the previously mentioned arguments that the performance of a single purpose (*ekārthakriyā*) alone is conceived as the ultimate auxiliary nature of auxiliaries. And since that [performance of a single purpose] certainly exists even for those things that have not yet come into contact at the outset, why would they not be auxiliaries?
The opponent says: Even that single purposeful action would not occur for things that lack mutual distinction.

If, however, it is admitted that even for those lacking mutual distinction there is that single purposeful action, then—since the capacity to produce it is accepted in each individual thing in that state—it would occur even separately, just as it does in that state.
For instance, even in that state, they act without any distinction from one another; why then does the objection that their individual performance of that specific action not follow?
Indeed, there is no difference whatsoever between these [atoms] in their combined and uncombined states.

If you say, "Let it be so; what is the fault?"—then, since it follows that there must be a separate extraction of the specific quality conducive to the production of the effect, you might think: "Therefore, the effect, such as a sprout, which by nature comes into being from that specific quality, would also possess that specific quality [even] from a mere auxiliary cause."
Here too, the entire response has been stated.

For instance, when it is asserted that entities which perish moment by moment are indeed without distinction between their aggregated and non-aggregated states— is this said with reference merely to some [trivial] difference,
or rather with reference to a difference capable of producing a specific excellence conducive to the arising of an effect?
If the first alternative is intended, that is incorrect;
for no state devoid of particularity whatsoever is possible, since there always exists a succession of particularities brought about by the connection with ever-new conditions.
For nothing is ever exclusively one thing, since there exists, as the case may be, the shadow, sunlight, wind, cold, and so forth of the supporting base;
nor, even when those are present, is that [object] exactly the same.
This is due to the difference in causes.
However, this much may be the case: a certain specific quality may be conducive to a particular effect, but not every [quality] is so for every [effect].
Showing that this has already been stated previously, he says: "by means of various successive conditions at every moment."

"Although conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*), which possess distinct capacities at every moment due to the conjunction of various successive conditions, appear to be similar because of some degree of uniformity as they form a continuum, nevertheless their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indeed distinct; therefore, only a specific [factor] is the cause of a specific [effect]. Thus.
"Because there is no identity among momentary entities due to the arising of successive [states]," thus it has been stated here most concisely.
And thus, in the phrase "there is no repeated statement for us," the double use of the word "again" (punar) is appropriate;
for it has already been stated in what manner the production of a specific quality occurs within the continuum of an entity.
In that regard, [the opponent claims]: "By its own nature, when the preceding moment ceases, a distinct moment arises from those very [causes]; thus there is the production of a distinction.

Now, if it is intended—on the basis of a distinction that produces a specific quality conducive to the arising of the effect—that those things which undergo the first contact are mutually undifferentiated, as before, that too is incorrect.

For what kind of things are the earth, seed, and so forth, which produce the distinction conducive to the arising of the effect? They are those which occur in immediate succession, being devoid of any intervention or the like.
Because its existence occurs only when those [causes] exist, and because the determination of what is a producer is based solely on this much;

and since such [causes] do not exist at all times, how could there be for them, even when separate, the initiation of specific qualities conducive to the production of an effect, from which it would follow that the effect could be produced even by them alone? He demonstrates this: "those whose locations are suitable are 'suitable-located' (yogyadeśāḥ)."
The state of that [proximity] is "being in a suitable location" (*yogyadeśatā*);
those for which this is the first among the various states such as being in an unobstructed location are described as such; and those various states themselves are likewise so described.

“Suitability of place,” such as being in a location that is not obstructed by others and so forth— these “particular states” that arise in earth, seeds, and the like, possess the nature of producing effects characterized by specific qualities conducive to the production of the result;
since seeds and the like are not always of this kind, how could they produce such specific qualities even when existing separately?”

This too has been stated previously: "In that regard, the collection of form, sense-faculties, and so forth, which exists in a location characterized by lack of obstruction and so on, is the cause capable of producing consciousness," according to this statement.
And because that [previous example] was merely an illustration,

here too it is indeed understood that the collection of factors such as the earth and the seed, existing in a location characterized by non-intervention and so forth, is the cause capable of producing a specific quality conducive to the arising of the effect;
and yet, such a specific quality does not exist at all times.
Because there is no cause that produces it;
for the specific condition (*pratyaya-viśeṣa*) which serves as the basis for their mutual approach and so forth is itself the cause of that [result].

He states that this too has already been explained previously: "And that from which those [conditions], being possessed of specific qualities, arise in order to produce the specificities conducive to the arising of the effect—that too has been stated more than once."
"That specific condition which is the basis for their mutual approach and so forth is the cause capable of producing that effect";

likewise, by this [statement]: "Those [atoms] which, through their respective conditions based on mutual approach and so forth, have come to reside in suitable locations and so on, attain the status of being causes of cognition simultaneously with the completion of their own nature."
For this too is understood here.
Therefore, even if there is no distinction among these [causes] due to their mutual impossibility,
who can prevent that which is produced by its own cause?

Nor is there, among entities that have already acquired their specific qualities from their own causes, any mutual expectation of those qualities, since it would be untenable to maintain that they acquire specific qualities from one another.

Furthermore, although each of those conditions—which produce the specific qualities conducive to the arising of the effect—is individually capable, the production of the effect cannot occur in fragments; rather, the entire effect must be produced by each [condition] acting in its totality.

Just as it has been stated more than once that there is no action consisting solely of individual factors— since neither the agent in isolation, nor the specific location such as the absence of intervention, nor the collection of elements such as soil and seed, when each exists separately, possesses the capacity [for production]—

and because of such statements as: "And since these [factors] do not exist prior to, after, or separately [from one another], the defects that arise from priority, posteriority, and separateness do not affect them, even though they are individually capable."

Therefore, since such a specific quality (*viśeṣa*)— which would depend solely on its own material cause— is not admitted, and thus [the production of] mere [causes] is impossible, how could there even be an effect mediated by the initiation of a specific quality conducive to the production of that effect?

Furthermore, from where is this arbitrary assumption derived, that the effects such as the sprout and so forth produce, through their mutual cooperation, a succession of specific qualities conducive to the production of the effect?

However, a specific quality conducive to the production of an effect arises merely through the occurrence [of causes] in a location free from obstructions and the like; therefore, he says: "And because there is a twofold nature of effects, it is thus divided.
How is there a twofold nature of effects?
To this he says: those produced immediately by auxiliaries located in positions free from obstructions and so forth, characterized as distinct moments that depend upon their own prior states.

Those specific qualities (*viśeṣa*)—which consist of a sequence where each subsequent moment is more distinguished than the preceding one—are the nature of a single effect whose property is such an origination.

Furthermore, there is another kind of effect which is the opposite: that which arises through the mere proximity of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) and does not depend on a succession of specific qualities produced by mutual interaction.
An example here is: "like a sprout and so forth";
by the inclusion of "and so forth," it means "like boiled rice and so forth.
Likewise, that sense-faculty which functions through impelling is like consciousness and so forth.
This qualification is intended to exclude the sense-faculties that have entered the interior chamber from the luminous [nature].
If it is asked, "Why is this so? [it is because] of the relationship between cause and effect (kāryakāraṇayoḥ).

Because of the difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*): for some effects have a nature produced by the mere presence of the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*), while others depend upon its transformation (*pariṇāma*).
A certain cause also possesses, by its very nature, the capacity to produce an effect through its mere presence, arising from its own causes alone;
it does not depend on a succession of specific qualities produced by mutual interaction for the performance of its own effect. Another cause, however, possesses a nature contrary to that.
Just as a certain thing has the nature of producing a rice sprout while another is its opposite,

and the rice sprout has the nature of being produced by its own seed rather than having the nature of being produced by seeds such as barley, the intrinsic natures of entities— which arise through the power of their own causes and are established by valid cognition— cannot be subjected to questioning.

However, regarding those things which are established by valid cognition as having the nature of producing a certain effect, a deliberation arises here: are they always of that very nature, or only at that specific time?

In that case, if it were always of that same nature, then—just as later—it would follow that it must perform its causal function even earlier; consequently, thinkers who investigate reality declare that there is a difference in nature between the states of being a producer and not being a producer, due to its having a different form, just as in the case of rice and barley seeds.

Furthermore, the recognition [of identity] based on the production of similar subsequent moments occurs through a sense of oneness, just as in the case of hair, nails, and the like that have been cut and grown back again; thus, there is no contradiction here.
And since there is a twofold division of effects due to the difference in the nature of their respective causes,
when that [cause] exists, it is the cause that has reached its final state which depends upon the mutual assistance of the continuum of those "cooperating factors," such as the earth and the seed.

Regarding its effect, such as the sprout and so forth, the cause of its production is that "initial" particularity—which consists in the state of a distinct second moment immediately following the first moment—that is conducive to the arising of the effect. This [particularity] does not arise from a particularity produced by those "cooperating causes" (sahakārin) themselves when they first come into contact with one another; rather, it exists solely due to a specific condition (pratyaya-viśeṣa) based on their mutual approach and so forth.

Then, from the first particularity— which is conducive to the production of the effect and which arises in the first moment— there arise, starting from that point, those "particularities" characterized by the increasingly superior subsequent moments produced by the auxiliary causes which have acquired their own particularities from other sources; these "are born from that," meaning they are born from the particularities produced by the auxiliaries.

Why? "Because that is its nature": because the first particular [moment], by virtue of being the basis for mutual proximity and so forth, has as its produced nature [the capacity] to be generated by auxiliary causes that have acquired particulars favorable to it through specific conditions, while remaining independent of mutual assistance; and because each subsequent particular has as its produced nature [the capacity] to be generated by particulars made conducive to the production of the effect by those auxiliary causes.
Since this is so, "therefore," there is no "infinite regress" as previously stated.

Now, [it might be argued that] even a seed and so forth situated in a granary would be approached by its auxiliary factors such as soil and the like only after having been modified by them, and likewise the soil and so forth would be approached by the seed only after being modified by it; thus there would be an infinite regress.

This is not the case, because we do not accept that kind of [mutual dependence]. Rather, we accept that this specific modification arises from human effort and other causes—such as the scattering of seeds in a field—which consists in the immediate contact between moist earth and the seed, and which produces a particular state conducive to the production of the effect.
Regarding this, as for what was stated by the opponent:

"Just as earth, seeds, and so forth, when undergoing their initial conjunction, produce a particularity conducive to the production of an effect without imparting any mutual distinction to one another;
likewise, even entities of stable nature, being restricted to that single effect, will exist without depending on any mutual distinctions produced [by others]."
Accepting that [position], he says: "In the same way, if even the non-momentary... and so forth.
If even the non-momentary produces an effect just as the momentary does, let it indeed do so;
no one prevents it.

However, if that nature by which it performs an action is defined as "having the property of performing the action without delay"—meaning its nature is such that it acts without obstruction—then, because a separate existence is possible, it would follow that "even alone" (not only when accompanied) "it would be so," meaning it would be the producer of that effect; this has been stated many times.

But if it lacks that nature—that is, if it is devoid of the nature of acting without delay—then "even at that time," even in the state of being accompanied, it remains "non-productive" just as before, since agency in another form was already refuted previously.

Thus, having refuted the cooperative causality (*sahakāritva*) of non-momentary entities through both their performance of a single purposeful action and the production of specific qualities, he concludes by saying, "Therefore," and so forth.

Since both types of cooperative causality are untenable, no entity whatsoever can be a cooperative cause for a non-momentary thing; consequently, even in its solitary state, it would produce its own effect.
Demonstrating what is logical for one who asserts that a non-momentary cause depends upon cooperative conditions, he says, "But for the most part," and so forth.

For one who maintains the doctrine of a permanent cause, if that cause produces an effect by depending on other conditions, then it is "evident" (*vyaktam*) that another nature must necessarily arise in that permanent cause which acts by depending on other conditions. It is not said that there is dependence for that which is "not an effect," meaning that which does not experience the state of being an effect.
For, that continuum of entities which resides in— that is, exists within— the "conjunction" or "assemblage" of auxiliary causes,
being for the most part— meaning generally— endowed with specific qualities produced by those auxiliary conditions, is seen to perform its own effect, just like a seed and so forth. (Hbṭ 138)
Therefore, it is analyzed in this way:
the inclusion of the term "mostly" (prāyaḥ) is for the purpose of excluding the collection of the sense faculties and so forth which act as projectors;
for it is impossible to conceive in any way a logical principle applicable to those [projectors] existing in non-momentary things, since their separate existence is possible.
However, it is not contradictory for that which was previously non-agential to subsequently give rise to a different intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that is agential;
for while it is not tenable that the very same non-agential entity possesses as its own nature an agential nature, it is not the case that it lacks such a nature altogether.
It is precisely for this reason that the term "different intrinsic nature" (svabhāvāntara) is employed.
In that case, one must simply accept that for that which has the nature of being non-productive, there is merely cessation by its own inherent tendency (*svarasanirodha*).
Consequently, everything is well-established.
Now, if it is thought: "If the productive nature were not already present even prior [to the effect], then the production of another productive nature would have to be desired for a permanent cause."
However, since that [nature] exists even prior [to the causal complex], its dependence on other conditions for its arising is also untenable; therefore, he says: "Of the agent," and so forth.

For if the nature of being an agent existed even prior to the state of completeness [of the causal complex], then its non-action would be illogical, because it would perform the action by virtue of that very nature even in the state of being combined [with other factors].
Since agency by way of another's form has already been refuted,
and since it does not act [in that manner],
therefore its nature did not exist previously.
And if this [destruction] were not produced even by other conditions, why would it depend on them in vain? [This concludes the discussion on causeless destruction.
Thus, because it is produced from that very nature...

Regarding this [objection]: "Whatever has a certain intrinsic nature (svabhāva), being produced from its own causes alone, remains of that very nature; it does not require another cause for that state to persist"—when a different kind of inconclusiveness (anekānta) has been raised against this statement made to avoid inconclusiveness, the Master stated "through connection with successive conditions" (*aparāparapratyayayogena*) and so forth, with the desire to refute it.

In this regard, having concluded the incidental discussion undertaken to demonstrate that the nature of cause and effect which belongs to momentary things is impossible in the case of non-momentary things, [the author], returning to the subject at hand, says: "Therefore, whatever is of such a nature," and so forth.

If there is no need for causes of destruction for an entity whose nature is not to endure, [one might think] it will exist for one whose nature is to endure; therefore, he says: "Even for that which has the nature of endurance," and so forth.
For even in the case of that which has the nature of stability (*sthitidharman*), there is no purpose whatsoever served by causes of destruction;

because its stable intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), produced from its own causes, cannot be altered by anything else, since it would entail the loss of its very essence as something stable if it were to become otherwise.
Granted that entities might not exist by themselves;

however, those that do exist do not abandon their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Now, if it is maintained that even that which has the property of stability undergoes transformation, then, upon the occurrence of that transformation, its [original] intrinsic nature—
In this way, there would be no such thing as a "nature whose very character is stability," because if a nature that is essentially unstable were to come into existence later,
its non-existence prior [to that] would be impossible;
for that which is of that nature cannot [be otherwise] in that state.
It is argued that the absence [of one thing] in another is only possible when they are in proximity;
therefore, because this would entail non-existence,
it has been stated that "the superimposition of contradictory properties is the defining characteristic of difference."

And this being the case, the very first conceptual construction—that an entity exists by its own nature as something whose characteristic is non-abiding—is already refuted. Regarding that first conceptual construction, the fault has already been stated: namely, that the cause of destruction would be redundant.
Now, suppose it were of the nature of a head.

One might argue that its nature as destruction arises for the first time while it is still non-existent, because otherwise its cessation would be impossible; therefore, he says: "And that which [is] from another," namely from a cause of destruction, while it is still existing as something characterized by stability, "becomes otherwise"—that is, it possesses the characteristic of a lack of stability.

This is "another" or distinct "nature" from the previous nature, which was produced by its own causes and was characterized by stability. Since this [new nature] is produced subsequently and has a different cause, how [could it be the same thing]?
"Could it have that as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?

If you say, "Because it appears as having that as its essence," then such an appearance would occur through similarity for one whose distinction [from the original] is unperceived, provided that this [new state] arises from something else while the previous intrinsic nature still exists.
Otherwise, how could the contradiction be resolved?
If it is argued that there is another nature [of the entity],
then how can that other nature belong to it?
For it is not logical that one thing has the intrinsic nature of another,
because that would lead to an over-extension;
why then should that which is the intrinsic nature of one not belong to the other as well?
To this he says: “A difference in intrinsic nature,” and so forth.
[The opponent asks: “Let it be a distinct entity; what is the fault in its having another intrinsic nature?

To this he says: “And thus,” meaning that if it were a distinct entity, the previous state of the thing—which arose from its own causes as something characterized by stability—would become something characterized by non-departure [from that state] when an intrinsic nature is produced by a cause of destruction.

That which is established does not possess the property of cessation, because it is occupied with the production of another entity that serves as the cause of its destruction; thus, there is no "alteration" or cessation of that thing characterized by stability.
For it is not logical that the cessation of one thing occurs upon the existence of another thing, such as a hammer or the like.
Because it would lead to an over-extension;
and it has already been stated that [the effect] arises through the destruction of that [cause].

But is it not observed that for copper and the like, which possess a solid nature, there arises another intrinsic state such as liquidity due to causes of destruction like fire; and yet, the preceding state does not possess the property of having perished? To this he says:
