"By this"—referring to what was just mentioned—"of the solid and so forth," the word "and so forth" including the liquid and so forth, there is the arising of another intrinsic state such as liquidity or solidity in copper, gold, and the like, due to fire, cold, wind, and so forth, while their established form [remains].

[The arguments] regarding copper and so forth have been "refuted," that is, rejected, because the same fault applies. How, then, is the production of another intrinsic nature possible, and how is the non-existence of the previous [nature]— which remains established with the property of non-decay— logical?

Thus he says: "In that case as well," regarding copper and so forth in their solid form, "because of the natural cessation" (*svarasanirodhitvāt*) of the preceding state—the solid, liquid, or other form—due to the absence of a cause for destruction; when "destruction" occurs through "fire and so forth"—the term "and so forth" including the sprinkling of water, cold wind, and the like—and through the "appropriating cause" (*upādāna*), which is characterized by an excellence produced by specific conditions such as mutual proximity and so on among the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), that copper and so forth in its solid form naturally ceases.

Precisely from that same material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), due to a specific transformation produced by the auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) such as fire and the conditions of the material cause (*upādāna-pratyaya*), "something else indeed"—that is, something different—arises with a nature characterized by fluidity, hardness, and so forth; for the mention of "fluidity" is an illustration [of other qualities].

It does not mean that the very same previously existing copper or the like, which possessed a fixed nature of hardness or fluidity, has merely undergone a transformation (*pariṇata*) into a nature of fluidity or hardness.
To this, the opponent says: "By whom was it stated... as follows:
"For that which possesses the property of stability, there is the arising of a nature of non-stability due to a cause of destruction; from that, destruction follows"—
by means of this, it is stated that "that which is a transformation from another is a different intrinsic nature," and so forth.
But rather, it is stability itself that is produced by its own causes; its unstable nature does not arise from a cause of destruction.
How is it known that "it is produced by its own causes as something whose very nature is stable"?
Because it persists even when causes of destruction such as fire are absent.
If a thing were produced by its own cause with the property of non-persistence by its very nature (*svabhāva*), then it would not persist even in the absence of those [causes].

For that which has the property of persistence by its very nature, another nature is restricted by its own causes alone, namely: "its destruction occurs by itself through something else," such as a contradictory factor like fire.
The term "from another" (*parasmāt*) is a fifth-case ablative used with the elision of the suffix *lyap* in the sense of an object; that is, it means "in relation to another.

This [entity] has arisen with its own nature determined solely by its own causes, such that it exists independently, even while you [the opponent] maintain that it depends upon something contradictory to itself.
It must be understood thus. As it has been said:
"That very intrinsic nature of his is such that it ceases by depending [on something else], just as the stream of other things [ceases] upon encountering a contradictory factor such as a hammer."
Now, one might object: if its destruction occurs by itself upon the presence of an opposing factor, it follows that it is causeless;

and since a restriction of place, time, and intrinsic nature is not tenable for what is causeless, [the author] says: "And yet"—it is not the case that so-called destruction is an intrinsic nature distinct from the thing destroyed, such that this fault would arise.
However, "destruction is simply the falling away from existence.
And because that [falling away] lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), its possession of a cause is not at all tenable;
for it does not belong to that [entity].
It is simply that this [entity] does not exist by itself;
therefore, since there is no thing that could come into being, for what is causality admitted?
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) says: "This does not transcend the two alternatives just mentioned."
What is this twofold conceptualization? It is such as:
"Is an entity eternal? and so forth.

Now, one might object that for something undergoing the state of impermanence (adharmatā) while persisting through a period of time, there is no room at all for the conceptualization of permanence. This is not so.

Even if that [duration] is accepted, it follows that permanence itself is accepted. For instance, if this entity characterized by a duration of one year is produced by its own causes, then at the completion of that year,
that very nature which was characterized by a duration of one year at the time of its initial arising— by virtue of which it remained for a year— [would persist].
That very same [nature] would persist even at the end of that [first year];
consequently, it would remain for another year thereafter.

Even at the end of that, because it does not abandon its inherent nature of persisting for the duration of the first produced year, there would follow the undesirable consequence of it persisting for yet further successive years.
Even if one accepts that things have the nature of persisting for a period of time, permanence itself has been accepted; thus, the conceptualization of permanence is difficult to avoid.

Furthermore, because one accepts that a thing ceases of its own accord when a cause of destruction is present, there is the conceptualization of impermanence, which is the conceptualization of a perishable nature.

For instance, that very intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of a thing which perishes of its own accord upon the presence of what is considered a cause of destruction belongs to it from the very moment it arises, since the entity is of a single nature.
Since it would follow that destruction occurs at that very moment, how could its nature of persisting for another time be possible?

When this alternative has been raised, if one accepts the subsequent alternative, then its persistence over another time is precisely what is severed; thus, he must accept the alternative of permanence itself.

In that case, if he accepts that it perishes by itself upon the presence of a cause of destruction, he is saying that it was permanent previously and later becomes impermanent, having a perishable nature.
“And by speaking thus, he asserts two entities.
The word “and” (*ca*) refers to what is about to be stated.
Of what kind are these two entities?
That which possesses two distinct natures, eternal and non-eternal, is thus [described].
One who asserts the subsequent destruction of that very same eternal nature previously held to be eternal, declares its destruction at every moment;
otherwise, by the logic already stated, destruction would be impossible even later.

If, on the other hand, its destruction does not occur at every moment, then because that [destruction] would remain impossible even later, it follows that there is never any destruction; thus, the cause of destruction is incapable and utterly ineffective with respect to the nature previously intended to be eternal. [Objection: But surely you have not admitted any efficacy for the cause of destruction, since [the entity] itself undergoes destruction upon encountering a contrary factor. [Reply: No.
For this very reason, it follows that destruction would have [the cause] as its basis;
otherwise, why would this [cause] be required for something that performs no function at all?
For the nature of being a cause is defined by the requirement of dependence.
If it is argued that it is their own causes that are at fault here, in that they employ [the cause] toward something that is ineffective even though there is a need for it—
then what is this misplaced insistence on their part that they employ it in such a manner?
Therefore, causes appear most appropriate only when they are employed precisely in relation to that which is to be assisted.
Otherwise, even those things which are of the nature of effects would not respect that restriction.
And how can something that accomplishes nothing be called a "contradictory"?
For it possesses no distinction whatsoever from that which is intended to be non-contradictory; thus, this [objection] is trivial.

As for what was also stated— "Just as for other proponents of momentariness, the stream of jars and the like ceases in dependence on a hammer or similar causes even though they are ineffective [in producing destruction], so too for us, an entity persists for a period of time"—
that too is said out of ignorance of the doctrines of others.
For us, there is no such thing as a "stream" distinct from the moments that could cease upon the proximity of a hammer or other instruments which have no causal efficacy;
indeed, there are only moments,
and these do not depend on a hammer or the like for their own cessation.
Because they cease by their own inherent nature (*svarasataḥ*).

However, that cessation of theirs—which is characterized by the functioning of potsherds and so forth, and which occurs through a process of exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—is such that when it exists, for the world which clings to unity, jars and the like are said to have "ceased," because the cause of delusion has been removed: namely, the appearance of a subsequent state similar [to the preceding one].
Such is common usage;
in that regard, it is not at all the case that hammers and other such tools are ineffective,
for they exist only when those [effects] exist.

[The opponent argues: "Because the pot-moment, assisted by cooperating factors such as a swift mallet, arises from a specific condition consisting in the mutual approach [of its parts]; because the shards and so forth possess the property of coming into being; and because that [pot] has the nature of producing them—therefore, there is no fault. Desiring to avoid the consequence of admitting two distinct natures (*svabhāva*), the other says: "Not before," and so forth.
Why is this so?
Because it possesses a single intrinsic nature (*ekasvabhāvatvāt*).
For that which always possesses a single intrinsic nature, there is only permanence at all times; it is impossible for it to subsequently possess an impermanent intrinsic nature.

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) says: "In that case, how can that entity—which is eternally of a permanent nature by its very essence and does not 'enter into destruction,' meaning it does not undergo it—be said to have perished at all?
Why? Because the permanent nature of that essence and the destruction, which is of an impermanent form, are of a mutually exclusive nature, being characterized by their mutual exclusion."

Summing up, he says: "Since it is thus established that destruction is not at all tenable for things whose nature is stability, therefore, if the destruction of an existing thing produced by causes is necessarily admitted by others when its destruction occurs, then [it must be said that] it perishes by way of the nature of destruction—
that is, 'destruction' means it perishes and does not remain."
The suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) due to its frequent application (*bahulavacanāt*).
That which has this nature is "that which has destruction as its nature" (*vināśasvabhāvena*), meaning that which has non-abiding as its characteristic (*asthitidharmaṇā*).

By means of that existing entity whose form is produced (*kṛtakarūpeṇa satā vastunā*), it "must come to be" from its own causes; otherwise, for those things that exist with a produced nature and are admitted to have the necessity of [eventual] occurrence, destruction itself would be impossible.

If it is argued, "Let it be so," he replies: "Even so"—that is, even if [the entity] has the nature of perishing by itself, and not merely the nature of being imperishable—it was already stated during the presentation of the first alternative that a cause of destruction is useless because a change in intrinsic nature (svabhāvānyathātva) is impossible;
it is not being said again.
Since this is so, the passage beginning with "by that" (*tena*) and so forth is easy to understand.

Thus, having established— through the lack of dependence on destruction and through its incapacity and futility— that the existence characterized by being produced lacks a cause for that [destruction], as shown by the former teachers, one should now see how this [reason] functions as a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) in the case of the contrary.
Showing this, he says: "Therefore, destruction," and so forth.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things that are independent with respect to a certain state are necessarily restricted to that state;
for example, the final causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*) in the production of its own effect.

And since an entity that has been produced is independent [of a cause for its destruction], it is accepted by others as being subject to inevitable destruction; this is the application of a *prasaṅga* based on a *svabhāvahetu*, which serves as the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the contrapositive, as demonstrated by the former masters.
"Therefore" means: given that [destruction] is necessarily tied to the existence of that [entity].

Because destruction is not occasional, destruction occurs immediately after arising; thus, that entity which "exists"—characterized by being produced—is "perishable," meaning its nature is such that it must perish. Since the cessation of existence characterized by being produced follows upon the cessation of the probandum-property (sādhyadharma), namely perishability, the establishment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is achieved for the momentariness of existence characterized by being produced, because the identity between existence—considered without dependence [on external causes]—and momentariness is established.
This is because there is also certainty regarding the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that serve as its basis.

Thus, with respect to the former teachers, since that which exists is uncreated, it lacks the definition of permanence—namely, "that which exists and is without cause is permanent"—and therefore its permanence does not exist.

Furthermore, it has been demonstrated by others that whatever exists and possesses origination must necessarily be subject to destruction according to the aforementioned reasoning, and thus cannot endure for any length of time.
[44. General demonstration of the identity-pervasion between existence and momentariness:

When, however, it is stated in general that "whatever exists is necessarily momentary," without regard for the distinction of existence characterized as being either produced or unproduced, and by way of bold assertion (*prauḍhavāditā*) without depending on the opponent's own admission that even for the produced destruction is inevitable;
In that case, the independence of everything with respect to destruction is not established at all.
For it is only in the case of things like jars, where destruction is observed to occur, that independence is logical because of the impossibility of a cause for it.

As for those things such as mountains that are obstructed by space and so forth, or which are not seen entering into destruction, since there is no basis for necessarily admitting their perishability,

it is impossible to say that even at the end this thing perishes independently with respect to destruction— because there is no distinction [between the beginning and the end]— and therefore it must be determined to possess that state [of perishability] from the very beginning, as it depends upon its own nature.

Since it is not established that things are independent with respect to destruction, and since uncreated things such as space (*ākāśa*) and the like do depend upon a perishable nature, one perceives the impossibility of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)— which are the basis for [the opponent's argument]— because a perishable nature is not established for an existing thing through independence. Thinking that, at that time, the subverting proof characterized by the contradiction of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-virodha*) must be stated to establish identity (*tādātmya*), he raises the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) and says:

Even if [things] were perishable by their very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*), according to the reasoning already stated, there might be some thing— such as a mountain or the like— which, though produced, has its destruction unperceived because it is obstructed by space and so forth; or there might be something unproduced, such as space and the like, which, being existent, would not possess that nature— that is, it would have a non-perishable nature— even though [all things] are observed to perish.
The word "api" (even/also) is used in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*).
This [possibility] is suspected because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes its nature as perishable;

consequently, since it depends upon a perishable nature, its independence from such a nature is unestablished. Therefore, by virtue of that [dependence], the fact that existence (*sattva*) is the very nature of the probandum—momentariness—is unestablished, and thus the establishment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), which is based upon that [nature], does not occur.
But what is the reason for suspicion here, by which someone might be suspected of not having that nature? He says: "For everything is not the nature of everything.
Indeed, entities are seen to have diverse natures: some are with resistance (*sapratigha*), some are without resistance (*apratigha*);
likewise, they have natures such as blue, non-blue, and so forth.
Thus, the objection of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣāśaṅkā*) is that some [things] are perishable while others are suspected of having a non-perishable nature.
This is not so; one should not suspect that "some might even have a nature other than that," for if that were the case, it would entail its non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*).

And since that being the case, there would follow the consequence that it is a real entity (*vastu*), how could there be any suspicion that it lacks that nature [of momentariness]? Furthermore, why does the consequence of being a non-entity (*avastutva*) follow from non-momentariness?

Because the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of existence is established through its having momentariness as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); therefore, he says: "For power... and so forth.
[45. Existence is precisely the capacity for causal efficiency, and that belongs only to momentary things.
He thinks as follows: First of all, this must be investigated here—what characteristic is appropriate for the existence of these entities?

In that regard, the definition characterized by the connection with existence (*sattā*) is not [valid], because it is under-extended (*avyāpti*), as it does not apply to universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth;
or else, because it is over-extended (*ativyāpti*), as it applies even to things such as the son of a barren woman.

If it is asked, "Since the son of a barren woman and such things do not exist, how can they have a connection with existence? we say: No, because that would involve mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
For their non-existence follows precisely from the absence of a connection with existence, and that absence [of connection] follows from their non-existence.

And if there were a connection with existence (*sattā*) only for those things that already exist, then another definition of existence would have to be stated, and the connection with existence would be redundant, because the thing itself would be existent.
[Objection: "If it is argued that those [non-existent things] lack a connection with existence because they are devoid of the capacity for any causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-sāmarthya*),"...

This being the case, since only that which is endowed with the capacity for causal efficiency possesses existence, it follows that the very capacity for causal efficiency is the definition of an entity; thus, the connection with existence is redundant. "In this way" means: in such a manner.

Otherwise, how could universals (*sāmānya*) and the like possess existence as their own nature (*svarūpa*)? For the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) belongs to all things; therefore, that alone is the defining characteristic of an entity (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, the statement that "existence is that which is associated with arising, passing away, and stability" is also untenable.
Because permanence contradicts arising and passing away, these cannot coexist in a single substratum (*dharmin*).
If it is argued that there is arising and passing away in one sense, while there is permanence in another sense;
Just as origination and cessation are not the same as persistence,
and as persistence is not the same as origination and cessation, so too no single entity could possess the characteristics as they have been described.
For otherwise, it would be impossible for anything else to possess the characteristic of existence, since [the opponent] maintains that capacity exists even in the production of its own cognition.

Otherwise, the systematic arrangement of the six categories and so forth would be untenable; therefore, that [existence] alone is the defining characteristic of being (*bhāva*), while the absence of all causal capacities is, in turn, the defining characteristic of non-being (*abhāva*).

Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "all" is for the purpose of precluding the notion that non-being is merely the absence of capacity in relation to one thing while possessing it in relation to another, since every entity consists in the absence of the capacity [to produce] other entities.

But that which has no capacity whatsoever is said to be non-existence in an absolute sense. If it is argued that existence is defined solely by capacity, then existence would belong only to the non-momentary; consequently, the momentary nature of existence would not be established, so how could there be positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)? To this, he says: "And indeed, the non-momentary has no capacity for any effect, even in the case of the effect characterized as cognition. Therefore, how could it possess existence defined by that [capacity], as would be the case for things such as the past or the future?
For this reason, the momentary nature of an entity would not be established.

Now, one might object: since capacity is beyond the senses and because there is no necessity for causes to produce their effects, how could the absence of such capacity belong to a non-momentary entity, such that it could be excluded by its opposite—non-existence, which is characterized by the total absence of all capacity?

An existent entity would experience only momentariness, because [only then] would there be positive and negative concomitance; therefore, he says: "By means of succession and simultaneity," and so forth.

It is not that the absence of all causal capacities in the case of non-momentariness is stated on the basis of direct perception or the absence of an effect, but rather on the basis of the absence of its pervader.

For instance: causal activity is pervaded by both succession and simultaneity, since there is no other possible mode. Therefore, because those two—which are the pervaders of the capacity for causal activity—are incompatible with non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*), their cessation entails the cessation of the capacity for causal activity which they pervade. Thus, non-existence, characterized by the absence of all capacities, is drawn forth [as the consequence] when non-momentariness is present, via the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Because two contradictory properties cannot coexist in one place, existence, having excluded itself from non-momentary things, remains only within momentary things and thus experiences their very nature; hence:
"whatever exists is necessarily momentary."

Thus, the establishment—meaning the ascertainment—of pervasion, which consists of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), occurs. Now, one might object: since there is no other possible mode [of causal operation], it is said that an effect such as a sprout is produced by a seed and so forth only through either succession or simultaneity; but from what is this very absence of any other mode established for the nature of the effect?
If another mode [of existence] were to meet the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), how could there be absolute impossibility?

There would merely be a negation of its presence in a particular place and so forth. Since the ascertainment of non-existence applies only to things that do not meet the conditions for perception—namely, those that are remote—how can the absence of such [remote] things be established?

Therefore, since causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is possible through another mode, even if succession and simultaneity are excluded, there is no exclusion of the capacity for causal efficiency. Consequently, how could there be non-existence—characterized by the absence of all capacity—in the case of non-momentariness? [And] how, on that basis, could there be positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) between existence and the nature of momentariness? No; for there is no fault in either case.
For instance: "succession" (krama) refers to a sequence, the isolation of the sprout and so forth from other effects;
"simultaneity" (yaugapadya) also refers to its coexistence with other effects such as the seed;
and "alteration" (prakārāntara) refers to the sprout and so forth becoming otherwise even in the absence of those two states.

And when that nature of the sprout and so forth—whether accompanied by other things or alone—is ascertained through direct perception to be non-existent, then its very nature, having met the conditions for perception, is not perceived as being excluded from both successive and simultaneous existence. Since the object is perceptible, once its accompaniment by others or its isolation has been removed, direct perception arises manifesting a location and so forth devoid of it; thus, because the non-perception of its nature occurs, the operation of conventional usage characterized by the determination of non-existence and so forth proceeds.

And regarding that state of being such as a sprout and so forth, there is no contradiction whatsoever even if its exclusion from two specific states of space and time is denied, provided it exists either sequentially in another place and so on, or in some other state. Therefore,
since the absence of any other mode is established by direct perception itself, how could causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*) not be pervaded by succession and simultaneity?

The author of the treatise, however, will himself state—by means of the extension [of the argument] in the words, "By this, succession, non-succession, and so forth are also [refuted]"—that the absence of any other mode is established through perception itself.

Even though another mode might meet the conditions for non-perception (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), its very nature consists in being mutually exclusive of both succession and simultaneity; therefore, [the absence of that mode] is established based on its substratum.

For it is thus: since things that consist of mutual exclusion establish one by the negation of the other, if that [negation] were not established, there would be a contradiction between affirmation and negation; therefore, how could a third alternative consisting of the negation of both possibly exist? Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): where the establishment of one category occurs through the exclusion of another category, there no possibility for a third alternative exists.

For example, when one excludes a particular mode such as "blue" and establishes another mode that is not blue, such as "yellow," there exists the establishment of one mode by means of excluding the other mode, whether sequentially or simultaneously. This applies everywhere to any entity consisting of cause and effect, even when the excluded mode is not itself made an object of cognition; thus, this is a perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*).

Furthermore, there is the establishment of what is excluded from the specific mode being delimited, and the possibility of another mode characterized by its existence outside of that; for these two—identity and otherness—are defined by their mutual exclusion.
Nor should one suspect an infinite regress here due to the fear of further subverting arguments.
Because the contradiction previously established is merely being recalled;

in cases of the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*), it is the very proof of the contradiction— after demonstrating the presence of the reason (*hetu*) in an external locus— that constitutes the sublation (*bādhaka*),
and that [proof] exists here as well.

Therefore, since two contradictory things cannot coexist in one place, there is a certainty regarding the absence of the counter-positive—just as in the case of cold and hot sensations, or existence and non-existence. So how could there be an infinite regress?
In that regard, a non-momentary entity does not produce effects sequentially, because it remains unchanged from its state when it is not acting.
Furthermore, dependence upon auxiliary causes (sahakārin) is untenable for either of the two types of auxiliary causality, and thus it should not be put forward as an argument.
Furthermore, because it would follow that the action of all [factors] occurs at the very same time as a single action, since the nature of their respective causal factors exists at that very moment;
nor does it occur simultaneously.
Because it would contradict perception and other means of valid cognition,
and because it would entail the consequence of performing that action again;
if it is argued that this is not so because [the action] has already been performed, we say no.
Because its capacity does not perish;
otherwise, since there would have been no specific difference in its form as a non-producer even previously, there would be no production.
If it is argued that this is because what has already been produced cannot be produced again, [we reply:]...

In that case, there would follow the consequence of a distinction within a single effect based on its being capable or incapable [of producing it], just as in the case of the seeds of rice, *kodrava* grain, and so forth.

Furthermore, since it is eternal and acts simultaneously, because it exists even prior to that [action], the consequence is that the action must occur at that very time; and since it exists even earlier than that, the action could never occur simultaneously [with anything].

Moreover, for that which acts simultaneously at one time during the preceding and succeeding moments, there would otherwise be non-existence—characterized by a total lack of capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—at other times.
How could it not be momentary? Or, if action is admitted, it must be the position of succession;
and the fault in that has already been stated.

Thus, since it would follow that the sense bases such as the eye could not exist if they were non-momentary, existence occurs only in the case of momentariness; therefore, because the nature of existence is established as being perishable—namely, "whatever exists is necessarily momentary"—the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the form of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is established.
[This constitutes the 3rd section: the establishment of the causal relationship.]

Thus, having established the determination of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) as being based on the proof of identity (tādātmya) in the case of an essential reason (svabhāva-hetu), and since the proof of the causal relation (kāryakāraṇabhāva) is the basis for that [concomitance] in the case of an effect-reason (kārya-hetu)— and since that [proof], which is itself based on perception and non-perception (pratyakṣānupalambha), has already been shown— [the author], in order to remove another cause of error held by opponents, speaks while demonstrating its object:
“In another object”: when the object to be understood (*gamya*) is a thing distinct from the reason (*hetu*), it is an "effect-reason" (*kāryahetu*).
But when it is not another object, it is said to be an "essential-nature reason" (*svabhāvahetu*).
Why, then, is only the effect the reason when it is another object? He says: "Because of non-deviation" (*avyabhicārāt*); for only the effect is [non-deviant] with respect to another object.

It does not deviate from what was previously stated, nor is it otherwise; therefore, when another object is to be understood, the effect itself is called the logical reason (*hetu*) by virtue of its connection (*saṃyoga*).

As for the objection raised by the opponent—that there would be a universal contingency of the relationship between the signified and the signifier—this was addressed by the Teacher with the words beginning with "And not by anyone," and so forth.
Anticipating that an opponent might perhaps raise an objection even here regarding the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), he says: "The relation of cause and effect," and so forth.
For if the effect is stated as the reason, then its capacity to convey [the probandum] would be by virtue of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
And this being the case, it would follow that the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*) holds in every respect.
Just as the general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) of fire are cognizable, its particular properties (*viśeṣadharma*) such as being produced from grass or wood would also have to be cognizable.
Likewise, just as the particular properties of smoke are indicative, its general properties such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and earthiness (*pārthivatva*) would also become indicators.
Why? Because there is a relationship of producer and produced (*janyajanakabhāva*) in every respect.
For the relationship between the produced and the producer is called the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
And that [relationship] exists between fire and smoke not merely in part, but in every respect.

To explain: just as fire is the producer by way of general properties such as being fire, being a substance, and being existent, so too is it the producer by way of specific properties such as being produced from grass or being produced from leaves.

Just as smoke is produced by its own specific, inherent properties such as "smokeness" and "whiteness," so too is it produced by general properties such as "existence" (*sattva*) and "substantiality" (*dravyatva*).

Consequently, just as there is a cause-and-effect relationship between those two, so too would there necessarily be a relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamya-gamaka-bhāva*), because that [latter] is based precisely upon the former; such is the objection raised in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Here it is said: "The relationship of producer and produced does not exist in every respect. Consequently, how could there be a relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*) in that way?

If one asks why, [it is because] "in the absence of those"—that is, in the absence of those specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*) such as being produced from grass or from leaves—"of that which arises," namely smoke in its mere generality, there is an absence of "the necessity of its arising from them" (*tadutpattiniyama*), in the sense that it arises specifically from those particular properties.

Likewise, in the absence of that—that is, in the absence of fire—there is no such rule of origination (*tadutpatti-niyama*) whereby a general property (*sāmānya-dharma*) such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), which exists even when fire is absent, could be said to "belong to fire alone. Since this is not the case, how could there be a relationship of signifier and signified (*gamyagamaka-bhāva*) in every respect? For, in the absence of a rule of origination, it is not logical to establish a relationship between producer and produced (*janyajanaka-bhāva*).

Since this is so, "therefore the effect," such as smoke and the like, [is pervaded] by "as many inherent natures" (*svabhāvaiḥ*) as there are, such as the nature of being smoke (*dhūmatva*), etc.; here the third case ending is used in the sense of a defining characteristic (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇā*).
"Inseparable" (*avinābhāvi*) means that which does not exist without [the cause].
"Without which does it not exist?"—
the phrase "by as many intrinsic natures as there are in the cause" is also connected here.
It is understood that those very natures residing in the cause—without which the natures residing in the effect would not exist—are the cause of those [natures in the effect].

Where is there an inseparable connection (*avinābhāvin*)? It is "in the cause"; that is, within the domain of the cause. Another meaning is that "in the cause" is a locative case denoting the substratum (*ādhārasaptamī*).

Now, the effect is the indicator (*gamaka*) of those general properties residing in the cause—such as "fire-ness," "substance-ness," and so forth—as many as there are that are invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*) with them.

Why? He says: "Because of the necessity of its being their effect" (*tatkāryatvaniyamāt*); because of the existence of such a rule (*niyama*) that this [effect] is indeed the effect of those very general properties residing in the cause.
For the effect never deviates from those general properties at any time.

Having thus defined the aspect residing in the cause by means of the subsequent [verse], he now defines the aspect residing in the effect by means of the preceding [verse], saying: "And by those very [properties]," and so forth.

The effect, too, is the indicator (*gamaka*) of the properties residing in the cause through its own inherent properties; for instance, specific forms such as the state of being smoke (*dhūmatva*) and the quality of being pale-colored (*pāṇḍupārṇatva*), which occur in the interval, do not exist without those general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) residing in the cause.
Here too, the phrase "because of the necessity of being its effect" is required;
for there is a necessity of those very specific properties residing in the effect being effects in relation to the general properties residing in the cause.
For those specific properties residing in the effect never exist without the general properties residing in the cause;
therefore, the restriction that they alone constitute the effect applies,
and not to others such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth.
Thus, for you,
it is only the general properties of the cause that are to be understood, not its specific properties; likewise,
only the specific properties of the effect are the indicators, not its general properties.
This is because of the restriction that [the effect] must be produced by that [cause].

However, those specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*) of the cause—by which there would be a restriction that only certain effects are produced by it—are not [invariably] indicative, as they do not apply to the effect in general. Furthermore, even those general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) of the effect, such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth, lack the capacity to indicate [the cause], precisely because they lack the restriction of being produced by that [specific cause].

If [the absence] is understood through the relation of cause and effect, how could the relation of the signified and the signifier (gamyagamakabhāva) result in being non-existent in every respect, as it would for the opponents?
[2. Even though the relation of producer and produced exists in every respect, the relation of signified and signifier does not likewise exist.
Anticipating the objection that this would entail an undesirable consequence for the opponent, he says: "In part," and so forth.

For if it is maintained that only the general properties of the cause are to be inferred, while only the specific properties of the effect are the inferential indicators— on the basis of the restriction that [the effect] must be the result of that [cause]— then, alas, a relationship of producer and produced would obtain only between partial aspects.
It would follow that only the general properties of the cause are the producers, not its specific properties.

It might be argued that for an effect as well, only its specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*) are produced, not its general properties (*sāmānyadharma*); and since the relationship between producer and produced is intended to hold in every respect, there would be a contradiction with one's own tenet. He resolves this: "There is no consequence of a producer-produced relationship [occurring] by way of parts."
Because a real entity is admitted to be impartite, it is accepted in its entirety; furthermore, the relationship between the signifier and the signified is intended to exist in every respect.
Thus he says: "produced from that," and so forth.
For if that specific quality produced in the effect by those specific qualities residing in the cause can be apprehended,
then— since it is desired that the specific qualities residing in the cause are cognized through the apprehension of the specific quality produced by them—

it follows that the universal properties such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth, which have smoke-ness (*dhūmatva*) and the like as their specific marks (*liṅga-viśeṣa*) and limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), are also intended to be the indicators (*gamaka*).

For instance, when there is the perception of the smoke of agarwood, there indeed occurs the inference of its fire; and by means of the qualification "smokeness," there is the inference of fire through [the universal] "substanceness" and so forth.

It is not the case that because a relation of produced and producer exists in every respect, the relation of the signified and the signifier exists in exactly that same way, since the latter depends upon cognition.
For it is thus: a logical mark (liṅga) does not function as a means of cognition by its mere existence, because it is a communicator (jñāpaka).
Indeed, a communicator makes known the object to be communicated only by depending upon its own ascertainment, and not otherwise.

How then is it said that "in the absence of that [cause], there is no necessity for the arising of that [effect]"? For if one were to accept a causal relationship in every respect, then in the absence of the cause, the effect itself would simply not exist. To this he says: "unqualified," and so forth.

This means that if one takes up merely the effect in its unqualified state—devoid of the apprehension of the specific quality produced by that [cause] and lacking the adjunct of a specific logical mark (*liṅga*)—[then the aforementioned objection holds].

Or, if one intends to refer to an undifferentiated generality— such as "substance-ness" (dravyatva) and so forth— then there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra), because smoke exists even in the absence of specific qualities belonging to its cause, and because substance-ness and the like exist even in the absence of fire; therefore, a causal relationship of produced and producer is not accepted in any such case.
And because of that absence, there is the relationship between the signified and the signifier;
however, this is not the case when one intends to express a specific distinction,
since in that instance there is no deviation.
For instance: if smoke in general exists even in the absence of specific qualities such as being produced from grass or leaves, but no specific quality produced by those [causes] exists,
and yet that [specificity] could be apprehended—
In that case, the specific property (*viśeṣa*) is indeed cognizable, because only that which is ascertained can function as a logical mark (*liṅga*).

Likewise, although the mere existence of substantiality (*dravyatva*) and being (*sattva*) may occur even in the absence of fire, they do not possess the nature of smoke; nevertheless, since that which is qualified by such [smoke] is non-deviant, its status as a means of cognition (*gamaka*) cannot be denied.
[3. Dispelling the doubt that the cognition of the causal relation is extremely difficult to obtain:

Anticipating an opportunity for an opponent’s objection here, he says: "Even though some [effect], such as smoke, exists at some time from some [cause], such as fire, every such smoke—that is, of the same kind as that which was once seen to arise from fire—is [the effect]."

"Born from such a [cause]" (*tathāvidhajanmā*) means one whose birth is from exactly that kind of thing from which that single instance was observed. From what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this "being born from such a cause" determined, such that it is said: "In the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) are based on the establishment of the causal relationship"?

For instance: even if it is understood through perception and non-perception that a certain smoke is the effect of a causal complex such as fire, does this much establish that another [smoke] of the same kind is also the effect of that same [complex]?
No, because perception and non-perception do not operate with respect to that other case.
Let it be that only that specific instance toward which those two [means of knowledge] operate is the effect of that [cause].
But what has happened to anything other than that [fire], such that its birth could proceed from such [a cause]?
For if it were so, why would one not also admit that a particular instance of smoke— since it is seen to be produced by fire and the like— is likewise produced by a jar or some other object?
Because there is no distinction in terms of being something else;
what fault is there in this being the case?

If this is argued, then, because there is an absence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no certainty regarding such a birth; and since there is a suspicion of birth even from what is not of that nature, the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of such smoke and the like with fire and the like are not established.
How, then, can the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) possess the capacity to produce cognition?

For it is not the case that the very same specific smoke—which was understood through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) to be restricted to a particular place, time, and state, and caused by a specific fire—whose positive and negative concomitances are to be apprehended [as universal].
Because that [specific individual] cannot exist in another place and so forth;
what then?

Since it is precisely such a universal nature (*sāmānyātman*) that serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*), and since there is a suspicion that it could arise even from something not of that kind, how could there be positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with such a thing? As it has been said:
“Because of the differences in state, place, and time, the capacities [of things] vary;
thus, the comprehension of entities through inference is extremely difficult.
To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) replies: “No,”
"Of that which does not arise from that," and so forth.

He thinks as follows: although here, at one time, the nature of smoke and the like is ascertained through perception and non-perception as being produced by a causal complex such as fire, the possibility that such [smoke] might arise even from what is not such [a complex] is still suspected.

In this regard, compared to that specific smoke which was once ascertained as being produced by the causal complex of fire and so on, another specific instance of smoke might be of the same kind even if it arises from something different—because things possess diverse causal potencies.

It might be suspected that this could happen; however, since that [smoke] too has been ascertained to be produced by a causal complex such as fire and the like, it remains exactly of that nature even in relation to something other than those. In that case, if the birth of such a thing from something else were to occur without being of that same nature, then a nature of that kind would not have the causal complex of fire and the like as its productive cause; consequently, even for smoke as it is actually observed, the causal complex of fire and the like— [The text continues: —would not be its cause. Therefore, because the production of smoke from something other than fire and the like is never observed, and because its production from fire and the like is observed, the nature of smoke is established as having fire and the like as its cause. Thus, the exclusion of its production from anything other than that is understood through the observation of its own nature (*svabhāvapratibandha*). It is precisely for this reason that the Master [Dharmakīrti] stated: "Because there is no deviation from the nature of things. This is because the nature of things is fixed by the very fact that they are produced from a specific causal complex. Therefore, the non-deviation of the effect from its cause is established through the observation of its own nature. Furthermore, when one says, "This is smoke because it arises from fire," the word "because" (*yasmāt*) expresses the reason (*hetu*), while the phrase "it arises from fire" expresses the logical ground (*liṅga*). Since the logical ground is the reason, and the reason is the logical ground, the two are synonymous. For example, just as the words "this is Devadatta" and "this is the son of the Brahmin" refer to the same person, so too the expressions "this is smoke" and "this arises from fire" refer to the same object. Thus, the logical ground is nothing other than the reason. Consequently, the statement "this is smoke because it arises from fire" is a formulation of the reason (*hetuvākya*). Alternatively, the word "because" may express the logical ground, and the phrase "it arises from fire" may express the reason. In this case, the logical ground is the reason, and the reason is the logical ground. It follows that there must be a cause;
for such a nature [of smoke] would have to be produced by a cause distinct from the causal complex consisting of fire and so forth.
Consequently, since the causal complex of fire and so forth would not be its cause, even that smoke which was seen by me to arise from it on one occasion would likewise not exist.
For that which is not the cause of something does not arise from it even once,
because that would entail the consequence of it being causeless.
In the phrase "not arising from that" (*atadbhāvinaḥ*), the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the intended causes such as fire and so forth.
That is not that; it is not of its characteristics, it is not of such a nature— such as the head of Śakra and so forth— and it has the property of arising from what is not that.

For that very kind of smoke-entity which does not arise from something other than its cause, because of the contradiction with its existence in the absence of "that"—namely fire and so forth—even "once" (sakṛdapi), at any single time—such a nature arises from such a causal complex as fire and so forth. Therefore, it is understood that such a cause produces such an effect; this is established by perception and non-perception operating just once.
So, whence can there be any suspicion of deviation?

Therefore, since smoke is observed to arise once from a specific causal complex such as fire, and because that smoke possesses a nature produced by that [complex], it arises only from such a [complex];
thus, the certainty of positive and negative concomitance is established: "Wherever there is smoke, there is the causal complex of fire and so forth."

Alternatively, it is explained otherwise: here, the establishment of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) based on perception and non-perception was previously stated in order to demonstrate positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
However, that is incorrect.

For instance, regarding "some" smoke—namely, the first [instance] arising immediately after the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of fire and so forth—at the time of its "first production," [the following applies].

“Even though there is the existence [or] arising from some causal complex such as fire and so forth, ‘all’ smoke is ‘of that same kind’—that is, just as the smoke existing in the first moment is, it is of that same kind in the second and subsequent moments as well, because it is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as being non-different from its preceding moments.

‘Born from such [a cause]’ means: that which has its birth from a cause characterized by a specific causal complex of fire, fuel, and so forth, exactly as the first moment of smoke arose, is ‘born from such [a cause].’”
"Why? Because that [smoke] and so forth do not exist at all.
And thus, since it is observed that something which arises from one thing is also seen to arise from another, there would be a lack of confidence in every case.

Thinking this, he says: "And likewise," because smoke could exist even from non-fire, and its existence from the head of Śakra and so forth would not be contradictory, [it would follow that it could exist] through fire as well.
"If you think that there is indeed no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) for smoke"—this is the doubt raised as the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
As it has been said:
"If things are momentary, how could they have a functioning that depends upon anything?"
For those things whose existence occurs from something other than their well-known causes, [there is no dependence].
"Therefore, just as smoke cannot possibly arise from what is not fire, who could prevent its arising from the head of Śakra?

To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) replies: "Smoke produced by a specific causal complex consisting of fire and fuel is not exactly the same as that which arises from smoke itself, due to the difference in their causes."
Because even that which is determined to be similar due to some degree of similarity is nonetheless of a different nature;

for a subsequent moment produced by the same causal complex of fire and fuel is indeed different from the first moment, and likewise, another [subsequent] moment produced by a different complex of fire and fuel is different from the first; thus, such smoke cannot arise from [that very same] smoke.
One should not have any lack of confidence in this regard.

For instance, just as the second moment of smoke produced by the first moment of smoke is of the same nature as that [first moment], so too the second moment of smoke is produced only by another first moment of smoke, and not by a third moment and so forth;
the same should be stated everywhere, including for the third moment onwards, and for sprouts and other such things.

If it is asked, "Whence, then, does this distinction arise? he says: "Of that which does not arise from that"—meaning smoke whose nature is not to arise from something other than fire, fuel, and so forth, and which is indistinguishable from its first moment—"even once," that is, even at one time, "from that," meaning from the causal complex consisting of fire and so forth, "due to non-existence," because its coming into being would be impossible.

For just as the second moment is similar in relation to the first, so too is the first in relation to that [second]; since there is no difference in their similarity, if such a thing were to exist from what is not fire, then such a thing would not have the nature of being produced by fire, and thus it would never arise from that [fire] even once. Or, if it does arise, then by manifesting itself as having the nature of being produced by that [fire], how could it arise from something else?
Therefore, since that which arises from something of a different nature is itself of a different nature, there is no deviation [from the rule].
[4. Although smokes produced by different causes are not identical, they are perceived as being identical due to their similarity.

But surely, since all moments of smoke are useful for purposeful action—such as scratching the throat, causing tears to flow from the eyes, or turning things black—how could they not possess an identical nature?
No, for even that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), whose form is conditioned by the distinction between moments, lacks such [permanence], and thus the same fault applies there as well.
If it is asked, "How then does the conventional usage of 'smoke' occur everywhere in the world? [the answer is:
it is due to the force of the determination of oneness based on the production of subsequent similar [moments], and because the conventional usage of a momentary entity is impossible.
If it is asked, "When there is similarity, why is there not identity?
[the answer is: because that which is similar is other than that which is identical.
For instance, the *gavaya* is similar to a cow, but it is not identical to it.
For it is precisely because another [cognition] is of that same nature.
How could the conceit of being "of that nature" (tādṛśa), which arises among those of dull intellect even regarding what is not of that nature from the perspective of ultimate reality, be averted?
For instance, even the ascertainment of reality cannot be prevented by those of limited vision with respect to what is not that [reality].
How much more so, then, the determination (*adhyavasāya*) that it is of such a nature? As it has been said (Hbṭ 157):
"In a continuum where color and shape are identical, [this determination] arises."
“Why then would people have the notion of identity regarding a single continuum? Thus it is said.
However, those who contemplate reality accept that entities possess such-and-such a nature due to the distinction between such-and-such causes, but they do not accept their identity [of nature].

For if something of such a nature were to arise even from what is not of such a nature, then its nature would be produced by that; consequently, that which does not arise from it would never arise from it even once.
Establishing this very point, he says: "In mutual dependence," and so forth.
For, in relation to the cause, the effect has the nature of being produced; and in relation to the effect, the cause has the nature of producing.
For by whatever cause something is seen to arise, that [cause] is understood to have the nature of producing it, and the other [effect] is understood to be produced by it;
otherwise, its existence from that [cause] would be impossible.
And because it is impossible for the other [type of smoke] to be produced by that [cause].
If this is indeed the case, what is established regarding the subject at hand?
To this he says: "In that case," meaning when this principle holds, "if smoke" is of such a kind as the first [kind] produced by the causal complex of fire and so forth, then...

If [the smoke] existing in the second and subsequent moments were to arise from "another" collection of causes such as fire and fuel— distinct from that which was determined to have the nature of producing it, namely the first moment of smoke generated by the collection of fire,

fuel, and so forth— then the nature of such smoke, being of that kind, would not have "that produced nature," meaning it would not be produced by the collection of fire and so forth, but rather would be produced by smoke itself. Consequently, it could not arise even once from that collection of fire and so forth.
"It would not come to be.

For if such an intrinsic nature were to arise from something else, it would possess an intrinsic nature produced by that [other cause], rather than an intrinsic nature produced by fire and so forth; how, then, would its arising from that [fire] even once be logical?
Here is the illustration: "like other things.

For just as an object distinct [from the cause], which is not intended to be produced by it, arises from something else and thus does not possess the nature of being produced by that [cause]—nor does it possess the nature of being produced by the causal complex of fire and so forth—and therefore does not arise from it even once;
in the same way, smoke of such a kind [is understood]. Thus, when it arises from that [fire], it is understood to be of a different kind altogether.

It might be thought: "Even though that [smoke] has a nature not produced by such [causes] as fire, it is produced by force from the causal complex of fire and so forth; what fault is there on the part of that poor thing? To this he says: "Nor even... It is not only that [the smoke] itself, by virtue of having a nature not produced by those [causes], would not arise from them;
rather, even the causal complex of fire and so forth would not produce such smoke—namely, the kind that exists in the second and subsequent moments. (Hbṭ 158)
Why?
Because it does not have the nature of producing that [effect].

For if such a thing were to arise from something else, then that [other cause] alone would possess the nature of producing it, and not the causal complex of fire and so forth; how then could that which is devoid of the nature of producing it bring it about?
An illustration of this is as follows: "Like another causal complex.
Just as another causal complex, which is not intended to have the nature of producing that [specific effect], does not produce it, so too is the causal complex of fire and other factors.
For indeed, that [complex] proceeds precisely by following its own inherent nature.

Then from what would that causal totality arise? [5. Regarding the production of like and unlike effects: even if smoke has a nature produced by a causal totality such as fire and so forth, it is of such a kind; and even if it has a nature produced by smoke, just as that very same smoke has both a nature produced by fuel and a nature produced by fire.

It might be thought: "Smoke, though its nature is produced by a causal totality such as fire and so forth, is of such a kind; and although it has a nature produced by smoke, just as that very same smoke has both a nature produced by fuel and a nature produced by fire."
It occurs as follows: even such smoke, by virtue of having a nature produced by both causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), would arise from both; therefore, he says:

"And not"—indeed, for such smoke, there is no [nature] "produced by that and not that," meaning neither that which is produced by the causal complex of fire and so forth, nor that which is produced by smoke.
“An intrinsic nature is logical,” meaning it is consistent with reason.
Why? “Because it has a single intrinsic nature,” since there is no difference in such a form of smoke;
for even when there is a difference in time, its such-like nature does not differ.
For if there were a difference [in nature] such that one thing arose from another of a different kind, dispute would be impossible.
If that [thing] were produced by causes of both similar and dissimilar kinds, then it would necessarily possess a nature that is both similar and dissimilar.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Smoke and non-smoke," and so forth.

By the word "smoke," such a nature as is produced by the causal complex of fire and so forth is intended; by the word "non-smoke," a different kind [of nature] produced by a different cause, distinct from that which is produced by smoke, is meant.
And it is precisely through being produced by such or not-such causes that their respective natures as such or not-such must be understood, according to the principle to be explained hereafter.

Therefore, because of the nature of fire as characterized by smoke—namely, its nature of producing both smoke and non-smoke, that is, its nature of producing such and non-such [effects]—this [fire], as it comes into being in such and non-such ways, would possess a nature of smoke and non-smoke, that is, a nature of being such and non-such.
Why then would it be of such a nature alone? To answer "Why is this so?", he says: "Of the natures of effects," and so forth.

For those natures of effects which are mutually incompatible must be produced by causal complexes that possess mutually distinct natures; they are not inherent, because that would entail the consequence of being causeless.
Therefore, smoke arising from such and non-such [causes] would necessarily possess such and non-such natures.

It might be thought: "In the case of having such-and-such or not-such-and-such intrinsic natures, there is no dependence upon such-and-such or not-such-and-such causes, because causes are required only for the mere production of effects. To this he says: "And if there were no dependence on causes"—that is, if there were no dependence on such-and-such or not-such-and-such causes regarding the state of being such-and-such or not-such-and-such—then it would follow that such-and-suchness [and its opposite] are "without cause" (*ahetukatva*).

For there is no other "arising" (utpatti) apart from the coming-to-be of such-and-such a nature after not having existed, wherein even those things independent of causes of such-and-such a nature would nonetheless depend upon them.
Therefore, by the word "arising," it is precisely the state of having such-and-such a nature that is expressed.
In that case, if one accepts dependence on a cause, how could there not be dependence on a cause regarding that very state of being such-and-such?

Therefore, since the distinction between the natures of effects as being similar or dissimilar arises precisely from the similarity or dissimilarity of the causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), how could that which is of one nature arise from something of a different nature? As for what was said— that "just as a single smoke is produced by fire and fuel which are of different characteristics, so too a single-characterized effect will arise even from a different complex of causes"—
that is incorrect.

For we do not deny that things which are distinct [from one another] can be productive; indeed, even though they are mutually distinct, those factors—whose nature consists in the proximity of the transformation of their own causes and who are restricted to that particular state—produce that single effect. However, because there is a restriction on the nature of the produced and the producer through their mutual dependence, it is said that such an effect arises only from such [causes] and not from something else, since the latter lacks the nature of producing that specific effect.
Because even in the absence of that [specific cause], if it were to arise from something else, there would be no necessity regarding its production;
and if there is no necessity, the relationship of cause and effect is untenable.
However, if—like fire assisted by the material cause of fuel—it is assisted by that material cause, then like the fuel, it would be restricted to that state, even if it were not of that nature.

If smoke and the like were to produce such smoke, and this were understood through perception and non-perception—just as in the case of fire and so forth—then who would not accept that it too is a producer of such [smoke], given the restriction of its nature to produce that?

However, if such [smoke] occurs even in the absence of that [fire], then because there is no restriction on the nature of those two as produced and producer, how could there be a causal relationship? For such [an effect] arising from something of a different kind would be entirely causeless.

Since this is so, "therefore" that specific causal complex consisting of fire, fuel, and so forth must be understood as "that which" initially "produces smoke," and not any other; and that smoke is initial, being produced by "that specific causal complex of fire and so forth," and not any other.
Thus, because of the restriction of the nature of the produced and the producer—consisting of the relationship between effect and cause—in the manner described above.

When the specific cause of a particular effect has been once ascertained through perception and non-perception, it follows that the production of such an effect cannot occur from a "dissimilar" cause—that is, from a cause of a different nature; however, this does not preclude the production of a dissimilar effect from a dissimilar cause.
Thus, having established that the nature of a similar or dissimilar effect is produced by a similar or dissimilar cause, he concludes as follows:

“Therefore,” because a particular effect has been observed and ascertained through perception and non-perception to arise from a particular cause, it “does not deviate”; that is, such an effect does not arise from anything other than that [cause].
For this reason, “when the causal relationship is established,” for such an effect, there is only such [a cause].

When there is the certainty that [the effect] has a cause, then by the aforementioned reasoning, the "pervasion of the effect by the cause"— consisting of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)— is established. Not understanding this meaning— that "there is no production from a heterogeneous [cause]" means that there is no production from a cause dissimilar to the observed cause,
i.e., from a cause of a different kind— the opponent objects, thinking that the intended meaning here is that "the effect is not produced from a heterogeneous cause," and says:

"But surely," [one might object], "it is observed that some effect arises from a cause even of a different class; how then is there no contradiction with observation regarding the claim that there is no production from what is of a different class?

To explain how this is so, he says: "For example, from cow dung and so forth"—by the inclusion of "and so forth," horn, moonstones, and the like are meant—"lotus roots and so forth"—by the inclusion of "and so forth," pond water and the like are meant.
For instance: the production of a lotus stalk from cow dung, of an arrow from a horn, and of water from a moonstone occurs.
Yet cow dung and the like are not of a different genus (*vijātīya*) from the lotus stalk and so forth; why then is it said that "there is no production from what is of a different genus"?
The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*), demonstrating the error of the opponent, says: "There is no production from what is of a different genus."
For the intended meaning here is that whatever arises from a particular cause does not arise from something of a different nature than that;
it is not meant that it does not arise from something heterogeneous to the effect.
Nor is there any deviation (vyabhicāra) in this regard.

Thus he says: "For indeed, such a thing as the form of cow-dung and so forth is the 'cause' (*nimitta*) for that [lotus root] of Śāluka and the like; that is to say, it is the cause of the initial moment—the first point of commencement—of the continuum of the lotus root and so forth. Therefore, there is no non-difference of cause for the beginning of the continuum of the lotus root and so forth, because its production does not arise from something of a different nature."
Because everything, such as that [sprout] and so forth, has cow-dung and other things as its cause;

however, when there occurs a process characterized by the production of successive moments in a continuous series where each subsequent moment is caused by the preceding moment—such as in the case of an arrow—then existence arises from the arrow.

Thus, that which arises from horns and the like is not of the same nature as the arrow and so forth, whereas that which is of the nature of the arrow and so forth consists of those successive moments.
Since an entity such as a horn does not arise from such [causes], it is impossible for such a thing to originate from a cause belonging to a different genus from its observed causes;
thus, there is a determination of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).

Even when lotus roots (*śālūka*) and the like are held to be dependent on their own preceding species and proceed in an beginningless continuum, there is still no deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because even though some may arise from cow dung and similar substances, they lack the requisite similarity (*tādṛśatva*).
Demonstrating this, he says: "And there exists," and so forth.

There is indeed a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*)—that is, a mutual dissimilarity—between those two lotus stalks (*śālūka*), one produced from cow dung and the other produced from something else, even though their form (*rūpa*) is identical, provided that for one the series of lotus stalks has cow dung and the like as its cause, while for the other it always has its own kind as its cause.
If it is asked, "How can there be a difference in nature when the form is identical?", he says: "For not," and so forth.

Because the mere identity of form is not the cause for the "suchness" (tādṛśatva)—that is, the being of that kind—of entities; for if that were the case, then because of the similarity of form between a lotus born from cow dung and one born from something else, they would possess that very same nature and there would be no distinction of genus.
Why is this so? He says: "Even for those whose forms are non-different," and so forth.

For even among certain entities that possess an identical form, a difference in genus (*jāti*) is observed based on some other specific characteristic (*viśeṣa*) distinct from that form; therefore, identity of form alone is not the basis for the unity of genus.
To illustrate: even when there is identity of form, a distinction is sometimes observed between flowers, as in the case of two sun-like blue and non-blue blossoms.
In some cases, it is from the fruit, as in the case of the two types of *karkoṭakī*—the barren and the otherwise;

in some cases, from the taste, as in the case of the two types of cucumber—the wild and the cultivated; and in some cases, from the fragrance, as in the case of the two types of *campaka*—those produced from trees and those from elsewhere.
In some cases, due to the influence of [a particular] power, it is like the case of two *harītakī* fruits, where the utility of touch is lost;
therefore, although the notion "this is that very same thing" is based on the similarity of form...

Thus, although recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) imagines a similarity between two *śālaka* insects—one born from cow dung and the other from elsewhere—it must nevertheless be understood that there is indeed a difference in their genus (*jāti*) because they are produced by distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*);
they do not belong to a single genus.
For this very reason, since recognition is erroneous, the "suchness" (*tādṛśatva*) imagined by it is unreal.
Faults in the production of a non-distinct effect from a distinct causal complex:

Furthermore, if—on the basis of recognition—it is held that things such as lotus stalks produced from cow dung and other materials, or smoke produced from fire and other causes, possess an identical nature despite being dependent on distinct causal complexes; #
"What would be the fault?"—to this he says: "For otherwise," and so forth.

For if [the causal complex] that produces a lotus and the like consists either of its own kind accompanied by other conditions characterized by its own nature, or of things such as cow-dung which are independent of its own kind;

Or, if from a causal complex that is dissimilar— characterized by such things as the kindling of fire for smoke, or having the nature of Indra’s head and so forth, yet consisting of smoke and the like— an effect that is itself non-dissimilar and of that same nature, such as smoke or a water-lily bulb, were to arise, then [the principle of] "the cause" [would be violated].

Considering that the difference and non-difference— that is, the distinctness and non-distinctness— of an effect from its causal complex (sāmagrī) by way of difference and non-difference would consist in its being of the same class or of a different class, it follows that for the "entirety" (viśvasya), the whole mass of entities, difference and non-difference would be "causeless" (ahetuka) in terms of their being of the same class or of a different class.
Therefore, wherever the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is of a different nature, even if there is some similarity due to certain commonalities, the effect remains of a distinct genus (*vijātīya*).

Now, one might object: "Even when there is a difference in the causal complexes—such as smoke and fuel—the learned do not acknowledge a difference in the genus (*jāti*) of the smoke, because the exclusion of what is not that nature (*atadrūpaparāvṛtti*) is identical in both cases."
This is not a fault,
because even though there are subtle internal class-differences based on the distinction between moments, the exclusion of heterogeneous things based on the gross continuum remains the same.

Just as the universal "cow" is established by the exclusion of non-cows despite internal class-differences such as *śābaleya* and so forth, so too is the determination of all smoke as belonging to a single continuum [established].
Because they are identical in being the basis for a single uniform cognition, even though there is a difference in their material causes and moments.
If it is asked, "How is this so for the first smoke produced from fuel? it is not so;
for all smokes conform to the nature of the fuel from which they arise.
For instance, the fumes of incense, camphor, sandalwood, and so forth, indeed conform to the specific varieties of those substances;

and the fumes of wicks made from substances that cure coughs, asthma, and other ailments likewise conform to them, because they follow the nature of their taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*).

Nor is there a state of being of a different genus (*vijātīyatva*) due to a difference in form (*ākāra*), because homogeneity and heterogeneity are not based on the non-difference or difference of forms;
for instance, [it is not the case that] rice sprouts and the like [are homogeneous simply because they share a common form].
They imitate the form of the first smoke and so forth, yet they do not fail to experience their belonging to that same class based on the exclusion of non-rice-grains and the like.
