Therefore, fuel alone is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), which, having received a specific quality through auxiliary conditions such as fire and so forth, produces such an effect as smoke in the form of embers and the like; enough of this over-elaboration.

Now, one might object: "If indeed no difference in the effect arises despite a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), then, since that [effect] is absent even when there is a difference in the causes, let it be causeless;
but what follows for its non-difference, such that both are said to be causeless? To this, he says: "For instance," and so forth.

For when, despite a difference in the causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), no difference arises in the effect, that effect is [erroneously held to be] causeless; indeed, it is not possible for that which does not exist even when the cause is present to possess causality in any way whatsoever. In that case, as for this non-difference of the effect, since it has arisen while there is a difference between the two causal complexes, how can it possibly possess causality?
For just as there is no possession of a cause for that which does not exist when a cause is present, how could there be possession of a cause for that which exists even when a cause is absent?
If it is argued that this is not so because the very distinction of causes is based on non-distinction [of the effect],
then this distinction would never find a foothold anywhere.

Because even in the case of rice, kodrava grain, and so forth, there is no difference in their causes despite the difference in their effects; for if one were to postulate [a cause] without a specific basis (nimitta), there would be no distinction [between them].

Furthermore, since the non-difference of appearance is observed due to some cause of error, even though there is ultimately a difference [between things], [the opponent might argue that the distinction is merely apparent].

It might be argued: "For one who maintains that such [an effect] arises even from what is not of that nature, the causelessness of both difference and non-difference is indeed accepted; only entities themselves possess causes. To this, he says: "And distinct from that..."
And so forth.
For there exists no nature of entities whatsoever that is distinct from difference and non-difference, which could possess a cause even if those two were themselves uncaused.
This is because [such a nature] would be other than those two.

For [otherwise] there would follow the consequence of an absence of relation in the form "these two possess difference and non-difference," and because if one were to postulate another relation distinct from that, there would be the fault of infinite regress.

Even if there were non-difference, since both difference and non-difference, as well as the intrinsic nature of an entity, would abide solely within themselves and because they do not confer any benefit upon one another, how could there be any relation? Furthermore, if one maintains that the intrinsic nature of an entity arises from its own causes alone and is produced neither different nor non-different from anything else,
then even when those [causes] exist, since there is no alteration of the intrinsic nature, how could the entity's nature be either different or non-different?
Now, if difference and non-difference were to be established as the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity by virtue of a difference and non-difference that are distinct [from it],

then if those two [difference and non-difference] are themselves distinct, the intrinsic nature of the entity remains exactly as it was; thus, there could be no difference or non-difference of that [entity] from anything whatsoever in terms of its own form.

Furthermore, if one again postulates difference and non-difference on the basis of that [entity], the nature of the entity remains in that same state, and there is an infinite regress regarding difference and non-difference.
Alternatively, if they are non-different, it would follow that the very nature of the entity is being produced by difference and non-difference;
however, it is impossible for it to be produced by means of another form.
Furthermore, because that [existence] arises later from another cause, it would follow that it is something other than the former;
nor is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of an entity produced, since it is already established by its own cause alone.

Alternatively, if one imagines that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity arises from its own causes as something possessing a nature both distinct and non-distinct [from those causes], then distinction and non-distinction—which possess a separate existence—would be redundant;
for the cognitions of distinction and non-distinction would be established from that very [intrinsic nature] alone.

Therefore, since it is illogical for distinction and non-distinction to exist as the specific (*viśeṣa*) and the universal (*sāmānya*) as imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas and others, the intrinsic nature of the entity itself is what is expressed by the words "distinction" and "non-distinction. If these two were causeless, it would follow that the intrinsic nature of the entity itself is causeless.
Consequently, because things would lack a cause, they would either exist eternally or not exist at all;
for if things were causeless, if they existed at any time, they would exist at all times, and if they did not exist at any time, they would likewise never exist.
However, it is illogical for existence to be occasional.
Why?
Because if that which is depended upon were itself causeless, nothing would exist.
Because it is logical that those things which are "occasional"— meaning they exist at certain times— occur when that cause to be depended upon exists and do not occur when it is absent,
and not otherwise;
therefore, one must not accept that an effect of non-dissimilar character arises from a cause of dissimilar character.
Because, according to the reasoning already stated, it would follow that [effects] are causeless and so forth;

furthermore, he states another fault regarding the production of a non-distinct effect from a distinct causal complex: "And there is a fixed application" (*vyavasthāvān*)—that is, a specific determination—in the world, regarding "the things to be accomplished" (*sādhyeṣu*), such as jars and cloth, "of the means of accomplishment" (*sādhanānām*), such as clay and thread.

One who desires a jar would employ only a lump of clay for that purpose and not threads, and one who desires a cloth would employ only threads and not a lump of clay; such [distinctions] would not exist.

Why? He says: "Because of the restriction of the capacities"—that is, the specific powers characterized as particular excellences of the natures—of the "causes," which are the causal complexes (*sāmagrī*). Only a certain complex [is restricted] to a certain [effect]. (Hbṭ 165)

If you argue that it is because [a specific cause] is employed for a specific effect and not another, such that "only a certain thing," like clay and so forth, is taken up for the accomplishment of "only a certain thing," like a jar and so forth, and "not another" such as thread and so forth which is dissimilar to it—[we reply:
this is because "of that very thing," such as clay, there is "capacity"—that is, suitability—"in that regard," such as in the jar; whereas "another," such as thread, lacks capacity therein.

Why does only that [specific cause] have the capacity for that [effect] and not another? To this he says: "Because of the difference between those two"—namely, clay and so forth, and thread and so forth—due to their having the nature of producing that [effect], such as a jar, and due to their having the other nature, namely, the nature of not producing a jar and so forth; that is, because of their distinctness.
For there is no such thing as a "nature of producing or not producing" that is actually other than the very form of clay, thread, and so on.

But when it is not accepted that there is a restricted capacity even among causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) that are mutually distinct— since it is admitted that a non-distinct effect can arise even from what is distinct— then, [the argument follows]: "even from something distinct from that which has the nature of producing it," that is, from something distinct from the causal complex characterized by fire, fuel, and so forth, which has the nature of producing smoke and the like, [an effect would arise] from the head of Śakra and so on, by way of momentariness.

Or, if it is intended that smoke and so forth— which are produced by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consisting of fire, fuel, and so on— arise at that very moment, then there would be "no restriction of its generative capacity," meaning no restriction of the capacity to produce the specific effect such as the intended smoke. "Therefore" (*iti*), "whatever" effect "might arise from whatever" cause, [would follow].

It is not the case that everything arises from everything exactly as it is seen; otherwise, everything would arise from everything. Therefore, one must admit a specific restriction of causal capacities among causes.

Therefore, even if a result produced by a dissimilar causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is perceived as having a similar form due to some degree of resemblance, it remains entirely different [in its true nature]; thus, it is established that everything of such a kind is born from a cause of that same nature. It might be argued: "Even though the causal complex is dissimilar, its capacity to produce an effect of that specific character is identical; therefore, the effect will possess that character. And because this occurs only for certain [complexes], there is no occasion for the fault previously stated. To this, he says: "But if there were equality in the capacity to produce that," and so forth.

The refutation already stated here in the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa)— beginning with "And smoke does not have a nature that is both produced by that [fire] and not produced by that"— and so forth, applies here as well.

Even granting this, he says: "Just as the capacity (*śakti*)—which is an excellence of its own nature (*ātmātiśaya*)—of the fuel, which undergoes a modification produced by fire as its auxiliary cause, is the cause for the differentiation of smoke through its own differentiation, exactly such [a capacity] belongs to Indra’s head or to smoke.

If that capacity, characterized as an excellence of its own nature, were the power to produce an effect distinct from the smoke generated by that causal complex (*sāmagrī*), then, given the identity of that capacity, it would be that very same thing consisting of fire, fuel, and so forth, merely stated under another name."
For it is impossible for that which is distinct from something else to possess an excellence whose nature is not distinct from it.
Indeed, that alone is fire which, imparting a transformation to the fuel, produces smoke;
and that alone is fuel which, undergoing a transformation induced by fire, causes the smoke to conform to its own genus.

And if you likewise accept this even for the head of Śakra and so forth, then there would be a dispute over nothing more than names, since you would be using such designations while accepting that the referent is not different.
Therefore, because it is thus, "the effect"— such as smoke and the like— having been "seen" once through perception and non-perception, [is established].

The cause, such as fuel and so forth, by its nature excluded from what is not that [effect], does not "deviate" with respect to the continuum or the moment—meaning it does not arise from anything else distinct from that which possesses those characteristics; thus, the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is established in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).
4. Examination of the Reason of Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhihetu*).
[1. The essential nature of non-apprehension, preceded by a demonstration of conflicting views:

Thus, in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), since it has been observed that whenever [the cause] exists, [the effect] occurs, through both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalambha*), such being the case for all [effects] of that kind...

It has been established that the birth [of an effect] occurs only from such a cause and not from something of a different kind; thus, when the existence of even a single individual effect is observed to arise from a specific cause, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is proven through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

However, regarding non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as previously described—which is based on the demonstration of the absence of other possible causes—there is no disagreement concerning its positive and negative concomitances.
However, they disagree regarding its very nature.

For instance, some, such as Īśvarasena and others, maintain that non-apprehension—which is merely the absence of apprehension—is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes known negation in the form of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).

Others, however, the Mīmāṃsakas, assert that it is a distinct means of valid cognition from perception and inference, consisting either of the self’s non-modification into the form of a cognition of the object to be negated, or of a cognition directed toward an object other than that [negated] thing, which makes negation known.
For cognition— whether of the nature of perception or inference— that has another entity as its object does not apprehend non-existence,
because it has a positive aspect (bhāvāṃśa) as its object, and the negative aspect (abhāvāṃśa) is distinct from that.
However, when it produces the cognition "it does not exist" regarding the aspect of non-existence, it receives the designation of "non-existence as a means of valid cognition" (*abhāvapramāṇa*),
just as the sense faculty receives the designation of "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) by virtue of generating the apprehension of its own object.

Likewise, others maintain that non-apprehension— characterized either as the presence of another thing or as the cognition thereof— is a means of establishing only non-existence itself, and not the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding non-existence.

Since the non-existence [of an object] is established through the mark (liṅga) of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), the conventional usage of that [non-existence] proceeds by itself. However, the Naiyāyikas maintain that the very cognition "it does not exist" is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) occurring immediately after the cognition that apprehends the bare locus and so forth; they do not assert it to be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of the determination of non-existence, which is of the nature of a mere void. That very [cognition] is what is designated by the term "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) with respect to the object to be negated, such as a jar.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction at all, then since the cognitions of the opponents have thus reached a divergence regarding non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), [the author], in order to refute that, first demonstrates the nature of non-apprehension, saying: "Of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension," and so forth.
‘Having reached the conditions for apprehension’ means:

the completeness of the other conditions for apprehension— namely, those designated as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)— as well as the specific nature of the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

The nature [of a thing] is such that, when other conditions for perception are present, it becomes directly perceived; this is how it was explained by the author of the treatise elsewhere (*Hbṭ* 168) in order to refute the misconceptions of the Naiyāyikas.

For they claim that by the term "attainment of the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*), they refer to the properties of substances, namely magnitude (*mahattva*), consisting of multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*), and form (*rūpa*).
"Perception occurs because of magnitude, because of possessing multiple substances, and because of color," according to this statement.

Thus, they declare that non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perception is possible even when a real object exists; therefore, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) for establishing the conventional usage of "non-existent.
For even in the case of visual rays, magnitude, possession of multiple substances, and color do not serve as causes for their own perception.
And yet, even with such non-perception, it is not possible to establish the conventional usage of its non-existence there.
As the author of the Bhāṣya said: "The non-perception by direct perception of that which is perceived through inference is not a reason for its non-existence."

"Because it is a sense faculty, like the skin and so forth, the eye must function by reaching its object (*prāpyakārin*); thus, by means of inference, a visual ray (*cākṣuṣo raśmi*) is perceived. How can its non-perception through direct perception (*pratyakṣato 'nupalabdhi*) establish the conventional usage of its non-existence? Thus, the Naiyāyikas state that the non-perception of something that meets the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntikī*) regarding the conventional usage of its non-existence. To refute this, [the author] demonstrates the true nature of meeting the conditions for perceptibility.
The author of the treatise stated:

"For when the completeness of other conditions for perception and the specific nature [of the object] as previously described are called 'attainment of the conditions for perception' (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*), rather than [merely] its largeness and so forth, then how could there be any occasion for error?
Because that [non-perception] is impossible when the thing actually exists."

However, properties such as magnitude (*mahattva*) cannot be denoted by the term "attainment of the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpti*) precisely because they are impossible [in this context].

For a substance (*dravya*) distinct from color-form (*rūpa*) and the other qualities does not appear in its own cognition through any other aspect that distinguishes it from the appearance of those [qualities].
Nor can that which does not so appear experience perceptibility through a form that distinguishes it from what is not itself, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

How, then, could there be the possibility of largeness and so forth for that which is non-existent? Nor is it possible for something that is not large by its own nature to possess largeness even through a connection with it.
Furthermore, if it were apprehended under another form, how could the cognition grasping it be non-erroneous?
Therefore, neither magnitude nor color is the perceiver of the substance;
for if it were apprehended in its own form, the nature of the substance would remain entirely beyond perception.
Furthermore, since the form of the substance is not perceived as distinct from that [magnitude or color], it does not possess such a capacity for apprehension.
Furthermore, neither magnitude nor color is admitted to exist at the time of the substance's arising,
because a substance is held to be the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of its qualities;
and since it acquires that state only once its own self-nature has been attained, the substance is indeed devoid of qualities in the first moment.

Furthermore, in its second moment, there is neither the abandonment of its prior form nor the manifestation of another form, by virtue of which it— having previously not attained the status of a substrate— might become a substrate through the connection with qualities such as magnitude (*mahattva*).
Moreover, that which is not a producer [of an effect] cannot be a substrate.
Furthermore, if it were a producer, it would necessarily be momentary,
because for that which is non-momentary, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is contradictory.
Therefore, how could there be the possibility of an inherent cause (*sāmavāyikāraṇa*)?
For it is designated as such because it produces an effect that has emerged from itself;

and this is not possible if [the entity] is momentary, nor if it is non-momentary, since there would be no substratum later for that which previously lacked a substratum. Furthermore, due to the impossibility of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), it cannot possess multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*); for it is only that which possesses multiple substances as its inherent causes in the form of constituent parts that is so designated.
And because it lacks substantiality (*dravya*), it does not possess multiple substances.
Even if existence (*sattva*) were present, we do not maintain that this [existence] meets the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) such as magnitude (*mahattva*) and so forth.
As for that which is [erroneously] imagined...

The author of the treatise demonstrated that this non-apprehension of something that has met the conditions for apprehensibility is not inconclusive regarding the establishment of the conventional usage of "non-existence": "Non-apprehension" of something other than the object to be negated— whether it be a cause or a pervader— that has "met the conditions for apprehensibility," is the "reason for the absence [of the effect]" and the "reason for the conventional usage of the absence of the pervaded."

The word "or" (*vā*) indicates that non-apprehension of that which is to be negated and which has reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is indeed the cause for the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*).

However, non-apprehension of that which has not reached the conditions for apprehension—which is characterized by the cessation of perception and inference—is a cause for doubt, because even when the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cease, the absence of the object is not established.
Nevertheless, it should be understood that due to the absence of the [necessary] cause, it serves as the cause for the negation of the conventional usage of its existence.
[2. Refutation of Īśvarasena, Kumārila, and others, in order to clarify one’s own intended non-apprehension:

In that regard, first, as for those who maintain that non-apprehension is merely the absence of apprehension, or—as stated in the words "or consciousness of another object"—who maintain that it is simply the consciousness of something other than that [object],...

In order to refute that [objection] and to demonstrate non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) characterized by the properties of the knower and the known, he first shows that apprehension itself is of two kinds, saying: "In this" statement of non-apprehension, when that apprehension which is heard as having the form of an action is considered as residing in the agent, then, while its being a property of "the one who apprehends"— that is, the agent— is being considered, "the cognition of that" belongs to the one who is apprehending.
That which is knowledge is called apprehension (*upalabdhi*).
And that which is apprehending—the complex of the intellect, the sense faculties, and the body—is said to be the producer of apprehension, being comprised within the preceding moment.
For it is thus: others say that the producer of apprehension, or its substratum, is the agent (*kartṛ*).

Nor is it possible for anything other than the sense faculties (*indriya*) and so forth to possess the capacity to produce [cognition], because the conventional designation of the causal relationship between effect and cause is based upon positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

And these two—positive and negative concomitance—are not possible for anything other than the sense faculties and so forth, because cognition occurs with necessity when the sense faculties and so forth are present.

For if, even when the sense faculties and so forth are present, cognition were sometimes not to arise, then that non-arising of the effect despite all other causes being present would indicate the deficiency of some other cause; thus, there would be a cause distinct from those [faculties].
It might be so conceived;
however, this is not the case.
Therefore, how could the self be accepted as being the causal condition for its own arising?

Because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), as it has been said: "When X exists, Y necessarily comes to be; if one were to postulate something other than that [X] as the cause of Y, there would be an infinite regress of causes in every case."
Since the status of being a substratum (āśrayatva) belongs only to that which produces [an effect], that too is not possible for the self (ātman).

If it is argued that it is a substratum because it is a stabilizer (sthāpaka), we say no; for if [the entity] were momentary, there would be no stability, and even if it were non-momentary, it would persist by itself without destruction.

For instance, the non-destruction of perception itself is called its "staying," not the absence of falling, because it lacks weight (*gurutva*). And the established doctrine (*kṛtānta*) of others is that "falling occurs due to weight through the absence of conjunction.
If it is argued that [perception] has a substratum (*āśraya*) by way of inherence (*samavāya*), [we reply:
surely even that [inherence] is held to exist only between things that stand in the relation of the supported and the supporter.
Nor does the substratum (ādhāra) contribute anything to a perception that is by nature non-falling;
furthermore, if inherence (samavāya) were the basis for being a substratum, it would follow that everything else would also possess that status,
since inherence is uniform across all entities.
Because it is apprehended as a unity,
and because causal efficiency is incompatible with both succession and simultaneity, this self has no existence; therefore, how could it possess the capacity to produce anything?
Or is it the state of being a substratum?
Enough of this grinding of what has already been ground.

Having thus demonstrated apprehension (*upalabdhi*), he demonstrates non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) by saying: "Therefore, non-apprehension is an apprehension that is distinct from the cognition of [that] apprehension, having as its object another entity, and consisting in cognition."
But how can perception itself be called non-perception?
To this he says: "In the intended [context]," and so forth.
Just as in a discussion concerning what is fit to be eaten and what is not, [something is called "non-eatable"] because it is other than the eatable intended [in that context].
"The village cock is not to be eaten";
even though it is edible for others,
it is so stated because it is other than that which is intended as edible in the context of what may and may not be touched.
And just as one who is untouchable, such as a *caṇḍāla* and so forth, is said to be "touchable" by someone other than that [untouchable person],
in the same way, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) should be understood as being nothing other than apprehension (*upalabdhi*).
Since the negative particle (*nañ*) has negation as its object, how can it have a positive entity as its object?

If this is argued, he says: "By way of exclusion (*paryudāsa-vṛtti*). By that function of the negative particle (*nañ*) which, through exclusion—meaning by the setting aside of the object to be negated—operates upon a qualified object, there is the status of being a positive entity (*bhāva-viṣayatā*) for the negative particle whose negation has not been grasped.

Where the affirmation is primary and the negation is understood through implication, where the subject of the affirmation is not expressed by its own word, and where there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), there the function is that of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
And the primacy of the affirmation is as follows:
"From the perception of what is intended, there occurs the perception of something else."

Thus, because the sentence prescribes the apprehension of something else, the negation of the intended apprehension is understood through the very power of that apprehension of another; for if the intended apprehension were not excluded, it would be impossible to prescribe "another" in relation to it. Therefore, by its own word, the negative particle (*nañ*) does not express that which possesses the character of a positive injunction.
What then does it do?
Because the word "other" (anya) is employed in the sentence by relying on the exclusionary negation (paryudāsa), it is "other perception" (anyopalabdhi) that is "non-perception" (anupalabdhi).

Furthermore, since the negative particle (nañ) has syntactic force (sāmarthya) with a nominal stem (subanta) and not with a verbal suffix (tiṅanta), there is a single unified sentence: "Non-perception is the absence of perception" (nopalabdhir anupalabdhiḥ).
Furthermore, *prasajyapratiṣedha* (non-presuppositional negation) should be understood as the opposite of this [implicative negation].

For in that case, the negation is primary, while the affirmation is understood by implication; there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), and the element subject to negation is connected with the negative particle (*nañ*) itself.

Having thus explained non-apprehension characterized as a property of the knower, he says—while establishing non-apprehension characterized as a property of the object—"In the state of being an apprehended property," and so forth.

When the apprehension (*upalabdhi*) of an object being perceived is intended with respect to the action residing in the object (*karmasthakriyā*), then apprehension should be understood as having the nature of the object (*viṣayasvabhāva*).
What is the nature of this object? He says: "In its own object," and so forth.

The nature of the object, characterized by its capacity to produce that cognition which has as its object the self-nature of the thing to be negated— such as a jar— is what is expressed by the term "perception" (*upalabdhi*).
If perception is the nature of the object, how can it be characterized as a capacity?
For fitness (*yogyatā*) is a property (*dharma*), and there is indeed a distinction between a property and its substratum (*dharmin*); therefore, he says: "Of fitness," and so forth.
For fitness, in the ultimate sense, is of the nature of an entity itself and does not differ from the nature of the thing (*vastu*).
Otherwise, an entity would not even be capable [of causal efficiency];
nor could it possess capability, because there would be no relation [between them].
It has already been stated that if one were to postulate such a relation, it would lead to an infinite regress.
Having thus established that perception (*upalabdhi*) is a property of the object, he now establishes non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) as well, saying: "Therefore, other than that," and so forth.

"Therefore" means other than the object of negation, such as a jar, which is capable of producing a cognition of its own object; that which is other [than that] is precisely the nature capable of producing perception—not its opposite—but rather the form of the location devoid of the jar. And that alone is what is expressed here by the term "non-perception."
Pointing out the same logic as before, he says: "As in the previous case.
Because it is distinct from the intended perception—like that which is inedible or untouchable—it functions by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

But how is this negative particle (*nañ*), being a general term functioning with another meaning, [understood] through exclusion as the non-perception of the place devoid of a jar, or rather, the non-perception of the cognition itself which is devoid of a jar?
But is this not the case for all things without distinction that are denotable by other words?
To this he says: "In which," and so forth.
"In which" means in a place, time, or state characterized by non-interruption and the like.

"When a certain object such as a location or a color is perceived, if another object such as a jar or a color is necessarily—that is, invariably—perceived, then that object, such as the jar or the color, is 'conjoined with it,' meaning conjoined with that location or color.
[Objection: How can there be the necessary perception of one thing when another is being perceived?
If this is argued, it is not so, because there is no difference in their capacity (*yogyatā*).
For the capacity to produce a cognition of their own respective objects is equal for both the location (*pradeśa*) and the jar.

Indeed, when the form of the location—being free from obstructions, distance, and so forth—imparts its own form to the cognition, then the form of the jar likewise imparts its own form to that same cognition in exactly the same way.
If their capacity is indeed equal to that [of the object], how can there be a connection between them given that they are established in their own respective natures?
To this, he says: "Because of the connection in a single cognition," etc.
For in a single cognition, both of those [the object and the cognition] are connected by way of their own respective forms, but not directly.
That cognition, arising in the form of two objects, demonstrates their connection within itself.
But why must that cognition necessarily take on the form of two objects, such that the connection between them occurs by means of that cognition?
To this he says: "When those two exist," and so forth.
If these two, which possess equal capacity and form, were both existent, then there would certainly not be a cognition restricted to a single form.
Why? Because it is impossible.
For this possibility does not exist: that of one alone appearing among two things that possess equal capacity and form, while the other does not.

For instance: since the capacity [to produce a cognition] is undifferentiated, who would not project their own form therein? Furthermore, the simultaneous appearance of multiple [objects] is established by experience;
and those who speak in contradiction to experience do not have words worthy of being heeded by the wise.
If it is argued that the misconception of simultaneity arises because of the rapidity of the mental processes, we say no;
for in the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*), it is illogical to assume such a misconception.

If it is argued that this is simply the nature of an instrument— that it accomplishes an action upon only one object and not many, and since the sense organ is an instrument, it cannot therefore be the cause of multiple cognitions— then [we reply]: no, because it would follow that such a state of being would apply everywhere.
How can a lamp or similar object produce cognition in many people located in different places?
If it is argued that there is no fault because the agents are distinct,
then since the agent is one, how can the action be directed toward multiple objects in different locations?
Does not such speech as "the nature of an instrument" and so forth float away [into meaninglessness]?
Furthermore, among entities that perish at every moment, neither the relation of agent, instrument, and so forth, nor any action whatsoever, is tenable from the perspective of ultimate reality.

Furthermore, since an effect conforms to the presence and absence of all its causal factors (*kāraka*), there is no excellence (*atiśaya*) belonging to any one of them by virtue of which it could be conceptually constructed as "this is the agent" or "this is the instrument," and so forth.
Therefore, how is it possible for there to be a cognition that is restricted to a single form from two things whose capacities are indistinguishable?
Thus, the co-occurrence within a single cognition is established;
and this very fact is the mark for the state of having an identical nature of fitness.

For, in the absence of an identical nature of fitness, it is not possible—just as in the case of color and taste—for two things to appear simultaneously in a cognition produced by a single sense organ.

In this regard, for those followers of the Sugata who hold the view that "even when many [objects] are included within a single sense-field (*ekāyatana*), only a single sensory cognition arises," there is indeed a primary conjunction with a single cognition.

However, for those who describe it thus: "Even there, distinct cognitions—each directed toward a different object, produced by a single sense organ, simultaneous, and having as their objects things present at once—are generated because they possess no difference in capacity regarding their own cognitions; it is for this very reason that they arise being determined as one in common worldly experience," for them, the designation of unity among simultaneous [cognitions] due to their being born of a single sense organ and having a single locus is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), based on such determination in the world.

If it is argued that even though [the object] is associated with that [negation] due to its association with a single cognition, why does the negative particle (*nañ*) not, in a general sense, convey everything else as being of that nature?
To this, he says: "Therefore," and so forth.
Because, since the capacity is undifferentiated, there is an association of both [the object and the negation] within a single cognition in the manner already described.

Therefore, since two things possess an undifferentiated nature of fitness, they alone are associated within a single cognition; thus, for those two things of such a nature, "otherness" (*anyatva*)—intended here in the context of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*)—is "mutually dependent" alone, and not dependent on all other objects.

However, in common worldly usage, although "otherness" expressed by the negative particle (*nañ*) is sometimes said to depend on all other objects by resorting to the logic of pervasion (*vyāpti*), [in this context it is not so].

Nevertheless, that [non-apprehension] is not accepted here because "proximity is relied upon. Proximity, characterized by co-occurrence within a single cognition (*ekajñānasaṃsarga*), is what is relied upon and nothing else, since this is an inquiry concerning the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Otherwise, non-apprehension would simply be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Therefore, those who contemplate reality must rely upon that kind of distinctness which is the basis for the non-deviation of non-apprehension;
and that [distinctness] is exactly as has been stated—this is the intended meaning.
Having thus established distinctness with respect to its association within a single cognition, he says "that alone," etc., while demonstrating non-apprehension.
When that very same location is described as being "other" than the aforementioned jar, then the cognition of that location as devoid of the jar is what constitutes non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*);
it is not, however, merely the absence of apprehension (*upalabdhyabhāva*) as [the opponent] naturally assumes,
because of the fault that will be stated later.
Alternatively, it is the nature of the location as distinct from the jar, and not the cognition itself as being distinct from it, as Kumārila stated: "Or [it is] the cognition of another object.

For just as a cognition having another object as its domain, when experienced, depends upon the recollection of the counter-positive to serve as the basis for the conventional usage of that absence, so too does the location as distinct from that [jar].

For instance, in the case of a certain cognizer, the cognition of non-existence arises in this way: "Since I experience a cognition that has only the form of a mere location and not even the form of a jar, therefore there is no jar here."
However, for someone else [the inference may be] as follows: "Since this place is seen alone and not accompanied by a jar, therefore there is no jar here.
Therefore, since both possess an equal capacity for producing the cognition of non-existence, it is logical to establish both as forms of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).

In this regard, when that cognition exists, there is the non-apprehension of the characteristics of the knower with respect to an action residing in the agent; when its intrinsic nature [the object] exists, there is the non-apprehension of the characteristics of the knowable with respect to an action residing in the object.
Having thus established non-apprehension through the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), he states "that [non-apprehension] is non-existence," etc., in order to show its probandum.

Even when a location or similar area— which meets the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*) and is devoid of all other things— is being observed, the non-perception of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), such as a jar, establishes its absence or the linguistic convention of its absence (*abhāva-vyavahāra*) whenever a memory of that object arises due to desire or other factors. Furthermore, the non-perception of a cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) and the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) both establish absence and the linguistic convention of absence.
The non-apprehension of intrinsic nature, however, results only in the conventional usage of non-existence.
And the conventional usage of non-existence is characterized by the operation of cognition and verbal designation;
in this regard, [one says], "There is no jar here."
Knowledge of such a form, a designation denoting such an object,
and the activity characterized by coming and going to that place by one who is free from doubt.

(Hbṭ 175) Having raised the possibility that Īśvarasena and Kumārila might find an opening for their arguments, and having already refuted their views by establishing the final system (*siddhāntavyavasthā*), [the author] speaks the words beginning with "How [can there be] the existence of another? specifically in order to refute their position.

For Īśvarasena thinks as follows: since non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is distinguished from the two types of reasons—effect (*kārya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*)—which are positive entities (*bhāvarūpa*), it must necessarily be of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvarūpa*);
otherwise, its separate treatment would be entirely purposeless.

Furthermore, you yourself describe the non-apprehension of another thing, such as a location distinct from the object to be negated, or the cognition thereof, as being of a positive nature; therefore, that which is thus designated must surely be the existence of something else (*anyabhāva*), which is [in fact] the non-existence of that [other thing].
And this is not tenable, because existence and non-existence are contradictory, and thus their identity is impossible.

Kumārila also thinks thus: "Let this non-apprehension of two kinds—characterized by the properties of the knower and the known—which you describe as having the nature of non-existence, serve as the means for the cognition of non-existence."
But how can that very existence—the positive aspect (bhāvāṃśa) of another object distinct from the negandum, or of a cognition other than the cognition of that [negandum]—be a non-existence?
And how could the negation or its cognition be a negative aspect (abhāvāṃśa)?
This is simply not tenable.

Because there is a distinction between the aspects of existence and non-existence by way of their nature as properties (*dharma*), even though there is no distinction between them in their nature as the substratum (*dharmin*), the determination of their apprehension or non-apprehension is established through their emergence and suppression. As it has been said:
"For we maintain that while the identity of the substratum remains, a distinction between the two properties is indeed accepted."

"Because it consists of emergence and suppression, apprehension also remains established. Showing that this has already been answered, he says: "The answer to this objection has already been stated: 'By way of exclusion (paryudāsa), through dependence.
Depending either on the object to be negated or on the cognition thereof, the object distinguished from that, or the cognition thereof, is called non-existence and non-apprehension."
This is the reply of Īśvarasena:
for the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is not exclusively a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), but also includes exclusion (*paryudāsa*);
therefore, it is not contradictory for the existence of something other [than that] to have the nature of a non-existence.
The fact that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is also of the nature of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), like other types of existence, will be explained later.
However, the separate treatment of non-apprehension from the reason of essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*) is due to the intention of the cognizer.
For the cognizer, when dealing with a reason of essential identity, is intent upon the cognition of a real entity.

In the case of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), however, one determines the cognition of absence; yet, in the ultimate sense, it is the very capacity of the locus (*pradeśa*) for the conventional usage of the negated object's absence—which is itself a real entity—that is being proven. Thus, the non-apprehension of essence (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is not distinct from the essence-reason (*svabhāvahetu*).

As for what Īśvarasena thinks—namely, that "non-apprehension is a mere negation that does not require connection with any other object"—the author, refuting that, says: "It is not a mere negation," and so forth.
Why? He says: "Because its proof is unestablished," and so forth.
For non-existence, which is characterized by the absence of all causal capacity, cannot be established as a means of proof— that is, as a cause for the establishment [of a thesis]—
because that [status of being a cause] is incompatible with its nature as the absence of all capacity.
Or, if it were a cause, how could it not possess causal capacity?
Or is it of the nature of an existent (*bhāva*)?
Since a real entity is characterized by causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*),

and since non-existence (*abhāva*) does not require auxiliary causes and cannot have any excellence added to it, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the cognition "it does not exist" would be produced eternally.
Consequently, because it would lack a means of proof (*sādhaka*), the very conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) could not be established.
Alternatively, no proof whatsoever for that absence of perception (*upalabdhyabhāva*), which consists of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), would be established;
for, being itself non-existent, it would have to be proven by another absence of perception.
If that [non-existence] were also [known] by another [means], there would be an infinite regress.
Furthermore, unlike a sense faculty, that which is unknown cannot be the cause for the cognition of negation;
for, being always present, it would follow that such a cognition would arise eternally, as it would not require any auxiliary conditions.
And these two points: how can there be the apprehension of a non-entity, or what could be the cause of such an apprehension?
Regarding the question, "How is that [absence] itself to be apprehended?", he will explain this himself in the following section.
He also states Kumārila’s reply: "Of that"—meaning of another thing whose nature is unassociated with a counter-correlate (pratiyogin), which is another entity.
For this [entity] does not possess a single nature that is commingled with other entities;
for if it were so, even the non-existent portion would not be established anywhere.

For such an entity, "the establishment of existence" (bhāvasiddhi)—that is, the establishment of the existent portion—is itself the establishment of the non-existence of the "other," namely the counter-correlate (pratiyogin), which is another entity; this is the establishment of the non-existent portion.
He considers that the establishment of the positive aspect (bhāvāṃśa) as you intend it follows from its very nature as the negative aspect (abhāvāṃśa).
For instance, even the negative aspect is designated as "absence" precisely by virtue of being unmixed with other forms; otherwise, such a designation would be impossible.

And since that [cognition] is the same with respect to the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*) as well, let that very thing be the non-existence, because its cause is the same; what is the use of postulating another distinct portion consisting of non-existence?
For this very reason, there is the qualification "of that which has an unmingled form.

Therefore, "thus" means for that reason, "even the existence of another"—that is, even the existence of another entity (*vastu*), which according to your view is the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*), and not merely the negative aspect (*abhāvāṃśa*), is what you consider to be non-existence.
We designate it in this way;
therefore, the fact that the positive aspect has the nature of non-existence is entirely consistent, and thus nothing is contradictory.

As it has been said: "By means of the non-perception of intrinsic nature, characterized by the attributes of the knower and the known, it is precisely the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) that is established, not non-existence itself."
Thus, in order to refute that [objection], it was stated: "Non-apprehension is not a mere negation,
because such a [mere] negation cannot serve as a means of proof."
Thus, in the second explanation, in order to demonstrate the proof for the statement that "non-apprehension is merely a negation," he says: "characterized by the existence of another," and so forth.

He thinks as follows: for the world first understands the absence of a jar simply from seeing the bare location, either through the perception of the cognition of the bare location or through the realization of the absence of the cognition of a jar; subsequently, it proceeds with the conventional usage of the absence of the jar.

Therefore, in accordance with worldly convention, non-existence— characterized by the presence of either a location other than the object to be negated or the cognition of that [other] object— is established by itself through the means of valid cognition, namely sensory perception and self-awareness; this is sufficient to establish the absence of a jar, both directly and indirectly, respectively.
And it is proper to establish the conventional usage of the absence of a jar in this very manner. Even with such an establishment, there is no injury whatsoever to our position.

For instance, even indirectly, that which is established through the non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) accepted by you is established from that very source; thus, when the mere negation is [itself] non-apprehension, in the demonstration of its proof—

This is the intended meaning: just as for you there are two kinds of non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) consisting of positive entities characterized by the knower and the known, so too for me there will be two kinds designated as non-apprehension, namely the absence of apprehension characterized by the knower and the known.

In this regard, by means of the existence of another thing characterized as an object of knowledge— which is established through direct perception— the absence of the object to be negated, which consists in the non-perception characterized as an object of knowledge, will be established under the designation of "non-apprehension" (anupalabdhi). Furthermore, by means of the existence of another thing characterized as a subject of knowledge— consisting in the cognition of the bare locus and established through self-awareness— the subject-property consisting in the absence of the cognition of the object to be negated will be established under the name of "non-apprehension."
And thus, how could there be an infinite regress such that the proof would remain unestablished?

In this regard, regarding the phrase "characterized by the existence of another," non-existence consists of the place—which is a positive entity distinct from the object of negation and its cognition—and the cognition thereof; it is so called because it is distinct from the intended positive entity, the object of negation, and the cognition of that object, and because it is [therefore] non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). (Hbṭ 178)
That which is accepted by you as established by its own nature through the means of valid cognition— namely, through sensory perception and self-awareness—
would establish the conventional usage of the absence of that object to be negated, characterized by the operation of cognition and verbal designation; or else,
it would do so "by the establishment of its establishment," that is, through the establishment of that aforementioned absence characterized as the existence of something else.

Or, if it is maintained that the establishment of its absence consists in the absence of that object to be negated or the absence of the cognition thereof— even so, there is no distinction whatsoever between the non-apprehension favored by you and the non-apprehension favored by us; therefore, why is our view rejected?

[Objection: "But surely, if this is accepted, there is indeed a distinction: non-apprehension characterized as the presence of another thing establishes the conventional usage of absence indirectly, whereas the other [type] does so directly. [Reply:

He says—there is no such distinction by which there would be a contradiction, since the establishment of the conventional usage of absence occurs through our intended non-apprehension, which is of the nature of absence and devoid of contact with a real entity.
However, as for any other particularity, even if it exists, because it does not constitute a sublation [of the object], it is effectively equivalent to non-existence.
Furthermore, regarding what was stated—
"there follows the consequence that the conventional usage of non-existence cannot be established due to the absence of a means of proof for that [non-existence]"— [the response is as follows]:

That too is incorrect, because that very "presence of another" (anyabhāva) intended by you—which consists of the ground as distinguished from the object to be negated—and the perception having that as its object, are asserted by you to be "non-perception" (*anupalabdhi*); whereas for us, non-perception is the absence of that [perception], which is the absence of the object to be negated. Thus, your position contradicts our own.
And why is it that the mark (*liṅga*) is not accepted as a means of proof (*sādhana*)?

For if that were the case, it would conform to worldly consensus. Furthermore, why is it that the establishment of the two kinds of non-existence (*abhāva*) is itself the establishment of that [non-existence], and no other thing to be established by it exists? This is intended to refute our own position, as it is something that transcends worldly understanding.
Thus ends the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

To this, he replies: "Because there is no other existence due to non-separate establishment (*apṛthaksiddhi*); since there is no separate establishment for its absence, how can there be the relation of sign and signified (*liṅgaliṅgitā*)?
Likewise, 'due to the absence of a connection,' there is no relation of sign and signified between the existence of another and its absence."

First, explaining the first reason, he says: "The existence of another thing, consisting of a location devoid of that [object], is not a means of proof (*sādhana*) for the absence of the object to be negated;
nor is the perception of that [other thing] a means of proving its absence"—this will be stated later.
The word "tāvat" is used for that very purpose.

Why is the existence of another thing not a means of proof? To this he says: "yatsiddhau"—upon the establishment, that is, the cognition, of which entity, [there is the establishment] of another. (Hbṭ 179)

When there is neither the establishment (*siddhi*) nor the cognition (*pratīti*) of an object, that object becomes the mark (*liṅga*) of that [other] object; this is the principle (*nyāya*) regarding the mark and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgaliṅgin*).
An example of this is: "like smoke and fire.
For instance, when fire is not cognized upon the cognition of smoke, then the relationship of mark and bearer of the mark exists between the two.
But this is not the case when fire is being perceived at the very same time as the perception of smoke.

If this is so, what follows from it? To this he says: "The existence (*bhāva*) of another thing," that is, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), "by the very establishment of that"—that is, by the very cognition of that—"is its non-existence" (*tadabhāva*).

The non-existence of that object to be negated is "established," meaning it is cognized; for the existence of something else is itself the nature of that non-existence, since the establishment of the one is characterized by the establishment of the other.

However, the Naiyāyikas maintain: "The non-existence of the object to be negated consists in absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) and is of the nature of a void (*tuccha*); how, then, can it have the nature of the existence of something else?"
Because existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory, how could the non-existence of that [object] be established merely by the establishment of the existence of something other than it?

To this he says: "Of that"—meaning of the presence of something else characterized as a location—"which has a form unassociated" (asaṃsṛṣṭarūpa), that is, whose nature is devoid of, or which is isolated from, the object to be negated, such as a jar or the like. By means of that [negation],...
Of an empty self.
By this, he states that even a mere location consists of a non-affirming negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).
How can the nature of an entity be a void form? Because it is contradictory.
If this is argued, we say no; for even that [other-existence] is of a non-existent nature (tuccharūpa) in terms of the form of the other.

For just as a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)—which does not involve a connection with another positive entity, which appears in an empty conceptual construction, and which is of a non-existent nature because it lacks the form of the object to be negated—is devoid of that [negated] form, so too is the existence of something other than that [object], which has a form unmixed with the object to be negated.
In that case, how could its nature as a non-entity (tuccha) be contradicted by that which is to be negated?
For this [negation] would be of a non-entity nature by its own nature, not by the nature of another;
otherwise, how could it be the "existence of another" or the "non-existence of another" therein?
For that which does not consist in the nature of the absence of something else is indeed that very thing,
just like its own essential nature;
consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the entire world possesses the nature of one another.

Therefore, it is faultless to say that all entities are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) in terms of another's form, even though they possess form in terms of their own form. What, then, is the difference between a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) and a presumptive negation (*paryudāsa*)? None at all; it is merely that in common worldly usage, a simple negation is said to be a mere non-existence that does not imply another positive form.
However, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is another form that is devoid of the other form;
it is not the case that the other form does not consist of the voidness of the other form.
Indeed, the other form is experienced precisely through its voidness of that [other] form. (Hbṭ 180)
How could it not have the nature of a non-presuppositional negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha) with respect to the form of another?
If it is argued that its cognition arises from that [other] by implication (sāmarthyāt), we say no; for implication is impossible when there is no cognition of the cause.

For if there were no identity [between the object and its absence], then cognition would occur as the cause of that [absence] only when there is the apprehension of the excluded [object] through a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), and not otherwise.

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the nature of that [excluded object]—which consists in its form being unmixed with anything else—as being the insubstantial nature of the object to be negated, is perception (*pratyakṣa*). It is from that very [perception] that [the absence is known], and not from what occurs at a later time, such as the cognition "there is no jar here."

Because of this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) since it apprehends what has already been apprehended and is thus a mere memory; for the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), which is the absence (*abhāva*) of another—such as a jar—which is non-existent there, is established, and it is precisely that locus (*pradeśa*) consisting of that absence which is apprehended by it.
Indeed, this locus is of two kinds: that whose nature is unmixed with a jar, being of a form excluded from it, and that which is other than it, namely, that which possesses a jar.

And the locus alone, insofar as its status as a substratum for the jar has not yet been apprehended, is grasped by perception through its distinction from that [jar]; thus, the difference from the jar and the absence of the jar are already grasped. Therefore, it is not for the sake of establishing the non-confusion of entities that one says, "This is not here."
For this reason, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be sought;
and since this will be explained in detail later on, let it rest for now.

Furthermore, since the non-existence of that [object] is established by the previously stated reasoning through the very establishment of the existence of something else, the existence of something else is not the logical mark (*liṅga*) for the absence of the object to be negated.
Explaining the second reason, he says: "And because of the absence of a connection.
There is no connection whatsoever between the existence of one thing and the non-existence of another; therefore, how could there be the relationship of sign and signified?
And when is this said?
When the nature of that non-existence as being the absence of another is considered from the perspective of what is not accepted by others;
for others maintain that the non-existence of a thing is a mere void, existing entirely separate from the existence of that other thing.

Otherwise, if by the logic already stated the very existence of another thing constitutes the nature of the absence of that [first] thing, then because of their identity (*tādātmya*), how could there be an absence of a relationship? Furthermore, its establishment through direct perception (*pratyakṣasiddhatā*) occurs precisely at that time,
and not by means of any other alternative position.

The phrase “And that belongs to it,” etc., is an elaboration of the very same point by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). The expression “inherence in a single object” (*ekārthasamavāya*) was stated according to the view of others; for according to others, such as the Naiyāyikas, the two properties known as "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) are indeed distinct, yet they both inhere in one and the same substratum (*dharmin*). Thus, there is a relation of inherence in a single object—the substratum—between the produced and the impermanent, or rather, [inherence] of the property. (Hbṭ 181)
The very same relationship is another example. Here, "inherence in a single object" refers to conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is expressed by the word "inherence" (*samavāya*).
This is because, since both conjunction and inherence are conceptual constructs, there is no regard for designating them as distinct.

According to others, however, fire and smoke are both inherent (*samaveta*) only in their own respective parts; thus, between them there is neither inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*) nor a relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). Therefore, the worldly (*laukika*) relationship is said to be that which consists in smoke being observed above fire.
The phrase “or the relationship of produced and producer (*janyajanakabhāvaḥ*)” expresses the ultimate (*pāramārthika*) relationship.
"Because, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), fire is the producer and the other [the fuel] is the produced.
Now, since the discussion was initiated with Īśvarasena, why is it stated that the relation as asserted by the Naiyāyikas is also absent in the presence of one thing and the absence of another?
True; however, it was stated incidentally for the purpose of refuting his view as well.

For it was stated incidentally that since the absence of the object to be negated is already established by a prior perception grasping another entity, no further perception in the form "there is no jar here" need be postulated for that purpose.

Now, however, this is stated as a corollary: when this absence is not established by a perception that apprehends another entity (*anyabhāva*), then you must accept another perception of the form "there is no jar here," arising from a sense-contact characterized by the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).
Furthermore, in the absence of a relation, it is not logical for there to be a qualifier-qualified relationship between the existence of another thing and its non-existence,
because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, how could perception of that non-existence arise from a sense-object contact characterized by such [a relationship]?

Having thus explained the nature of a relation, he states its impossibility in this case: "Not so. Just as there is a relation characterized by inherence in a single substratum (*ekārthasamavāya*) between producedness and impermanence, or between fire and smoke, no such relation exists between existence and non-existence by which the existence of something else could serve as the means of proving that non-existence.
Inherence in a single substratum occurs only between two things that subsist in one and the same objective entity (*dharmin*).
Furthermore, that "other-existence" (anyabhāva) which is called "space" (pradeśa) exists in its own constituent parts; in those [parts] where it resides, there is no absence of the jar.
For if this were so, it would follow that the jar is absent from the parts of the space, not from the space itself.
Moreover, this [absence] is not produced by the parts of the space.
For those [substances] that possess the nature of a substance initiate only another substance;
moreover, the absence of a jar is not a substance,
for only nine substances are accepted.
Furthermore, the definition of substance as that which possesses action and so forth does not exist therein;
nor does it subsist there in the form of a quality.
For indeed, [the categories] are only twenty-four. (Hbṭ 182)
Qualities (guṇas) are accepted [as distinct categories],

and this [non-existence] is not any one of them; nor is it of the nature of action (karman), because it is not included within the five types of action and because it lacks their defining characteristics.
For its definition begins with the words "consisting of a single substance" (*ekadravyam*) and so forth;
this is not possible in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*),
nor is it possible for it to have the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*) and so on.

It is precisely because of the absence of that nature [in the other] that there is no conjunction between the existence of one thing and the non-existence of another, as in the case of fire and smoke;
for conjunction is admitted only between two substances.
And it has been stated that the absence of that [entity] is not a substance;
nor is there a relationship of locus and located.
For that [cognition] is also said to be caused by conjunction,
as in "the jujube fruits are here in the bowl," or else it is caused by inherence.
"Here, in these threads, is the cloth. Furthermore, conjunction does not exist for non-existence, which is not of the nature of a substance; nor does inherence exist.
For it is accepted that only the five categories, beginning with substance, possess the quality of being inherent loci (*samavāyin*);
and non-existence (*abhāva*) is not included among those five. Furthermore, as long as there is no benefit conferred upon its own nature, the designation of "substratum" (*ādhāra*) is impossible.
Or, if there were assistance, it would be a relationship of producer and produced;
yet that non-existence is not something produced, because that would entail its being an effect.
Moreover, its being an effect is impossible,
because you define "being an effect" as either inherence in its own cause or inherence in existence (*sattā*).
However, that which is called "space" (pradeśa) is not the cause of this [non-existence],
for it is accepted that substance alone is the cause of the three— substance, quality, and action—
and non-existence does not possess the characteristics of substance and so forth.
Even if existence were inherent [in it], the locus of existence would be the object of the cognition "existent," but not the object of the cognition "non-existent.
Furthermore, since the absence of a jar is possible even when its location is absent, how could [existence] be the effect of that [absence]?
Nor does it possess differentiation according to each respective object,
because its objects are cognitions of a single form;
for if it were differentiated by the difference of its correlates, then that same consequence would follow even for universals and the like.

Since inherence (*samavāya*) has also been refuted immediately prior, how could there be an "effect-ness" consisting in inherence with the existence of its own cause for that which lacks such [inherence]? By this, the relationship of producer and produced is also excluded.
Therefore, because there is no connection whatsoever, the existence of another thing cannot be the means of proving the non-existence of that [other].
Showing another relationship, the opponent says: "There exists [a relation] in the object," and so forth.

For just as an object (*artha*) is the *viṣaya* (the object) and a word is the *viṣayin* (the subject), such that their relationship is one of *viṣaya-viṣayibhāva* (subject-object relation), so too will there be a relationship of *viṣaya-viṣayibhāva* between the presence of another thing and its absence.
The objection of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the absence of a jar is communicated by means of another presence called "the locus" (*pradeśa*).
The connection is that there would thus be a relationship between word and meaning.
Of what nature is it?
"It has the characteristic of cause and effect.
But how is it that a word has the status of being an effect of an object?

It is because, when there is the intention to communicate that object—that is, when there is the desire to express the communication of the object—one employs it, which is to say, one utters the word.
In that sense, by means of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) which revolves [toward the object], there would be a relationship between the word and [the object] characterized as cause and effect.

And although both the word and the object possess the nature of universals (*sāmānya*) conceptually constructed by the intellect, nevertheless, because the particular characteristic of the word (*śabdasvalakṣaṇa*)— which is the basis for the conceptualization of the word-universal— is brought forth by the speaker’s intention that manifests the object, [the connection occurs] through that medium.
The relationship between cause and effect is stated [as follows]:

"Or it is characterized by inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). This is stated according to what is established for others, for others conventionally maintain that the relationship between word and meaning is characterized by inseparable connection.
Therefore, a relationship consisting of the connected basis—the nature of the signified and the signifier—is appropriate as the relation between object and subject.

If it is argued that the same will apply to the cases of "absence when that is absent" (*tadabhāva*) and "presence when another is present" (*anyabhāva*), he says: "And this"—referring to the manner just described—"is not possible here," namely, in the cases of *tadabhāva* and *anyabhāva*.
For when there is the intention to demonstrate the absence of a jar, the application— that is, the production— of the "presence of another" characterized as the location does not occur;
because even prior to the intention to demonstrate the absence of the jar, the location is already produced from its own causes,
and furthermore, because even if that intention were present, the "presence of another" would still be absent.
And how, then, could there be a causal relationship between those two,
or an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) mediated by it, through which the relationship of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) might be postulated?

It might be thought: "Just as between a word and its object there is a subject-object relationship caused by the relation of the probandum and the probans, so too is it between the presence of one thing and the absence of another; it is on this basis alone that the word and its object serve as the example.
To this, he says: "For [only] when [the relationship] is established," and so forth.

For the relationship of the probandum and the probans between a word and its object is based on a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*); otherwise, if they were distinct entities, it would not be so.

Because that [relation] is not applicable, it is the same here as well: if the relationship of probandum and probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) were established between the absence of that [object] and the presence of something else, then, by means of that—that is, through the door of the relationship of probandum and probans—the relationship of object and subject (*viṣayaviṣayibhāva*) would exist.
However, that very relationship of probandum and probans is not established in the absence of a connection such as the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
Because it would follow that everything could be both the probandum and the means of proof.

If it is asked, "How is it that the sense faculty is the basis for the establishment of its own object? [the answer is: It arises from the production of a single cognition by the sense faculty and its object, due to a specific causal condition based on their mutual approach and so forth. (Hbṭ 184)
There is such a designation there,
but not so here, because that [designation] is inappropriate for the existence of one thing and the non-existence of another.
And since the relationship between the probandum and the probans, characterized by the state of being the sign and the signified, is the subject under discussion,
and since that is impossible without a connection, [the opponent might argue]:
"The relationship of probandum and probans between the presence of another thing and its absence is not based on any other connection, but is caused solely by the relationship of object and subject."

He says: "Otherwise"—if another relation is not accepted, but rather the relation of probandum and probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) arises from the relation of object and subject (*viṣayaviṣayibhāva*), and from that [probandum-probans relation] the relation of object and subject [arises], then this would result in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
And thus, when one of the two is unestablished, both would remain unestablished.

Furthermore, if it is intended that the non-existence (abhāva), which is the possessor of the mark (liṅgin), is established through the mark consisting of the existence of something else (anyabhāva), then the "aggregate" (samudāya) would be the probandum (sādhya). Since its absence is established solely by means of the existence of something else, it is not the case that the relationship of probandum and probans is impossible due to the mere absence of a connection. Moreover, the aggregate—characterized as the property and the property-possessor (dharmadharmilakṣaṇa) and existing in the form of a qualifier-qualified relationship—is the desired probandum; thus, there is the fault of its non-existence. This is the meaning of the word "and" (ca).

If it is argued that the probandum-status (*sādhyatā*) of the whole (*samudāya*) is never intended in any case, he says: "And likewise," even if one accepts the probandum-status of the property (*dharma*) alone as independent, [the following occurs]:
"The absence of a jar [is known] because of the existence of something other than it."

In such a formulation, the non-existence of the jar would follow at all places and at all times. For when a property that is subordinate to a subject is established in a particular location, its existence is logically appropriate only in that very place and at that very time, and not otherwise; therefore, one must admit that the entire aggregate is the probandum, and not the property alone.
Here the opponent says: It is not the case that the composite whole is the probandum (*sādhya*), nor is there a lack of connection between the presence of another thing and its absence.
Why?
Because [the text says] "the location and so forth," and so on.

In the statement, "There is no jar in this location," the locus (dharmin), such as the location, is qualified by the absence of the jar; it is established as distinct from a location that possesses a jar. Thus, its status as a qualifier is established, and not merely the jar's non-existence as something "isolated" (*kevala*) that has not attained the state of being a subordinate attribute (*guṇabhāva*) of any locus.
Therefore, since the composite whole is not the probandum (*sādhya*), how could there be any fault resulting from its [non-existence]?

Furthermore, in this position, the fault of a lack of connection between the "mark" (*liṅga*)—which consists of the presence of another—and the "possessor of the mark" (*liṅgin*)—characterized as the locus (*dharmin*) such as a specific place—is not at all entailed.
Why?

“Because of the connection” of the “other entity”— characterized as a place devoid of a jar and so forth— with the “locus,” such as that place itself, is due to the existence of identity (*tādātmya*) between them.
For instance, you yourself maintain that the connection between a locus such as sound and properties such as being produced is characterized precisely by identity.
The intention is that "it exists here";
therefore, he considers the statement "and because of the absence of a connection" to be incorrect.
