The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntavādī), however, considering that the previously stated absence of a relationship between the mark (liṅga)— namely, the existence of another thing— and the bearer of the property to be proven (liṅgin), which is characterized by the property to be proven and called the "absence of a jar," does not pertain to the locus (dharmin), and thus intends to connect this subsequent [objection] with it, says— showing the absence of a relationship even with the locus— "No;
there is no non-connection between the mark and the bearer of the mark"— whereby it is connected as "nor is there [non-connection]."
Likewise, it is not the case that the non-establishment of the collection [of reasons] is what is meant;
rather, for one who speaks thus, the very absence of a relationship between the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin) is precisely the non-establishment of the collection.
Why is this so?

Because that very place and so forth, which is established as the subject (*dharmin*), is the "existence of another" (*anyabhāva*), and because it possesses the characteristic of being a mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the existence of another.

He demonstrates this very point: for when a certain place and so forth is conceived by you as the subject, and it is said by the world that "the jar and so forth do not exist there," that very place and so forth, being unconnected with—that is, devoid of connection with—that jar and so forth, is the "existence of another."

Nothing else is accepted as the logical mark (liṅga), because "from the mere perception of that"— that is, from the mere perception of a location not in contact with a jar— the conceptual cognition (vikalpa) "the jar is not present" becomes accepted by this cognizer as a cognition of the object indicated by the mark (liṅgin).
Therefore, that very thing is "other-existence" (anyabhāva).
For that alone which, being perceived, produces the cognition of the probandum is called the "probans" (liṅga);
and a location or the like, when not conjoined with a jar, is just such [a probans].
Therefore, that very absence of another (anyabhāva), characterized as such, must be accepted as the logical mark (liṅga).

Consequently, how could there be the relationship of the sign and the signified (liṅga-liṅgibhāva)—that is, the state of being the mark or the state of being the marked—for that very absence of another, which does not even experience a distinction through its own exclusion (vyāvṛtti)?
For it is not possible for the logical mark itself to be the subject (dharmin).
Because the cognition of the probandum occurs only through the cognition of the locus (*dharmin*), it is impossible to follow the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth;

and since there is no other locus, how could there be a connection between that [locus] and a mark (*liṅga*) whose nature consists in the existence of something else, or how could there be the status of the whole (*samudāya*) as the probandum?

However, although sound and producedness (*kṛtakatva*) are identical in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), there is indeed a distinction between them based on the difference in their exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*).

Therefore, it is logical that even when the locus (*dharmin*), such as sound, is apprehended, if impermanence and so forth are not yet perceived, they are established by means of "producedness" and the like.

It might be argued: "By means of the conceptualization of universal and particular, the relationship of sign and signified (*liṅga-liṅgin*) will occur even for that which is one. To this he says: "And here," in the present case of the existence of another (*anyabhāva*), "the conceptualization of the state of universal and particular is not possible."

By which conceptualization of the universal and the particular would the universal become the reason (*hetu*) and the particular the subject (*dharmin*), such that there might be the establishment of a composite whole,
or the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*)?

To the question "Why is it not possible?", he says: "Precisely because of the cognition of that particularity"—that is, precisely because of the cognition of the particular place devoid of the jar—"there is the apprehension of its absence," namely, the absence of the jar.
Since it is the particularity itself that is the basis for the cognition of the absence of the jar, what is achieved there by the postulation of a universal?
If it is argued that this very particularity, when occurring elsewhere, will attain the nature of a universal; [the response follows].

He says: Since there is an absence of "concomitance" (anvaya)—that is, of persistence—of that specific location devoid of the jar "elsewhere," namely in a similar instance, how can it have the nature of a universal?
For this particularity, restricted by its own place, time, and state, does not persist in another.
Regarding this very point, he states the supporting reason: "In the meaning of the proposition," and so forth.
For if the specific locus (pradeśaviśeṣa) as distinct from the jar were indeed the subject (dharmin), and that very [locus] were intended as the reason (hetu),
then the reason— characterized as the subject— would be merely a part of the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā), which is the aggregate of the property and the subject.
Furthermore, since it does not experience a distinction even through the exclusion of a portion of the meaning of the thesis, its status as a logical reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Now, if this fault is to be avoided, and it is not maintained that the logical reason is merely a specific location devoid of a jar, [then...]
But since a mere location is devoid of the specific quality of being distinct from a jar, he says: "And it is not the case that wherever there is a mere location, there is the absence of a jar.
For if the mere location existed even in a place where a jar is present, the reason would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
The opponent, showing otherwise the relationship between the general and the particular, says: "In such a [location]..."

Since the mere location standing before one, devoid of a jar, is exactly the same as any other such location, how can there be any inconclusiveness (anekānta) regarding the non-existence of the jar everywhere?

The cognition of such a specific location is itself the cognition of the jar’s absence; therefore, the relationship of sign and signified (liṅga-liṅgitā) between the existence of another thing and the absence of that [jar] is untenable. Demonstrating this, he says: “But surely of that very [location],” etc.
That which is established as the subject (dharmin) is the specific location in its isolation, and it is precisely that isolation which is expressed by you through the qualifier “mere” (kevala).
That absence of the jar is called the "non-existence of the jar.

And that absence of the jar is established only upon the cognition of the bare location which serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*); it is not established at a later time as something entirely different from that, in another form, like fire [is established] from smoke.
Therefore, when the cognition of the probandum has already occurred "only upon the cognition of that" [mark], of what is this now the mark?
It does not belong to anything else; for while the absence of a jar—which was what was sought to be known—is established, nothing else has been sought to be known.
And when the cognition of the mere location itself results in the cognition of the absence of the jar, that which [occurs] at a subsequent time—
"In every place where there is only a bare location, there is an absence of the jar"—
this "following" (anugama), that is, the tracking or following along of the positive concomitance (anvaya), is useless, because the probandum has already been understood at the very outset.

Since this is so, it is established that "the existence of another" (anyabhāva), characterized as a mere location, cannot be the means of proof for non-existence, because there is no distinction between the probandum and the probans.

Thus, in order to demonstrate that the composite whole is the object of proof and that the logical mark lacks a connection with the locus (dharmin), the opponent stated: "Because non-existence is being proved as a qualification of the locus, such as a particular location."

Thus, this has already been refuted by the very critique of non-separable establishment (*apṛthaksiddhi*). However, when the relation [of the two] as object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) has been rejected, the opponent, demonstrating another kind of relation between the probandum and the probans, says: "There exists another relation between the presence of one thing and the absence of another, called opposition (*virodha*)."
"Therefore, because of the existence of a relationship, the non-existence [of one thing] will be established through the existence of another.
But the proponent of the final position (siddhāntin), not conceiving of any contradiction between the probandum and the probans, asks: "What is in contradiction with what?
The intention is that no contradiction between the probandum and the probans is possible here.

The opponent points out a contradiction based on a lack of understanding of the intended meaning: "By means of the existence of another"—that is, by means of the nature of a mere location—there is the non-existence of that which is desired to be cognized as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), such as a jar.

Demonstrating that this proponent speaks of what is unrelated, [the author] says: "Is it indeed the counter-correlate," such as a jar, that is desired to be cognized, such that a contradiction between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*) is asserted on the grounds that the counter-correlate is the object of cognition (*prameya*)? Thus, he shows the opponent's failure to state a valid connection.

If it is argued that the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is not what is intended to be cognized, but rather its absence (*tadabhāva*), he replies: "But as for the absence... [which is the absence of the counter-positive that is to be proven]...

[Kumārila, however, maintains that this aspect of absence is distinct from the aspect of existence; therefore, since the absence of X is not simply the existence of Y, how can the cognition of that [existence of Y] itself be the cognition of the absence of X?]
For this non-existence is divided into various types, such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth;
yet, since differentiation is not possible for that which is a non-entity (*avastu*), it must therefore be of the nature of a real entity (*vastu*). As it has been said:
"These distinctions could not belong to a non-entity; therefore, it possesses the nature of a real entity."
Nor is it logical that the aspect of non-existence is identical to the aspect of existence,
because the former is cognized through the power of sense-object contact,
whereas the cognition of the latter is caused by the absence of such contact. As it has been said:
"In conjunction with that, it is perceived as 'existent' (sat), and its nature as being existent is thus understood; however, the cognition 'this is not here' is caused by non-conjunction with that.
To the question, "How then can the very apprehension of that [object] constitute the exclusion of another?", he speaks in order to refute that objection.

The "isolation" (*kaivalya*) of that other, solitary region— which is its state of being alone (*ekākikatva*) or lack of assistance— is itself the "deficiency" (*vaikalya*), that is, the absence, of the "other," the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) such as a jar; therefore, it is precisely the existence of that other— the very positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*) intended by you— that constitutes the "absence of that," the negative aspect of the counter-correlate, and not something distinct from it.

It is called a "separate property" (dharmāntara) by the sons of the Sugata. Consequently, "the cognition of that very [property]" means precisely the cognition of that other-existence; and "the non-cognition of that" means the non-cognition of its counter-correlate (pratiyogin), which is to say, the cognition of absence. He thinks as follows: this portion of absence, which is postulated as a property of the real entity distinct from the portion of existence, experiences the nature of the absence of a jar and so forth solely through the deficiency of that [jar's] form, and not otherwise.
And that deficiency of its own form exists even in the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*) of another entity;
for if that [deficiency] were absent, its status as "another entity" would be lost.
Indeed, that which is not deficient in its own form does not experience otherness from it.
Just as its own essential nature [is not established], so too its non-existent aspect would not be established,
and it would follow that the entire universe is a single substance.

Consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence of simultaneous origination and so forth, and everything would be applicable everywhere; therefore, the positive nature of one entity must necessarily consist in the very absence of its opposite. And thus, the cognition of that [positive entity] itself is the cognition of the absence of its opposite.
Since the very conjunction of the sense organ with that [object] is itself the conjunction of the sense organ with the absence of anything other than it, why is it said:
"But the cognition 'this is not here' is thus caused by non-conjunction with that"?
If it is argued that this was stated with reference to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then this does not undermine our position;

for when a thing's nature is apprehended by perception through the arising of its own form, as consisting precisely of what is other than that [form], the subsequent [conceptualization]— *Hbṭ* 189— [does not affect the prior].
This is because we accept that conceptual construction (vikalpa) expresses [its object] exactly as it has been apprehended.

Furthermore, this detailed investigation into non-existence was established by one who, in the proof of the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), investigated both the non-existent object of knowledge (*prameya*) and the means of valid cognition itself; therefore, it should be understood from that very source.
Moreover, the cognition of the non-existence of something is necessarily nothing other than the cognition of the existence of something else.

Therefore, demonstrating that the postulation of a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for non-existence is not tenable— both for the sake of establishing the non-confusion of entities and for the sake of the conventional usage of non-existence, such as "this is not here"— he says: "Otherwise..."
If it is not accepted that the cognition of that [object] itself is the cognition of its absence,

then, in the case of "non-exclusion"— that is, the non-rejection— of that other thing which is of a different nature (atadrūpa) through the determination of its own form (*svarūpa*), there would be no cognition of its absence; consequently,
"there would be no determination of that at all"— meaning there would be no cognition of the own-form of that other object.
What is the reason?

Because of the "non-discrimination" (*aviveka*)—that is, the failure to distinguish, the failure to establish through distinction, and the failure to prove without confusion—between "that form and that which is not that form": namely, between the specific form of that object and of another object, which is distinct from the entire triple world, and that which is "not that form," which is the form of another and does not possess that [specific] form.

For that form [of the object] is indeed unmixed with the forms of all other things; if it were not thus represented by the perception produced through its capacity, but rather that perception arose with a merely indistinct form, then how could there be a determination of it by that [perception]? Indeed, it is not logical for a thing to be determined by a cognition that does not represent its form, just as a person with jaundice cannot determine a white conch shell through a cognition in which it appears yellow and does not represent the actual form of the white conch.
Or, if it were to conform to a specifically determined form, how could there be the exclusion of others from its determination?
Therefore, it is precisely because it does not conform to a specifically determined form that there is no exclusion of others;
and thus, there would be an absence of the determination of that [object].
If this were so, what would be the fault?

To this he says: "This conventional practice," which is recognized by all people, [arises] from the perception of some object such as fire; for the purpose of attaining that which is related to a certain place, and for the purpose of avoiding that which has been seen or not yet seen, there would be no such activity characterized by engagement and withdrawal.
What is the reason?
Because "this" cognizer, "even while seeing fire," does so through a perception in which there appears a mixed representation of that [fire] and its form;
otherwise, this [perception] would lose its nature as a form of seeing.

For instance, if one does not perceive even that which is mixed when unmixed things are not seen, then how could this perception of something belong to anyone at all, being like a mere clod of earth and such?
How then could a cognizer who possesses such a perception of the mixed see "only fire" and not water and so forth?
"But" because it is a cognition in which an object of mixed form appears, one "sees even water and so forth.
Therefore, how could "one seeking water not proceed there," toward that place containing fire?
Anticipating an opportunity for an opponent's objection, he says: "By non-perception," and so forth.
For by means of a cognition in which fire appears, the very nature of fire itself is perceived;
whereas the absence of water therein is established through the non-perception of water.

Thus, because of the discrimination between that which possesses such a nature and that which does not, by means of these two cognitions, the specific worldly transaction characterized by engagement and withdrawal is accomplished.
The proponent of the established tenet (siddhāntavādin) asks: "What is this so-called non-apprehension?
Anticipating that the opponent might say it is merely the absence of the apprehension of water, he replies with the words "If [there were] water," and so forth.
For Kumārila, however, the mere cessation of the apprehension of water—which is of the nature of a void—is not at all intended to be the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for non-existence.

For it is said: "The non-arising of perception and the other [means of knowledge] is called the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāva); it is either the non-modification (apariṇāma) of the self, or a cognition of another object."

However, this transformation of the self (ātman) in the form of a cognition appearing as the object to be negated must be admitted to be accompanied by a cognition appearing as another object, and not solitary; it is for the purpose of establishing this that [the opponent's position] is introduced.

Thus, let the cognition of the other object itself be the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding non-existence; what is the use of postulating a property called "non-transformation" of the self, which is itself devoid of any means of valid cognition?

Furthermore, you do not intend for that which is called "non-transformation" to be something entirely distinct from the transformation of the cognition of another object, because non-existence is accepted as being merely another state of being.

Moreover, the cognition of the other object must be understood as belonging specifically to that object which possesses a form with an equal capacity for cognition and is associated with the same act of consciousness, and not to any other;
for it is from the cognition of that [specific] object that the absence of its counter-positive is established.
For it is not logical that the non-existence of taste and so forth be cognized from the cognition of form, nor [is it logical] for those things separated by space and so forth;
moreover, the cognition of one object manifests only a specific form.
For if that [cognition] were to manifest another form, the very absence of the perception of water would not be established.
And thus, the absence of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is indeed manifested through perception.

This [argument] is introduced in order to demonstrate that, regarding the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of that absence, it results in nothing other than the non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as we define it.
In this regard, if the non-apprehension is a mere void (*tuccha-rūpa*) consisting in the absence of the apprehension of water, then how can it be an absence? (Hbṭ 191)
For someone, "comprehension" (pratipatti) means "ascertainment" (pariccheda), since ascertainment is a property of cognition (*jñāna*).
Now, if it is not intended that this [object] has the nature of comprehension, but rather that it is the cause of that [comprehension], he says: "or the cause of comprehension."
For it is not logical that non-existence—characterized by the absence of all causal capacity—should function as a cause for the cognition [of itself].

If it were to function as a cause, then, since it would never depend on auxiliary factors and would thus constantly produce the cognition of it, the cognizer would have only the cognition of non-existence;
there would be no room at all for any other cognition.

And it is not logical that the non-existence of this [perception] should produce the cognition of its absence when it itself is unknown; thus he says: "How is there the apprehension of that too?"—namely, of the absence of the perception of water?
If this absence of the perception of water were to produce the cognition of the absence of water while remaining itself unapprehended, then it would do so for anyone at all.
He states this very point: "of that"—the absence of the perception of water—or of something other than that water, such as fire.
Or [if one says] "consciousness is in another object";
therefore, because the non-modification of the self is established as distinct [from consciousness],

even if that [non-modification] were admitted in that case, since the non-modification of the self would be of the same nature as that [consciousness], it could not be established as different from it.

Furthermore, if the absence of water and so forth were perceived even when there is no cognition of that [water] or anything else, then why would the absence of water and so forth not be perceived even during states such as sleep?
That its absence would be perceived then as well has already been examined in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*; therefore, it should be understood from that very source.

By mentioning "obstruction" and so forth, he demonstrates this: the otherness (*anyatva*) of one thing from another object also depends precisely upon a form of capacity equivalent to that [otherness], and it cannot be accepted as independent of it.
Thus, the establishment of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is proven according to our description.

And when, in the manner thus described, the cognition of the absence of water through non-apprehension is not tenable, and the determinate form of the cognition appearing as fire is not admitted, then this cognizer who perceives fire— “even while seeing” the fire— by means of a cognition in which forms are conflated, [does not perceive it as such].

One does not determine, "This is fire, not water"; and because it appears even as the form of water despite not being determined as such, one who seeks that [water] would neither "stand still" nor "proceed"—that is, one seeking water would not proceed.
For that which is called "water" is defined as that which is capable of removing all thirst, heat, and so forth, and which appears in a cognition as a specific form unmixed with any other form.
"But this [object] appears as something else entirely, having a variegated form" (Hbṭ 192).
And "therefore," because it is impossible to simultaneously carry out two contradictory actions—namely, engagement and withdrawal—"the pursuer would encounter an insurmountable calamity.
Anticipating an opportunity for an opponent's objection here, he says: "For that very reason," and so forth.
I do not say that the cognition of the absence of water arises merely from the perception of the nature of the place as being devoid of water,
for that would entail the faults already mentioned;
rather, it is from the very sight of the solitary fire alone that the cognition of the absence of the other— the water— which does not appear there, occurs.
Because of the statement, "or consciousness [is directed] toward another object," the proponent of the established doctrine says: "How can one [be both]? and so forth.
By what capacity, moreover, does the perception of that one thing cause the understanding of the absence of others?
For instance, when that [one thing] is being perceived, one may understand that "only this exists";
but why should one realize that "anything other than that does not exist"?

"From the perception" (*darśanāt*) "of that very" (*tasyaiva*) fire and so forth which is being observed "in its isolated state" (*kevalasya*), meaning in a form unmixed with water, and from its appearing in the cognition of fire, the certainty arises: "water is not present."

For instance: if water were also present there just as fire is, then that too would appear as an object of cognition in perception just like the fire, because their capacity [to produce cognition] is indistinguishable with respect to their own cognition; thus, the appearance of only one of them would not be logical.

Therefore, the appearance of one thing is invariably concomitant with the non-existence of the other; hence, from that [appearance], a cognition arises regarding the non-existence of the other, and it produces the cognition that "there is no cognition of another object."
Likewise, another entity is described as such precisely because its own nature is unmixed with the nature of others;

and cognition of that [entity] is designated as "cognizing the other" only by virtue of having that very form, since otherwise such a designation would be impossible. Thus, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) states: "This very... and so forth, [arguing] that the cognition of the other is itself the cause for the conceptual construction of the absence of that [other].
Indeed, we have already stated this previously through such statements as: "When those two exist, there is no cognition restricted to a single form, because [such] is impossible.

Therefore, that very appearance of the solitary [object] unassociated with others is itself the non-existence of anything else, because that very solitary [object] consists in the non-existence of the other, and because any other part consisting of non-existence has been refuted.

Then, because the absence [of the other object] is manifested through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), by the force of that [perception], there arises a subsequent conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka*) in the form of a knowledge of non-existence (*nāstitājñāna*) which functions as conventional practice (*vyavahāra*).
However, nothing unapprehended is understood by it;

for if the cognition regarding another object—though its nature is direct perception—were to produce a cognition of the absence of that other when [the other] is not cognized, it could be established as a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) called "absence" (*abhāva*).

For it is thus: only that which is devoid of any other form is experienced as the single cognitive image of that [object]. Therefore, the experience of that [image] itself is the experience of its absence.
Indeed, even for conceptual cognition, there is no such thing as an "experience of absence" other than the experience of a nature devoid of that [object's] form.
Only its nature as conceptual construction (vikalpa) is superadded;
therefore, just as when fire has been determined by non-conceptual knowledge (nirvikalpajñāna),
one says, "There is fire here."
Thus, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is merely the engagement in conventional usage and is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) from that [perception], as was stated previously;

likewise, the cognition of non-existence is also conceptual, or rather, the cognition of another object by way of its result is not a separate means of valid cognition called "non-existence" distinct from perception.
Therefore, that which we have asserted regarding the apprehension of the absence of others [is correct].

"Since you yourself are stating that very same thing, why does it seem so harsh?"—this is said in derision because he has accepted a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called "non-existence" (*abhāva*) by not accepting [the opponent's position]. For indeed, this is now being stated by you out of necessity, not out of impartiality; otherwise, why was this not stated earlier? Since you have only exhausted yourself with a web of empty talk, the author concludes by saying: "Therefore, like one who does not see the shore," and so forth.
It is said that just as merchants aboard a ship release a bird with the hope that it might see the shore,
and when, after wandering everywhere, it does not find the shore, it returns to the very ship— so too should this be understood.
Since this position must necessarily be accepted, there is no purpose whatsoever in this direction which lacks any established foundation.

Thus, when it has been established that for one who desires a relationship of indicator and indicated (*liṅga-liṅgibhāva*) between the existence of another thing and the absence of that [thing], such a position is untenable due to the lack of a connection, and when the opponent objects: "In the absence of a connection, even through the cognition of the existence of another, there would be no cognition of the absence of that [thing]," [the author replies:]
It has indeed been stated that "it is not from any [inherent] connection," and so forth;
therefore, "the existence of another thing is itself the non-existence of that thing, and the cognition of the existence of another thing is itself the cognition of the non-existence of that thing."

Thus, while establishing this, the doctrine of non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*) postulated by Kumārila for the sake of ascertaining the non-existence of something has been incidentally refuted; now, however—
(Hbṭ 194) “And the establishment of the non-confusion of entities depends upon its validity.”
In order to refute this by raising an objection, he says: “If [it were] from the cognition of one alone,” and so forth.

For if the exclusion—that is, the negation—of another were established merely from the cognition of “one” in isolation, then the non-existence of all other things would be established without distinction in that very place where that single thing is perceived.
But it is not by way of grasping a specific [object] that [the capacity] belongs only to that which is in a state capable of producing its own cognition;
for, in this way, it is perceived as having a form distinct from objects whose capacity is equal,
because its cognition is restricted to that single form.
Likewise, it is also of a nature devoid of the object whose form consists of an incomparable capacity.

Consequently, since there is no distinction in its establishing the non-existence of anything other than that by virtue of having a form devoid of that [object], the cognition of the locus-form would establish the non-existence of taste and so forth just as it establishes the non-existence of the jar;
or else, it would not establish even the non-existence of the jar.

Furthermore, as for this qualification stated— namely, that "the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility is the means of proving non-existence"— that too need not be stated.
What is the reason?

Because even for those things that have not reached the conditions of perceptibility (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), there is indeed an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of them from that place by means of cognition having that single form (*tadekākāratayā*). For instance, just as those things that have reached the conditions of perceptibility do not appear in a cognition possessing that single form and are thereby excluded, so too it is with those that have not reached the conditions of perceptibility; what [difference is there]?

By this qualification, "of that which has reached the conditions for perception," when the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is thus established, if the exclusion of others (*tadanyavyavaccheda*)— that is, setting it apart and establishing it as distinct— is intended, then that is indeed accepted. Alternatively,
if it means the non-existence [of the object] at those specific places and times, [then that too is accepted].
That is incorrect;

for the capacity by which one establishes the non-existence of that which possesses a form of equal fitness and has reached the conditions of perceptibility cannot exist in that which possesses a form of unequal fitness or has not reached the conditions of perceptibility.
"Since those two exist, there can be no cognition restricted to a single form, because that is impossible"—

this is how the proof for their non-existence is established. And since this [proof] cannot be established elsewhere, he begins with the words "Because of the determination of a single nature," and so forth, in order to demonstrate this.

Because one determines the specific form of that single, individual self which appears in direct perception as being present before one, through the arising of a mental image of it and by generating an affirmative conceptualization (*vidhi-vikalpa*), [one excludes] everything "other than that"—that is, other than it, distinct from it—the "self" or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all that [is thus excluded]. From that... (Hbṭ 195)
"Exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*) means differentiation, separation, the establishment of distinctness, and the communication of an unmixed nature.
But how is it that through the very determination of its own nature, perception effects the exclusion of that [object] from other natures?
For perception, arising through the power of the object situated before it, should only apprehend that very form.
As for that entire collection of objects distinct from it, how could it serve as a delimiter for that Self standing before one?

Therefore, the means of knowledge known as non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*) must be accepted for the sake of delimiting it, because it is said: "The establishment of the non-confusion of entities depends upon its validity."
Therefore, he says: "Because of the cognition whose appearance is restricted to that [object's] own nature.
For the nature of a single object situated before one is unmixed with other forms;
because all things, by their very essence, are established in their own respective natures, they possess a nature that is not mixed with the form of others.
Otherwise, how could their non-confusion even be established by means of the pramāṇa of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*)?
For if that [non-existence] were used to prove the non-confusion of things whose forms are actually confused, it would follow that it is erroneous.

When a thing is not confused with the form of another, the manifestation which—by its very nature—is restricted to its own essence and unmixed with the manifestation of the form of another, [is what constitutes its identity].

For in perception, which arises through the power of the object as a single entity, the appearance of another form is impossible; otherwise, perception would lose its status due to the consequence of being erroneous.
As it has been said: "For that [cognition], arising through the power of the object, must conform to the very form of that [object].
This is because that cognition, whose appearance is restricted to that very nature, is experienced by perception through self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*).

For the very perception of that [object] is the "exclusion" (*vyavacchedana*)—that is, the differentiation—from what does not possess its form; and by the power of that [perception] alone, a subsequent conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka*) arises, which grasps what has already been grasped, consisting of the conviction regarding the state of non-confusion: "This is not of the nature of another."
Nothing new is cognized by that [subsequent cognition], because the self, which is unmixed with other forms, is already determined by perception itself, which conforms to its form.
Even if that cognition has a manifestation restricted to that very self, how can there be a separation of it from another self?
To this he says: "For that is not its nature," and so forth.

Because the nature (*ātman*) of that entity—which is unmixed with the forms of others—is not the nature of any other remaining entity, since everything else has a different intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) from it.
Otherwise, that [distinction] would be lost;
therefore, it is precisely the cognition whose manifestation is restricted to that very nature which constitutes the exclusion from others.
For knowledge does not take an object by the hand and turn one away from it;
rather, its "turning away" from another is said to be merely the imitation of a single self that is unmixed with the form of anything else.
Otherwise, if [knowledge] did not turn one away from other selves regarding its own object, [it would be ineffective].
In that case, if this object were not distinguished from another nature and were not established as separate, then there would also be a delimitation (*pariccheda*) of the other nature therein;
otherwise, the very non-delimitation of that [other]—which consists in the delimitation of a single nature—would take the form of its exclusion.

Consequently, since there would be no distinction from the other nature, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of delimiting it, which results in the absence of both engagement and withdrawal; such is the previous reductio ad absurdum.
For this [cognition] is not [of the form] "not seeing fire," and so forth.
He says "and that" in order to show that it does not merely exclude other things from one object, but excludes everything else even from that very object itself—
[the object] which stands before one, determined by its specific place, time, nature, and state, and whose essence is distinguished from other places and so forth.

Since this [object] exists precisely due to its own causes, the cognition perceiving it— by means of that very nature which is restricted to a specific place and so forth, and which thus conforms to such an intrinsic nature—
excludes the "deviation from that state," namely, the condition of existing with a different place, time, or intrinsic nature, of "this" object which is its own referent.
Then he distinguishes [it].

Why, again, does he establish it as distinct from that [other thing] by way of being in another location and so forth? To this he says: "For in this way," because when there is a distinction from that [other thing] by way of being in another location and so forth, the object determined by that location and so forth becomes delimited (*paricchinna*).
Because it conforms precisely to that form;

if there were otherwise-being— namely, being in another place and so forth— which, due to not conforming to that form, would be excluded from it, then both that state [of otherwise-being] and the restriction to that specific place and so forth would belong only to that which is currently perceived, and not to anything else situated in another place and so forth.

Since this is so, "therefore" (*iti*), [the word] "excludes" (*vyavacchindaty eva*)—that is, it indeed turns away—that which is of a different nature and possesses a different location and so forth, from that which is of such a nature and possesses that very location and so forth; thus it delimits that [object]. This is the conclusion of the first [point]. Likewise, "it excludes that which is of a different nature from that which is of such a nature"—this is how the conclusion of the second [point] should be formulated.
"In this way," by the logic thus stated, "of one" means of a single means of valid cognition, whether perception or inference; for that too is exactly like this.
Because it delimits its own object, "functioning" (vṛtti) or activity establishes all entities within "two groups," namely as being either identical or different.
Therefore, the non-confusion [of entities] is established solely by the force of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that delimits them;
what is the use of this conceptualization of non-existence (abhāva) as well?
(197) But is this not the operation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), namely: "This is not of another nature; otherwise, it would be of this nature"?
“Since perception is held to be non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), how can the establishment of their non-confusion (*asāṃkarya*) be derived from it?
To this, he says: “When that [perception], etc.
For that perception is successful only when it generates the conceptual constructions of affirmation and negation regarding its own object.

And it is accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only at that time, not at any other; for this very reason, although there is a determination of the nature of a single object in its entirety— since there is no part of it that has not been apprehended— it is not accepted as being a means of valid cognition with respect to [properties] such as momentariness, because the causes of error are present and it lacks the capacity to produce cognitions of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding them.

It might be thought: "Even when establishing the two-fold division [of existence and non-existence], let there be no postulation of non-existence as a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the sake of ensuring their non-confusion; rather, it will serve to establish the absence of any other alternative mode.

For it has not been demonstrated that perception has any function whatsoever in establishing that absence. To this he says: "By the exclusion of everything distinct from that," and so forth. Therefore, by the exclusion—that is, the separation—of all things whatsoever that are distinct from that which is being perceived, and by the concomitance (vyāpti) established through that very proof of such difference, there is the non-existence of any other mode that lies outside the categories of identity and difference.
It is established; therefore, even for that purpose, it is not logical to postulate non-existence as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Now, if it is thought: "Perception does not establish such a pervasion—that everything unperceived is other than what is being perceived—so how could the absence of a third category be established by perception itself?"

Since the postulation of non-existence as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would thus be futile, he says: "Of that"—of what is being postulated as a third category—"because there is no pervasion" due to its being other than the perceived [object], "by that"—namely, by perception—"there is no exclusion" (*avyavaccheda*), that is, no differentiation, of "that object" from its own domain;

and because that object, which is being postulated as a separate category, is not excluded from, nor differentiated from, its own domain, it follows once again that there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-determination of existence within its own domain.
For if that object—which has as its nature a self unmixed with all other forms—is not delimited by that [specific] nature, how can it be delimited by it?
Or, if it is delimited by that nature, how could there be no proof of the pervasion of everything else by way of being "other than that"?
Otherwise, even a single thing would not possess the state of being "other" than that.

"Because the sign (*nimitta*) is the same. Since this is so, when a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), has operated upon some object (*vastu*), it delimits that object by way of its specific nature.
It excludes that which is other than it and devoid of its nature, because it establishes [the object] as being distinct from that;
and it indicates the non-existence of a third category that falls outside of identity and difference.
This is because pervasion is established through the otherness of everything, or because the twofold nature of all things—which is the opposite of that [otherness]—is established.
Thus, this operation of a single means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) has just been described; having summarized it for the sake of easy comprehension:

Showing this, he says: "For instance," when a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, operates upon a certain object, that very object is "delimited" from other forms; it is distinguished from them and is apprehended as having a nature unmixed with them, because in ultimate reality it possesses that very nature, and because perception conforms to the form of the object as it actually exists.
Why does it exclude other forms?

Because it determines that very thing which is devoid of other forms as having a single form. Likewise, the phrase "and indeed different from that" excludes what is different from that which is being perceived.
Why?
Because it "from that," i.e., from its own object;
it does not merely differentiate its own object from others.
"Even that which is other [than itself] from its own object"—from what [source is this known]?

Because another form, being other, is not discerned therein in that objective support; and for that which is necessarily undiscerned, there is necessarily a state of being other than that which is discerned.

Since this is so, therefore that very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which delimits a single object, establishes the absence of other modes, not a [separate] means of valid cognition called "non-existence" (*abhāva*).
Why is this so?

When that object is being perceived, because it is seen as distinct from others, the "otherness" (*anyatva*) of that other thing which is not delimited therein is its "distinctness from what is seen" (*dṛṣṭatadanyatva*). By means of that, everything excluded from it is established; therefore, [it is] not [the case that...].

And because that which is other than this [object] does not exist as something standing before one, and because that very object—which is excluded from all other entities—is established as the mode of appearance being perceived in its true nature;
applying this same principle elsewhere, he says: "By this, succession, non-succession, and so forth," etc.
By this aforementioned principle, a cognition arises that conforms to the form of a single, specifically determined entity.
Excluding everything that has a form contrary to that [specific object] from its own domain, it establishes a twofold division and the absence of a third possibility.
Thus, whatever pairs of mutually exclusive forms there may be—such as succession and simultaneity, permanence and impermanence, and so forth—they have been explained.
For instance, the intellect, while perceiving the succession of an effect as its lack of assistance from anything else, thereby distinguishes its non-succession as its association with other effects.

Consequently, the possibility of a third mode [of existence] is excluded by the fact that duality is established through either succession or non-succession; for everything that arises as an effect, being distinct from successive occurrence, must exist as a second mode [namely, non-successive]. Thus, momentariness is defined as perishing immediately after arising; at the very time of establishing this cognition, the intellect [perceives] its opposite nature.
Because it is excluded from its own object and established as something other than that in a different manner, there is no possibility of a third category.

Having thus demonstrated the establishment of non-confusion based on a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he concludes by saying: "In this way," according to the reasoning already stated, because of the perception of "one" thing—that is, of a specific nature—whatever belongs to that perceived thing [is distinct] from that...

The "exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*)—that is, the differentiation—from the nature of that [perceived object] consists of its being either of a nature possessing a fitness equal to that [other], or its being the opposite, or its being deficient in that form;
this occurs because the perceived object appears in a different form from the unperceived nature.

Thus, through the exclusion of that object's own domain from having the nature of anything else—the description here emphasizing the existence of the state itself—"exclusion" is established, which means non-confusion is proven.

If it is intended here that, because this [cognition] is without distinction, there would be no establishment of the non-existence of everything else, then that is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
For everything is indeed, without distinction, excluded from its own object by a cognition having a single form,
since no other form whatsoever appears therein.

Now, he shows that it is not tenable to maintain that the non-existence of that [specific object] at that place and time constitutes the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of everything else that is its opposite; [he says]: "Not of that place and time. For where that specific entity, which is distinct from the entire triple world, is perceived, there [one must exclude] all other entities—whether they be of a nature similar to it in terms of capacity (*yogyatā*), or otherwise.
Or rather, exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is negation (*pratiṣedha*).
For by whatever cause there is a negation of that which possesses a form of equal fitness [to appear] but does not appear therein,
when that [cause] exists, because a cognition restricted to that single form is impossible, that [cognition], arising as inseparable from the absence of that [object], [constitutes] its negation.

Since the cause [of perception]— namely, that which brings about [cognition]— is not possible in the case of something that has reached the conditions for non-perception (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) or in something whose nature lacks a corresponding capacity (*atulyayogyatārūpa*), how could its absence be established?

Concluding this very point, he says: "Therefore, everything that is not of that nature and possesses a form contrary to it would be established by a cognition having a single form of that [object]; and "it would also possess its place and time," meaning it would have those same place and time as that which is appearing.
Like what?
"Like taste, form, and so forth.

For even when a cognition manifesting as a form distinguishes a taste—which lacks that form—from its own object, and even if it establishes the non-confusion between them, the absence [of the taste] from the place and time of that [form] is not thereby established.
Consequently, how could there be an absence of everything—even those things whose capacities for manifestation are dissimilar—within that [place and time]?
Or else, the qualification "of that which has reached the conditions for perception" would not have been stated.

For this reason, the proof of the non-existence of something, somewhere, or at some time, is established through the aforementioned non-perception— specifically, from a non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perception, consisting in the perception of its own nature as a form possessing equivalent capability—
but not by way of generality, as others claim.

"Where the five means of valid cognition do not arise with respect to the nature of an object, there the means of valid cognition called non-existence (abhāva-pramāṇa) functions for the purpose of awakening one to the existence of that object.
For it is not the case that the absence of an object is established merely by the non-operation of the five means of valid cognition when the conditions for perception have been met.
"Even though that [object] exists, it is possible for the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) not to operate due to its remoteness in terms of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth.
Having thus concluded this incidental discussion, [the author addresses] what was stated by the opponent:
"Why is that very 'presence of another' (*anyabhāva*) and the perception whose object is that [other] not a proof for the non-existence of that [object]?"

Thus, having refuted the status of the existence of another thing as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the non-existence of that [specific] thing, he says—refuting the perception whose object is that [existence of another]—"Regarding the object which is the existence of another," and so forth.
As for what was further stated:
"Why is the perception whose object is the existence of another not a means of establishing that non-existence?"
Thus, for us, that [non-perception] is intended only as a means of proving the absence of that [object], and not as a logical mark (*liṅga*) in the manner you have described.
What is the reason?

For even in that case, when the non-existence (*abhāva*) is to be established as distinct from the other entity (*anyabhāva*) which is the object of perception, the absence of a relationship is equal to the absence [of the entity itself].
Indeed, there is no relationship—such as inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*) or the like—between that perception, which consists of the other entity, and that absence.
Demonstrating the equality of this point with the argument "because they are not established separately" (*apṛthaksiddheḥ*), he says: "In the manifestation of the mark," and so forth.

As for this perception of another entity which is stated to be a logical mark (*liṅga*), since its very manifestation—at the time of its arising or at the time of its cognition—consists of the form of a place devoid of that [other entity], the absence of that [entity] is established at that very moment.
For it is thus: the experience of a cognition perceiving another entity as distinct from the appearance of that [absent entity] is itself the experience of its absence.
He establishes that very point: for a cognizer, having first apprehended the existence of another thing distinct from that [object], does not subsequently—

after having established the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) based on the cognition of that other thing being present when the former is absent— apprehend its absence by means of a valid cognition (pramāṇa) that proves the necessary connection (pratibandha).
What then?

One who apprehends that other thing, which has a nature distinct from it, simultaneously apprehends the non-existence of its counter-positive, because that very thing consists in the nature of the non-existence of that [counter-positive].
For instance, the perception of a bare location whose nature is not intermingled with the location occupied by a jar is itself the perception of the absence of the jar.
Indeed, [the statements] "there is no jar here" and "this place does not possess a jar" [are nothing other than such a perception].
"There is something other than the jar"— this is one kind of distinction in meaning.
Therefore, the perception of the bare location precisely as being "other than the jar" is itself the perception of the absence of the jar.
If it is asked: "How is it known that the cognition 'there is no jar here' is merely a memory, because it apprehends what has already been apprehended?"
Immediately after perception, and without the mediation of the means characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [one cognizes]:
"This object in this location exists as distinct from the jar," and "But this thing, the jar, does not exist."

Thus, because it is established by means of these two alternatives [regarding] the posterior [position], there is no recourse here to positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Furthermore: when the example is unestablished, the apprehension of the absence of [the reason] within its own nature is the proof of that non-existence.
He demonstrates that very point by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words, "And that [is] of that," and so forth.
If it is argued that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) also exists here,
he replies with the words, "For it is not possible in this way," and so forth.
Why is it not possible to demonstrate [the pervasion]?
Because of the apprehension of that one [thing]: because the specific form of the apprehension of that single thing, which is not associated with anything else, does not exist anywhere else.
Now, if it is argued that the cause is the generality of the apprehension of what is distinct from that—namely, wherever there is the apprehension of a ground distinct from a jar, there [is fire]...

Regarding that, the absence of a jar is, for example, as in a location previously experienced as devoid of a jar; thus he says: "When a general demonstration is being made," even in the case of the illustrative example, there is no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) such as perception to establish the absence of the jar in the previously experienced location devoid of a jar, because [such a demonstration] consists in the apprehension of another existing thing.

However, that very perception of something other than it (*tadanya-bhāva-upalabdhi*) is what establishes the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*), which is characterized by its absence (*tad-abhāva*).

And just as that [perception] requires an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the sake of establishing that absence in the subject of the thesis (*sādhya-dharmin*), so too does it require one in the case of the example. Likewise, since it would require another example for that [example] as well, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of examples.
And in the case of infinite regress, there would be no cognition of the absence of that [object] anywhere.
Since this is so, "therefore, the establishment of the absence of that [object] does not arise from any mark whatsoever," whether it be the existence of something other than it or its own perception.
If the existence of something other than it does not establish its absence, [then how could it do so?]
But how does it establish [non-existence] by way of a logical mark (*liṅga*)?
To this he says: "That non-existence (*anyabhāva*)" is established by the definition of perception—because perception itself is non-perception insofar as it is other than the intended apprehension.
Being established by that non-perception characterized by such a definition, it would establish the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*).
Because, with respect to the action residing in the locus [of the substratum], the non-existence of anything other than that consists in the nature of non-apprehension.
But where would this [non-apprehension] establish the conventional usage of non-existence? It establishes it when the cognition of a deluded person is the object to be proven.

For one who, being undeluded regarding the apprehension of an object, nevertheless remembers the subject [of that perception], the conventional usage of its non-existence is based precisely on direct perception; thus, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) does not function as a logical mark (*liṅga*) in that case. This has already been well-discussed elsewhere, so let us stop this digression here. [3. Having divided non-apprehension into three types, the analysis thereof.]

Thus, having established the essential nature of non-apprehension by refuting all opposing views, [the author] says, for the purpose of explaining its divisions: "This aforementioned non-apprehension is threefold.
How so?
When the causal relationship has been established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that proves it, there is the non-apprehension of the cause.
Of what kind [of non-existence]? Of that which is established as non-existent (*siddhābhāva*).

Likewise, when the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) has been established, it is by the very force of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes it, that the pervader is established as being precisely that which is non-existent; otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) itself remains unestablished.
And as for what was stated as "the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature," thus there are three types of non-apprehension.

But how is the conventional usage of the absence of both cause and pervader established, such that their absence is said to be proven? To this he says: "In that regard, [it applies] to the cause and the pervader as well"—meaning not only to that [object] for which the conventional usage of absence is directly established.
It is established as follows:

in the case of the non-perception of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), the "establishment of the absence of the intrinsic nature" refers to the establishment of another thing that is distinct from it; this very establishment of the other entity is so called because it is the cause for the establishment of the conventional usage of its absence.

That [absence], which is the non-existence of the cause or the pervader, is "established in that manner"—that is, established through the perception of the existence of another thing—which constitutes the conventional usage of absence regarding the effect or the pervaded, both of which are the objects to be negated.

When, because these two have dissimilar objects, the perception of things possessing specific qualities is not established, then [the non-apprehension] "proves either absence or the conventional usage of absence.
The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of conjunction.

Now, one might ask: even in the case of the non-perception of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), is non-existence established as a logical mark (*liṅga*)? To this he says: "But in the case of the non-perception of an intrinsic nature," and so forth.

It is only the "conventional usage of non-existence" (*abhāvavyavahāra*) [that is established], not non-existence itself, because that [non-existence] is already established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Anticipating an objection from the opponent here, he says: "If," then, that non-existent conventional usage is established by which two [factors]—namely, the cause (*kāraṇa*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*)—being present, by what means?

By non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) consisting of the nature of perception (*pratyakṣātmikā*), which is the establishment of "that other thing"—that is, of an entity devoid of the cause and the pervader.
It establishes both the absence of another thing—whether it be an effect or a pervaded—and the conventional usage of its non-existence.

And that perception of the presence of something else serves as the means for establishing the conventional usage of non-existence for those two, namely the cause and the pervader, only when they have reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*); it does not do so otherwise.
This being accepted, how could those two—the non-perception of the cause and the non-perception of the pervader—apply to an object that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*)?
The application [of the reason] concerns the object [in question].

When a formulation of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is made for reasons based on effect (*kārya*) or essential nature (*svabhāva*), such as: "Wherever fire is absent, there smoke is also absent," or likewise, "Wherever a tree is absent, or momentariness is absent, there a *śiṃśapā* is absent, or existence is absent"—since this formulation of negative concomitance occurs by encompassing all things without exception; [this is the case when the reason is applied to the subject].
For at that time, all objects other than the fire and the tree are not perceived as non-momentary. Consequently,

how can the non-apprehension characterized by the apprehension of what is distinct from them— the non-apprehension defined by the characteristic of apprehension— be established for the counter-correlate (pratiyogin), given that its fulfillment of the conditions for apprehensibility is unproven?

And if that were so, how could the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the effects-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*) be established through a pervasion that includes all instances?
Or, if it is not so established, how could these two possess the capacity to prove [the probandum]?
Therefore, the negative concomitance must be accepted based merely on the non-observation [of the probans] in some particular case.
In some cases, however, there is positive concomitance (*anvaya*) through mere observation;
thus, the opponent considers the proclamation of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) to be purposeless.

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) says: "By no means" is the application of the non-perception of the cause or the pervader (*kāraṇavyāpakānupalabdhi*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatayā*) when the object is beyond perception (*parokṣa*), at the time of demonstrating negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). This is because the non-perception of the cause or the pervader—# [is not a valid cognition in that context].
It is not at all employed as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Why?

Because there is no certainty regarding the "mark" (*liṅga*)—characterized by the non-perception of the cause or the pervader, or characterized by the absence of that [object]—since those two types of non-perception are of the nature of doubt, and its absence is itself uncertain.
How, then, is the application of these two intended at that time?
To this he says: "Only," and so forth.
For, by means of that which establishes the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between the cause and the pervader—(Hbt 204)

When the relationship— characterized either as origination from that (*tadutpatti*) or as identity (*tādātmya*)— has been established by the aforementioned means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which proves the state of the pervaded and the pervader, then wherever there is an absence of those two whose relationship is thus established, there must necessarily and invariably be an absence of the other [term], whether it be the effect or the pervaded; otherwise, the fallacy of having no cause would follow.

And because it would follow that [the reason] lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), how could there be a recollection of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) by means of that [recollection]? It is for the purpose of demonstrating this point that these two—non-perception of the cause and non-perception of the pervader (*kāraṇavyāpakānupalabdhi*)—are employed.

However, when the proof is based on the power of perception and non-perception, then in whatever case something is seen upon the perception of one thing, or not seen upon its non-perception, let its existence or non-existence apply only to that [specific] case; why, then, should it apply everywhere?
Is it so?
For, although a concomitance is observed in some instances among things like cows and horses whose natures are not interconnected, such concomitance does not occur everywhere.

However, in the case of a person, if there were no essential connection, the observation that when one thing exists or does not exist, another thing always exists or does not exist would have to be considered a mere accidental coincidence. Thus he said:

“Diverse potencies are seen in substances due to differences in place and other factors; therefore, it is not logical to determine the existence of a potency observed in one instance as being present elsewhere.
Thus, a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the probandum and the probans must necessarily be admitted.
That very [reason] must be indicated through the application of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
And since it cannot be made known without demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*) through positive and negative concomitance, [the text says]:
"wherever...".
Thus it is made known by the inclusion of all categories of entities.
For when an invariable concomitance is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it necessarily follows that wherever there is an effect, there must be a cause;
and wherever that [cause] is absent, there too the effect must be absent. Otherwise, if the effect were to exist in the absence of its cause, that effect would be devoid of a cause altogether.
And consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence of [the cause] being eternally present as a substantial entity (sattva) and so forth.

Likewise, wherever something has a certain intrinsic nature (svabhāva), there that very state must exist; otherwise, it would be nothing but a non-entity (nairātmya). Thus, it was already stated previously that the necessary connection (pratibandha) can only be demonstrated through the presentation of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) by means of pervasion (vyāpti), and not otherwise.

[The detailed exposition is concluded. Having thus demonstrated that the presence of the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) exists only in those reasons characterized as effect, essential nature, and non-perception— because the valid means of proof (*pramāṇa*) establishing them exist there, and not elsewhere— the author concludes by saying:

"Thus"— this very property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), characterized as the non-apprehension of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) or the effect (*kārya*), possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) because of the existence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*). And since it possesses positive and negative concomitance due to the existence of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish that connection, "thus"— for that reason— it is "pervaded by a part of that" (*tadaṃśena vyāptaḥ*), because the pervasion by that part is ascertained precisely through the ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance, as was stated previously.

Furthermore, because of the statement regarding the pervasion by its parts, only the three-featured—meaning "only that which possesses the three forms" (trirūpa)—is the probans (*hetu*) that makes [the object] known, and not anything else with different characteristics or another type. This is because, when the aforementioned three features are present, any other feature is redundant; and when the aforementioned three features are absent, even if one imagines another feature, there is no certainty (*avyabhicāra*), and thus it cannot serve as a means of knowledge.

Why is it that only a reason possessing the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*)—and no other kind—is a means of cognition? [The author] shows this by stating, "because of the non-deviation from its own property to be proven" (*svasādhyadharmāvyabhicārāt*). Since only that which possesses the three characteristics does not deviate from its own property to be proven, and since being a means of cognition consists precisely in this non-deviation from the property to be proven, the postulation of any other form [of reason] is useless. Furthermore, if one were to postulate another form while abandoning the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) based on the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), there would still be an absence of non-deviation from the property to be proven.

Thus, by this [explanation], regarding the statement "that [reason] is indeed threefold," it means that "that reason" possesses exactly three characteristics because of the "necessity" (niyamāt)—that is, the inevitable presence—of the non-deviation from its own probandum-property (*svasādhyadharma*). Furthermore, if one does not accept the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by the part of that [probandum] as the basis for the connection, then even if other forms are postulated, "the others are fallacious reasons" (*hetvābhāsāḥ*); that is, they are distinct from the aforementioned three-characterized [reason] due to their association with other forms.

When these pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are examined, they are shown to be another point: because the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), which is the non-deviation from their own probandum-property (*svasādhyadharma*), is absent in them.
[5. Refutation of those who assert additional characteristics for the definition of a reason.
As it has been stated: "The reason possesses only three characteristics, not others."

Thus, showing the disagreement of others on this point, he says: "Others hold that the reason has six characteristics. The Naiyāyikas, Mīmāṃsakas, and others believe this. What, then, are the six forms of the reason desired by them?
He says: "And these three," namely those called *pakṣadharma* (property of the subject), *anvaya* (positive concomitance), and *vyatireka* (negative concomitance).
Likewise, the fourth characteristic is "having an uncontradicted object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*).

That whose object—characterized by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—is "uncontradicted," meaning not refuted by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is so described; the state of being such is its "nature" (*tattva*), which is another characteristic. Similarly, "having a singular number as intended" (*vivakṣitaikasaṃkhyatva*) is yet another characteristic.
That which has the number one belonging to its causal substance (*hetudravya*) is "unitary" (*ekasaṃkhya*).

That universal of the reason (*hetusāmānya*) which has as its substratum that intended unitary causal substance is "possessing the intended number one. Its state (*tadbhāva*) constitutes another form [of the reason].

If the state of being a reason (*hetutva*) occurs in a causal individual delimited by the number one and devoid of a counter-reason (*pratihetu*), then it possesses the capacity to prove (*gamakatva*); however, it does not possess this capacity when accompanied by a counter-reason, even if it is associated with the number two.
This means that no other counter-reason (*hetvantara*)—namely, a contradictory non-deviant reason (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*)—is presented.
Likewise, "being known" (*jñātatva*) is the state of being an object of cognition;
for it is not logical that a reason which is unknown should be a prover by its mere existence alone.

In this regard, among these various forms [of the reason], that which is called "having an uncontradicted object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) does not constitute a separate definition apart from the existence of an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), which consists of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) based on a necessary bond (*pratibandha*).
Since that [inseparable connection] is already expressed by the very statement [of the definition], it need not be stated separately.
Why is it not a separate characteristic? Because there is a contradiction between sublation (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).

For instance, even when invariable concomitance exists as previously described, those who consider the possibility of sublation to exist [in that case] state "having a non-sublated object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) as another essential feature (*rūpāntara*).
And this possibility of that [coexistence] is not possible, because there is a "contradiction" with non-deviation (*avinābhāva*), characterized by the impossibility of existing together.
Demonstrating that very contradiction, he says: "For non-deviation... and so forth.
For the inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of the reason is said to be its presence only when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is present;

however, sublation (*bādhā*) occurs when that [property] is absent. For if a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were to operate toward the absence of that [property] while it is indeed present, then because that [cognition] would be erroneous, it would simply lack the status of a valid cognition—so how could there be sublation?

Therefore, that reason, possessing those characteristics— that is, being inseparable from the probandum— must exist in the subject (*dharmin*). And in this case, why would the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) not be present,
such that there would be room for sublation (*bādhā*)?

Therefore, there is an impossibility of the coexistence of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) and sublation by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabādhā*), because the presence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in the subject (*dharmin*)— which is established by invariable concomitance— and its absence— established by sublation by a means of valid cognition— are contradictory due to being characterized by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthiti*).
Consequently, they cannot exist in a single subject.
To clarify that very contradiction, he says by way of mocking others: "For perception and inference," and so forth.
Indeed, when perception and inference subvert the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), they "seize him by the neck" and "expel him" from his own locus, the subject (dharmin).

And since the reason exists only when that property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) exists—due to its being invariably concomitant with it—it seizes that property to be proven by the throat as it is being led away, and forcibly establishes it right there in the subject (*dharmin*). Oh, how great indeed is the distress of "entities" characterized as the properties to be proven!
For, being constrained by two machines and deprived of breath, they have reached nothing but death.

Showing that there is no contradiction between sublation (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) because their objects are distinct, [the author] says: "Elsewhere"—that is, setting aside the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), the reason is invariably concomitant with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), but not in the subject of the thesis itself. Therefore, how could there be a contradiction between sublation and invariable concomitance? For sublation establishes the absence of the property to be proven elsewhere, whereas the reason establishes its presence elsewhere.

And thus, even though such an inseparable relation (avinābhāva) exists, since there is no possibility of sublation (bādha), the other characteristic—having a non-sublated object (abādhitaviṣayatva)—is possible.
