Even when such an inseparable relation and the other characteristics such as having a non-sublated object are accepted, [the author] speaks with a tone of derision toward others in order to refute the status of being a "pseudo-reason" (hetvābhāsa) that was attributed to those other characteristics: "The pseudo-reasons are others than these," [meaning they arise from the presence of other characteristics].

So then, does this wretched and pitiable subject (*sādhyadharmin*)—having married a eunuch (*ṣaṇḍha*) and having settled upon that [eunuch] as a reason (*hetu*) incapable of producing the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—now seek a "son" characterized by that very property to be proven?
He clarifies this very point: "For which [reason], even though the property to be proven is absent in the subject, its presence is nevertheless asserted."
Because the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is admitted to exist elsewhere than in the subject (*sādhyadharmin*).
Having demonstrated that [concomitance] in such a manner within the subject, how can it be said that "the subject possesses the property to be proven" (*sādhyadharma*)?

For even though wateriness (*ambhastva*) is invariably concomitant with salinity (*lavaṇatva*) in the ocean, when salinity is intended to be proven as a property in water other than that [ocean], the establishment of salinity does not follow from the mere presence of wateriness.
Anticipating an opponent’s objection regarding the scope for an alternative argument, he says: "For this very reason," and so forth.
He explains this very point: "It might be [argued] as follows" is your [opponent's] view:

because the reason (hetu) could exist in the locus (dharmin) even otherwise—that is, even in the absence of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma)—since such is observed in cases like water and the like.

And because inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is accepted even when excluding the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), for this very reason, a subject whose property is not sublated by the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is so called.

If, by means of perception and inference, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)— which is the object of the logical reason (*hetu*)— is not sublated in the subject of the thesis, as for example the saltiness [of water] is not sublated in the case of "water-ness," [then it is a valid subject].
In that case, it possesses the capacity to convey [the meaning],
but not otherwise;
for we do not accept that the probandum is established by mere inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) in other instances, and thus the aforementioned fault does not apply.

The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntavādin) says: "In that case, what now?"—if, because the inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitā*) of the reason with the subject is not admitted, there is an absence of proof for the probandum (*sādhya*), and another characteristic, namely "having an unsublated object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), is stated for the sake of proving it, then the reason has no efficacy whatsoever. Why? Because "by the very fact of being unsublated," the probandum is established even without the reason; thus, the reason is entirely ineffective (*akiñcitkara*).

For in this case, there are two alternatives: when the subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) operates, would the absence of the probandum (*sādhya-abhāva*) be necessary or unnecessary?

If the first alternative holds, then the absence of the probandum is indeed necessary when the subverting means of valid cognition operates, because it exists only when that [cognition] is present and is absent when it is not.

Therefore, when there is "non-sublation"—that is, in the absence of the operation of a subverting means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—since the absence of the probandum, which is necessarily concomitant with that [sublation], is also absent, the "establishment of the probandum" certainly occurs; thus, the reason is indeed redundant and should not even be presented.
Consequently, for what could "having a non-sublated object" be a distinct characteristic (rūpāntara)?
It might be thought: "Let it be that the reason lacks capacity when there is an absence of the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*);

however, when a subverting proof of the probandum (*sādhya*) operates upon the locus (*dharmin*), then the reason will possess the capacity to establish the probandum. To this, he says: "Even in the case of subversion" (*bādhāyām api*). If a subverting proof operates, then because that [proof] establishes the absence of the probandum in the locus, even by Brahmā himself—

Since it is impossible to bring about that state [of the probandum], how much less so by means of a fallacious reason (*śaṭha-hetu*)? For this very reason, you yourselves state "having an unsublated object" as another characteristic of the reason (*sādhana*). Now, if the absence of the probandum is not certain when a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) operates—because [the probandum] may still exist even in its absence—this is the second [alternative].

Even if that [absence] is accepted as the locus (*pakṣa*), it demonstrates the lack of capacity for non-sublation; thus he says: "In the case of non-restriction," when the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is intended while a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*) is operative, this consequence follows:
"There would be both a subverting means of valid cognition and the possibility of the absence of the probandum"—therefore, there is no establishment of the probandum.

“The capacity [of the reason] consists in the absence of sublation; for even when that [absence of sublation] exists, the non-existence of the probandum may still be possible, and thus even that which possesses it is merely a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

Regarding the statement, “The reason is useless because the probandum is established by the absence of sublation alone,” the opponent, demonstrating the meaning otherwise and establishing the capacity of the reason, says: “It is not the mere absence of sublation...”
What is intended by "my lack of affliction"? It is the non-perception of affliction.

And that non-perception [of sublation] might occur for a person due to a deficiency in their capacity, even when sublation is possible in certain places and so forth. Therefore, since the probandum is not established merely by the non-perception of sublation, a reason must necessarily be stated for its establishment; thus, that is the domain of the application of the reason. For, when the reason is establishing its own probandum, how could it be incapable?

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) says: Why indeed does one fear that perception which constitutes the sublation (*bādhā*), and not the sublation itself, such that you disregard even a possible sublation and maintain that [the reason] must be employed when there is no perception of it? Perhaps an opponent might say: "What will that wretched sublation do, even if it exists?"
The perception of that [object] itself is the demoness.
Therefore, for that very reason, there is fear; and since the cause must indeed be employed when that [demoness] is absent, he says: "In that case," and so forth.

Thus, disregarding whether or not there is sublation (bādhā) from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), he asks by means of a rhetorical question (*kāku*): "When there is no perception of sublation, should it be employed?"
Someone might say: "This has already been stated; why is it being asked?
To this he replies: "For what purpose is it employed?
The intention is that even if no sublation is perceived, if such [sublation] were possible, there would be an impossibility of establishing the probandum by means of the probans.

The opponent, whose intention is not understood, says: "For the sake of establishing the probandum (*sādhyasiddhyartha*). He thinks that since validity is accepted when there is an absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*), the establishment of the probandum from that [reason] is entirely uncontradicted. The proponent of the established tenet (*siddhāntavādī*), suspecting that the establishment of the probandum is impossible even when no subversion is perceived if such subversion actually exists, asks: "Does that [reason] ever... and so forth. Does it occur to you that this reason might establish the probandum even while subversion is present, such that you do not exert effort toward ascertaining the absence of that subversion and yet still employ the reason?
If it is argued that [the reason] is "employed" in this way,

then even when there is sublation (*bādhā*), if one accepts the capacity of the probandum and the probans, the characteristic of a logical reason (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*) would not be "having a non-sublated object."
What is the reason?
Even when there is sublation, this reason possesses "capacity" because its capacity is acknowledged;
for that by which the probandum could not be established is said to be the definition of a [valid] reason.

(210) It might be thought that, in the ultimate sense, the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*) is the state of not being contradicted by non-perception (*anupalabhyamānabādhatva*), and not the state of having an uncontradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*); therefore, he says: "And thus," and so forth.

For this being the case, even though the existence of a sublation (*bādhā*) is possible, one would have to accept it and yet proceed with the application of the reason (*hetu*) based merely on its non-perception.

Indeed, if the application of the reason were not intended while accepting the possibility of sublation, then one would have to apply the reason based on mere non-perception despite the presence of doubt;
for even among existing things, there is the possibility of their non-perception in some way or another, and [the rule] applies to the application of a reason when there is doubt.
Activity itself would not be tenable.
Therefore, whoever engages in action even when there is doubt must do so by accepting the positive possibility [of the object's existence].
And thus, just as a reason is employed after accepting the non-perception of sublation when such sublation is not perceived, it should likewise be employed even when that [sublation] is perceived.

Since there would be no distinction between the perception and non-perception of that sublation (*bādhā*) if its existence were admitted, even the characteristic of a reason (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*) as "not being subject to sublation" is not tenable. Thus, how could validity possibly occur in the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) when there is no [logical] connection?
Anticipating an opportunity for an opponent to speak, he says: "Not in the case of sublation," and so forth.
Indeed, when sublation (*bādhā*) is present, the capacity of the reason (*hetu*) is not admitted; therefore, how could there be an application [of the reason] even when that [sublation] is perceived?

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) says: "If this is so"—if it is admitted that the reason is incapable when sublation exists—then a reason for which the impossibility of sublation has not been determined does not deserve to be employed merely on the basis of the non-perception of sublation.
What is the reason?
It is so that, even in the case where sublation (*bādhā*) is possible, there may not be "an incapacity" of the "reason already employed" to establish the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*).

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) says: when no sublation is perceived, because of the absence of sublation, and in the absence of any cognition that perceives its existence...

If you think that the capacity [of words] for objects must necessarily exist because of the reason that [otherwise] objects would be non-existent, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) says: "Is perception a sublation? and so forth.
For perception is the effect of objects, and an effect does not pervade its cause.
For causes do not necessarily possess their effects, since the possibility of obstruction or deficiency exists.
Therefore, how can there be an absence of sublation upon the absence of a non-pervasive perception?
For this reason, the incapacity caused by the possibility of sublation would not occur;

and this is indeed accepted even by our opponents, since even for that which is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), no sublation is perceived at the time of its arising, yet it may occur at a later time. (Hbṭ 211)
Because when a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) arises, the lack of validity (*aprāmāṇya*) is admitted.

Now, even if the perception of that which is not all-pervasive (*avyāpaka*) ceases, the subversion ceases as well: "For falsity (*mithyātva*) ceases effortlessly through the absence of defects (*doṣa*) and ignorance (*ajñāna*)."
Thus, by this very same reasoning, he says that since sublation ceases upon the cessation of [erroneous] cognition, the reason is nevertheless useless.
Why?
Because the probandum is established even without the employment of a reason, simply from the non-perception of sublation (*bādhānupalambhāt*).
What is the reason?
Because contradiction is impossible when there is non-perception.
For it is thus: you maintain that where there is no perception of contradiction, that contradiction does not exist in reality.

And where that [subject] does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there the absence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) also does not exist in the ultimate sense; otherwise, it would be impossible for there to be an absence of sublation (*bādhā*) in the ultimate sense.

Consequently, since the absence of the absence of the property to be proven constitutes its presence, the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*)—according to your own view—is rendered useless by the reason (*hetu*).
Now, if you maintain that there is no contradiction with reasoning, and thus do not accept that the cessation of sublation follows from the cessation of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), [then...]

To this, he says: "Even if the apprehension [of the reason] has ceased, if the sublation (*bādhā*) is held not to have ceased, then the incapacity of the reason remains as it was when the sublation was apprehended; thus, there is no application of the reason. For whom, then, could 'having an unsublated object' be a distinct characteristic (*rūpāntara*) of the reason? Summing this up, he says: "Therefore, with respect to its own probandum," and so forth.
Since, in this way, if one accepts that the reason is invariably concomitant with the probandum in all cases through pervasion (*vyāpti*), and external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) is thus intended,
it follows that the employment of the reason becomes useless; therefore, a reason that— “otherwise than by the presence or absence of its own probandum”— that is,
existing neither when its own probandum is present nor when it is absent, does not "bring about" (*bhāvayati*) or establish any probandum in the subject (*dharmin*).

"One does not exclude" means one does not negate its opposite; "thus," for one who performs neither affirmation nor negation, "the introduction"—that is, the formal application—"is not effective. Therefore, by one who desires the application of a reason, an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between the reason and its own probandum must necessarily be admitted in all cases.
And that [invariable concomitance] is based on a necessary connection;
furthermore, as stated previously, this [connection] depends merely upon observation and non-observation.

Since that [necessary connection] is accepted, the contradiction between sublation (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is established; thus, concluding [the argument], he says: "Therefore, not... and so forth.
For that very reason, non-sublation (*abādha*) does not constitute a distinct form [of the probans].

Even if it is granted that non-sublation is understood when there is inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), because sublation (*bādhā*) and inseparable concomitance cannot coexist, why is it not nonetheless a distinct form?

Thus, for this reason he says: “That name,” and so forth. For that [name] would, according to the actual state of things, be a further qualification; and it deserves to be treated by the authors of the definitions as a distinct characteristic (rūpāntara) of that qualification whose absence would occur even when another [qualification] is present.
For the relationship of qualifier and qualified exists when there is both possibility and deviation, not in the case of mere possibility alone.
He provides an example, beginning with "Just as," and so forth.
For even though there is a connection with the subject (*dharmin*), audibility and the like do not exist in the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
Furthermore, even though visibility and the like exist in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), there is no connection with the subject (*sādhyadharmin*), namely sound.
Therefore, because these two—possibility and deviation—are present, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is established and adopted as a distinct definition.

If it is argued that the same will apply here as well, he says: "And this" [definition] which was just mentioned is not possible when there is non-deviation from the absence of contradiction (*abādhā*).

Since non-deviation is absent when there is no necessary concomitance with the probandum (*satyavinābhāva*), and since sublation (*bādhā*) is impossible [in that case] due to the absence of deviation, how could there be a relationship of qualifier and qualified, or how could it deserve to be included as a separate category?

Thus, sublation is possible only in the case of a reason that is either *viruddha* (contradictory)—which has necessary concomitance with the opposite of the probandum—or a reason that possesses necessary concomitance with the probandum itself.

According to the method explained, it is called a "pseudo-reason" (*hetvābhāsa*) because it is a valid reason only when its contrapositive is true, but it is termed a pseudo-reason when it is employed in a domain where it does not apply.

Since this is so, "therefore" (*iti*), the absence of that [sublation]—the lack of sublation (*bādhāviraha*)—need not be stated as a separate definition for these two, namely the probans and the contradictory [reason], which consist of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), distinct from inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*);

for, since there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it is impossible for it to be a different form [of the definition]. Furthermore, when inseparable connection exists, sublation is impossible because of their contradiction.

Therefore, when there is the employment of a reason possessing the characteristics as previously stated, there is no possibility of defects— such as contradiction by perception and so forth— even in the case of a thesis whose meaning is already understood, because those [defects] have already been excluded by the very definition of the reason.
So how can the absence of sublation be stated as a further feature (*rūpāntara*) of the reason?
The underlying intention is that describing those things which are impossible is fruitless.
If it is argued that there is a possibility [of occurrence] when [the reason] is used alone, he says:
"Nor even," and so forth.
For when the application of a reason (*hetu*) is absent, a mere thesis (*pratijñā*) is not employed at all,
because it is accepted as having the reason as its object.
Consequently, the authors of treatises should not state defects of the thesis, such as its being contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣaviruddha*).
However, since Diṅnāga’s venerable teacher observed a misconception regarding the reversal of the provable and the unprovable (*sādhyāsādhyaviparyaya*),

he formulated a definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) even for that which is unfit for formal employment. Thus, while the status of being a non-thesis (*apakṣatva*) was already established by logical necessity, the term "contradicted" (*nirākṛta*) was employed to designate that which is opposed by valid cognition (*pramāṇaviruddha*).
The definition of the subject (pakṣa) is not over-extended, as it is clearly delimited;
for only that which is doubted is the object to be proven (sādhya),
since no means of proof can operate against that which is already sublated by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Having thus refuted the state of having an uncontradicted object, he speaks while refuting another aspect: "By this"— namely, by the demonstration that contradiction is impossible when there is invariable concomitance— "the intention to express a singular number" is also "answered," that is, rejected, as being the opposite of the fault known as *viruddhāvyabhicārī* (the non-deviant contradictory).

The opponent asks: "How?"—in what manner is there a lack of coexistence between sublation (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), such that the same [lack of coexistence] would apply to the presence of a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) and invariable concomitance as well, whereby the intended expression of a single number (i.e., the status of being a valid reason) might be rejected in that very same way? The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*), demonstrating their equality, says: "One," and so forth.
For how can a single reason, when endowed with the [required] characteristics, be non-deviant from its own probandum?
It would be so only if it existed exclusively where its own probandum exists.
Otherwise, its defining characteristic, namely "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*), would be lost.

In whatever locus (*dharmin*) that [reason] exists as a single instance of that characteristic, how could another counter-reason (*pratihetu*)—which is contradictory to it and yet possesses the characteristics of a reason—also exist in that very same locus? For when there is the existence of another property that is contradictory to and subverts what is to be proven (*sādhya*) by one reason, there can be no absence of it.

Because [the reason] exists, there is an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*); thus, it is equal to the sublation (*bādhā*) [of the opponent's position], and since it is equal by virtue of the impossibility of sublation, it is refuted by the very refutation of that [opponent's counter-reason].
To state another objection against this very point, he says, beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*), while posing an alternative:

"In reality" (*vastutaḥ*), that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), for whom a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is not possible—is such a person [the possessor] of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) or of error (*viparyaya*)?

Is the reason intended as that which possesses the cognition of the opposite of the thesis (sādhya) presented [by the opponent]—since its definition is said to be the possession of the intended singular number—or rather, is it that for which no counter-reason (pratihetu) capable of proving the opposite of that thesis has been shown, even though such a one exists in reality?
Not seeing the fault in this, the opponent says: "What follows from this? and so forth.
"If it be granted that either the prior or the subsequent [reason] is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), what fault is there in that?

To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) replies: "If a reason for which a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is impossible is accepted as a cause of correct cognition and so forth,"
This "absence of that characteristic" (tadālakṣaṇa) refers to the state of having a single intended number.
Why?
Because it is impossible to determine [the presence of] a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) in reality; that for which this is so is described as such.
This is stated from the perspective of the opponent's view;
for the opponent, even in the absence of a causal connection, desires an invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) based on mere observation and non-observation.
Consequently, there is the possibility of such a counter-reason (pratihetu) arising for him.
Even if it were not perceived, one might think it could exist at some time; therefore, its non-existence is determined in reality.

However, for us—who maintain that inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is based on a necessary connection (*pratibandha*)—the impossibility of a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is indeed well-ascertained. For when a necessary connection characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or origination (*tadutpatti*) is established through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the absence of the reason] follows by virtue of that inseparable concomitance caused by such a connection.

Once a [proponent's] reason has established its own probandum, it is then suspected that there might exist a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) with the same characteristics as that [original reason], which establishes a meaning contrary to it, within that very same subject (*dharmin*),
because it is impossible for entities to possess two contradictory natures.

Because the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) is the defining characteristic of difference (*bhedalakṣaṇa*), and because when there is the possibility of a proof for a contradictory property, it is impossible for that very first [reason], which is invariably concomitant with its own probandum, to be established as existing therein by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It might be argued: "Even if we are unable to ascertain the non-existence of a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) under discussion, nevertheless, the state of having no possible counter-reason is intended to be established by the principle of 'singularity' (*ekasaṃkhyatva*)."
Why is it not the characteristic of the reason (*hetu*)? To this he says: "For [it does not belong] to that which is of an uncertain nature," and so forth.

Because for a property (*dharma*) that serves as the proponent of the reason, if its own-nature (*svabhāva*) is uncertain, it cannot possess the status of being a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)—that is, the state of being a property that establishes [the probandum].
Just as the previous argument—that "the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) is doubtful"—is a proof;

nor is there any reason that would have a doubtful definition, for if that were so, nothing at all could be a reason, or else there would be an absence of reasons. This serves to support the statement [in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*]: "The fallacies of the reason (hetvābhāsa) are others than those. Thus, this has also been applied here.
It might be thought: let that [reason] for which a counter-reason (*pratiyogin*) is observed be non-reason (*ahetu*) due to the presence of a counter-reason;
however, that for which no counter-reason is observed is, in reality, one for whom a counter-reason is impossible.
For in that case, the possibility of a counter-reason in reality is not even suspected.
For, in the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*), it is impossible to entertain a doubt regarding subversion. As it has been said:
"As long as no knowledge of subversion has arisen, there is no groundless suspicion.
Regarding this, he says: "For when the characteristic is equal," and so forth.

When a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) that is suspected to exist has a characteristic equal to [the original reason]—that is, one whose nature consists of an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) based merely on observation and non-observation—the possibility of such a counter-reason, which acts as an opponent and a sublater (*bādhaka*), is seen; and for those [reasons] which possess that same equal characteristic...
Even when no counter-positive is perceived, it gives rise to doubt concerning the possibility of a counter-argument. What is the reason?
Because there is no distinction between one whose counter-positive is unperceived and one whose counter-positive is perceived.
For there is no distinction between it and the other such that its possibility would not be suspected; rather,
its non-perception might be attributed to defects in the person's faculties and so forth— so why is this being said?
"Nor is doubt [justified] without a basis in valid cognition.

Now, if it is maintained that a specific feature—characterized by a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) and serving to ascertain the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*)—is required for a reason whose counter-positive has not been observed, so that from this the suspicion regarding the possibility of a counter-positive might cease;
then, provided such a specific feature exists, that very specific feature must be the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the reason.
What is the reason?

Because, due to that specific distinction, the reason—being one-sidedly certain (*ekāntena niścaya*) and having its counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) eliminated—determines its own probandum (*svasādhya*) in such a subject (*dharmī*), since a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is impossible therein.

That which does not possess such [a distinction], being devoid of that specific quality and having a counter-reason observed, lacks the defining characteristic [of a valid reason] and would therefore not be a reason.
And likewise, even if a counter-reason is observed against a reason that is not [a valid] reason,
what has happened to that [valid] reason such that, for the sake of its exclusion, the intention to express the number "one" is made with respect to it?

He says that because that [possibility of a counter-reason] is excluded by the very statement of the aforementioned inseparable connection (avinābhāva): "And thus, when there is no counter-reason associated with those specific qualifications of the reason, the intention to specify a single number is useless—that is, it serves no purpose.

For if one accepts the aforementioned qualifications, a counter-reason possessing those characteristics is impossible; so of what would there be an exclusion by means of the intention to specify a single number, such that this [specification] would have any utility?

The intention to specify the number "one" in the definition of a valid reason (*hetu*) is made for the purpose of excluding the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) known as the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).

Furthermore, since it is impossible in reality for a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) to be established when a specific reason characterized by an essential connection (*pratibandha*) is intended, the "non-erroneous contradictory" does not even constitute a fallacious reason.
Therefore, in the absence of anything to be excluded, what is the purpose of intending the number "one"?

Showing this, he says: "Therefore," because of the acceptance of the specific characteristic of the connection [between the reason and the property to be proven], "the definition of the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) known as the 'non-deviant contradictory' (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) would be lost"—that is, it would not be possible.
What, then, is the definition of that non-deviant contradictory?
He says: "its own definition" (*svalakṣaṇa*), and so forth.

The definition of the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) is as follows: when two reasons, each possessing its own specific characteristic, are presented together in a single locus (*dharmin*) such that they function to prove mutually contradictory conclusions through contradiction, it is called "non-erroneous contradictory.
This, however, is not possible if one accepts the existence of an essential connection (*pratibandha*).

For when a single reason, which possesses an essential connection (*tādātmya*) or a causal connection (*tadutpatti*) with its own probandum, is possible in a certain locus (*dharmin*), a second reason characterized by those same [connections] could not possibly exist in that very same locus;
this is because it is impossible for entities to possess two contradictory natures,
since the superimposition of contradictory properties is the defining characteristic of difference.
How, then, could there be any possibility for a second, non-deviant reason (*avyabhicārin*) to exist in that case?
Now, if the definition of the "non-deviant contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) is lost when such a lack of distinction exists,
or if the intention to specify a singular number is rendered useless, [then what follows?]

Nevertheless, there is no consequence of [falling into] the absence of a reason; why was it said, "or the absence of a reason"? To this he says: "And not"—indeed not—"of that" [reason], namely the specific [reason] characterized by its logical connection (*pratibandha*), because it is ascertained that, in reality, there is no possibility of a counter-reason (*pratihetu*).

“Essential nature” (*svarūpa*) is indicated by you as being characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) and causal origination (*tadutpatti*), just as it has been indicated by us. Having understood (*pratītya*)—that is, having apprehended—that form, we perceive the possibility or impossibility of a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
Where that specific distinction does not exist, there the possibility of a counter-positive is imagined in inference based on scripture (*āgama*).
However, where that specific distinction does exist, as in inference proceeding by the force of real entities (*vastubala*), there the counter-positive is impossible.
Since this is so, that distinction does not exist for you at all—it is simply that the distinction is not known by you.
Therefore, even in every case where a counter-example (*pratiyogin*) is not perceived, there must still be a suspicion regarding that counter-example.
Strengthening that very suspicion, he says: "Even for one whose counter-reason has been observed," and so forth.

For even in the case of that which has a counter-positive observed previously through the perception of its counter-correlate, no distinction whatsoever is perceived from another [instance] where the counter-positive has never been seen at any time; for, based on such observation, one could not know "here a counter-positive is possible,
but elsewhere it is not," since positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), which are based solely on observation and non-observation, are identical in all cases.
Nevertheless, because a counter-positive has been observed there previously, the suspicion that a counter-positive exists everywhere in things possessing those same characteristics does not cease.
It might be argued: "In those cases where a counter-positive is possible, it is necessarily perceived at some time;
however, in those cases where it is not perceived even in a human lifetime, it simply does not exist."
(Hbṭ 217) "In that case, such a reason will exist; so how can there be an absence of a reason for us?
To this, he says: "And not," and so forth.
For even in those cases where a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is possible, that counter-reason is not always perceived by cognizers;
for the perception of those who do not see everything does not pervade the existence of all things, because of the presence of obstacles and deficiencies.

But surely, where the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is never perceived by the cognizer at all, how can a suspicion regarding it be raised? And thus it has been said: "When no subverting cognition (*bādhajñāna*) has arisen, suspicion is without basis."
Likewise, another [verse] states: "For he who, out of delusion, might imagine an obstacle even where none exists, being possessed by doubt in all worldly transactions, shall go to his destruction."
Therefore, he says: "But [the cognition] possessing excellence," and so forth.

For instance, we have observed that in certain cognizers of exceptionally sharp intellect, there exists a superior wisdom capable of conceiving counter-arguments; as was seen when the Buddhists presented arguments against the authority of the Vedas—arguments whose counterparts had not been perceived by the lineage of their disciples prior to the appearance of Kumārila.

By that very person endowed with superior wisdom, counter-reasons (*pratihetu*) were conceived; therefore, because of seeing those [counter-reasons], even regarding cases where no counter-reason has been seen throughout one's life, the suspicion regarding them does not cease.
Consequently, how can it be said that such suspicion is without basis (*niṣpramāṇika*)?
Indeed, the passage beginning with "for when the characteristics are equal" (*tulyalakṣaṇe hi*) has already stated the cause for the suspicion that a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is possible.
Nor can one who suspects the possibility of a counter-example be turned away by mere verbal abuse such as "for he would be imagining," on the grounds that the cause for such a suspicion might exist.
Therefore, he must state some reason capable of dispelling the suspicion of a counter-example, as we have stated:

"In the case of an essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*), once identity is ascertained by virtue of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the contrapositive, there is a determination of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) therein;
and in the case of an effect-reason (*kārya-hetu*), there is such ascertainment because the relation of cause and effect is established through the aforementioned perception and non-perception."

Since, in this way, the suspicion regarding a counter-positive does not cease anywhere in your system, for that reason there is uncertainty concerning the possibility or impossibility of a counter-positive,
in the form: "In this case a counter-positive is possible, but in that case it is not possible."

Therefore, since the characteristic of a reason (*hetu*)—namely, that its counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is impossible in reality—is not certain for those who maintain that one should intend [to state] only a single number [of reasons], no reason at all would exist.
For a reason cannot be one whose characteristic is uncertain; such is the conclusion.

Thus, having refuted this alternative—"Is that which is in fact incapable of having a counter-reason intended as the cause of the error of right knowledge?"—and desiring to refute the second alternative, he says: "Or, one for whom a counter-reason has not been shown" is intended as the cause of the error of right knowledge; such is the connection [of the words].
And pointing out that this position is indeed favored even by the teacher Dignāga, the opponent says: "As the teacher Dignāga said."
What does he say? "In that case, then," and so forth.
When the Master Dignāga stated, "For audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) cannot in any way be a cause of exclusion (*vyavaccheda-hetutva*)," the opponent replied:
"In that case, when a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*) accepts 'soundness' (*śabdatva*) as an eternal particular universal (*sāmānya-viśe�ṣa*), then this [reason] characterized by audibility—"

"The property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) would indeed be the reason [for proving permanence], as in: 'Sound is eternal because it is audible, like the nature of sound (*śabdatva*). When this was stated by the opponent, the Teacher said: 'If someone were to put forward here, with respect to the subject called "sound," a reason for impermanence characterized by being produced (*kṛtakatva*), being dependent on effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*), and so forth...'"
"Otherwise, the Vaiśeṣika and others would not have to present [a counter-reason], and in that case, this unexhibited counter-reason would simply be a valid reason.
When the venerable Teacher has thus been granted the role of witness, the author of the treatise, raising his arm and crying out, says: "Now, this... and so forth.
For when some explain that even the Teacher himself intended this, a very great calamity has ensued: [the work] would be unfit for publication because it was spoken by one's own Guru.

Indeed, it is not proper to proclaim the faults of one's gurus; for those who uphold justice, that which ought not to be concealed must remain unhidden. Thus, whether we should revile our gurus or disregard justice—both being impossible—how can this most grievous calamity be endured?
"Not in any way.

But what is the fault here that makes this so grievous? He says: "This very reason," characterized by audibility, "having made" the entities—such as sound and so forth—"possessed of that nature," meaning having made them identical with their own probandum, namely the reality of permanence, that audibility [is then abandoned]."
Having "joined" those persons—such as the Mīmāṃsakas, Grammarians, and others—for whom [the Buddha] is an authority, with "prosperity," namely heaven, and with "the supreme good," namely liberation;
for it is thus: by cultivating the reality of things, one attains heaven as long as one has not yet abandoned the afflictions.
By abandoning the afflictions (*kleśas*), one becomes intent upon *nirvāṇa*.

Alternatively, once the eternality of sound is realized, through the authority of the Veda, by performing the *agnihotra* sacrifice prescribed therein, one attains heaven; and through the study of the Vedānta, one attains the supreme goal (*apavarga*).
Furthermore, at a later time, by a person such as a Vaiśeṣika who possesses "insight" (*pratibhā*)—that is, a specific kind of wisdom—one [proceeds] by means of "another reason" (*hetvantara*).

By means of the "illustration" of the counter-reason (*pratihetu*), that "capacity for proving its permanence" which it previously possessed when the counter-reason had not been presented is "uprooted," meaning it is removed.
Having displaced those entities from their state of possessing permanence, [the capacity is eliminated].
And having caused those persons who take that [Veda] as their authority to fall from the wealth of heaven and liberation, the reason characterized by audibility—
being unable to save itself due to a deficiency of power— goes to the forest of penance like a king deprived of his kingdom through his own misdeeds; what can we say to this?
Having thus mocked [the opponent], he points out the fault in this position, saying: "The capacity of a person" and so forth.
For when a reason is accepted as a valid reason even though its counter-reason has not been shown, then the status of being a proof is admitted to be produced merely by a person's ingenuity.
Consequently, in reality, nothing would be established as either a proof or a non-proof.

For instance: when a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is not presented, it is a proof (*sādhana*); but when one is presented, it is no longer a proof. Thus, the status of being a proof would come to depend upon the intellectual capacity of the person.

Furthermore, if a reason is accepted as a valid reason even when a counter-reason has not been presented, two alternatives arise: is the reason, in the ultimate sense, necessarily concomitant with that property (*taddharmabhāvī*), or is it not?
Or does it not possess that property?

Regarding the first alternative, he says: "And that" reason, which is first employed, "if by its very nature" exists "only when" that probandum-property exists—such being its character, because of the acceptance of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) as described by us.
If it is accepted [that it is so], then how could it be made otherwise? How could that which does not possess those properties be made so by another cause?
Not in any way. What is the reason?
Regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things characterized by their causes—

namely, that "the probandum-property (*sādhyadharma*) exists as a real entity"— because there is an absence of its being otherwise, that is, an absence of its opposite, and because both [reasons] are invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvitva*) with their respective probandum-properties,
if both were present in a single locus (*dharmī*) by virtue of their very nature, then two contradictory natures would belong to one and the same thing.
Furthermore, two contradictory natures cannot belong to a single entity, because the superimposition of contradictory properties would entail the loss of its unity.

Now, regarding the second alternative: if it were "not possessing that property" (*ataddharmabhāvī*), meaning it has the nature of occurring even when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is absent—since no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is admitted—then how could it be so "even at other times," that is, even in a state where a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) has not been demonstrated?
“Of what is it a proof?
It is not a proof even then,
let alone in the state where a counter-reason has been demonstrated.
Summing up, he says: "Therefore, by their very nature," and so forth.

Since the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities cannot be altered in this way, and since a single entity possessing two contradictory natures is impossible, therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), [the reason] possesses the aforementioned characteristics of being inseparable (*avinābhāvin*) from its respective probandum (*sādhya*).

Because a counter-reason characterized by either effect or essential nature— that is, characterized as an effect or an essential nature— is impossible for those two [types of reasons], "the designation of a single number being without a defining characteristic" means that the intended singularity of number does not constitute a defining characteristic.
What is the reason?
Thus he says: "Because there is nothing to be excluded.

For a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is described as that which is to be excluded from the intended singularity [of the reason]; yet such a counter-reason simply does not exist in the case of an effect or an essential nature (*svabhāva*) that possess their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). How, then, could there be a definition of a [valid] reason in such cases?

Thus, the meaning of the statement "the others are fallacious reasons" (*hetvābhāsāstato 'pare*) has been explained as follows: when the occurrence of these two aforementioned forms is impossible due to the absence of the stated invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), they remain fallacious reasons even if another form is admitted.
To refute [the opponent's claim regarding] "being known" (*jñātatva*), he says: "As for cognition, moreover," and so forth.

The state of having an uncontradicted object and the state of having the intended singular number belong only to the effects-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*), because, given their invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), there is no possibility of a contradicting reason (*bādhaka*) or a counter-reason (*pratihetu*). It has been stated that even though they possess the property of being a mark (*liṅgadharmatva*), they do not constitute the definition [of a valid reason] due to the absence of anything to be excluded (*vyavacchedya*). Knowledge (*jñāna*), however, is simply the state of being known (*jñātatva*).
Because it is designated by means of an abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya) referring to that very [cognition] itself;
for instance, "knowability" (jñātatva) is said to be the ground for the application of the word "cognition" (jñāna),
and that is indeed cognition itself.
Because when that [object] arises, there is the conventional usage "it is known.
And since that [knowledge] is not the essential nature (*ātmarūpa*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*), how could it be the definition of a logical mark?

Even if a generic form (*sāmānyākāra*) appearing in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is established as being the logical mark, nevertheless, knowledge does not possess the property of being a logical mark.
For this [conceptual construction] is not an independent indicator (*liṅga*).

As it has been said: "Because independent conceptual distinctions depend upon [words] whose meanings are conventional, when there is a comprehension of an object based on an object imagined by those [conceptions], there would be no attainment of the actual object at all" (Hbṭ 221).
Therefore, it is established that this [conceptual cognition] has as its logical mark (*liṅga*) precisely the apprehension of an external object.

This is because, in the conceptual construction of the probandum and the probans, there is an abandonment of the perception of the real thing (*vastu*), and because the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not occur in any [conceptual] concomitance.

However, conceptual cognitions—recalling only the property of that [real thing] and displaying various positive and negative concomitances—are non-deceptive with respect to the real thing, due to an indirect connection (*paramparayā pratibandha*).
It has already been largely stated that [the object] is based on the designation of signs such as the "effect" (kārya) and so forth;
yet knowledge is not the essential nature (ātmarūpa) of that effect and the rest.
Furthermore, the generic form (sāmānyākāra) appearing in conceptual construction is by no means the very self (ātmabhūta) of that conceptual construction.

Because that which is formless is contradictory to the nature of a real entity (*vastu*), and because that circle of conceptual reflections lacks the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*). For how could there be the nature of a universal for something that, although unsublated, is determined as external, and although non-pervasive, is determined as pervasive? And if it were such [a universal], how could it have the nature of a conceptual construction? As it has been said:
"And how could that which is non-different from cognition become a separate object?"
"Therefore, this apprehension of a single nature in objects is a false appearance.
Thus, [the reason] does not possess the property of being a mark (liṅgadharmatā) of the cognition.
Proving this very point, he says: "Of what form... and so forth.

When the inquiry is underway as to what kind of reason (*hetu*) the object to be inferred (*anumeya-artha*) is to be known from, the treatise-authors describe the essential nature of that indicative mark (*liṅga*) which is non-contradictory for the cognizer—the person—by means of seeing whose form this cognizer [understands]:
"That in which such a form is possible is the means of proof (*sādhana*); that which is devoid of such a form is not a means of proof."

Having thus established [the distinction] through this analysis, one relies upon activity based on the conviction that the means of accomplishment (sādhana) established therein brings about the presence of the desired object.

Likewise, when this principle is established, that which constitutes the essential nature (*ātmarūpa*) of this logical mark (*liṅga*) must be its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), such as its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth, but not that which is its extrinsic form (*pararūpa*). It might be argued: "Since a known logical mark is the means of accomplishment, it is indeed appropriate that the cognition which serves to establish the probandum (*sādhya*) should be the defining characteristic of the logical mark. To this, he says: "In the arising of comprehension," and so forth.

If the definition of a logical mark (*liṅga*) is intended merely as that which is useful for the production of the cognition of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), then an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) follows. He states this very point: "In this way, if the definition of a logical mark consists merely in being useful for the production of a cognition, then the object to be known (*prameya*), the person (*puruṣa*)—that is, the knower (*pramātṛ*)—and by the word 'etcetera' (*ādi*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), and so forth, as well as light, mental attention (*manaskāra*), and the like, would all possess the definition of a logical mark."

Regarding this, he states the reason: "For even when those [objects], such as the object of cognition (*prameya*) and so forth, do not exist, there is no cognition of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*).
To this, the opponent, seeking to bring about an undesirable consequence, says: "In that case, the inclusion of the term 'ascertained' (*niścita*)," and so on.
If cognition, by virtue of having the nature of another, does not constitute the definition of a mark, then as for this which was stated by the Teacher—
Regarding the statement, "Its presence in the subject (*anumeya*) and in what is similar to it, and its absence in what is not [similar],
must be ascertained," the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) has been made; however, that need not be done, as it is already accepted by you.
For instance: certainty is indeed the very form of another [the object] for the logical mark (*liṅga*).
If that [certainty] is its defining characteristic, why is it not accepted as cognition? For certainty is nothing but consciousness, since this [mark] is a particularity thereof.

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) says: "It is not that [the reason] should not be stated; rather, it must certainly be stated, because the purpose of that formulation of the certainty [of the reason] is to demonstrate its nature as a logical mark (liṅga).
Demonstrating that very fact of having another purpose, he says: "In the similar class (sapakṣa) and the dissimilar class (vipakṣa)," and so forth.
For opponents maintain that a reason is indicative merely by its presence in the similar class and its mere absence from the dissimilar class.
The term "ascertained" (*niścita*) is employed for the purpose of making it known that a reason is not capable of establishing the probandum merely by being seen among them;

for it is observed that even when presence and absence exist—that is, when they are actually present—the reason lacks the capacity to convey [the conclusion], as in the case of: "He is dark-complexioned, because he is his son," and so forth.

For this reason, it should be understood that the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) is included in the definition statement in order to make known the following meaning: that a logical reason (*hetu*) is a prover when it is characterized by its presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), by its absolute absence in every dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), and by its presence— characterized by the nature of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*)— in the similar class while being absent in every dissimilar class.

This is what is meant: a logical reason (*hetu*) becomes a means of cognition (*gamaka*) precisely through those two—the presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the absence in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*)—which have been ascertained by the operation of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*);
it does not become so merely through some kind of casual observation. To make this point known, the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) has been employed.
Concluding the present topic, he says: "Therefore," and so forth.
Since the term "ascertained" was employed solely to indicate the presence and absence of the specific [property] itself,
and not to denote another form,
it is not tenable for that which is not of the nature of the self to serve as a definition.
Therefore, the other form [of the cognition] does not constitute a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*).
For, by that other form consisting of cognition and so forth, no specific feature of the nature of the logical mark is expressed.
But surely others also accept a reason as indicative by virtue of its presence in the similar class (sapakṣa) and absence from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa);
since it is the observation and non-observation of these two that establish them, for what purpose is the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (niścita)?
Thus, for this reason he says: "For those two," and so forth.

Although opponents maintain that a logical reason (*hetu*) is indicated solely by presence and absence, they nevertheless establish presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and absolute absence in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*) based merely on observation and non-observation; yet, on that basis alone, those two [presence and absence] are not established as being of such a nature.
Since it is possible for things that lack an invariable connection (pratibandha) to be observed or not observed in some way regarding their presence or absence in certain cases,

therefore those two— the presence [of the reason] only in the similar class (sapakṣa) and the absolute absence [of it] in the dissimilar class (asapakṣa)— must be understood as being established by the operation of that very means of valid cognition which proves its existence, namely, the means of proving identity (tādātmya) and causality (tadutpatti).

Why? Because there is no other means [to establish it]. For that [certainty] would only occur if one were to accept that the reason exists only in the similar class (sapakṣa)—that is, when the concomitance of all things possessing the reason with the probandum is observed—and if one were to observe its absolute non-existence in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa)—that is, when all things lacking the probandum are perceived as being devoid of the reason. But this is not accepted. Therefore, since there is no other way, the certainty of the reason's presence in the similar class and its absence in the dissimilar class cannot be established. Thus, the definition of a valid reason is unestablished. Consequently, because the three characteristics of a reason are impossible, inference is not established. Since inference is not established, neither is the scripture (āgama) established, for scripture is merely a form of inference based on the word of a reliable person (āpta). Furthermore, perception (pratyakṣa) is not established either, because it is understood through inference by means of the characteristic of "being free from conceptual construction" (kalpanāpoḍha). Therefore, since the four means of valid cognition are not established, all worldly and transcendental activities based upon them are likewise not established. Thus, the entire world would fall into total ruin. Therefore, the certainty of the reason's presence in the similar class and its absence in the dissimilar class must necessarily be accepted. And since that certainty is not possible otherwise, the existence of a necessary connection (pratibandha) between the reason and the probandum must be admitted. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the existence of a necessary connection is not possible without the establishment of causality (tadutpatti) or essential identity (tādātmya). Therefore, the existence of a necessary connection is established only through the establishment of these two. Hence, it is said: "Because there is no other means. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the existence of a necessary connection is not possible without the establishment of the two types of non-perception (anupalabdhi): the non-perception of the perceptible (dṛśyānupalabdhi) and the non-perception of the cause (kāraṇānupalabdhi). Therefore, the existence of a necessary connection is established only through the establishment of these two. Hence, it is said: "Because there is no other means. This is the meaning.
