And this is not possible for one who does not perceive everything.

Since there is no other means [of knowledge], for that reason the word "ascertained" (*niścita*) was employed by the author of the definition in the definition itself, in order to demonstrate those two specific states of existence and non-existence.

But surely, the ascertainment [of these] is obtained from the mere statement of existence and non-existence through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); otherwise, their very existence would not be established.
Therefore, he says: "Even though," and so forth.

By the very statement—"Presence in the object of inference and in what is similar to it, and absence in its absence"—which merely expresses the existence and non-existence in the similar (sapakṣa) and dissimilar (asapakṣa) instances without depending on the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (niścita), the occurrence of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes that existence and non-existence is indeed implied.
But how can there be an implication of its occurrence [in the subject] merely by stating its presence and absence, without the apprehension of a certainty?

To this he says: "Otherwise," if the occurrence of the means of valid cognition that establishes it were not implied, then there would be "non-establishment" of the existence—that is, the determination of the essential nature—of those very two, namely, presence and absence in the similar and dissimilar instances.

Why is there no proof? He says: because the determination of the existence of the object of knowledge—characterized as being or non-being—and its establishment of its own nature, are dependent upon that which is the existence or arising of "cognition," that is, apprehension.
For objects do not [exist] by themselves independently of apprehension. (Hbṭ 224)
[Otherwise] all things would be established as everything, because it would follow that everything could be established as anything.

Therefore, the determination that "this is of such a form" and not "of such a form" is established solely through the arising of a cognition possessing that specific aspect (*tadākāra*). Since this is so, in every treatise or in the world, the very establishment of the existence of an object of knowledge (*jñeya-sattā-vyavasthā*)—even without an explicit mention of its ascertainment—"draws forth" or implies "the means of establishing that," which is the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes its existence.

Furthermore, the connection [of the verse] is as follows: because the composition of a treatise (*śāstra*) is for the sake of others, the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes those [objects] is implied.

But what kind of treatise composition is it, which—being for the sake of others—implies the means of valid cognition that establishes the existence of the objects of knowledge as determined by itself?
To this he says: “The three-fold mark (*liṅga*) is, for you, that which brings about correspondence with and leads to the attainment of the desired object.”
Even if the composition of this treatise is indeed for the sake of others, how does it imply the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes it? To this he says:

"Those practitioners who do not know its form"—that is, the nature or essence of that three-fold logical mark (*liṅga*) as taught in the treatise—"for them there is no engagement with the desired object on the basis of that three-fold mark taught in the treatise."
Because that which makes an unknown object known does not induce action by its mere existence;

since this is so, therefore—precisely because it is a characteristic of others and because it is informative to others—it is established that knowledge resides in the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) as the inducer of action.

Thus, although the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) is redundant, nevertheless, those two—the presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the absence from the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*)—are indeed the [essential] features of the logical mark.

Some, such as the Naiyāyikas and others, state that the two [characteristics] specified by the Teacher are "existence only in the similar class (sapakṣa)" and "non-existence only in the dissimilar class (asapakṣa)."
Others establish [the relationship] by mere observation and non-observation— those observations and non-observations which do not actually prove a necessary connection— merely on that basis,

saying "from this very fact. Therefore, the word "ascertained" (*niścita*) was employed by the Teacher in the definition for the purpose of excluding those disputants, and it has been accepted by us as well.
If, however, there were no misconception on the part of others, then this [reasoning] would not be employed at all.

Why, then, are existence and non-existence—characterized by presence and absence with respect to the subject matter, and consisting of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as they pertain to similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*)—not accepted? To this he says: "Even though they exist," and so forth.

Even when there is an observation of the presence of the reason in some similar instances (sapakṣa) and an observation of its absence in some dissimilar instances (asapakṣa), as in the case of "He is dark-skinned because he is that man's son," there remains doubt regarding both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).

For instance: positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is the presence of the reason wherever the probandum exists; and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is the absence of the reason wherever the probandum is absent, by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Now, even if the presence of the reason is observed in some instances where the probandum exists, its existence in that manner does not necessarily follow for all cases merely on that basis.
Because there is no necessity of coexistence for things whose natures are unconnected;

likewise, even if one observes the absence of the probandum in some instances where the reason is absent, it does not follow that the reason must necessarily be absent whenever that probandum is absent,
because that which is not dependent on another does not necessarily cease when the other ceases.

Therefore, since the existence and non-existence in the similar and dissimilar instances as described are established only through the operation of the means of valid cognition that establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), and not otherwise, [the author] says "therefore" and so forth, demonstrating that the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) was made precisely for the purpose of refuting misconceptions.
He says "by us" because, regarding the inclusion of the term "ascertained" made by the Teacher (Dignāga), this is our own accepted view elsewhere; thus he says "by us."
Thus, having established that the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) is included for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions—
and that it need not be employed when no such misconception exists— he says, “Since...,” etc., demonstrating by this very logic that "knownness" (*jñātatva*) is not a distinct property.
The phrase “separately from this” means separately from the threefold nature (*trairūpya*) consisting of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth.
Why? Because it is "understood"—that is, apprehended—by that very statement of the three-fold character (*trairūpya*), through the implication of the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for that [character].
Like what? "Like the meaning of the application (*upanaya*), because of its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).

Just as the meaning of the application of the reason is understood by the mere statement of its being a property of the subject, since that [statement] consists in demonstrating the existence of the reason in the subject (*dharmin*).
And since the statement of the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) possesses that very form [of the three characteristics], the application (upanaya) is not a separate form from it;
likewise, knowledge [of the conclusion] arises from the three characteristics, because it is understood by the statement of those very characteristics.
Here, the opponent, seeking to establish an undesirable consequence, says: "Even in the case of positive and negative concomitance," and so forth.

If knowledge is obtained through the force of the statement of the three characteristics alone, then it should not be mentioned separately from that. "Alas! then negative concomitance should not be mentioned separately from positive concomitance, nor positive concomitance separately from negative concomitance.
What is the reason?
Because both [the positive and negative concomitances] are understood from the employment of either the positive or the negative concomitance;
and yet, they have been stated separately.
Likewise, since "cognizedness" (jñātatva) also possesses the three characteristics [of a valid reason], it should also be stated separately as something to be understood.
To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) replies: "No, because of the reason," and so forth.
There is no distinctness between positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), but rather they are simply different forms of the same thing.
For instance, positive concomitance of the reason (*hetu*) is defined as its presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Furthermore, negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is non-existence in the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*).
These two do not imply one another nor are they mutually included, because affirmation and negation are of different natures.
And it is not logical that what is of a nature distinct from something else should be included within it.
Now, if positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are of distinct natures, how then is it said that the logical mark (*liṅga*) possesses three forms?

For it is not possible for two mutually distinct entities to constitute the very nature of this [mark], since the distinction between things is characterized by a difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

This is not a fault, because we state that [the two types of inference] are not included within those two [methods of proof] only insofar as positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are established— or not— by those two methods, and not otherwise.
And how are these two established?
By taking recourse to a distinction made through exclusion;
thus, these two possess distinct natures.

Furthermore, even though there is a difference in their conceptual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), there is no difference in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*); thus, it is said that "a single logical mark (*liṅga*) possesses three characteristics.
How then is it stated previously that "there is no difference whatsoever between these two in terms of their referent (*artha*)"?
"Is it because of a difference in application?
To this he says: "A single sentence," and so forth.

We do not say that a single sentence, whether employed by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), conveys both positive and negative concomitance as having distinct characteristics; rather, [we say] it conveys a single meaning.
Because two things that are mutually distinct can indeed constitute the meaning of a single sentence.
On this point, the opponent says: "But not in that very case," and so forth.

The intended meaning is as follows: the objection regarding mutual inclusion is raised by relying on the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) established by the defining statement (lakṣaṇavākya).
And that [non-existence] indeed exists; for instance, in the defining statement "existence only there," by virtue of its meaning, its non-existence is understood in the absence of that [object].
And here, "necessarily non-existence in the absence of that" implies "existence when that exists."
For when there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*), the absence of one thing does not entail the absence of another.
And that necessary connection consists precisely in the form of existence [of the one] when the other exists, by way of identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from it (*tadutpatti*).

Consequently, since both [presence and absence] are understood through a single, specific defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*) that establishes presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and absence in the dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*), a second statement need not be made.
And thus, because they are included within the meaning of a single sentence, it is difficult to maintain that these two possess distinct natures.
Consequently, what was stated— that "even positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are not separate"— is indeed the case.
"That remains in that very same state.
To this, the proponent of the established tenet (siddhāntavādin) says: "This statement..."
In that very context, [the statement] beginning with "existence" and so forth "implies both," which means it establishes them.
Why?
Because of its capacity—that is, because it possesses the power to convey both meanings.
If one asks, "How so?
he says: "Even of a single sentence. Of what kind [of sentence]?
Because the statement of the rule—

namely, "existence only in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and non-existence only in the dissimilar class (*asapakṣa*)," which is restrictive— is necessarily concomitant with the implication of the second [part], that is, necessarily concomitant with the presentation of the second [part].

“Nor does the mere presentation of both [reasons] by a single statement imply that they possess a single nature, because even objects with distinct natures can be presented by a single sentence. Furthermore, although both [reasons] are understood from a single definition-statement, the fact that they are ‘stated separately’ is for the sake of restricting their formal application (*prayoganiyamārtha*). In the case of an application based on similarity (*sādharmya*), [the dissimilar instance is implied]; in the case of an application based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)...”

A statement [of similarity] should not be made when there is an application of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-prayoga*), nor should a statement of similarity be made when there is an application of dissimilarity; furthermore, it is not for the purpose of establishing another form that has not been understood through a single expression.

Nor, in that way, is there an establishment of the existence of the object of knowledge (*jñeya-sattā*) by means of the statement of the three forms (*trairūpya*), which serves as the basis for cognition, for the sake of providing a preliminary indication.

Furthermore, since the three-fold nature of the cognition based on the treatise (*śāstra*) has already been established by the composition of that treatise itself, there is no purpose in stating it again once that cognition has been obtained; thus, its separate mention is not logical.

It might be argued: "In that case, even if they are isolated, the two [the object and the cognition] will still not be included within the meaning of a single sentence, as they would possess mutually non-different natures."
Precisely because they are included within the meaning of a single sentence, he says: "But not the two alone"— that is, independently of the meaning of a single sentence,
the presence and absence in the similar and dissimilar instances do not imply one another or become included merely by virtue of being contained therein,
for we observe that even meanings of distinct forms are included within a single sentence.

But surely, even if existence and non-existence possess a restriction, they are each merely individual; if they imply one another, that consequence would apply to them even when they are isolated. To this, he says: "And possessing a restriction" means as presented by a sentence containing a limitation (*sāvadhāraṇa*); they are "not merely individual," but rather only together.
Why?

“Because a restrictive statement (*niyama*)—that is, a sentence possessing an exclusive emphasis—is of a dual nature (*ubhayarūpatvāt*), consisting in the demonstration of both existence and non-existence.
Thus, by means of a restrictive sentence, neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) alone is expressed;

rather, because the second is included within it, the two are expressed together by a single sentence as mutually inclusive. Concluding the argument for the sake of the one being instructed, he says: ‘Therefore,’ in that very case [of] the similar instance (*sapakṣa*)...”
By this statement, "existence only in the similar class" (*sapakṣe bhāva eva*), it is not said that there is existence [of the reason] only in the similar class.
What then?
Regarding "absence in the non-concordant class" (*asapakṣe 'bhāvaḥ*):
if it were the case that by the other statement, "absence in the non-concordant class," only absence were expressed and not presence in the concordant class (*sapakṣe bhāvaḥ*) as well,
then by that exclusive statement, either presence or absence would imply the second by virtue of being its very nature, such that there would be no separate mention of these two.

Therefore, when positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are intended as presence (*bhāva*) and absence (*abhāva*), they are indeed of distinct forms; how then could there not be a difference between them?
Alternatively, if they are expressed by a single rule-governed sentence, then since both are understood from that very sentence, a separate statement should not have been made at all.

However, it has been stated that this was done not for the sake of making known what was not already understood, but rather for the purpose of establishing a formal rule for the application (*prayoga*).

It might be thought: just as positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), characterized respectively by existence and non-existence, are not identical with one another and thus possess distinct natures from each other, so too cognition is indeed distinct from the three-fold nature (*trailakṣaṇya*) taught in the treatises that define it;
it is not included within that [three-fold nature].
To the objection that "therefore there will be another form [of existence]," he says: "It is not so.

Just as positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), characterized by presence and absence, are mutually non-inclusive, knowledge is not similarly non-included within the three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*) taught in the treatises that define the characteristics of others.
Why?

Because of "being characterized by others" (*paropalakṣaṇāt*). Others are characterized; that is, they are caused to have a cognition whose object is the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) by means of which treatise (*śāstra*). Therefore, because the three-fold nature that is cognized is not distinct from the apprehended cognition—namely, the three-fold nature within the apprehended cognition—[the treatise is considered a means of valid cognition].
“Thus,” therefore, there is no other definition [of the mark] than the three-fold character (*trairūpya*).

This is the collective meaning here: if "cognizedness" (*jñātatva*)—the ground for the application of the word "knowledge"—is, according to the manner stated, said to be knowledge itself, then it is not something distinct from the nature of that mark; thus, it is not its definition.

Alternatively, even if "cognizedness" is said to be the state of being an object (*karmabhāva*) dependent upon knowledge, since the establishment of the existence of the knowable depends upon the existence of knowledge, it is precisely the establishment of the three-fold character that establishes its existence.
It implies knowledge;
therefore, since the status of being an action (karmabhāva), though dependent on that [knowledge], is established even without being explicitly stated, its separate mention need not be made.
Likewise, because it is not distinct from the three characteristics (trailakṣaṇya) derived from the knowledge not yet grasped as taught in the treatise intended for the instruction of others.
Having thus refuted the three-fold nature [of the reason], such as having an uncontradicted object, he concludes by saying: "Therefore, the reason does not possess six characteristics.
What then?
It possesses only three characteristics.
This lamp of the method of the Sage’s final doctrine, which has destroyed the entire path of fallacious reasoning—
May that merit which has been accumulated by this expansion bring about supreme purification for the world.
The *Hetubinduṭīkā* is completed. May this [work], which is of such a nature, be for the eternal benefit of the three worlds. May you strive toward that which is of such a form.
She is the bridge for men and the awakener of the Tathāgata’s doctrine. // 2 //
... on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, on a Sunday. May there be auspiciousness and great glory!
He did not receive the teacher’s instruction, nor did he understand the reality;
consequently, his intellect made no effort toward its growth, nor was it even able to stir.
The vital principle and the lunar light have taken up their residence within it;
that very [light], through its powers, [manifests] elsewhere in various ways, for the natures of the universe are indeed manifold. // 2 //
O lover of Rohiṇī!
O abode of all arts!
O lord of the stars! O sovereign of the night!
O treasure-house of nectar, while recollecting the moon— whose body is surrendered to the qualities of the essence of *kādambarī*— one should remain absorbed in those very qualities.
